P.title: The baby on the Dawes card
P.hook: Enrolled at 7½ months. A 19-year-old farmer on his 1918 draft card. Three generations under his roof in 1940.
body: Simon was the youngest person on the family's 1899 Choctaw enrollment card, listed at 7½ months old. His mother Betsy and his grandmother Emeline Tims, who was the midwife at his birth on 4 May 1899, both swore affidavits so he could be enrolled. He was given Dawes Roll No. 3492 and his own land allotment near his parents'.
On his WWI draft card (12 September 1918) he was 19, a farmer working for his father at Corinne, of medium height and build, with black hair and brown eyes.

By 1940 he and Frances owned a $400 farm at Jeter, in a county where nearly three of every four farmers were tenants, and were raising five children: Ethel 13, Leonard 10, Junior 6, Bernice 3 and a baby daughter. Frances's parents Robert and Lizzie Pisachubbe and her orphaned nieces and nephews lived with them. Simon had three years of schooling and had worked all 52 weeks of 1939. His 1990 obituary called him a retired farmer and a Methodist who had lived in the Hugo area for 64 years; he left 17 grandchildren and 20 great-grandchildren. He and Frances, who married in 1925, are buried at Long Creek Cemetery near Hugo.

The card shows how close the timing was. His mother's family applied on 1 May 1899, three days before he was born, so his birth affidavit was added later. It was enrolled on 19 December 1899, but the affidavit was irregular and was returned for correction, and the corrected one was filed on 20 February 1900. At four he received a 160-acre homestead, the northeast quarter of Section 11, Township 5 South, Range 19 East, and he was issued a citizenship certificate at Hugo on 6 December 1907.

His wife's family on the Dawes cards: her mother Lizzie was Roll No. 3738 on Card 1363, written there as the 7-year-old daughter of Legion and Molsey Austin of Fowlerville, and her father Robert Pisachubbe was Roll No. 4467 on Card 1580 at Goodland. The two families lived forty miles apart in 1899 and joined in 1925 when Simon married their daughter Frances.
kv: NE¼ Sec. 11, T5S R19E, 160 acres (selected 2 Oct 1903)
Legion and Molsey Austin; Joseph and Eunice Pisachubbe

P.name: Frances (Pisachubbe) Thompson

imgs.cap: Frances's grave marker

P.place: Daughter of Robert Pisachubbe and Lizzie Austin, both from full-blood Choctaw families. Married Simon Thompson in 1925. Her grave marker at Long Creek Cemetery reads 1907–1979; the 1940 census gave her age as 31.
kv: Already sharing a home at Jeter with Simon and her parents; married at about 17
Legion and Molsey Austin (Card 1363, Towson County, 1896 Nos. 199-200); Joseph and Eunice Pisachubbe (Card 1580, Kiamitia County)
Born 1907, after the 4 March 1906 cutoff for newborns
P.src: U.S. Censuses (Ancestry); Dawes Cards 1363 and 1580; Newborn Card 1203; Act of Congress approved 26 April 1906 (birth affidavit forms); 1930 and 1940 U.S. censuses.
body: Frances Pisachubbe was born in 1907, after the rolls had closed to new births. The April 1906 act that let the Commission add newborns asked each parent to swear the child was "living March 4, 1906," so she has no Dawes card, unlike her cousin Colbert, whose card 1203 was sworn in 1906. Her place in the record is the family around her: her father Robert and grandmother Eunice on Card 1580, her mother Lizzie and grandparents Legion and Molsey Austin on Card 1363.

Her grandmother Eunice died 19 May 1927, leaving Robert and William H. Pisachubbe as her only heirs. Her other grandmother, Molsey, appears in the 1915-16 list of restriction-removal cases as "Molsey Pisachubbi, Austin," and her mother Lizzie appears in the same list as "Lizzie Pisachubbee, nee Austin." Frances married Simon Thompson in 1925, whose own enrollment affidavit had been sworn in 1899 by his grandmother Emeline Tims. By 1930 the young couple shared a house at Jeter with her parents, and in 1940 they owned a $400 farm there with five children.

P.title: Judge and Choctaw senator
P.hook: Spencer Academy, Mount Hermon and Roanoke College, then county clerk, legislator and judge in Cedar County.
body: A full-blood Choctaw (Dawes Roll No. 3487), born in Cedar County in December 1861, two miles west of High Hill church. His Dawes card names his parents as John and Betsy Thompson, both dead by 1899; his son Joel said John died when Joseph was nine.

A sketch of Joseph printed in 1891, while he was still a young man, says he was educated at Spencer Academy and at 'Mount Harmon Institute, Northfield' (D. L. Moody's Mount Hermon School for boys in Massachusetts), and finished at Roanoke College in Salem, Virginia, where he stayed until 1886. Joel remembered it in a different order: three years at Roanoke, then three years at a college in Massachusetts studying law.

The 1885 Choctaw census shows him at 24 in Cedar County, farming 20 acres of his own with a horse, six cattle and 30 hogs. The 1891 sketch says he began as a schoolteacher, was appointed county clerk of Cedar County in 1889, and the next year was elected to the lower house of the Choctaw Council, 'one of the youngest members of the legislature.' Joel said he later served as County Judge of Cedar County, holding court at Sulphur Springs near present-day Rattan, and about six years as a Senator.

He married Betsy Tims in 1889. They started in a one-room log house. In 1901 he built a big white house with two front rooms, a wide hall, an L-shaped kitchen and dining room, and lots of porches, 300 yards from High Hill Methodist Church. He sat on the school board, raised an orphan boy named Wister Davis, and named a son Peter Pitchlyn Thompson after the Choctaw chief.

The 1910 census, taken on the special Indian schedule, shows Joseph at 48 farming his own allotment free of mortgage in Wilson Township, Choctaw County. He gave both his parents' birthplace as Mississippi, which fits a family that came west on the Removal. Living with them was 19-year-old "David Wister," the orphan the family raised, whom Joel remembered as Wister Davis. Their nearest neighbors were Henry W. Thompson, probably Joseph's brother, and two Tims households, one headed by James Tims, very likely Betsy's brother Jimmie.

Joel said his father was 'second of nine children' and that the 1901 house stood on a farm that raised 'plenty of hogs' and 'lots to eat.' He added that his father 'was always interested in the government of his people.' The county officers Joel named were Robert S. Frazier, High Sheriff, and Noah Frazier, Clerk, with James Brown Tims as a representative in the Council.

Joseph's name is in the federal record again after statehood. He filed a petition on 27 August 1908 from Fort Towson, and again on 10 September 1915 from Corinne, when the Secretary of the Interior approved removal of restrictions on his land on 28 March 1916. In 1903 he had gone to Atoka to pick out the allotments for his wife and children.

A correction to the neighborhood: the Henry W. Thompson who lived near Joseph in 1910 is on Dawes Card 1282, filed the same day as Joseph's, and the card gives his parents as Simon and Lucy Thompson, not John and Betsy. He is told on his own page.

quotes.t: He could have sentenced criminals to be shot, but I don't know whether he did or not. I do know that he had lots of them whipped at the old whipping post on the Sulphur Springs Court ground.
quotes.c: Joel J. Thompson, 1937

quotes.t: Dad could go out early any morning and kill a deer within a quarter of a mile of the house… We boys would listen for his gun to fire, then we would run to get the deer and bring it in.
quotes.c: Joel J. Thompson, 1937

quotes.t: He was always interested in the government of his people.
quotes.c: Joel J. Thompson, 1937

P.note: The 1891 sketch heads him 'Joseph B. Thompson,' probably a printer's error; everything else in it fits. It also calls his father 'Rev. John Thompson,' a Presbyterian minister in Cedar County for twenty years, which does not fit Joel's memory that John died about 1870. Roanoke College had about 35 Choctaw students between 1876 and 1896, but Joseph does not appear in the 1881-82 catalogue; that fits the sketch, which has him at Mount Hermon first, but the 1882-86 catalogues have not been seen. Joseph's terms as judge and senator have not yet been found in Choctaw Nation records. A Find a Grave memorial gives his birth as 1862 and has him at High Hill, but his burial there is unverified; his death in 1927 comes from family files. The orphan he raised is 'Wister Davis' in Joel's interview. Paragraph 5 guesses that Henry W. Thompson, a 1910 neighbor, was Joseph's brother; the last paragraph corrects that from Dawes Card 1282, which names Henry's parents as Simon and Lucy Thompson.
P.src: H. F. O'Beirne, Leaders and Leading Men of the Indian Territory, vol. 1 (1891), p. 162; 1885 Choctaw census, Cedar County (NARA M595, roll 623); Dawes Card 1283; WPA Indian-Pioneer Papers, interviews #7392 and #7418 (Joel J. Thompson, Hugo, 1937); 1910 U.S. Census, Indian Population schedule, Wilson Twp, Choctaw Co., Okla., ED 64, sheet 11A; 1920 U.S. Census, Wilson, Choctaw Co; Allotment files and restriction-removal ledgers, 1903-1916; Dawes Cards 1282 and 1283.

imgs.cap: Dawes Card 1283: Joseph, Betsy and their children, with the 1902 approval stamp

1910 U.S. Indian Population census, Wilson Township, Choctaw County, Oklahoma, enumerated 22 April 1910: the household of Joseph P. Thompson with wife Betsy and their children Alexander, Joel, Peter, Simon, Joseph Jr. and Jancy, plus nephew David Wister.

P.title: Betsy and the Dawes rolls
P.hook: Choctaw by Blood, Roll No. 3488, and the girl from the Pine Ridge school.
body: The family applied for Choctaw enrollment on 1 May 1899. The Secretary of the Interior approved it on 12 December 1902. Betsy was Choctaw by Blood, Dawes Roll No. 3488, Card 1283, and received a land allotment that included a 160-acre homestead north of Doaksville.

She went to school at the old Pine Ridge mission near Doaksville, founded by the missionary Cyrus Kingsbury in the 1830s, where the Choctaw Nation's Chuwahla Female Seminary opened in 1844. Her son Joel said her family was "quite prominent in public affairs." Her brother James Brown "Jimmie" Tims served in the Choctaw Council as a Representative.

An 1891 sketch of her husband calls her 'Miss Betsey Ann Tims' and names their first child, Alexander, born in March 1890. Her parents were Vinson and Emeline Tims; her brothers and sisters included James, Mitchell, John, Rev. Robert Tims, Willie, Rosie and Calvin.

Her son Joel added a correction to the family story about her schooling: he believed it 'was after the Mission school had been suspended and that it was very likely neighborhood schools which she attended, schools held at the old Academy site.' Whatever the building, she remembered it. Her father's name on the card is written 'Vincent Tims,' dead by 1899, and her mother 'Emiline Tims,' still on the 1896 roll in Towson County.

Joel named seven children who lived to be grown: Alex B., Joel J., Peter Pitchlyn, Simon W., Joseph W., Jincy and Marietta. A daughter, Ella, died in May 1899, and the card also notes a newborn card, No. 1410, under the Act of 3 March 1905. In March 1920 her own petition from Corinne to lift restrictions on her land was approved.

quotes.t: She always told us, as we passed that old Pine Ridge school site, "There is where I went to school."
quotes.c: Joel J. Thompson, 1937

quotes.t: Mother attended Pine Ridge Academy, a school for girls.
quotes.c: Joel J. Thompson, 1937

P.note: Her birth year is 1870 in the family tree; her age on the card (28 in May 1899) and Find a Grave and a local Tims history give 1871. Her 1925 death comes from Joel's interview, and the memorial at High Hill is a placeholder, not a known grave. The 1910 census says she had borne seven children, six living, while Joel names seven who grew up plus Ella.

imgs.cap: Robert's WWI draft card, Speer, 5 June 1917
His WWII "old man's draft" card, 1942
Dawes Card 1580: Eunice Pisachubbe's family, Kiamitia County, 1899

P.title: The Pisachubbes of Speer and Jeter
P.hook: A full-blood Choctaw farmer who registered for both world wars and lived with his daughter's family in 1940.
body: Full-blood Choctaw, Dawes Roll No. 4467, enrolled at age 11 on his widowed mother Eunice's card. In 1917 he was 28, married with one child, farming for himself at Speer; the registrar wrote "Indian" for race, black eyes and black hair, medium height, slender. In 1942, at 53, he registered again for the WWII draft of older men, still at Speer, naming his wife Lizzie.
In 1940 he and Lizzie were living with their daughter Frances and son-in-law Simon Thompson at Jeter, with their niece Alice and nephews Eli and Edward: twelve people in the house.

The three young relatives were orphans. Robert's older brother, William Harrison Pisachubbe, had married Lizzie's younger sister Adline Austin, so two Pisachubbe brothers had married two Austin sisters, and their children were double first cousins of Frances. Adline died at Speer in 1929 and William Harrison in 1937.

William Harrison's obituary in the Hugo Daily News (11 May 1937) gave a family history from his relative Judge T. W. Hunter: the Pisachubbes came from Mississippi with the first group of Choctaw exiles in 1832 and settled at Fort Coffee, near present-day Spiro. His funeral was held at the family home near the Long Creek school house, with Choctaw Presbyterian minister Rev. Logan Harlin officiating.
The name Pisachubbe ends the way many Choctaw war-names do; its exact meaning is not recorded.

The county land records bring his land forward. A 1979 decree of heirship for his daughter Frances Pisachubbe Thompson covers Section 29, Township 5 South, Range 17 East, the same section as his allotment. An order in his own estate was entered in 1982.

His 1896 census number was Kiamitia No. 10433, listed right after his mother, and the 1899 card gives his age as 11 and his father as the dead Joseph Pisachubbe. He was approved as Choctaw by Blood No. 4467 on 12 December 1902. His wife Lizzie came from the Austin family of Fowlerville (Card 1363), whose roll numbers ran 3736 to 3740; her brother James, who died in 1899 before enrollment, was struck off by the Department on 16 September 1904.
P.src: Dawes Cards 1580 and 1363; WWI Draft Registration, 1917; WWII Draft Registration, 1942; 1940 U.S. Census, Jeter; Hugo Daily News, 11 May 1937; Find a Grave (Speer and Long Creek cemeteries); Allotment file for Roll 4467; Choctaw County Clerk records (1979-091763, 1982-115102); Dawes Cards 1580 and 1363.

quotes.t: He was a full blood Choctaw Indian, and was well known among the white people as well as among members of his tribe.
quotes.c: Hugo Daily News, 11 May 1937, on William Harrison Pisachubbe

P.note: The Fort Coffee migration story is family tradition printed in a newspaper; it has not been matched to a removal-era roll.

P.name: Lizzie (Austin) Pisachubbe

imgs.cap: Dawes Card 1363: Legion and Molsey Austin's family, Towson County, 1899

P.place: Full-blood Choctaw, Dawes Roll No. 3738, from Fowlerville (now Valliant). Her baby brother James died in April 1899, weeks before the family applied for enrollment. Her younger sister Adline married Robert's brother William Harrison Pisachubbe. Age 42 in 1940, living with her daughter Frances at Jeter; buried at Long Creek Cemetery.
body: Lizzie is Roll No. 3738 on Dawes Card 1363, filled out on 21 May 1899 for her father Legion and mother Molsey, who are written full-blood Choctaw. She was 7 years old on the card (10 on the final roll, which counted her age in 1902). She had an infant brother, James, who died in April 1899, and a baby sister, Adline, born on 5 August 1900. Adline later married William Harrison Pisachubbe, and Lizzie married his younger brother Robert.

In the same 1915-16 list of land-restriction cases, in a later section dated June to September 1915, appears "Lizzie Pisachubbee, née Austin," an application to free her inherited land from federal restrictions.
kv: Choctaw by Blood No. 3738, full-blood, Card 1363
P.src: Dawes Card 1363; House Committee on Indian Affairs, Five Civilized Tribes of Indians, hearings (1916), list of removal-of-restriction cases, Choctaws.

P.name: Vinson Tims

imgs.cap: Vinson W. Tims marker, High Hill
1896 Choctaw census, Towson County: Vinson, Emeline and family, with brother Edward's household below

P.place: Lived north of Doaksville in the High Hill neighborhood, where he and Emeline farmed. Brother of Judge Edward Ward Tims. His marker at High Hill is a memorial only and gives 1891 as his death year, but he appears on the 1896 Choctaw census. His grandson said he was buried at the old home place.
P.title: The old place north of Doaksville
P.hook: Vinson Tims farmed north of Doaksville, where his daughter Betsy married Joseph Thompson in 1889 and where he is said to be buried.
body: Vinson W. Tims was born in 1838, the elder son of the Doaksville trader Vincent B. Tims. He and Emeline farmed in the High Hill neighborhood of Towson County, 'about four miles north and a little west of Doaksville,' on land later called the Charley Blankenship place. Their children included James, Mitchell, Betsy (Mrs. Joseph Thompson), John, Rev. Robert Tims, Willie, Rosie (Mrs. James Wilson) and Calvin.
Betsy married Joseph Thompson at that house in 1889. Joel remembered his grandparents as 'buried there at the old place,' which fits the marker at High Hill, a cenotaph whose dates cannot be read.

A memorial for him at High Hill Cemetery gives 1838 to 25 October 1891. The 1896 Choctaw census, pictured here, appears to list Vinson with Emeline and their family in Towson County, and on the 1899 card Betsy's father is named 'Vincent Tims,' dead. So his death date is unsettled: 1891 on the memorial, after 1896 if the census line is his.

A memoir of his son Robert, printed in 1944 in the Methodist Indian Mission's minutes, says Robert was "the son of Vincent and Emiline Tims." That is the same first name the 1899 Dawes card gives for Betsy's father, so the family's own church record used "Vincent" for him where the High Hill marker says "Vinson."

Vinson never enrolled, because he was gone by 1899, but his name is on the cards of his children. Written by Dawes clerks in 1899, it appears as "Vinson W. Tims" on James B.'s card, "Vincent Tims" on the cards of Betsy, Robert and Willie, and "Benson Tims" on Mitchell's. In every case the column marks him dead and gives Towson County, where the family lived.
kv: Towson Co., about 4 miles north and a little west of Doaksville
James, Mitchell, Betsy, John, Robert, Willie, Rosie, Calvin
P.note: The date of Vinson's death is in conflict: 25 October 1891 on a Find a Grave memorial and in a local history, against a listing in the 1896 census. The marker is a cenotaph, and his grandson said he was buried at the old home place.
P.src: Find a Grave memorial 10596388; Joel J. Thompson interview #7392; 1896 Choctaw census, Towson County; Hughes (2020); Minutes of the Indian Mission of Oklahoma, 14-17 Sept. 1944, p. 31, memoir of Robert James Tims

P.name: Emeline (Steadman) Tims
P.title: The midwife of Doaksville
P.hook: ¼ Choctaw, daughter of a white man and a Choctaw woman named O-we-na. She delivered her own grandson.
body: Born 26 January 1842, Emeline was enrolled as Choctaw by Blood, Roll No. 1947, one-quarter blood, with her sons Johnny and Calvin on Card 778. Her father John Steadman was a white man ("non-citizen"); her mother O-we-na was Choctaw of Towson County.

She and Vinson farmed in the High Hill neighborhood north of Doaksville. Their children included James, Mitchell, Betsy (Mrs. Joseph Thompson), John, Rev. Robert Tims, Willie, Rosie and Calvin, and several of them later lived around Spencerville.

When her grandson Simon was born on 4 May 1899, Emeline attended as the midwife. On 17 October 1899 she swore before a notary at Doaksville that "there was born to her on said date a male child… said to have been named Simon Thompson," the affidavit that put Simon on the rolls. She died on 16 March 1918 and is buried at High Hill Cemetery.

Her grandson Joel did not remember her maiden name ('Grandmother Tims first name was Emmaline'), so the name Steadman comes from the Dawes records, not family memory. Joel placed her home 'about four miles north and a little west of Doaksville,' in Towson County, 'known as the Charley Blankenship place now.' A local history says six or seven miles. Betsy and Joseph were married there in 1889.

Emeline and Vinson are 'buried there at the old place,' Joel said. A memorial at High Hill Cemetery for Emeline, created by the Choctaw County Genealogical Society, gives her dates, while a photograph of a Tims headstone in a local history is captioned Hampton Chapel Cemetery, which may belong to a child. Her husband's marker at High Hill is a cenotaph.

Her name is printed "Emiline" in the 1944 memoir of her son, the Rev. Robert James Tims, which says he was born six miles north of Fort Towson and was "the son of Vincent and Emiline Tims." The Methodist Indian Mission minutes also give the date and place of birth of another son, James Brown Tims: 25 June 1864, at Doaksville.

Her name is on more Dawes cards than her own. Card 778 enrolls her with Johnny and Calvin; the cards of her sons James B. (510), Robert (816), Mitchell (850) and Willie (1268) each name "Emiline Tims" as mother, and so do the cards of her daughters Rosanna (1281) and Betsy (1283). The men's father is written variously as "Vinson W. Tims," "Vincent Tims" and "Benson Tims," always dead by 1899. In the 1900s she kept being asked to vouch for births.

Her daughter Rosanna was first on her own Card 778, enrolled on 24 April 1899, and moved to her husband James Wilson's Card 1281 in October 1900; the notary who sorted out the name wrote that Rosanna's "mother name is Emaline Times." Emeline swore as midwife to the birth of Rosanna's son (23 March 1903) and, signing as "midwife" on 29 April 1905, of Betsy's son Joseph W. (5 March 1903), swore with Rosanna to the birth of Rosanna's daughter Candace (16 June 1905), and swore with Mildred to the birth of Mitchell's son Vincenta (1904; the Commission acknowledged the affidavits in April 1905).
P.src: Dawes Card 778; enrollment affidavit, card 1283 file (1899); 1896 Choctaw census; Find a Grave (High Hill Cemetery, Choctaw County Genealogical Society); Hughes, 'Trader V. B. Tims of Doaksville' (2020); Find a Grave memorial 185528783; Joel J. Thompson interview #7392; Minutes of the Indian Mission of Oklahoma of the Methodist Church, 1941 (p. 28) and 1944 (p. 31); Dawes Cards 510, 816, 850, 1268, 1283; Newborn Card 1410 jacket; Card 850 jacket; Dawes Card 1281 and jackets 7-1281, 7-1410, 7-850; Newborn Card 1171; Minor Card 150.

P.name: Eunice (Gardner) Pisachubbe

imgs.cap: Dawes Card 1580, Eunice is line 1
Choctaw County court petition in the estate of Eunice Pisachubbe, Roll No. 4465: her sons Robert and William, her only heirs, ask approval of a full-blood deed. It records her death on 19 May 1927.

P.place: Full-blood Choctaw of Goodland, Kiamitia County, the Presbyterian mission settlement whose school survives as Goodland Academy. A widow in 1899 raising her sons William Harrison and Robert and a ward, Edward Pisachubbe, son of Simpson and Sallie. Daughter of Jackson and Viney Gardner of Blue County.
body: After Eunice died on 19 May 1927, her sons Robert and William H. Pisachubbe, "the lawful issue of the marriage between Joseph Pisachubbe and Eunice Pisachubbe," petitioned the Choctaw County court to approve the sale of her allotment of about 159 acres for $1,200. As full-blood Choctaw land, it could not be sold without a judge's approval. The petition also records that Joseph had died long before her and that she never remarried.

Eunice's Dawes card, 1580, was made out for Kiamitia County, post office Goodland, on 10 May 1899. It lists "Pisachubbe, Eunice," age 49, full-blood, Roll No. 4465, with her parents named as "Jackson Gardner" and "Viney Gardner," both dead, of Blue County. Her sons William H., 16 (on the 1896 roll as "William Harrison"), and Robert, 11, are on lines 2 and 3, fathered by "Joseph Pisachubbe," dead. Line 4 is not a son: Edward Pisachubbe, 17, is written as her ward, with his own dead parents named as Simpson and Sallie Pisachubbe of Jackson County, and the card notes that he was the husband of Frances Byington, Card 956.

The tribal-enrollment columns of Card 1580 add the 1896 census numbers: Eunice is Kiamitia County No. 10432, her son Robert No. 10433 and the ward Edward Pisachubbe No. 10434, the three of them on consecutive lines of one household. William is not with them. He appears on the same card as No. 5759, a far earlier number, with a note "No. 2 on 1896 roll as William Harrison," which fits the 1911 finding that he was also listed separately as a student at Armstrong Academy and enrolled twice. All four were approved by the Secretary of the Interior on 12 December 1902.

A note on the card sends the reader on for William's child: "For child of No. 2 see N.B. (Apr. 26, '06) Card No. 1203," the 1906 newborn card for his son Colbert. On the back of the 1911 duplicate-enrollment file, the Commissioner's letter of 1 August 1911 lists the testimony of four witnesses taken to settle the question: William H. Pisachubbe, Eunice Pisachubbe, Harrison Nohio and Thomas Hunter.

P.name: Joseph Pisachubbe
P.place: Kiamitia County, Choctaw Nation. Named as the father of William Harrison and Robert on Dawes Card 1580; dead by May 1899. A 1937 obituary says the family came from Mississippi in 1832 and first settled at Fort Coffee.
P.note: His parents are given in trees as Pisachubbe, also called Wilson, and Nancy Te-hol-ba-ta-bi, but the link is not proven. The Nancy found on the Dawes roll was about 72 in the late 1890s, so she would have been about twelve in 1839, too young to be his mother.
body: Joseph Pisachubbe is on his family's Dawes card only as a dead father: Card 1580 writes him as the father of William H. and Robert, "dead," of Kiamitia County. He had no card of his own. Eunice's 1927 petition says he died long before her.

In the father column of both sons' lines the year column is marked "Dead" and the county Kiamitia. William H.'s line carries 1896 census No. 5759 and Robert's No. 10433, so the two boys were enrolled in different parts of the 1896 Kiamitia County roll. Nothing on the card gives his death year. He therefore died before the 1896 census and before the youngest son was 11 in 1899, which puts his death between about 1883 and 1896.

His own parents are unproven. The Commission's files carry a "Case Pisachubbi" at Idabel (jacket 7-1277) and a "Sarah Pisachubbi," Roll 3471, in a 1913 report on Choctaw land cases, but nothing in either connects them to Joseph (lead only).

P.name: John & Betsy Thompson
P.place: Full-blood Choctaw of Cedar County, named as Joseph's parents on his 1899 Dawes card, both dead. Joel said John died when Joseph was nine and was buried near the family home toward Spencer Academy, and that his grandmother's people "had some sort of a Choctaw name" and had not taken an English one.
P.src: Dawes Card 1283; WPA interview #7392 (Joel J. Thompson, 1937); Dawes Card 1283.
body: Joseph's Dawes card is the only record that names them. Card 1283 writes his parents as "John Thompson," dead, of Cedar County, and "Betsy Thompson," dead, of Cedar County. Joseph's son Joel said his grandfather John died when Joseph was a boy, and that Joseph was the second of nine children. Henry W. Thompson of the next card, 1282, is not named as their son; his parents are given as Simon and Lucy Thompson.

P.name: Legion Austin

imgs.cap: Dawes Card 1363, Legion is line 1
Dawes Card 1363: Legion and Molsey Austin, their children, and their parents' names
Legion Austin's affidavit for his son James, born 15 November 1898, sworn at Fowlerville in May 1899 with Leonidas Willis as neighbor-witness

P.place: Full blood. On the 1896 roll as "Legend Austin." Son of Ata-sa-ha-bi and Lotima of Towson County. His 1899 card gives his age as 33, but in November 1902 he testified he was "about fifty," and he had a grown daughter, Viny, born about 1879 to an earlier wife, Betsy. He also raised his nephew Nicholas Greenwood.
body: Dawes Card 1363, line 1, lists 'Austin, Legion,' 33, male, full blood, on the 1896 census of Towson County as No. 199, living near Fowlerville. The card names his father as Ata-sa-ha-bi and his mother as Lotima, both dead and both of Towson County. His wife Molsey is on line 2, with her parents Brazil and Siney of Red River, also dead.
Fowlerville's post office was established on 7 July 1894 and renamed Valliant on 23 June 1902,, so the post office name changed in 1902.

The application was filed on 21 May 1899 for Towson County, post office Fowlerville. The card lists five people: Legion, Molsey, their daughter Lizzie, a son James who died in April 1899, and a baby daughter Adline, born on 5 August 1900. Legion himself wrote to the Commission from Garvin in October 1900 asking for a blank application for an infant child; the Commission sent it on 9 October. The baby was enrolled on 4 June 1901, as a Commission letter of 5 June 1901 to William Swink at Fowlerville records: "Adline Austin, the infant daughter of Leageon and Muley Austin, born August 5, 1900," the clerk's spellings of Legion and Molsey.

James was a son of about a year old. The card carries the note that he "died April, 1899," and that proof of death was filed. His line has a red rule through it, and the Department cancelled his enrollment on 16 September 1904.

The card's tribal-enrollment columns tie him to the 1896 Choctaw census: Towson County, No. 199, with Molsey at No. 200 and Lizzie at No. 201, and the clerk's note "No. 1 on 1896 roll as Legend Austin." The Commission approved lines 1, 2, 3 and 5 on 12 December 1902. On the final roll he is Choctaw by Blood No. 3736 and the age beside his name is 36, three years more than the 33 written on the 1899 card. The ages on one card do not agree with each other, or with his own testimony in November 1902 that he was "about fifty".

He signed by mark. On the affidavit for his infant son James, sworn at Fowlerville in early May 1899, the clerk crossed out the form's printed "Affidavit of Mother" and wrote "Father" above it, and Legion, "33 years of age and a citizen by blood," swore as the husband of Molsey that the boy was born 15 November 1898. The man who vouched for the birth was a neighbor, Leonidas Willis, who also signed with a mark and is written in as "a Neighbor," not a physician. Nobody named a doctor or midwife for that birth.

P.name: Molsey Austin
P.place: Full blood. Daughter of Brazil and Siney of Red River County.
body: Molsey is on Dawes Card 1363, line 2, wife of Legion Austin, a full-blood Choctaw. Her parents are named on the card as Brazil and Siney, both dead, of Red River; the jacket affidavit ties her to Legion.

In the 1915-16 list of land-restriction cases sent to Congress, a Choctaw entry reads "Molsey Pisachubbi, Austin," which by the table's habit of giving a married woman's maiden name after her married name suggests that by then Molsey Austin carried the name Pisachubbi.

Molsey is Roll No. 3737, Towson County, No. 200 on the 1896 census, and the card gives her age as 22 in 1899; the final-roll age beside her name is 25. She gave the same figure herself on 19 April 1901, when she swore to the birth of her daughter Adline and signed with her mark as "Mulcy Austin," "25 years of age and a citizen by blood" and "the lawful wife of Leageon Austin." She was therefore born about 1875 to 1877. Adline was her third child on the card: Lizzie, about 1892; James, born 15 November 1898 and dead within five months; Adline, 5 August 1900.

The woman who delivered Adline was a midwife, Sinie Hall, who also signed by mark, with the same two witnesses as Molsey, J. R. Moore (reading uncertain) and Sallie Johnson. The notary was William Swink of Fowlerville. Molsey's own mother is written on the card as "Siney," in quotation marks; whether the midwife Sinie Hall was kin to her is not stated anywhere (lead).
P.src: House Committee on Indian Affairs, Five Civilized Tribes of Indians, hearings (1916), "Removal of restriction cases received in the Indian Office since Jan. 1, 1915," Choctaws, p. 93; Dawes Card 1363 (front and back) and jacket 7-1363, NARA Dawes Enrollment Jackets (Choctaw by Blood).

P.name: Vincent B. Tims
P.title: Witness to the Treaty of Doaksville
P.hook: His name is on the 1837 treaty, and his trading post fed Choctaw families arriving from Mississippi.
body: On 17 January 1837, "at Doaksville, near Fort Towson, in the Choctaw country," the Choctaw and Chickasaw nations signed the treaty that let the Chickasaws settle inside the Choctaw Nation. The witness list reads: Wm. Armstrong, Henry R. Carter, Josiah S. Doak, Vincent B. Tims, Daniel McCurtain (U.S. Interpreter)… followed by the marks of the three Choctaw district chiefs.

Born in South Carolina (family accounts say Chester County), Vincent was a trader and the partner of Josiah Doak, whose trading post gave Doaksville its name; a missionary later remembered the town's founders as "Josiah Doak and Vinson Brown Tims, an Irishman." Doak & Tims held the government contract to feed Choctaw families arriving on Removal, at 13 cents a ration, and handled the annuity payments that drew crowds to Doaksville. Notices in the Arkansas Intelligencer dissolved the partnership in 1844.

On 29 May 1847 he bought the Dancing Rabbit Creek treaty allotment of Henry Graves, "son of Chief Netachachie," one of the three district chiefs whose marks appear on the 1837 treaty. That December the Washington (Arkansas) Telegraph reported that "Jos. R. Berthelet and Vincent B. Tims of the Choctaw Nation" were invited within the bar at the Red River Raft Convention, which pressed Congress to clear the great logjam that blocked steamboats on the Red River.

He and his full-blood Choctaw wife stayed at Doaksville the rest of their lives. Family accounts say Vincent died at Doaksville in June 1864, while Confederate troops held Fort Towson a mile away, but he was still signing letters as the Confederate postmaster there on 9 September and 1 November 1864 (see "A postmaster's letters, August to November 1864").

The trader's origins, in the one local history that traces him, are modest: 'Born in South Carolina, V.B. Tims is said to be of Irish descent.' He came to the Doaksville area with Josiah Doak in the early 1830s. In March 1843 he ran an office there for letters to the Agent for Claims, and in February 1844 the partnership with Doak was dissolved 'by mutual agreement,' after which he kept the business on his own.

Three of his children are known by name: Vinson W. (born 1838), Edward Ward (born 1842) and a daughter, Phoebe, who died before final enrollment. His grandson Joel said that 'Venson Brown Tims' was the first postmaster at Doaksville and that Edward succeeded him on his death. The postmaster rolls show Edward appointed on 24 October 1887 and a 'V. B. Tims' on 17 May 1871, seven years after the family date of Vincent's death. Local history says that in 1861 he was 'designated' to be Indian Agent for the Choctaws had the Confederacy won, but this rests on one source.

An 1891 sketch of William Gardner, a Choctaw merchant born in 1830, says that "after he had been to work for E. B. Tims, the sutler at Doaksville," he opened his own store at Hamilton, in Blue County (O'Beirne, Leaders and Leading Men of the Indian Territory, p. 124). The book prints the initials "E. B." rather than "V. B.," but the trade and the town point to the Doaksville trader, so this is probably Vincent.

Two more records show him as a man of business. A New Orleans commission house advertising in the Washington (Arkansas) Telegraph of 10 December 1845 named "Doak & Tims, Doaksville, C. Nation" among its references, next to Maj. William Armstrong of the Choctaw Agency. And a list of stockholders in the Cairo & Fulton Railroad Company of Arkansas, to June 1854, includes "V. B. Tims, Choctaw Nation," with 10 shares at $25 each, among other Choctaw Nation stockholders; the road was chartered to link Cairo, on the Mississippi, with Fulton on the Red River.

The signed army contracts behind the thirteen-cents-a-ration figure are printed in House Report No. 271 (1843): contracts nos. 41 and 42 of 1 January 1838 and no. 44 of 1 January 1839, each naming "Doak & Tims." They are told under "Thirteen cents a ration."

In April 1841 a clerk in the Doaksville trading house wrote home that "Mr. Tims one of the men I am living with is now in New York purchasing a stock of goods." The letters, printed in the Chronicles of Oklahoma in 1931, are told under "Mr. Tims one of the men I am living with."

The U.S. Official Register prints the post office he is remembered for. The edition for 30 September 1877 (Post-Office Department, p. 537, the Arkansas list, which also carries the Choctaw Nation offices) reads across: "Doaksville," "Choctaw," "V. B. Tims," "37 77", a year's compensation of $37.77. The 1871 Register's Arkansas list (p. 502) likewise carries a "V. B. Tims" among the postmasters on the page that holds Doaksville. The initials are the trader's. Whether the postmaster of the 1870s was Vincent himself or his son Vinson, who would have used the same initials, the printed register does not say.

The Dawes card of his son Edward names Vincent's wife. On Card 1437 Edward W. Tims's parents are written "Vincent B. Tims," dead, a non-citizen, and "Betsy Tims," dead, of Towson County. Betsy Thompson, born in 1870, was a granddaughter of that Betsy Tims and shared her name.
P.note: Vincent was white, so the family's Choctaw citizenship came through his wife, whose name has not been found. His date of death is given as 14 June 1864 in a descendants' account and 17 June 1864 in family files, but he signed letters as Doaksville's Confederate postmaster on 9 September and 1 November 1864, so both dates look wrong. The postmaster rolls name a 'V. B. Tims' on 17 May 1871, which may be Vincent himself. The 'first postmaster' detail rests on Joel's memory, and the Confederate office had an earlier postmaster, J. P. Kingsbury, in 1862-63. A card for his son Edward may name Vincent's wife.

P.name: John Steadman
P.place: A non-citizen (white) man, named as Emeline's father on her 1899 Dawes card (Card 778) and dead by then. Family says he was Irish; no record has confirmed it.
body: Card 778 gives him one line, in the father column for line 1, Emeline Tims: "John Steadman," the year marked "Dead," and the county column reading "Non Citz" (non-citizen). That is how a clerk wrote a white man who had not been adopted into the Nation: he is the one name on the whole card whose county is not a Choctaw county.

Emeline's own 1896 census entry is Towson County No. 12116, written there as "Emeline Tims." The Dawes clerk gave her age as 57 against a final-roll age of 60, and her blood as one-quarter Choctaw. Her mother O-we-na is the only parent on the card with a Choctaw county; her father is the only one marked as a non-citizen. The family story that he was Irish is not on the card, and no record seen names his birthplace (lead).

P.name: O-we-na
P.place: Choctaw, of Towson County. Named as Emeline's mother on Dawes Card 778, dead by 1899. A Choctaw given name; its meaning is not recorded.
body: The card writes her name "O-we-na" with the year marked "Dead" and the county Towson. She is the only parent on Card 778 with a county of her own, and it is the same Towson County in which her daughter Emeline was enrolled in 1896 (No. 12116) and lived near Doaksville in 1899. The Choctaw hyphenated spelling is the clerk's attempt to write a sound; no other record found carries her.

P.name: Jackson & Viney Gardner
P.place: Blue County, Choctaw Nation. Named as Eunice's parents on Dawes Card 1580, both dead by May 1899.
body: Their daughter Eunice's Dawes card, 1580, names them as her parents: "Jackson Gardner," dead, of Blue County, and "Viney Gardner," dead, of Blue County. Eunice was 49 when the card was filled out on 10 May 1899.

Eunice is Kiamitia No. 10432, so her husband's county and not her parents' decided where she was enrolled. Blue County held Armstrong Academy, the Choctaw boys' school where William Harrison's name turned up on a student list in August 1899.

Laws of the Choctaw Nation (1894) show how the county map stood in her parents' day: Blue County sent one senator in the Pushmataha District, beside Kiamichi, Atoka and Jack's Fork counties, and in 1886 the Council cut a new Jackson County out of Kiamitia, Blue and Atoka counties. Several well-known Choctaw Gardners lived in Blue County, among them Samuel G. Gardner, who was its probate judge, but no record ties Jackson and Viney to them (lead).

P.name: Brazil & Siney
P.place: Red River County, Choctaw Nation. Named as Molsey's parents on Dawes Card 1363, both dead by 1899; the clerk wrote "Siney" in quotation marks.
body: Named on Dawes Card 1363 as the father of Molsey Austin, dead and formerly of Red River, with Siney as mother. The card spells the mother's name in quotation marks, which may mean a nickname.

Molsey herself was enrolled in Towson County, so she had crossed over from Red River County to marry or live near Legion before the 1896 census, where she is No. 200. The first name Brazil is the clerk's English rendering of a name that may have been something else.

P.name: Ata-sa-ha-bi & Lotima
P.place: Towson County, Choctaw Nation. Named only by their Choctaw names as Legion Austin's parents on Dawes Card 1363, both dead by 1899. Ata-sa-ha-bi ends in -abi, like many Choctaw war-names.
P.src: Dawes Card 1363 (NARA); Dawes Card 1363.
body: Named on Dawes Card 1363 as the father of Legion Austin, dead and formerly of Towson County, with Lotima as mother. The name appears to end in the Choctaw war-name element abi ('killer'); its exact meaning is not recorded.

The card writes "Ded" beside both names. Because Legion was already on the 1896 census, the clerk copied them from that roll rather than taking them from anyone's mouth in 1899, and neither has a number of their own. The card gives no year of death, only that both were gone by May 1899.

P.name: Mary Ellen Hulsey
P.place: Born 22 August 1938 at Broken Bow; died 4 November 2002 in Hugo. The 2-year-old "Mary" on the 1940 census at South Fork, Arkansas. Buried in Woodlawn Cemetery beside William Thompson Jr.
body: Mary Ellen Hulsey was born on 22 August 1938 at Broken Bow, Oklahoma, the fifth of Oscar and Katie's children. In April 1940 she was 2, living with her parents and four older brothers and sisters at South Fork in Montgomery County, Arkansas. She married William 'Junior' Thompson Jr. (1934-2007), and died on 4 November 2002 at Hugo. She is buried at Woodlawn Cemetery in Choctaw County.

P.name: Oscar Franklin Hulsey
P.title: A WPA laborer in the Ouachitas
P.hook: Out of work 48 weeks of 1939, on a government job, with five children in a rented house.
body: Born at Hot Springs, Arkansas, on 27 October 1910. In April 1940 the census taker found Oscar, 29, and Katie, 29, renting a house valued at $2 at South Fork in Montgomery County, Arkansas, with Leon 11, Delis 9, Benney 6, Glen 4 and Mary 2. Oscar was a laborer in "Government work" (the Depression-era WPA), had been unemployed 48 weeks, had worked 16 weeks in 1939 and earned $140. He had five years of schooling.

He had married Katie Stevenson on 27 October 1927, his 17th birthday; she had turned 17 twelve days earlier. He registered for the WWII draft at Mount Ida on 16 October 1940. The family later moved to the lumber towns of McCurtain County, Oklahoma. Oscar died at his home at Holly Creek on 17 June 1982, at 71, and was buried at Wheelock Cemetery near Millerton, the old Choctaw mission ground.

Oscar and Katie had seven children: Franklin Leon (1929-2015), Delphia (1931-2005), Bennie George (1933-1947), Glen (1935-2001), Mary Ellen (1938-2002), Charlie (1940-2010) and Willis Delane (1943-2004). Mary Ellen was born at Broken Bow, Oklahoma, and the family was back in Montgomery County by 1940.

Oscar's obituary in the McCurtain Gazette of 20 June 1982 says he was born at Hot Springs, 'lived in the area for many years,' and died at his home at Holly Creek, between Broken Bow and Wright City in the old sawmill country. His funeral was held at 2 p.m. on Sunday at Wheelock Cemetery, with Rev. Bob Lewis officiating. He was survived by four sons, two daughters, two sisters, four brothers, ten grandchildren and nine great-grandchildren.

Wheelock was the Presbyterian mission to the Choctaws; its church was organized in December 1832 by Rev. Alfred Wright, whose 1853 gravestone in the same graveyard is copied in a 1914 book. Oscar was buried among the missionaries' graves in 1982.

E. P.place: Born 15 October 1910 at Danville, Arkansas, daughter of Frank and Jane Stevenson. Married Oscar Hulsey on 27 October 1927. A homemaker, she moved to Hugo in 1947 and died there on 30 January 2009, at 98.

P.hook: She was a baby at Danville, Arkansas, married at 17, raised seven children, moved to Hugo in 1947 and lived to be 98.
body: Katie Cornelia Stevenson was born on 15 October 1910 at Danville, Yell County, Arkansas, the daughter of Gilbert Franklin 'Frank' Stevenson and Parsis Jane (O'Neal) Stevenson. By 1920 she was 'Kate, 9,' on a rented farm in McCurtain County, Oklahoma. She married Oscar Hulsey on 27 October 1927, twelve days after turning 17.

She moved to Hugo in 1947. She died on 30 January 2009 at 98, with services on 2 February and burial in Mount Olivet Cemetery. Her obituary counted 16 grandchildren, 32 great-grandchildren and 26 great-great-grandchildren, and noted that she was preceded in death by daughters Delphia and Mary and sons Willis, Bennie and Glen.

Katie was the youngest of seven children listed in the 1910 census at Danville: Delphia, Willie, George, Frank, Elisha, Eddie and herself, born in Indiana, Texas, Oklahoma and Arkansas. Her brother Horace Edward "Eddie" (1907-1998) ended his life in Portland, Oregon; her brother George Sherman died at Kilgore, Texas, in 1978. Her aunt Mary Wilson of Tuttle, Oklahoma, lived to 100, and her father's first cousin James Baxter Stevenson preached in Yell County, Arkansas, in 1883-85 (his son Eugene Hendrix became a Rhodes Scholar). See "Seven children in the 1910 census."

P.title: A preacher at Camp Pike
P.hook: In 1918 he was building the Army's big WWI training camp near Little Rock.
body: A preacher from Hot Springs, Arkansas. On his WWI draft card (12 September 1918) he was 42, living at Story in Montgomery County, Arkansas, and working as a laborer for the Stewart-McGehee Construction Company at Camp Pike, the Army's big training camp near Little Rock. The card describes him as short and slender, with blue eyes and black hair. His wife was Sarah Rebecca (Graves) Hulsey.

He married Sarah Rebecca Graves on 22 December 1901, when she was 17, and they had ten children, among them Oscar, born in 1910. He died on 5 August 1935 and is buried in Breashears Cemetery, east of Story, where Benjamin F. Hulsey, believed to be his father, also lies.

Rebecca and George Washington Hulsey had ten children: William Roy (1904), John Wesley (1906), Noah (1908), Oscar Franklin (1910), Fred (1913), Ruby Ellen (Stipe, 1915), Grady (1918), Louis Daniel (1920), Grace Irene (Dunagan, 1923) and George Paul (1925). Oscar was the fourth. Rebecca was 17 at the wedding and 41 when the last child was born.

Find a Grave records his burial at Breashears Cemetery near Fannie in Montgomery County, Arkansas, with a death date of 5 August 1935, and names his father as Benjamin Franklin Hulsey and ten children. That date differs from the 22 December 1935 in the family tree, so the exact day is still to be confirmed from a death certificate or obituary.

Oscar's 1982 obituary says he was survived by two sisters and four brothers. Since Oscar had eight siblings, at least two of them had died before 1982. Each of the children after Oscar now has an entry of his or her own.
When he died on 5 August 1935, the oldest child, William Roy, was about 30 and the youngest, George Paul, about 9 or 10; his widow, Sarah Rebecca, was 51. She died at Bandon, Oregon in 1972.

Camp Pike was under heavy strain when he signed. Eleven days after the draft card, on 23 September 1918, the camp base hospital admitted 214 influenza cases in a single day, and by the end of October 12,393 men had reported sick with the disease. See "The camp where George Hulsey was working when the influenza came."
P.src: WWI Draft Registration, Little Rock, Ark., 1918. Find a Grave (Breashears Cemetery, Montgomery Co., Ark.); 1910, 1920 and 1930 U.S. Censuses; Find a Grave Index (Breashears Cemetery); Opie et al., Epidemic Respiratory Disease (1921), pp. 15–17 and 52; Montgomery County ARGenWeb, 'Breashears Cemetery, Story' (argenweb.net/montgomery/breashears_cemetery.htm; photo study, June 2020)
P.note: His headstone gives his birth as 24 December 1876; his draft card age of 42 points to late 1875 or 1876. The date 22 December appears in some trees as his death, but it is the date of his marriage. Which church he preached for is not recorded; the only church named in the Story cemetery records is the Story Church of God, but nothing ties him to it. Occupation caveat: the records cited here give his work as laborer at Camp Pike (1918 draft card) and tenant or renting farmer (1920, 1930 censuses); none of them calls him a preacher, so 'Rev.' rests on family usage. The Find a Grave death date 5 Aug 1935 and the family-tree 22 Dec 1935 conflict (see above).

P.title: From the Georgia mountains to Story, Arkansas
P.hook: A blacksmith's son from Union County, Georgia, who may have ridden with the Union cavalry at sixteen.
body: Benjamin Franklin Hulsey was born on 2 February 1847 in Union County, in the north Georgia mountains. In the 1850 census he was 3, in the household of Salathiel ("Salathel Halsey") and Elizabeth Hulsey; his father was a blacksmith.

By the Civil War he was in Arkansas. The roster of Company D, 4th Arkansas Cavalry, a Union regiment recruited in Montgomery County in the winter of 1863–64, lists a private "Hulsey, Benjamin F." He would have been 16 or 17. His grave memorial says instead that he served in a Confederate 4th Arkansas Cavalry, but that unit's Company H was raised in Benton County.

He married Sylvania Susane Partin in 1868 and, after her death in 1889, Lucy Lee Morgan in Montgomery County in 1893. He named a son Martin Salatheil Hulsey after his own father. He died at Story on 16 December 1924 and is buried in Breashears Cemetery, the same small cemetery where Rev. George Washington Hulsey was buried in 1935.

His parents were Salathiel, a blacksmith, and Elizabeth (Estel) Hulsey. His first wife, Sylvania Susane Partin (1849-1889), is the likely mother of George Washington Hulsey; his second, Lucy Lee Morgan (1878-1947), he married in Montgomery County on 25 September 1893.

The Hot Springs Sentinel-Record of 13 February 1910 printed the Garland County real estate transfers for 1 to 9 February, and one entry reads: "B. F. Hulsey and wife to C. Floyd Huff, W. 1/2 of N.W. 1/4, sec. 10, Tp. 2 S., R. 19 west, $175." The notice gives no first name or home town, so it may be Benjamin, whose son George Washington was farming in Garland County in 1910, or another B. F. Hulsey.

A transcription of the 1850 Union County, Georgia census lists the household of Salathiel Hulsey with a Benjamin aged 6, which would give a birth about 1844 and not 2 February 1847; the household also has brothers Robert R. (17), Jesse (10) and Jennings (8) and sisters Maryann, Elizabeth, Lillean and Nancy. A Robert R. Hulsey, 27, was already in Hempstead County, Arkansas by 1860 (lead).

His regiment, the 4th Arkansas Cavalry (Union), was organized at Little Rock in December 1863 and skirmished at Cedar Glade on 1 March 1864, the date a Montgomery County petition to Little Rock says Dr. Brown of Cedar Glades was shot down and a wife and baby wounded. A summary of the regiment's marches is told under "The 4th Arkansas Cavalry: Union men from the Ouachita hills."
P.note: That Benjamin was G. W. Hulsey's father rests on grave memorials, a shared cemetery and family naming; it has not been confirmed by a census or death record. The same Union company roster lists a private Gilliam Graves, whom trees place as Sarah Rebecca Graves's grandfather; that link is also unproven. Birth year conflict: the family record (and this entry's first paragraph) give 2 February 1847, which would make him 3 in 1850; the 1850 Union Co., Ga. census as transcribed by the San Diego Genealogical Society gives Benjamin age 6 (b. c.1844); neither the census page nor a birth record has been seen, so 1844 and 1847 are both open. The grave memorial's Confederate 4th Arkansas Cavalry service conflicts with the Union Company D roster.
P.src: 1850 U.S. Census, Union Co., Ga.; Index to Compiled Service Records of Union Soldiers from Arkansas (NARA M383), Co. D, 4th Arkansas Cavalry (ARGenWeb roster); Find a Grave (Breashears Cemetery, Montgomery Co., Ark.); The Sentinel-Record (Hot Springs, Ark.), 13 Feb 1910, p. 4 (http://www.loc.gov/resource/sn89051285/1910-02-13/ed-1/?sp=4); San Diego Genealogical Society, Hulsey Families (2000), 1850 Union Co., Ga; Montgomery County ARGenWeb, 'Breashears Cemetery, Story' (argenweb.net/montgomery/breashears_cemetery.htm; photo study, June 2020)

P.name: Sarah Rebecah Graves
P.place: Born 5 May 1884 (her grave memorial says St. Francis County, its biography Little Rock). Married G. W. Hulsey in 1901 at 17. Died at Bandon, Oregon, on 23 December 1972, at 88.
P.hook: Born on 5 May 1884, the day her mother died, she married George Washington Hulsey at 17 and lived to be 88.
body: Sarah Rebecca Graves was born on 5 May 1884. Her mother, Margaret Crumpton, had married Jesse Graves in Garland County on 31 January 1884 and died the day Sarah Rebecca was born. Sarah grew up among half-brothers and sisters from her father's first and third marriages: Abraham Nicholas, Catherine Eunice, Greenbury and Vestal, Lucinda, William Vestal, Pearl Mae and Cora Ellen.

On 22 December 1901 she married George Washington Hulsey in Arkansas. They lived in Sulphur Township, and by 1920 had moved to McCurtain County, Oklahoma; she was in Oklahoma in 1943. She died on 23 December 1972 at Bandon, Coos County, Oregon, and is buried in Hawthorne Memorial Gardens, Grants Pass.

Her stepmother, Nancy (Wilborn) Kyle Cuttler, married Jesse Graves when Sarah Rebecca was five, and she had half-siblings and stepsiblings from three marriages. Her mother's maiden name is Cornett on the evidence of the 1880 census, where Margaret Crumpton is living with her mother Rebecca Cornett; the name Rebecca may come from that grandmother (lead).

She had ten children between 1904 and 1925. She was widowed in 1935 at 51 and died in Oregon in 1972, her grandson Glen, Oscar's son, died at Veneta, Oregon in 2001, and the family may have followed western timber work (lead).
kv: Hawthorne Memorial Gardens, Grants Pass, Josephine Co., Oregon; died 23 Dec 1972, Coos Co., Oregon (Find a Grave memorial 94352588)
P.note: Her birthplace is given as St. Francis County on one memorial and Little Rock on another; her mother's maiden name is Speer or Cornett. The identification of her father with Jesse King Graves is probable, not proven.
P.src: Graves Family Association, Gen. 242; Find a Grave memorial for Sarah Rebecca Hulsey (94352588); Find a Grave Index (Hawthorne Memorial Gardens)

P.hook: Born 17 November 1861 at Pulaski, Tennessee, the son of a Methodist preacher; he carried his family from Indiana to Arkansas to Oklahoma.
body: Gilbert Franklin Stevenson was born on 17 November 1861 at Pulaski, Giles County, Tennessee, the son of the Rev. Abner Arrington Stevenson and Martha Still (Watson) Stevenson; he was apparently named for an uncle, Rev. Gilbert Stevenson. He was 8 in 1870 and 18 in 1880 in his father's household.

His wife Parsis Jane O'Neal came from Gibson County, Indiana, and their first children, Iva Myrtle (1884), Adison Galiton (1886) and Nellie Vashti (1889), were likely born there. A later group, Frank Lester (1902), Horace Edward (1907) and Katie Cornelia (15 October 1910, at Danville, Arkansas), were born in the West. The 1910 census calls him a clergyman, 51, renting at Danville, married 25 years, with seven children born in Indiana, Texas, Oklahoma and Arkansas.

In January 1919 his mother-in-law Vashti's obituary names her daughter as 'Mrs. Frank Stevenson of Valiant, Oklahoma.' In 1920 he farmed a rented place on South Millerton Road in McCurtain County. He died at Hugo on 9 May 1950 and is buried at Mount Olivet Cemetery.

In January 1881, when Frank was 19, the Giles County paper noted that his father had "abandoned the idea of going to Texas." That May it reported that "Judge Geo. Stevenson, son of Rev. A. Stevenson, returned from Texas last week," probably Frank's brother George W. Texas was in the family's talk long before Frank himself preached there.

The Mount Olivet canvass of 2000 lists 'Stevenson Frank N. 1860 1950' in Block 2, next to a Parsis Jane Stevenson. That confirms a stone with his death year and a birth year one year off his family record; the census ages of 1870, 1880 and 1910 range from 1859 to 1862, so the difference is not unusual.

Gilbert was five months old when the first Federal troops reached Pulaski in April 1862. Goodspeed's county history says the county was "continually overrun with both Federal and Confederate soldiers" until the war ended, and that in 1863 the Federals relieved the whole county of "horses, cattle and grain." His first cousins Coleman and Wilbur Stevenson served in the Confederate 32nd Tennessee.

Frank was one of fifteen children of Rev. Abner A. and Martha (Watson) Stevenson, and the twin of George Washington Stevenson, born on the same day; a family history written from the Stevenson family sketches lists both. The 1870 census household in Giles County names Gilbert and George W., both 8, with Mack (Wilson McAlister), 5, and Manerva Jane, 3, and in 1880 the household lists Gilbert F., 18, a farmer, with Wilson M. and Jane M. His brothers and sisters are described in "Fifteen children at Bee Spring."

The 1910 census at Danville lists the seven children at home: Delphia, 18, born in Indiana; Willie, 16, Texas; George, 12, Indiana; Frank, 8, Texas; Elisha, 6, Texas; Eddie, 2, Oklahoma; and Katie, a baby, Arkansas. That count of seven does not match the earlier list of Iva Myrtle, Adison Galiton and Nellie Vashti, whose connection to Frank is not documented; see "Katie Stevenson's brothers and sisters."

P.name: Rev. Abner Arrington Stevenson
P.place: Born 16 March 1816 in Giles County, Tennessee, son of Rev. Elam Stevenson. A Methodist preacher for 54 years who also farmed; the 1880 census lists him as a "Farming Preacher" with his son Gilbert F., 18. Buried at Bee Spring Cemetery, Pulaski.
P.src: 1870 and 1880 U.S. Census, District 10, Giles Co., Tenn.; Goodspeed, History of Giles County (1886); family letter of 1932; Pisgah History and Elam Stevenson family letter (Giles Co. TN, AHGP); Find a Grave memorials for Abner and Martha Stevenson; Goodspeed, History of Tennessee (1886), Giles County, Biographical Appendix, p. 872; The Pulaski Citizen, 21 Feb 1878 p. 3, 21 Nov 1878 p. 3, 28 Aug 1879 p. 3, 27 Jan 1881 p. 2, 5 May 1881 p. 2, 29 May 1884 p. 3 (Library of Congress, sn85033964); Goodspeed, History of Tennessee (1886), Giles County Biographical Appendix, p. 872; History of Methodist Churches and Institutions in Middle Tennessee, 1787-1956 (1956), 'Bee Spring Memorial' by Sterling E. Stovall, historian (archive.org/details/historyofmethodi00cart); Goodspeed, History of Tennessee (1886), Giles County, pp. 872-873; Casey family history, pp. 3-108 to 3-120; 1870 and 1880 census as printed on WikiTree Stevenson-12558.
P.hook: A Giles County farmer and preacher whose family letter says he preached 54 years.
body: Abner Arrington Stevenson was born on 16 March 1816 in Giles County, Tennessee, the son of the Rev. Elam Stevenson and Lydia Payne, and was one of five Methodist-preaching brothers. A grandnephew's letter of 1932 records the family totals: 'Uncle Abner 54 years.' A church history of the circuit calls him 'a Godly man' who 'lived to be very old.'

In 1880 he gave his occupation as 'Farming Preacher.' His wife was Martha Still Watson (1823-1887), daughter of David Milton Watson, and their son Gilbert Franklin was born in 1861. Abner died on 30 July 1896 and is buried at Bee Spring Cemetery, the church his father founded.

Goodspeed's 1886 list of Elam and Lydia Stevenson's eleven children names him fourth, as "Abner A.," between James C. and Willis M. (page 872). The list comes from the sketch of his nephew Coleman L., the son of his brother William P.

The Pulaski Citizen shows him at work and at home. On 21 November 1878 the Mt. Pisgah circuit appointments gave him "Blooming Grove, 4th Sunday, 11 a. m." In January 1881 the paper reported that he had "abandoned the idea of going to Texas and will remain where he is now living," and that May his son "Judge Geo. Stevenson" "returned from Texas last week." In May 1884 a column noted two sermons at Rocky Point, "one by Abner Stevenson."
Abner's nephew Coleman L. Stevenson, son of his brother William P., enlisted in 1862 in the 32nd Tennessee and served to the end of the war (Goodspeed, History of Tennessee, 1886, p. 872).

Goodspeed's History of Tennessee (1886) shows two of Abner's nephews in Confederate service, Coleman L. and Wilbur M., sons of his brother William P., in the 32nd Tennessee Regiment. Abner's own Union or Confederate sympathies are not recorded in anything seen. The county around his Pulaski-area farm was crossed by Federal and Confederate troops throughout the war (see the Giles County story).

Abner and Martha Watson were married on 8 December 1838 and had fifteen children between 1840 and 1866; the twins Gilbert Franklin and George Washington were the twelfth and thirteenth. One son, James Willis, became a Methodist minister and lived to 1943; Frank was called a clergyman in 1910. The children are listed in "Fifteen children at Bee Spring." One of his sons-in-law, John Newton Andrew, married three Stevenson women in succession.

P.name: Salathiel & Elizabeth Hulsey
P.place: A blacksmith in Hall County, Georgia, in 1840 and Union County in 1850, with his wife Elizabeth (maiden name given as Estel) and son Benjamin, 3. Their place in our line depends on Benjamin being G. W. Hulsey's father, which is not yet proven.
P.src: 1840 U.S. Census, Hall Co., Ga.; 1850 U.S. Census, Union Co., Ga. (as cited on Find a Grave and WikiTree); 1850 U.S. Census, Union Co., Ga., as transcribed in San Diego Genealogical Society, Families: Hulsey (archive.org sdgsfamilies64); San Diego Genealogical Society, Hulsey Families (2000).
body: Salathiel Hulsey was a blacksmith in Union County, Georgia, and in 1850 the census taker found him with his wife Elizabeth and a three-year-old son, Benjamin Franklin. Benjamin later named a son Martin Salatheil Hulsey for him. He died in the early 1850s. Trees name his parents as Jesse Hamilton Hulsey and Mary Tharp, but no record supports this.

The 1850 Union County, Georgia census, as transcribed in the San Diego Genealogical Society Hulsey file, lists Salatheil Hulsey, 43, born Georgia, with Elizabeth, 35, and Maryann 19, Robert R. 17, Elizabeth 12, Jesse 10, Jennings 8, Benjamin 6, Lillean 3 and Nancy 1, plus Arminda Burnet 20 and J. C. Bell 23. His son Robert R. is in Hempstead County, Arkansas by 1860, aged 27, with a one-year-old son named Salathel G. (lead for the identification).
The Benjamin of that household is 6, not 3, which would put his birth about 1844 and not 2 February 1847; that difference has not been settled. The original census film should be checked.
P.note: The transcription gives Salathiel's age as 43 in 1850, about 1807, and Elizabeth's as 35; the household has eight children including Benjamin. Trees naming his parents as Jesse Hamilton Hulsey and Mary Tharp are unsupported. Benjamin's age conflicts inside the sources: the first paragraph says a three-year-old Benjamin (b. 2 Feb 1847, family record), the 1850 transcription says 6 (b. c.1844).
kv: Salatheil 43, Elizabeth 35, Maryann 19, Robert R. 17, Elizabeth 12, Jesse 10, Jennings 8, Benjamin 6, Lillean 3, Nancy 1 (Union Co., Ga.)

P.name: Parsis Jane (O'Neal) Stevenson
P.place: Born at Princeton, Indiana; died in Hugo. Daughter of Union soldier Daniel W. O'Neal.
body: Parsis Jane O'Neal was born in 1868, the fourth of the ten children of Daniel Waters O'Neal and Vashti Pearson in Gibson County, Indiana. She married Frank Stevenson, and by the time of her mother's obituary in January 1919 she was 'Mrs. Frank Stevenson of Valiant, Oklahoma.' She died in 1956, aged about 88.

Parsis was the fourth of ten children. The 1880 census, in Columbia Township, Gibson County, lists her at 11 as "Works At Home," with brothers William (16), John (13), George J. (4, born in Missouri) and Daniel G. (2). Her sisters were Mary Elizabeth (1860-1960, who lived to 100), the infant J. A. (1871), Nora (1884) and, much later, Charity Louisa (1887-1979). WikiTree gives her birth as 26 March 1868 and death as 26 January 1956 at Hugo. The Find a Grave memorial that WikiTree cites for her grave at Hugo is titled "Parsis Jane O'Neal Louderback"; see "A sixteen-year-old bride in Pulaski County."

The 1910 census names her children at Danville as Delphia, Willie, George, Frank, Elisha, Eddie and Katie. Her son George Sherman Stevenson died on 3 June 1978 at Kilgore, Texas, and she appears as his mother on the death certificate. The brothers who stayed in Indiana and her sister Mary Wilson of Tuttle, Oklahoma, are told in their own stories.

P.name: Daniel Waters O'Neal
P.title: Union soldier, 42nd Indiana
P.hook: Enlisted in 1861 and marched through a Kentucky winter of mud and measles. How long he served is a family puzzle.
body: Daniel Waters O'Neal was born on 25 October 1838 in Tennessee, the year before his parents settled in Gibson County, Indiana. He married Vashti Pearson on 5 January 1860. On 21 October 1861, at 23, he was mustered in as a private in Company F, 42nd Indiana Infantry, the company raised at Oakland City.

The regiment's first winter was its hardest. At Calhoun, Kentucky, the men camped on ground "fully ankle-deep in mud in its best parts," and within twenty days a third of them were in the hospital, many with measles. At Sacramento, Kentucky, they raided the hen-roosts and were arrested until the chaplain talked them free. When they marched into Nashville on 25 February 1862 they found an unlocked pork-house, and by the time headquarters sent a search party "not an ounce of the meat could be found."

A family biography says Daniel was discharged for disability, blindness, at Nashville on 15 March 1862. The regimental rosters list him with no remark, which usually meant a man served out his three years. Company F went on to Perryville, Stones River, Chickamauga, Missionary Ridge and the Atlanta campaign.

Daniel farmed in Gibson County, and he and Vashti raised ten children, among them Parsis Jane, born in 1868. He is buried in Somerville Cemetery under a family stone, with a side stone reading "DANIEL with Co. F. 42 Reg. Ind. Vol." His father, Archibald O'Neal, died in 1841; his widowed mother, Parses Shaw, later married Hugh Watt.

Daniel's funeral was held by Rev. Wright at the United Presbyterian Church of Somerville. He and Vashti lie in the same plot. A twenty-five-foot limestone monument to Company F was raised in 1893 at Oakland City, and it is said to carry the name 'D. O'Neal'; the stone has not been seen, so the name on it is unconfirmed.

The 1884 History of Gibson County prints the roll of Company F, and beside his name it reads: "O'Neal, Daniel W., vet. mustered out July 21, '65." (page 115). "Vet." marks a man who reenlisted as a veteran when the 42nd did in January 1864, and 21 July 1865 is the day the regiment mustered out. If the roll is right, Daniel stayed in Company F to the end of the war rather than leaving in March 1862, and the regiment's later campaigns at Chickamauga, Atlanta and Bentonville would have included him. His application for an invalid pension in December 1865, five months after the muster-out, fits a man who came home with the regiment.

Gil. R. Stormont's 1913 booklet says the Company F monument at Oakland City, dedicated in September 1893, carries "the names of all the original members of the company and the recruits, 143 in number," and beneath a scroll "Starved to death at Andersonville" the names of eleven company men who died as prisoners after Chickamauga. See the stories on the monument and on Company F's war.

Calhoun left a story that the regiment itself told. In Horrall's telling, Col. James G. Jones kept a canteen of whisky in his quarters against "the bad weather and poisonous miasma" of the Calhoun camp, and one morning found it empty: "That d——d Lieutenant-Colonel Denby has been at my canteen, drank it all." The sentinel before headquarters, "being also a little afraid of malaria," had emptied it himself. The same camp sent a third of the men to the hospital within twenty days, and of the measles cases a few "transferred to Evansville died." The story of Daniel's company and its captain is told under "Company F: the men around Daniel O'Neal" and "Captain Cockrum: Stones River to Libby Prison."

Of his ten children, WikiTree traces seven to adulthood: Mary Elizabeth (1860-1960), William Allen (1863-1933), John Sherman (1866-1940), Parsis Jane (1868-1956), George Johnson (1875-1965), Daniel Clinton (1878-1954) and David Commodore (1881-1955), plus the youngest daughter Charity Louisa (1887-1979). William was born in Tennessee, probably in 1863 while Daniel was in the army, though the 1880 census says Indiana; George, in 1880, says Missouri. Three of the five sons died at Somerville, one at Evansville and one in Pike County, all within about thirty miles of the farm. Mary and Parsis went west. Their stories are told under the O'Neal family entries.

P.name: Vashti Pearson
P.place: Born 18 May 1844, daughter of John and Elizabeth Pearson. Married Daniel O'Neal on 5 January 1860. A member of the United Brethren Church of Somerville, Gibson County, Indiana; died there on 16 January 1919.
body: Vashti Elizabeth Pearson was born on 18 May 1844 and married Daniel O'Neal on 5 January 1860. She died at Somerville, Indiana, on 16 January 1919 of 'apoplexy, 6 hrs.' Her obituary says she 'professed faith in Christ early in life' and was a faithful member of the United Brethren Church of Somerville. She was survived by her husband, five sons (William, John, George, Clinton and Commodore), and two daughters, Mrs. Frank Stevenson of Valiant, Oklahoma, and Mrs. Fred Skomp of Somerville, and by a brother, James Pearson, of Elberfeld, Indiana.

The ten children were Mary Elizabeth (1860-1960, who lived to 100), William Allen (1863), John Sherman (1866, born the year after the war), Parsis Jane (1868), J. A. (1871, died an infant), George Johnson (1875), Daniel Clinton (1878), David Commodore (1881), Nora (1884, died an infant) and Charity Louisa (1887).

The 1884 county history says that in 1827 "Solomon Brown and William Pearson had charge of the poor" in Columbia Township, so a Pearson family was in the township long before Vashti was born in 1844. No record links that William to her father John.

Her five surviving sons (William Allen, John Sherman, George Johnson, Daniel Clinton and David Commodore) all lived into their fifties or later, and three died at Somerville. Her two daughters named in the obituary were Mrs. Frank Stevenson (Parsis) and Mrs. Fred Skomp (Charity Louisa); the eldest daughter, Mary Elizabeth, was alive in Oklahoma in 1919 but is not named in the notice as printed. Charity and Fred Skomp later lived at Hobart and Valparaiso in northern Indiana.

P.title: A family of Methodist preachers
P.hook: Frank Stevenson's grandfather rode into Tennessee by pack horse, built a church, and raised five preacher sons.
body: Elam Stevenson was born on 24 September 1787 in what is now Alexander County, North Carolina, the son of James and Jane Stevenson, who were Presbyterians. He was the first of his family to join the Methodists. He married Lydia Payne in Burke County, and in 1813 he was licensed to preach and moved his family to Giles County, Tennessee, travelling by pack horse because there were no wagon roads.

In 1815 he was the chief founder of Bee Spring Methodist Episcopal Church near Pulaski, buying 15 acres for $20. He preached for more than sixty years, was ordained an elder in 1859, and died in 1875; Lydia had died in 1872. Family tradition says he was buried under the pulpit. The church was destroyed by a tornado in 1909.
Five of his eight sons became Methodist preachers, and the family reckoned 292 years of preaching among Elam and his sons.

Our line runs through Rev. Abner Arrington Stevenson (1816–1896). In 1880 Abner, 63, gave his occupation as "Farming Preacher," and his household in Giles County included his wife Martha and their son Gilbert F., 18: the Frank Stevenson who later brought his family to Hugo. Frank was apparently named for his uncle Gilbert.

Goodspeed's History of Tennessee (1886) prints the family's own roll of children, in the sketch of Elam's grandson Coleman L. Stevenson of Giles County. Coleman's grandparents were "Rev. Elam and Lydia Stevenson, natives of North Carolina, who were married about 1805, and located in Giles County, Tenn., about 1813. To them were born these children: Katherine, William P., James C., Abner A., Willis M., Minerva J., John B., Thomas C., Amanda, Elam A. and Gilbert. The grandfather died in 1875 and the grandmother in 1872." That is eleven children, eight of them sons. Coleman's father William P. "has four brothers who are ministers of the gospel, and his father was also a very prominent Methodist Episcopal minister."
His own letter to the church historian McFerrin, written in 1869, is told under "In his own words, 1869."

The Pulaski Citizen of 18 March 1875 carried his death notice: "Died, at the residence of W. M. Stevenson, near Bethany, on the 13th inst., Rev. Elam Stevenson, in his 88th year." It called him "this venerable minister of God" and said he "had been greatly afflicted, but never complained." In May 1878 another Citizen writer, describing the Bee Spring graveyard, wrote of "old Father Stevenson and his beloved consort" as among "the founders and upholders of Methodism at Bee Spring."

A neighbor's recollection, "Old Times in Giles" in the Pulaski Citizen of 25 September 1884, places the family near Bee Spring church in 1815 or 1816 and calls him "a Methodist preacher all his life"; it is told under that title.

The 1956 history of Middle Tennessee Methodist churches says of Bee Spring that Elam Stevenson organized it in 1815, helped by Stephen Loyd, Meshack Boice and James McCowan, and that the 1855 frame church was destroyed by the tornado of 29 April 1909. Of the old site only the cemetery remained, 'sadly neglected.'

Elam's eleven children, as the Casey family history reconstructs them: Catherine A. (1808-1888, Mrs. William Hamilton, Limestone County, Alabama); William Payne (1810-1892); James Calvin (1813-1899); Abner Arrington (1816-1896); Willis McKendree (1818-1900); Minerva J. (1820, an infant who died that December); John Baxter (1821); Thomas Coleman (1825-1906); Lydia Amanda (1827-1901); Elam Augustus (1829-1886, who moved to Arkansas); and Gilbert Worth (b. 1830), a schoolteacher and minister who married Martha J. Tharp. Some of their stories are told under their own names.

The stone over Elam and Lydia at Bee Spring reads, on his side, "Nearly 62 years a minister of the gospel. He was pure in heart and life," and on hers, "Nearly 70 years a Methodist. She consecrated her household to God and the church." She died on 6 March 1872, a day the cemetery list and the Casey history agree on.

P.name: Archibald O'Neal
P.place: A Tennessean by birth and a farmer, he came to Gibson County, Indiana, in 1839 and died there on 25 April 1841.
body: Archibald O'Neal came to Gibson County, Indiana, in 1839 and, in the words of the 1884 county history, 'was a Tennessean by birth.' He was a farmer, and died on 25 April 1841. His widow Parses, 'a native of Lawrenceburg, Ohio,' later married Hugh Watt, and in 1884 was still living on the old home farm. His son Daniel, born in Tennessee the year before, grew up there and enlisted in 1861.

The book prints his death date twice, and the two differ. The township narrative says "He died April 25, 1841" (page 212), while the directory on page 239, listing him under his widow, reads "Died Ap'l 22,'41," "First Husband of Mrs. P. W.," with birthplace "Tennessee" and the year 1839 for his arrival. The printed dates are three days apart, and no grave record has been seen to choose between them.
P.note: The 1884 history says he was born in Tennessee, while online trees say Virginia. His parents in trees (Charles and Martha O'Neal) rest on an uncited memorial and are doubtful.

P.name: Parses (Shaw) O'Neal Watt
P.place: A native of "Lawrenceburg, Ohio," per the 1884 county history. Widowed in 1841; later married Hugh Watt and was still living on the old home farm in 1884. Died in 1901.
body: Parses Shaw was born about 1811 and, as the 1884 county history puts it, was 'a native of Lawrenceburg, Ohio,' who 'came to this county in 1839' with her husband Archibald O'Neal. After he died in 1841 she married Hugh Watt, and in 1884 she was still on the old home farm. She died in 1901.

The township directory in the 1884 county history lists her as "Watt, Mrs. Parsis," farming on Section 32 at Oakland City. The two men in her story are listed directly beneath her. One is "Archibald O'Neal," "First Husband of Mrs. P. W.," born in Tennessee, came in 1839, "Died Ap'l 22,'41." The other is "Watt, Hugh," the "Second" husband, who died "Sept. 20,'71" and was born in "County Down, Irel'd." (page 239). So Hugh Watt was an Irishman from County Down who died in 1871, thirteen years before the book was printed, and Parses was living on the old O'Neal farm as his widow.

P.name: Noble Shaw
P.place: Guilford County, North Carolina.
body: The Greensboro newspaper The Times of 26 March 1857 carries the administrators' notice for the sale of his 268-acre farm near the Oak Ridge Institute, signed by J. H. Leak and Sicily Shaw. It is told under "Noble Shaw's land, advertised at Oak Ridge in 1857."

Hinshaw's Quaker records and the Dover Monthly Meeting register list Noble Shaw, born 22 April 1787, with Sicily Shaw his wife and their children: Aaron, born 16 December 1809; Parris, born 7 July 1817 and died 30 May 1818; and Mary, born 17 November 1820. A later note records that Noble died on 25 December 1855. One caution: this register shows a Parris who died as a baby in 1818, so it does not by itself prove that Parses Shaw, who lived to 1901 and married into the O'Neal line, was this couple's daughter. Another child born around 1811 could simply be missing from the page.
