P.name: Aden Nordyke

imgs.cap: The Marmon "Wasp," winner of the first Indianapolis 500 in 1911
Marriage license of Henry Nordyke and Rebecca Perkins, New Jersey, 1731

P.title: Quakers and the first Indy 500
P.hook: A New Jersey Quaker family that moved west, a grandson who fought for the Union, and a cousin whose firm won the first Indianapolis 500.
body: The Nordykes were Quakers from Burlington County, New Jersey. Henry Nordyke married Rebecca Perkins there in 1731. Their descendants moved to Guilford County, North Carolina, then on to Ohio and Indiana with the Quaker migration away from slavery.

Aden was the oldest son of Abraham Nordyke and Mary Rogers, born in Burlington County in 1762. An Ohio county history says that while the family lived in Georgia he was shot in the arm during an Indian attack. He married Martha Johnson at Deep River, Guilford County, in 1787, and later moved on to Indiana, where he died in 1842.

An 1899 biography of Captain Adin Nordyke of the 63rd Indiana calls his father Robert Nordyke "son of Adin and Sarah Nordyke," and his mother Elizabeth Shaw. If this is our Aden, the captain was his grandson. Raised a Quaker, he "still holds to that doctrine," yet he fought at Resaca, Atlanta, Allatoona, Franklin and Nashville. Since our Sicily Nordyke married Noble Shaw, the two Guilford County families were probably linked twice.

Aden's brother Micajah moved to Clinton County, Ohio, in 1806 and gave the land for the East Fork Friends burying ground at New Vienna. Micajah's son Ellis, born in 1807, was a Quaker millwright who founded a flour-mill machinery works at Richmond, Indiana, with his son Addison. Daniel W. Marmon joined in 1866, and the firm moved to Indianapolis in 1876 as Nordyke & Marmon. On 30 May 1911 Ray Harroun drove its yellow No. 32 Marmon "Wasp" to victory in the first Indianapolis 500, averaging 74.6 miles per hour.

Hinshaw's Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy, vol. 1, carries a Quaker entry dated 12 December 1787: "Martha, dt Robert & Cecilia, Surry Co., m Adin Nordyke." If this is Aden's wife, her parents were Robert and Cecilia of Surry County, and the Quaker entry for the marriage is dated 12 December 1787. The name would also fit Aden's daughter Sicily, a form of Cecilia. The entry as printed gives no surname for Martha, so the link to Martha Johnson stays a lead. Hinshaw also lists Aden's children with Martha beginning "Sicily b. 8-2-1790. Mary 2-15-1792."

Deep River Monthly Meeting recorded the marriage intention of Adin Nordyke and Martha Johnson on 12 December 1787, naming his parents as Abraham and Mary Nordyke. It ties Aden to the Abraham Nordyke and Mary Rogers household that had come south from Burlington, New Jersey.
P.note: The 1899 biography names Adin's wife as Sarah, not Martha Johnson, so either Aden married twice or the captain descends from another Adin. Ellis being Micajah's son rests on cemetery records and a family account; it is very likely but not proven by a single document. Sources disagree on whether the Richmond works began in 1851 or 1859.

P.place: Burlington County, New Jersey Quakers, married 1 June 1761. They moved through Virginia, Georgia, North Carolina and Tennessee before settling in Clinton County, Ohio, in 1806. Their children included Aden, Israel, Benajah, Beulah, Micajah, Daniel, Phebe and Hiram.
body: A Nordyke family history, the Terrell-Nordyke Genealogy (1960), gives Abraham and Mary's moves in order: members of Chesterfield Monthly Meeting in New Jersey; to Virginia and Hopewell Monthly Meeting near Winchester in 1771; eight years in Georgia; transferred to Deep River Meeting in North Carolina in 1788; to Lost Creek Meeting near Knoxville, Tennessee, in 1798; and in 1805 to a new farm near New Vienna, Clinton County, Ohio, where they helped start East Fork Meeting. Mary died in 1814; Abraham's burial at East Fork was recorded in 1825, at 89. The full route is told under 'Six homes in forty-four years.'

P.name: John Winfred Moffitt

imgs.cap: USS Chief (AM-315), the minesweeper he served on in 1946 (photo from 1952)

P.title: Navy corpsman in the Pacific
P.hook: Born at Frogville. Trained as a Navy medic at 18 and served on a floating drydock that came under air attack at Leyte.
body: Born 25 October 1925 at Frogville, Oklahoma, a Red River community of about 40 families, to Grady and Mary Moffitt; his older brothers were Alvin, Odis and Dois. In 1930 the family was living with his mother's parents in Martin County, Texas, and in 1940 he was "Johnnie," 14, at 411 North H Street in Hugo.

He enlisted in the U.S. Navy on 17 December 1943, at 18, and trained at the Navy Hospital Corps School in San Diego, the school for corpsmen (medics). From the day it was commissioned, 22 March 1944, he served on ARD-19, a floating drydock towed across the Pacific to Manus and then to Leyte in the Philippines. In late November 1944, while ARD-19 held the mine-damaged destroyer USS Ross, a Japanese fighter crashed into the dock and started gasoline fires, and the crews shot down a second attacker. ARD-19 earned a battle star for Leyte, then moved to Subic Bay on Luzon, where it kept repairing ships until after the war. For nearly all his time aboard, its commanding officer had a name much like his: Lieutenant Commander Allan P. Moffat.

By the start of 1946 he was aboard the minesweeper USS Chief, which had swept mines off Japan and was on occupation duty at Nagoya and Sasebo until March 1946, when she sailed home to San Francisco. He was discharged on 9 May 1946 and married Faye Smith in Paris, Texas, on 12 June 1947. He was a Baptist, and lived in Hugo until his death in 1990.
P.note: His exact role during the attack is not recorded, and his rate is not confirmed. The muster index labels his second ship MCM 14, a mix-up with a later ship; AM-315 is correct. The rolls run past his 9 May 1946 discharge, probably because the index follows roll dates. His service file can be requested from the National Personnel Records Center.
P.src: U.S. Navy muster rolls, 1943–46; VA BIRLS death file; 1940 U.S. Census, Hugo; obituary, The Paris News, Sept. 1990; ship histories (DANFS, NavSource). 1930 U.S. Census, Martin Co., Tex.

P.name: Woodford "Grady" Moffitt

imgs.cap: Grady's WWI draft registration, 5 June 1917

P.title: Timberman at Ervin, laborer in the Depression
P.hook: Tall, stout and gray-eyed in 1917. Nine children and almost no work in 1939.
body: Born 6 November 1891 at Mountain View, Arkansas, the youngest of Henry and Hannah Moffitt's children at home in 1900. In 1910, at 18, he was living with his widowed mother in Stone County and working in the timber, apparently making barrel staves.

When he registered for the WWI draft on 5 June 1917 he was 25, working as a timberman for C. D. Neese at Ervin, Oklahoma, married and supporting a wife, his mother and a child. The card describes him as tall and stout, with gray eyes and dark hair.

In February 1920 he was a tenant farmer in Wilson Township, Choctaw County, with Mary, sons Alvin and Odis, and a nephew and niece; his brother Tom farmed next door. In April 1930 the family, now with six boys, was living with Mary's parents on a farm near Stanton, Martin County, Texas, and Grady, a road-work laborer, was out of work.

The 1940 census shows the family renting at 411 North H Street in Hugo: Grady, 48, a laborer with five years of schooling, had been unemployed 50 weeks, worked 12 weeks in 1939 and earned $100. At home were Mary ("Manile"), 44, and the children Odis 21, Dais 19, Johnnie 14, the twins Alton and Eldon 11, Donald 8, and two little ones.

Grady and Mary lost two children at three years old, Jimmie Gaynell (1923–1926) and Henry Wayne (1934–1937), and their son Dois died in 1947. Grady died on 21 June 1972 and is buried beside Mary at Shoat Springs Cemetery near Hugo.

On his 1942 "old man's" draft card, Grady is 50, living on North Broadway in Hugo, listed as unemployed, with his birthplace given as Stone County, Arkansas. The person who would always know his address is "Mrs. Mannie Moffitt," Mary's nickname in the census too.

body: Mary was born on 4 June 1895 in Alabama and is the "May, 5" in her parents' 1900 household at Gilbert, Etowah County. Her parents were John Morgan and Lizzie (Newton) Shackleford. She married Grady Moffitt about 1914 and bore at least eleven children, two of whom died as toddlers.
In 1930 she and Grady and their six boys were living with her parents in Martin County, Texas. She died in Paris, Texas, on 26 August 1962 and is buried beside Grady at Shoat Springs Cemetery, Hugo.
P.note: Where her middle name Tinsley came from is unknown. Her Texas death certificate should name her parents.

P.name: Henry H. Moffitt
P.place: Born in Lawrence County, Arkansas; died at Mountain View, Stone County, at 46.
P.title: Henry and Hannah in the Ozarks
P.hook: From Randolph County to the Stone County hills: a farm owned free and clear, and a widow who kept going for 22 years.
body: Henry was born in August 1855 in Lawrence County, Arkansas, the son of Nathan and Rebecca Moffitt, and appears as "Henry, 4" in their 1860 household. He and Hannah Grimes married about 1876. In June 1880 they were farming in Janes Creek Township, Randolph County, with daughter Josephine, 3, and son Jesse, 1.

By 1889 they were in Stone County, where son Tom was born at St. James, the old Buck Horn settlement. In May 1864 Buck Horn had seen the county's bloodiest Civil War fight, when Jo Shelby's Confederates attacked a band of bushwhackers. Grady was born near Mountain View in 1891, the year after the town incorporated.

The 1900 census, taken in Franklin Township, shows Henry as a farmer who owned his farm free of mortgage, with Hannah and five children at home: Jesse, Gimsa, Bertha, Tom and Woodford (Grady), 8. Henry died at Mountain View the next year, at 46. No grave has been found for him.

Hannah, who could not read or write, kept the family going. In 1910 she was a widow renting a house with Tom, a railroad section hand, and Grady, who worked in the timber. She had borne seven children, six still living. She died at Herpel, a Rocky Bayou settlement east of Mountain View, on 4 April 1923, and her stone in Herpel Cemetery reads "Wife of Henry H Moffitt."

P.name: Nathan H. Moffitt
P.place: Born in Randolph County, North Carolina; moved west and died in Oregon County, Missouri.
P.title: A wheelwright on the move
P.hook: Four censuses follow Nathan from North Carolina to Arkansas to Missouri, and from owning land to owning almost nothing.
body: Nathan was born in 1814 in Randolph County, North Carolina, a son of Robert and Martha (Chamness) Moffitt, and grew up in the Centre Quaker Meeting community, which hosted meetings of the North Carolina Manumission Society in those years. He married Rebecca Williams in Randolph County on 13 October 1835.

The 1850 census shows the family's route in its children's birthplaces: the older children were born in North Carolina up to about 1842, the younger ones in Arkansas from about 1843. In 1850 Nathan, 36, was farming in Strawberry Township, Lawrence County, Arkansas, with Rebecca and eight children.

By 1860 he was working as a wheelwright near Smithville, with land worth $1,200 and personal property worth $1,000, and the family had grown to include twin girls born in 1859. Henry, our ancestor, was 4.

The Civil War brought raiders on both sides to Lawrence County. By June 1870 Nathan and Rebecca had moved to Dent County, Missouri, where he was farming with no land of his own and $300 in personal property. Nathan died in Oregon County, Missouri, in 1873, the year his son Patrick married there.

Rebecca's sisters-in-law included Thalitha Williams (born 1804 at Deep River), who married Nathan's brother William C. on 7 August 1827. Whether the two Williams women were sisters is not shown. His father's will of 1796 names "my son Robart Moffitt" executor and leaves him 250 acres bought of William Cox, and his mother's 1820 will lists "my three sons." He is in the Randolph County censuses of 1830 and 1840.

The Centre Monthly Meeting certificate of 20 September 1797 reads: Robert Moffitt, son of William Moffitt deceased and Mary his wife, of Randolph County, and Martha Chamness, daughter of Joseph Chamness and Margaret his wife, both deceased, were married in a public meeting of the Quakers at Providence. Among the signing witnesses are William Moffitt, Joseph Chamness, Hannah Chamness and Mary Moffitt.

P.title: A Regulator the Governor wouldn't pardon
P.hook: One of thirteen men left out of Governor Tryon's 1768 pardon.
body: The Regulators were backcountry farmers in North Carolina who rose up (1766–1771) against corrupt officials and illegal fees. William Moffitt of Deep River was in the movement from its start: in August 1766 the inhabitants of Deep River chose "Wm Cox and Wm Masset" (a misreading of Maffet) to attend the Regulators' first general meeting. In 1768 he signed their petitions alongside the movement's leaders, Herman Husband and James Hunter, and on 21 May 1768 he was named first on the committee to carry their grievances to the Governor.

On 3 October 1768, at Hillsborough, Royal Governor William Tryon pardoned the Regulators except thirteen named men, and "William Moffitt" is one of them. He was never outlawed, and a general pardon in 1769 covered "all persons concerned in the said late Insurrection." His name is on the memorial trail at Alamance Battleground, and James Otis listed him among "the patriots of upper Carolina" in his 1901 boys' novel The Boy Spies with the Regulators.

William married Mary Davies at Cane Creek Quaker Meeting on 2 April 1763, when he was 23. He and Hugh Moffitt, probably his brother, married sisters, and Hugh ran the first mill on Richland Creek, which gave the community of Moffitt, North Carolina, its name; the Moffitt's Mills post office lasted from 1823 to 1935.

His will, dated 13 March 1796, begins "I William Moffitt of Randolph County in the province of North Carolina, being weak in body." It leaves "my Loveing Wife Mary" the wagon, the still, the tools and the stock, divides his land among sons Robert, William and David, and leaves money to daughters Naomi, Catharine, Hannah, Mary and Margaret. Robert, our ancestor, received the 250 acres bought of William Cox and was named executor with his mother. The Quaker records of Centre Meeting show Robert, "son of William & Mary," marrying Martha Chamness in 1797.

William and Mary had eight children: Naomi (born 11 June 1763), Catharine (1765), Hannah (22 December 1771), Mary (1773), Margaret (1774), Robert (1778), William (1781) and David (4 February 1785). All five daughters and three sons are named in Mary's will.

Family legend says the Moffitts came from Dumfriesshire, Scotland, descended from a "Robert Bruce Moffitt" born in 1716. No record names such a man. The Alamance Battleground Book of Remembrance instead says William was born about 1740 in Donegal, Ireland, to Robert and Martha Steward Moffitt and came through Philadelphia, which fits Ulster Scots, but that entry has no citations.

His part in the committee's account of the deputy sheriff's missing Act is told in "The Act nobody could find," and his name on the Regulators' letter, address and indictment of September 1768 in "September 1768: a letter, an address and an indictment." A Cox family history of 1955 adds two earlier court-record items: a deed proved by "Wm. Moffitt" in May 1765 and his witnessing of William Cox's will, proved at Hillsborough in February 1767.

The Moffitt Genealogy of 1928, compiled by Frank Moffitt for the descendants of Silas Moffitt of Hamilton County, Indiana, gives that family's own tradition of William's origins: sons of "Robert and Margaret Moffat" who "migrated to Donegal County, Ireland," and whose children included James, Charles, William, Adam, Margaret, Catharine, Robert, Mary, Hugh, Patrick and John. It says that "William married Mary Davis and Hugh married Hannah Davis, both being daughters of Charles Davis," and that Mary Moffitt Wilkinson, "our own foremother," was "said to have been their fifth child," married to William Wilkinson, "an Englishman, on the 26th day of the 3rd month, 1795." This agrees with the "Mary Wilkinson" of William's will, and the two witnesses to that will, Hugh and Charles Moffitt, match two of the brothers in the book's list. The parents differ from the Book of Remembrance's Robert and Martha Steward Moffitt, so the Donegal family is tradition, not record.

The book also repeats a story about "the Davis millions." Hamilton County heirs, it says, raised money to send an agent to the old country to look into an inheritance, but "this supposed wealth, like the fortune at the foot of the rainbow, was always just out of reach."

WikiTree quotes the Bible Record of Abijah Moffitt for William's parents: Robert Moffitt, born in Scotland and later of County Donegal, and Margaret Stuart, with eleven children, six of whom came to America. It adds that William and his brother Hugh both married Davis daughters in North Carolina, which matches William's 1763 marriage to Mary Davies. The Alamance Battleground Book gives the mother as Martha Steward. Both accounts are family-based, not contemporary records.

P.title: Mary Moffitt's Quaker will
P.hook: The Regulator's widow outlived him by more than twenty years and dated her will the Quaker way.
body: Mary Davies married William Moffitt at Cane Creek Monthly Meeting on 2 April 1763, at 22. Her sister Hannah married Hugh Moffitt. When William died in the late 1790s, Mary kept the wagon, the still and the stock, and a share of the home plantation for her widowhood.

Her own will is dated "the 23rd day of the 9th month, 1820," in the Quaker style. It names her daughters Naomi Mackie, Catharine Cox, Hannah Cox, Mary Wilkinson and Margaret Moffitt, and "my three sons" Robert, William and David. It was filed in 1822, about when she died.

Mary was a daughter of Charles and Hannah (Matson) Davies. A family account written in the back of the Cane Creek meeting's minute book says Charles "was brought over the ocean and sold to pay his passage," that is, he came as an indentured servant. He married Hannah, "daughter of John Matson of Merion," in Pennsylvania in February 1733, and the family followed the Quaker migration south: Goshen Meeting in Pennsylvania, Hopewell and Fairfax meetings in Virginia, and Cane Creek in North Carolina by about 1751.

Charles was recorded as a minister at Cane Creek in 1761 and disowned by the meeting in 1766 after complaining that the women's minutes were "mixed with an untruth." He died on 13 May 1801. Hannah lived to about 97 and died at Cane Creek on 25 October 1812. All eight of their children married; two daughters married Moffitts and two married men named Thomas Cox.

Mary was born about 1741 in Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania, according to family-tree profiles, and died in February 1822 in Randolph County. Her father's 1732 or 1733 marriage to Hannah Matson was by Radnor Meeting, with her grandfather's consent. Charles Davies bought 187 acres in Orange County on 2 August 1758.

P.name: Joseph Chamness & Margaret Norton
P.place: Married 17 March 1763 at Cane Creek Meeting. Joseph, born 1740 in Baltimore County, Maryland, was Anthony's eldest son and became the meeting's recorder of marriage certificates. Margaret, a daughter of Edward and Elizabeth Norton, bore eleven children and died in 1784; their daughter Martha married Robert Moffitt.
P.src: Cane Creek MM marriage certificate (1763) and Centre MM births, in Hinshaw vol. 1 and Hanson (1922); U.S., Quaker Meeting Records, 1681-1935 (Cane Creek MM, marriage of Joseph Chamness and Margret Norton, 17 Mar 1763)
body: Joseph died on 17 May 1818 in Randolph County and is buried at Providence Cemetery. After Margaret's death in 1784 he married Hannah Beeson on 6 March 1786 at Deep River Meeting. Margaret's children included Sarah Elliott, William, Elizabeth Pierson and Martha, who married Robert Moffitt.

Zimri Hanson's 1922 Chamness history prints the text of their Cane Creek certificate and its twelve witnesses, among them both sets of parents; it is told under "Two weddings at Cane Creek, sixteen days apart."

The Cane Creek Monthly Meeting certificate of 17 March 1763 names the couple and both sets of parents: Joseph Chamness, son of Anthony and Sarah Chamness of Orange County, and Margret Norton, daughter of Edward and Elizabeth Norton of Rowan County. Anthony and Sarah Chamness and Edward and Elizabeth Norton signed as witnesses, which is the record tying this branch back to the Chamness and Norton families.
P.note: Joseph's birth is given as 3 May 1740 in one source and 3 November 1740 in another; Margaret's is given as 3 November 1740. Martha, born 1778, is not the same Martha as Anthony's daughter born in 1747.

P.title: An indentured boy from London
P.hook: Bound for seven years' service in Maryland at 15, he ended up a landowner and overseer of a Quaker meeting.
body: Cane Creek's records say Anthony Chamness was the son of John and Ann, born about 1713 in East Smithfield, London. On 9 February 1724/5, giving his age as 15 and his home as Whitechapel, he bound himself to John Cooke, a London victualler, for seven years' service in "Maryland (his Majesty's Plantation in America)."
On 24 November 1735 he married Sarah Cole in St. Paul's Parish, Baltimore County; her own family's story is told under Sarah (Cole) Chamness.

The Chamnesses moved with the Quakers from Gunpowder Meeting in Maryland to Monocacy (1741), Carver's Creek in North Carolina (1749), and Cane Creek, where Anthony received a 490-acre grant in June 1751. When Cane Creek Monthly Meeting was organized that year he was named its overseer. His farm, a mile west of the meetinghouse, had a grist mill. He married three times and died on 20 September 1777.

His son Joseph, born in Baltimore County in 1740, married Margaret Norton at Cane Creek in 1763 and later farmed near Providence in Randolph County. Joseph's daughter Martha married Robert Moffitt at Centre Meeting in 1797.

Anthony married three times: Sarah Cole in 1735; then Rachel Haworth, the widow of Stephanus Haworth, who died on 19 March 1775 and is buried at Deep River; and, on 9 May 1776, Margaret Evans Williams, a widow. He made his will on 24 November 1776 in what was then Chatham County and died the next September.

A Hussey family genealogy written in 1928 by Charles Chaney Baker records a Chamness tradition that differs from the indenture. Baker quotes a letter of 30 April 1917 from Dr. John M. Hussey of Somerville, New Jersey, stating "that Martha Chamness, who married Stephen Hussey, was the daughter of Anthony Chamness and his wife, Sarah Cole; that Anthony Chamness had been kidnapped in England as a child and brought to America where he was 'bound out' till he reached a certain age; that he was the heir of an estate in England, which he had to go to England in order to claim but his wife would not consent to his going." Baker thought the inheritance "somewhat of a myth," since immigrants often told such stories. The kidnapping tale and the indenture of February 1724/5, in which a fifteen-year-old of Whitechapel bound himself to a London victualler for service in Maryland, may be two tellings of one event. The same book dates Martha's marriage to Stephen Hussey to September 1762.
He and his wife Sarah signed as witnesses at their son Joseph's wedding at Cane Creek on 17th of the 3rd month 1763; Hanson's 1922 history prints the certificate and the witness list.

The London parents of Anthony's father John Chamness are not shown by any cited birth record. WikiTree proposes Anthony Chamness and Ann Pitts, who married at St James, Duke's Place, on 23 September 1686, but John's baptism in November 1682 is earlier than that wedding.

Zimri Hanson's 1922 Chamness history describes the home Anthony and Sarah kept near Cane Creek, as remembered by a neighbor about a century earlier: "The farm lay a mile west of Cane Creek Friends church, was a good body of land and lay fine. The dwelling was large, perhaps 20x80 feet, consisted of two main rooms, made of hewn oak logs, with two shed rooms with porch the whole length on the front side." A small creek ran through the farm with a grist mill, and in the barn stood "a stationary thrashing machine propelled by horse power," to which neighbors hauled their wheat. Hanson calls the home "one of hospitality, and a kind of social center," and says Sarah taught her daughters to spin and weave. The family register in his book lists the children's births in Baltimore County, Maryland, then in Frederick County, Maryland (1742 to 1746), then in Orange County, North Carolina (1749 to 1761). Sarah, he writes, was "the mother of thirteen children" and died probably about 1773; he adds a tradition that Anthony was drafted for the army but not forced into it because of his conscience, and judges that tradition "barely credible" given his age.
P.src: Transcribed indenture (1724/5); Hinshaw, Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy, vol. 1 (Cane Creek and Centre MM); Zimri Hanson, History and Genealogy of the American Descendants of John and Ann Chamness (1922); wills of Joseph Cole (1720/21) and William Cole (1769), abstracted in Barnes, Baltimore County Families 1659–1759; Charles Chaney Baker, The Hussey Ancestry of Charles Chaney Baker and Harry Delphia Baker (Los Angeles, 1928), notes on authorities; WikiTree Chamness-43 (https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Chamness-43); From Whence We Came: Cane Creek Meeting Sesquibicentennial Reunion (Snow Camp, N.C., c. 2000), archive.org/details/fromwhencewecame00cane; Zimri Hanson, History and Genealogy of the American Descendants of John and Ann Chamness of London (1922), chapter on Anthony and Sarah Chamness, https://archive.org/details/historygenealogy00hans
kv: Signed as witness to son Joseph's marriage certificate, Cane Creek (Hanson 1922, p. 18)
Large Chamness stone placed in the Cane Creek Friends cemetery in 1975 for Anthony and Sarah; modern commemoration, not an original marker

The two do not agree, and the repository holding the indenture is not cited, so the story is probable rather than proven. Family stories of a French Huguenot or Norman noble origin have no support.

P.place: Born at Hagansport, Franklin County, Texas; died in Hugo.
P.title: Neighbors at Hagansport
P.hook: In 1910 Oscar Smith, 19, and Pearl Satterfield, 11, lived a few doors apart in the same Texas farm community. Four years later they married.
body: Charles Oscar Smith was born on 29 May 1889 at Hagansport, Franklin County, Texas, a farm community that grew up around a Sulphur River crossing called Hagan's Port. In the 1880s it had about 150 people, a gin, a mill, four churches and a one-room school.

In June 1900 the census found "Oscar," 10, in the Franklin County household of John and Emma Smith, with Vera, Luina, Lona, Allie and baby Jimmie. John owned his farm free of mortgage. Emma died on 15 March 1905, at 37, and her stone at Hagansport reads "Emma / Wife of / J.B. SMITH / Gone but not forgotten."

By April 1910 John B. Smith had remarried, and Oscar, 19, was working on the home farm. The same census taker, on the same day, recorded the Satterfield family a few doors away: John C. and Samantha, lately from Kentucky, and their daughter Pearl, 11. Oscar and Artie Pearl Satterfield married in 1914.

They later crossed the Red River to Choctaw County, Oklahoma. Charles died on 17 August 1971 and Artie on 21 July 1983, and they are buried together in Grant Cemetery, south of Hugo. John B. Smith died in 1918 and lies beside Emma at Hagansport, in a grave "marked with a wooden stob."

His 1942 draft card gives his name as Charlie Oscar Smith, 52, of Forney in Choctaw County, with mail at Hugo Route 1, working on a farm. He gives his birthplace as 'Higgensport, Texas,' the Franklin County community more often spelled Hagansport, and names Mrs. Pearl Smith as the person who would always know his address.

P.name: John C. Satterfield & Samantha (Johnson)
P.place: Farmed at Horse Mill, Butler County, Kentucky, in 1900, with seven children at home.
P.title: From Butler County to the Red River
P.hook: A Kentucky farm family that moved to Texas about 1907 and ended up around Soper and Hugo.
body: John C. Satterfield was born in 1864 in Allen County, Kentucky. In 1880, at 16, he was a farm laborer at Renfrow, Butler County, in the household of his father, James H. Satterfield, with his brothers and sisters. His mother, Melissa Gibson, had died in 1877.

A widower with three children, Henry, Martha and John, he married Samantha D. "Mantha" Johnson, about 20, in 1892. In 1900 they were farming at Horse Mill, Butler County, with seven children at home. Their son Wavey Lincoln was born near Morgantown in 1895 and later served as a private in the U.S. Army in World War I; Artie Pearl followed in 1898.

About 1907 the family moved to Franklin County, Texas. In April 1910 John, 46, was renting a farm at Hagansport, with Wavey, Pearl, James, Ira and little Stella. John died in Franklin County a few years later. On 28 July 1917 Samantha married Bird Alexander "Alex" Stephens at Mount Vernon, Texas, and they moved across the Red River to Choctaw County, Oklahoma. She died there in 1928 and is buried as Samantha Stephens in Soper Cemetery.
His father's family is described under James Henry Satterfield and Melissa Gibson.

Samantha's husband John C. had a larger family than the two households show. His full brothers and sisters, children of James H. and Melissa, included Sidney Rufus (1865-1949), James Doiser (1867-1929, who went to Clay County, Arkansas) and A. M. (born in Minnesota in 1870, died 1892). His nine half-siblings by Lucinda Phelps lived mostly around Texarkana. He and his brother Sidney both married women of the Clark-Johnson family of Butler County.

The farm John C. Satterfield rented at Hagansport in 1910 was in a county where, by the government's 1908 soil survey, tenants on the usual share plan gave up half the crop, and farms averaged under 80 acres. The Hagansport soil was heavy clay that stayed sticky after rain and suited cotton better than corn. See the story on renting on shares at Hagansport.
kv: Renting a farm at Hagansport, Franklin Co., Texas, with Samantha and five children
b. 28 Mar 1872, Ky.; d. 1 Oct 1928, Choctaw Co., Okla.
Samantha m. Bird Alexander Stephens, 28 Jul 1917
P.note: A family biography places John's death between 1912 and 1916; no grave or death record has been found, so the 1919 date in family trees is uncertain.

Satterfield; Find a Grave (Samantha D. Stephens, Soper Cemetery, with family biography); Find a Grave (Wavey Lincoln Satterfield); Soil Survey of Franklin County, Texas (1908), pp. 931-947.

P.name: Thomas Rogers & Ann Staples
P.title: Three wills from Quaker New Jersey
P.hook: A grandfather's will names Ann Staples, her husband Thomas Rogers, and their daughter Mary, who married into the Nordyke family.
body: Thomas Rogers married Ann Staples on 30 October 1736 at Upper Springfield Meeting in Burlington County, New Jersey. When Ann's father Thomas Staples wrote his will on 25 October 1758, he named his daughter "Ann, wife of Thomas Rogers" and his granddaughters "Mehetable and Mary Rogers." That Mary Rogers married Abraham Nordyke in 1761, which ties the Rogers family directly to the Nordykes.

Thomas Rogers's own father, John Rodgers of Burlington, left him a fifth of his estate in a will proved in 1767. Ann's mother Mehitable was the daughter of Hananiah Gaunt of Springfield Township, whose 1720 will names "Mahitable Staples" and his son-in-law Thomas Staples.
Together the three wills carry this Quaker family back to the early 1700s in Burlington County, one of the first English settlements on the Delaware River.

body: A Burlington County administration of 6 December 1748 may belong to the next generation of this family: "Staples, Thomas, Jun'r, of Burlington Co., innholder," died without a will, and administration went to Thomas Rogers, the husband of Ann Staples, with John Deacon and John Antram of the City of Burlington as bondsmen. The inventory was only 30 pounds 7 shillings, and the account of June 1749 shows payments to Joseph Scattergood, Joshua Raper's executor, and John Rogers. If this Thomas Jr. was Ann's brother, it fits Thomas Rogers acting for the estate. Probable, not proven.

P.src: Will of Hananiah Gaunt, 1720, Calendar of New Jersey Wills; WikiTree Gaunt-14, citing McLean (NGSQ 1974) and the Calendar of New Jersey Wills; E. M. Woodward and John F. Hageman, History of Burlington and Mercer Counties, New Jersey (Philadelphia, 1883), Springfield Township, p. 438.
body: Hananiah married Dorothy Butler, daughter of Thomas Butler of Sandwich, on 10 May 1678; their intention was posted at Sandwich Friends Meeting on 3 May. They lived at Dartmouth, Massachusetts, until about 1685 and then took up 500 acres at Hananicon in Springfield Township, New Jersey. His father was Peter Gaunt of Sandwich (d. 1678).

He is named in the county history's Springfield Township chapter as an established neighbor by the 1680s. Citing "Revel's Book of Surveys, remaining in the Secretary of State's office in Trenton," the history says that land was "surveyed for William Biddle, at Oneanickon, 8th month, 1686, two hundred and seventy acres of land, and in 4th month, 1689, one tract of two hundred and thirty acres, and two other tracts, containing together three hundred and twenty-three acres, making altogether eight hundred and twenty-three acres, adjoining lands of Hannaniah Gauntt, John Days, Peter Harvey, Charles Read, Samuel Barker, Daniel Leeds, Michael Buffin, John Browne, and John Shinn." That puts Hananiah Gaunt on land of his own beside the Biddle tracts in Springfield, about thirty years before his will of 1720.

The New Jersey record of his deeds, told under "Hananiah Gaunt's deeds: 500 acres, a hundred sold, and a share of West Jersey," shows him as "of Rhode Island, yeoman" when he bought 500 acres from George Hutcheson on 11 May 1685, and selling 100 acres to William Bustill, carpenter, on 18 May 1687.

P.name: Sarah (Cole) Chamness
P.title: A murder trial in early Maryland
P.hook: Anthony Chamness's wife came from a Baltimore County family whose patriarch was murdered.
body: Anthony Chamness, the London boy indentured to Maryland, married Sarah Cole on 24 November 1735. Her father Joseph Cole had died young: his will, written 22 January 1720/1 in Baltimore County, names his wife Susanna and his little daughter Sarah. Nearly fifty years later her uncle William Cole's 1769 will still called her "dau. and heir of testator's bro. Joseph." The Cane Creek Quaker records in North Carolina name her as "daughter of Joseph and Susanna Cole."

Joseph was the son of John Cole and Johanna (Hannah) Garrett. Johanna's father, Dennis Garrett, was murdered. John Cole testified at the trial of a Captain John Oldton for the killing of his father-in-law.

Dennis's widow Barbara remarried, to John Broad. In August 1712, as Barbara Garrett Broad, she deeded property to "her grandson Dennis Garrett Cole, s. of John and Hannah Cole," a boy named for the grandfather he never knew.

quotes.t: Sarah, dau. and heir of testator's bro. Joseph.
quotes.c: Will of William Cole, 1769

P.note: The murder trial and the 1712 deed come from Robert Barnes's Baltimore County Families, which abstracts court and land records; the original court papers have not been seen yet.

P.name: Charles Davies & Hannah Matson
P.place: Quakers. Married at Radnor Meeting, Pennsylvania, in February 1733, and settled at Cane Creek, North Carolina, about 1751. Charles died in 1801 and Hannah in 1812.
P.src: Radnor MM marriage certificate (1732/3); Davis, Davis: A Quaker Family (1985); Hinshaw vol. 1; U.S., Quaker Meeting Records, 1681-1935 (Cane Creek MM minutes, 6 Dec 1766)
body: Charles Davies bought 187 acres from Henry McCullogh on 2 August 1758, land that later fell in Chatham County, and was on the 1755 Orange County poll list. He died 13 May 1801 and is buried at Cane Creek Meeting cemetery, Snow Camp. His children's spouses included Thomas Vestal, two men named Thomas Cox, William and Hugh Moffitt, and Owen Williams and Abraham Ozbun, the latter two successive husbands of Abigail.

Charles Davies had moved from Pennsylvania to Cane Creek, North Carolina by the 1760s. The Cane Creek minutes for 6 December 1766 record that he was complained of for charging the women's minute with an untruth, and that after repeated labor to show him how unreasonable this was, the meeting disowned him.
P.note: The marriage is given as 9 Feb 1732 (old style, meaning 1733) and 9 Dec 1732 in different sources. Details of his youth differ: the Cane Creek family account says he was sold to pay his passage, and a Find a Grave note says he was indentured to a Quaker family in Philadelphia.

The Nottingham Monthly Meeting certificate describes the bridegroom as Edward Norton of West Nottingham in Chester County, son of the late Edward Norton of the Parish of Armagh in the Kingdom of Ireland, and the bride as Elizabeth Brown, daughter of William and Elizabeth Brown of West Nottingham. It is the document that names the Irish father, Edward Norton of Armagh, and shows Brown and Cowgill relatives among the signers.

P.name: William Brown & Ann Mercer
P.place: William Brown came from England in 1682 and was one of the first settlers of the Nottingham Quaker settlement on the Pennsylvania–Maryland line. Ann was his second wife.
P.src: Maryland Quaker Records: Nottingham Monthly Meeting; WikiTree Brown-2504 and Mercer-123, citing Wellingborough MM and Northamptonshire QM registers
body: Quaker registers at Wellingborough, Northamptonshire, enter William Brown's birth in 1658 as the son of Richard and Margery Browne. His first wife was Dorothy, in England; Ann Mercer was his second (1684), followed by Catherine Williams (1699) and Mary Matthews (1711). Ann was the daughter of Thomas Mercer of Andover. WikiTree puts his arrival in Pennsylvania between June 1682 and 1684, because two men named William Brown shipped goods in those years.

His move to the Nottingham Lots, where the plat gives him Lots 23 and 33 and his brother and son the lots beside them, is told under "Lots 23 and 33: William Brown on the Nottingham Lots," and his talk with his brother James about George Keith, "he is in a wrong spirit," under the Marcus Hook story. A 1902 history of the Brick Meeting House says that he "was the first Friend to settle on the Nottingham lots" and that the first meeting was held at his house in 1704.

P.name: James Henry Satterfield & Melissa Gibson
P.title: The family story in an 1885 county history
P.hook: A Kentucky history book printed James Satterfield's own account of three generations.
body: In 1885 the book Kentucky: A History of the State printed short biographies of farmers and businessmen county by county. One of them was James H. Satterfield, then of Butler County (pages 676–677), and it reads like his own account of the family.

It says his father, Henry Satterfield, was a native of Maury County, Tennessee, and died in 1861. Henry married Mary, daughter of John M. Garrison of Allen County. Henry was the son of Ephraim Satterfield, "a native of Virginia, who died about 1850."

James married Melissa A. Gibson, "daughter of James and Cynthia (Woodcock) Gibson, of Allen County." The Allen County marriage register confirms the wedding on 17 September 1859. The sketch lists their children as Henry W., John C., Sidney R., James D., Martha A. and Mary C. John C., born in February 1864, is our John C. Satterfield, who later farmed at Horse Mill in Butler County. Melissa died in 1877.

After Melissa died in 1877, James married Lucinda Belle Phelps on 2 June 1878 in Butler County, according to a copy of the marriage bond cited by a family group sheet. They had nine children between 1879 and 1899. Several of those half-siblings of John C. married in Bowie County, Texas, or nearby Arkansas between 1909 and 1917, and James himself died in Bowie County on 24 November 1922 (the sheet also gives 1924).

The sketch says more than the family papers do. James "was born April 14, 1838, in Allen County, Ky., where he grew to manhood. In 1867 he removed to Dakota County, Minn., and in 1875 he returned to Kentucky, and located in Warren County. In 1876 he settled in Butler County, where he has since resided." James spent eight years in Minnesota; if the family went with him, John C. was three when they left and eleven when they came back.

The sketch gives his war service as brief: "In 1861 he enlisted in the Ninth Kentucky (Federal) Infantry, remaining in the field but three months, after which he was engaged in the recruiting service." It dates his first marriage to "September 15, 1859," two days before the 17 September date on the Allen County register, names his second wife as Lucinda B., "daughter of Solomon and Sarah J. (Deweese) Phelps, of this county," and lists the three children of that marriage, Martha B., Alonzo T. and Minnie E.
By 1885 he was well off for a farmer: "Mr. Satterfield is a farmer, and owns 1,340 acres of land, where he now resides, and 425 acres in Tennessee."

Find a Grave names Melissa's death as 2 May 1877 and gives James's birth as 14 April 1837 and his death as 28 November 1922 at Redwater in Bowie County, buried at Reed Cemetery. A daughter, A. M., was born in Minnesota in 1870, and a son, James Doiser, in Allen County in February 1867.

body: The 1885 sketch of their son James describes Henry as "a native of Maury County, Tenn.; died in 1861, at the age of fifty years," which puts his birth about 1811, and says he married "Mary, daughter of John M. Garrison, of Allen County, Ky." It names their twelve children, with the daughters' married names as of 1885: Louisa J. (Roy), David E., Samuel A., James H., Ruth M. (Massey), John E., Euphema P. (Liles), Hettie C. (Jones), Martha C. (deceased), Sarah E. (Hues), Joseph W. H. and Abraham W. (Kentucky: A History of the State, Butler County, p. 676.)

Mary Garrison was born on 17 October 1811 and died on 2 March 1896 (WikiTree Garrison-5361). Her probable mother, Martha 'Patsey' Cannon, married John M. Garrison at Wilson County, Tennessee, on 6 December 1809.

A Warren County lawsuit names an S. A. Satterfield: in 1871 James Clark & Co. and H. T. Clark sued A. W. Garrison and S. A. Satterfield in the Warren Circuit Court over lot 74 in Bowling Green (Garrison v. Clark, 151 Ky. 565, 1913). The 1885 sketch lists a son "Samuel A." of Henry and Mary (Garrison) Satterfield, but the court opinion gives only initials, so this is a lead.

P.name: John Milton Garrison
P.place: Allen County, Kentucky.
P.src: Kentucky: A History of the State (1885); Find a Grave; Kentucky: A History of the State (1885), Butler County, p. 676; Laws of Kentucky (Acts passed at the session of the General Assembly), 1847-48, ch. 600 sec. 6, p. 410 (archive.org item actspassedatses72kentgoog); Acts of the General Assembly of Kentucky, 1847-48, p. 410; WikiTree Garrison-4365.
body: The 1885 sketch of his grandson James H. Satterfield calls him "John M. Garrison, of Allen County, Ky." and follows the name with the parenthesis "(now living at the age of seventy-five years)." With his death in 1860 recorded on a grave memorial, the parenthesis most likely describes his daughter Mary, Henry Satterfield's widow, who would have been seventy-four or seventy-five in 1885 (Kentucky: A History of the State, Butler County, p. 676).

Kentucky's own published laws confirm the split between John M. Garrison and his wife. Chapter 600 of the Laws of Kentucky for the December 1847 session, "An act to divorce Elizabeth A. King, and others," reads in Section 6: "That the marriage contract now existing between John M. Garrison, and his wife, Patsey Garrison, be and the same is hereby dissolved, and they are hereby restored to all the rights and privileges of unmarried persons." It was approved in February 1848 (page 410). The legislature divorced several couples in the one act, a common practice before the courts took over.

The 1810 census for Warren County, as WikiTree transcribes it for "John M Garreson," counts one slave in his household of five; transcribed returns for 1820, 1830 and 1840 in Allen County count none. By act of the Kentucky General Assembly of 1847-48 his marriage to Patsey Cannon was dissolved, and WikiTree says he then married Sarah Stamps, the neighbor whose children he had fathered during the marriage and had the legislature declare legitimate. The legitimation act has not been found. See the story on John M. Garrison and the General Assembly.

body: Middletown Monthly Meeting records Elizabeth Cowgill's birth on 24 June 1694 to John Cowgill and Bridget (Croasdale) Cowgill. Her father came from Yorkshire on the Lamb in 1682 and later moved to New Castle County, Delaware.

Elizabeth Cowgill's sister Ellin (born in December 1700) married William Jr.'s brother Thomas Brown in 1718/9, so two Cowgill sisters married two Brown brothers. After William Jr.'s death about 1727 his widow Margaret (Davis) Brown married William Kirk, and Elizabeth's orphaned daughter married Edward Norton at West Nottingham on 16 October 1739. P.name: Gilliam Graves
P.title: A 45-year-old farmer joins the Union army at Cedar Glades
P.hook: Born on Toms Creek, North Carolina, he served on Georgia juries, farmed in the Arkansas hills and enlisted in 1864 at 45.
body: Gilliam Graves was born about 1813 in North Carolina, on Toms Creek in Randolph County. On 18 August 1832 he married Mary Tyler there. By 1840 he was in Cherokee County, Georgia, where he served on county juries in December 1835 and on 5 November 1838. By 1853 he was on the tax lists of Montgomery County, Arkansas, at Cedar Glades, and in 1860 the census taker wrote his name as 'Galem' Graves.

On 14 January 1864 he volunteered at Cedar Glades for the Union army, in Company D, 4th Arkansas. He was 45, a farmer, five feet ten inches tall, with black eyes. He deserted on 12 October 1864 and returned on 25 December 1864. His second marriage, on 18 August 1845 in Montgomery County, was to Delila Hawthorne. His third wife was Mary 'Polly' (Gray) Washburn.
He died, supposedly killed by robbers, in January 1876 in Garland County, and is buried beside Polly in Mountain Valley Cemetery. His son Jesse is the Graves who stands behind our Sarah Rebecca.

The Graves family genealogy is the only source for Gilliam's parents. WikiTree's William Gilliam Graves (Graves-8557, 12 Dec 1813 - 22 Oct 1876) has no parents attached, and no WikiTree profile gives a sourced father.

The Graves genealogy records his later years in detail. He appears on the Montgomery County tax lists in 1853-59, 1861, 1865, 1867-68, 1871 and 1872, and in the 1860 census, under the name "Galem Graves," with children Sarah 15 (born Georgia), Aaron 13 and John 11 (Alabama), Julia 9 and Nancy 5 (Arkansas). No record of his family has been found for the 1850 and 1870 censuses.

In January 1854 he was made guardian of the children of Samuel and Sarah Graves, and again in April 1861 of the minor heirs (see the story of Samuel and Sarah's children). His first wife, Mary Tyler, married him in Randolph County on 18 August 1832; a Charles Tyler, 79, is on the 1850 Cherokee County, Georgia census with a boy, William D. Graves, 10, born Georgia, who may be Gilliam's son left with his grandfather (lead).

His third wife, Polly Gray Washburn, died about 1879; his second, Delila Hawthorne, died about 1860 at Cedar Glades. His family tradition, recorded twice in the genealogy, makes his father an American Indian (lead; no record seen).

The Union 4th Arkansas Cavalry at Cedar Glades was a company of neighbors. A petition of 10 March 1864 from Union men of Montgomery County said "Dr. Brown, of Cedar Glades, was shot down" on 1 March, and a cemetery index lists the men who enlisted with Gilliam on 14 January: William Haskins, 45, John Stroud, 45, John Tidwell, 32, born in Blount County, Alabama, and others. See the stories 'Dr. Brown, of Cedar Glades, was shot down' and 'Who signed up beside Gilliam Graves.'

The regiment he joined was the 4th Arkansas Cavalry (Union), organized at Little Rock in December 1863. Its Company L wrote from Montgomery County on 10 March 1864 that wives and children of Union men at Cedar Glades were being shot, and a battalion of the regiment fought through the county in July. His desertion on 12 October 1864 and return on 25 December 1864 fall in the period of the autumn expedition from Little Rock to Fort Smith, but no record places his company on it. The full story is told under "The 4th Arkansas Cavalry: Union men from the Ouachita hills."

P.name: Jesse King Graves
P.title: From Alabama to the Cedar Glades
P.hook: Jesse Graves, born in Alabama, married three times and is buried by rocks in the yard of his old home in Garland County.
body: Jesse S. Graves, probably the Jesse King Graves of our tree, was born about 1855 in Blount County, Alabama, a son of Gilliam Graves, who had earlier lived in Cherokee County, Georgia, and Randolph County, North Carolina. Gilliam settled the family at Cedar Glades in Montgomery County, Arkansas.

At about 16, Jesse married Sarah Emma Fisher on 2 April 1871 at Jack Phillips's home in Mountain Township, Montgomery County. They had four children, and in 1880 the family was in Garland County. On 31 January 1884 he married Margaret Crumpton. She died on 5 May 1884, the same day their daughter Sarah Rebecca was born.

He married a third time, to Nancy (Wilborn) Kyle Cuttler, on 19 September 1889, and had four more children. Jesse died in 1910 and was buried in the yard of his former home on Walnut Valley Road, with the grave marked only by rocks. His daughter Sarah Rebecca had married George Washington Hulsey on 22 December 1901.

Two details of the genealogy differ from the usual story. The Montgomery County marriage record, Book A, page 278, gives Jesse's age at his marriage as 18 and his bride Emma Fisher's as 15, which puts his birth about 1853 rather than 1855. And Margaret Crumpton's mother is named in the 1880 census as Rebecca Cornett, which supports Cornett over Speer for Margaret's maiden name.

His second wife, Margaret, brought two Crumpton sons, John and Henry; his third, Nancy, brought Isaac Kyle, Prince Cuttler and a Cindy Sutton about Sarah Rebecca's age. The family therefore grew up with half- and step-siblings of three marriages. In 2002 he was named on a list of burials in McGill Cemetery, Garland County, though the genealogy places his grave in the yard of his old home on Walnut Valley Road.
His widow Nancy, who lived to 20 November 1932, is on the 1920 census with their daughter Lucinda and son-in-law Benjamin Hogue.

His daughter Sarah Rebecca, born 5 May 1884, is named in the same genealogy, but the link to our Jesse King Graves is probable, not proven.
