P.title: Six brothers from Donegal and the extra T
P.hook: A descendant's Bible record says Robert Moffitt of Donegal had eleven children, and that six sons came to America and agreed to end the name in 'itt'.
body: The Bible Record of Abijah Moffitt, quoted on WikiTree, says Robert Moffitt was born in Scotland, went to Ireland when young, and there married Margaret Stuart. It names eleven children: James, Charles, William, Adam, Margaret, Mary, Catheren, Robert, Hugh, John and Patrick.

According to the record, John crossed first and went back to Ireland; liking the country, he returned with five brothers to Philadelphia. From there they went to North Carolina, to what became Chatham and Randolph counties. William, Adam and Charles died in North Carolina. Hugh went to Ohio in 1798 or 1799 and died near Chillicothe about 1800. Robert started back for Ireland and was never heard of again, and was supposed lost at sea. Patrick never left Ireland. The record adds that 'William and Hugh married Davis daughters of North Carolina,' which matches William Moffitt's marriage to Mary Davies at Cane Creek in 1763.

Family tradition explains the spelling: the brothers agreed to end the name in 'itt' so that kin could recognize each other wherever it turned up. That part is tradition, not record. North Carolina papers of the 1760s write the name Maffet, Moffit and Moffitt.

The Alamance Battleground Book of Remembrance gives William's parents as Robert and Martha Steward Moffitt, without citations. The two accounts agree on Robert and Donegal and differ on whether his wife was Margaret or Martha. Neither names Robert's own parents; the Moffat ancestors that appear on WikiTree for Robert have no sources.

The 1928 Moffitt Genealogy, compiled by Frank Moffitt for the descendants of Silas Moffitt of Hamilton County, Indiana, tells the crossing differently from the Bible Record: "William came first, alone, and went back," and then "he and five other brothers afterward came to Philadelphia and remained there for some time." It says all of Robert and Margaret's children but Catharine and Patrick crossed. Hanna's The Scotch-Irish (1902), which does not mention this family, says eastern Donegal was settled from Ayrshire and Galloway by the Cunninghams and Stewarts, which fits the bride's surname but names no parish.
P.src: WikiTree Moffitt-289 (quoting the Bible Record of Abijah Moffitt) and Moffitt-65; Moffitt Genealogy (1928), pp. 1-3; Hanna, The Scotch-Irish (1902)
P.note: A descendant's record, not a contemporary one. WikiTree gives Margaret's death as 1770 in Lancaster Co., Pa., which does not fit a family that stayed in Donegal; treat as unreliable. The claim that she was 'a near relative of King James II' is tradition only. Conflicts between the accounts: the Bible Record says John crossed first and names the wife Margaret Stuart; the 1928 Moffitt Genealogy says William crossed first; the Alamance Battleground book names the wife Martha Steward. Marked lead for that reason.

P.name: Richard & Margery Browne
P.place: Richard Browne 'of Boasworth' and his wife Margery were Quakers at Wellingborough, Northamptonshire. Their sons James and William both settled in the Nottingham lots on the Pennsylvania-Maryland line.
kv: c.1620, Husbands Bosworth, Leicestershire (Northamptonshire FHS inference)
Nine reported; births of James (1656), William (1658) and Jeremiah (1660) are in the Wellingborough Quaker register
P.title: Stripped of their property for fines
P.hook: William Brown's memories, written into the Nottingham Quaker minutes in 1786, say his parents lost most of what they owned to fines for their faith.
body: The Wellingborough Monthly Meeting in Northamptonshire entered the births of Richard and Margery Browne's sons James (1656), William (1658) and Jeremiah (1660), and the county quarterly meeting's entry for William names his mother. Richard 'of Boasworth', probably Husbands Bosworth in Leicestershire, was buried in 1662.

Forty years after William Brown died, a great-nephew set down William's stories in the minutes of East Nottingham Meeting on the 28th day of the 1st month 1786, and Gilbert Cope printed them in The Browns of Nottingham (1864). They say Richard had leaned toward both the Baptists and the Puritans and was reputed a teacher among both, and that about 1663 William's parents 'had suffered greatly and were much stripped of their property for fines &c.' The memorial miscalls the father 'William senior'; the registers give Richard.

James Brown reached Pennsylvania by 1677. William followed between 1682 and 1684, after marrying Dorothy in England, and married three more times in Pennsylvania, the second time to Ann Mercer in 1684. He died in West Nottingham on 1 October 1746.

The East Nottingham memorandum tells how the Brownes became Friends when William Dewsbury sat at their table, how Richard's wife asked why he had brought "that madman" into the house, and how his landlord made him pay his rent twice because he would not swear that it was paid. It is told under "A madman at the table."
P.src: WikiTree Browne-440, Brown-2504, Unknown-278288, citing Wellingborough MM and Northamptonshire QM Quaker registers; Cope, The Browns of Nottingham (1864)
P.note: Birth registers name both parents. The place of origin and exact arrival year are inferences or unresolved. Evidence: probable (registers are cited only through WikiTree and Cope).

P.name: Thomas & Ann Mercer
P.place: Quakers of Ringwood and Andover, Hampshire. Ann died before the voyage; Thomas crossed about 1682–83 with their daughter Ann and settled in Aston Township, Chester County, Pennsylvania, where he died on 22 November 1694. A 1709 Quaker list of public Friends who died in Pennsylvania names him and 'Ann Browne daughtr of said Thoms Mercer', who died in 1696.
kv: Born 24th day of the 12th month 1666/7, Ringwood Meeting; m. William Brown 1684
P.src: WikiTree Mercer-123 and Mercer-124, citing the Quaker birth register and the 1709 'Catalogue of Eighty-seven Publick Friends'
P.note: Evidence: probable (WikiTree citing the Quaker birth register). Thomas's own parents are not known.

P.name: John & Bridget (Croasdale) Cowgill
P.place: John Cowgill came from Yorkshire in 1682 with his widowed mother and married Bridget Croasdale at Neshaminy, Bucks County, in 1693. About 1713 he moved to New Castle County, Delaware, and built a tan-yard. Their daughter Elizabeth married William Brown Jr.
kv: Born 24 Jun 1694, Middletown Twp., Bucks Co.; d. c.1721
P.title: Aboard the Lamb, 1682
P.hook: John Cowgill crossed as a servant in a shipload of Yorkshire Quakers; the family of the girl he later married was on the same ship.
body: In 1682 a group of Quaker families from the Settle Meeting in Yorkshire, carrying what Friends call the Settle Certificate, sailed for William Penn's new province on the Lamb and reached Pennsylvania in October. The certificate lists 'Ellen Cowgill widow & her children'. Her son John, probably about seventeen, came as a servant to Cuthbert Hayhurst.

The Croasdale family was on the same certificate: Thomas and Agnes Croasdale and six children, who took up 500 acres on Neshaminy Creek in Bucks County. On 19 October 1693 John married their daughter Bridget, whose birth in August 1671 is in the Settle Meeting register.

Bridget died on 26 April 1701 and left four children, among them Elizabeth, born 24 June 1694, who would marry William Brown Jr. in 1715. John married Rachel (Baker) Bunting, a widow, in 1703 or 1704. About 1713 or 1714 he moved to New Castle County, Delaware, where he asked for land on Blackbird Creek in 1718 because he had built a tan-yard there. He died in 1731.
P.src: WikiTree Cowgill-28, Cowgill-353 and Croasdale-11, citing Middletown MM minutes and McCracken, The Welcome Claimants (1985)
P.note: Elizabeth's birth is in the Middletown minutes naming both parents. The servant detail comes from McCracken as quoted on WikiTree. Our older note says 'of Duck Creek'; WikiTree's land records name the Appoquinimink and Blackbird Creek tracts. Evidence: probable (WikiTree and McCracken cite the minutes; no original seen).

P.name: Ellen Cowgill
P.place: A widow when she sailed on the Lamb in 1682; the certificate reads 'Ellen Cowgill widow & her children', and her children Edmund, Jennet, John and Jane came with her. She settled at Middletown, Bucks County, Pennsylvania, and is buried in the Middletown cemetery. Her husband's name is not documented: tradition says Ralph Cowgill, but the Cowgill family association thinks Edmund Cowgill, baptized 1634 at Thornton in Craven. The maiden name Stackhouse of Giggleswick is traditional and disputed.
P.src: WikiTree Stackhouse-56 and Cowgill-16, citing the 1682 Settle Certificate and Cowgill Cousins research; WikiTree Cowgill-16 and Stackhouse-56; Stackhouse-58 (https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Stackhouse-58)
P.note: Evidence: probable (mother only). Do not state a father.
body: WikiTree flags two problems with this profile. The long-held belief that Ellen's husband was Ralph Cowgill (said to have been hanged in 1682 as a Quaker) has no documentation, and the Cowgill family association suggests her husband was more likely Edmund Cowgill of Thornton in Craven. Her maiden name is also disputed: some books give 'Stackhurst', and several Stackhouse histories say she was not a Stackhouse. A Thomas Stackhouse of Giggleswick (1601-1686) and Anna Evans, named in the compiled Stackhouse genealogy as her parents, are therefore not added.

Her sons John and Ralph both arrived as servants. John came to Cuthbert Hayhurst, the Yorkshire minister who died in March 1683. A Bucks County record lists Ralph Cowgill among the servants of Randolph Blackshaw who came on the Friend's Adventure and arrived on 28 September 1682, each "to serve 4 years, and to have 50 acres of land apiece." This is told under "Two sons in service."

P.name: Thomas & Agnes (Hawthornewaite) Croasdale
P.place: Quakers of the Settle Meeting in Yorkshire, married on 1 May 1664 (recorded by Lancaster Monthly Meeting). They sailed on the Lamb in July 1682 with six children and took up 500 acres on Neshaminy Creek, Bucks County, Pennsylvania, as members of Middletown Meeting. Thomas died within two years of arriving (the profile gives 1682 and 1684); Agnes administered his estate and died on 20 October 1686.
kv: Born 20 May 1644; died 1682 or 1684, Middletown, Bucks Co., Pa.
Bridget, born 30 Aug 1671, m. John Cowgill 1693
P.src: WikiTree Croasdale-9, Hawthornewaite-1 and Croasdale-11, citing Quaker registers and Potts, Our Family Ancestors (1895); WikiTree Croasdale-17 and Hawthornthwaite-8
P.note: Evidence: probable (WikiTree and the compiled Potts family book cite registers naming both parents; no register page seen).
body: WikiTree makes Thomas the son of William Croasdale of Newhey (d. 1666, buried at Settle Meeting) and Elizabeth Hayhurst, and Agnes the daughter of William Hawthornthwaite, who died in 1633 when she was a baby; the William Croasdale link is called 'highly probable' by the authors cited.

Thomas died on 2 November 1684 and his estate was appraised at 47 pounds 9 shillings, with the 500 acres "not prized." Agnes's inventory, appraised by Nicholas Waln and Robert Heaton, lists her brass and pewter, "one Bed wth ye bedding," "3 Cows 2 Bullocks 1 Heifer" and the land at 50 pounds, for a total of 106 pounds 5 shillings. Both are told under "Three cows, two mares and 500 acres."

P.name: Dorothy (Butler) Gaunt
P.place: Born at Sandwich, Plymouth Colony, on 23 January 1649/50, the daughter of Thomas Butler. She married Hananiah Gaunt there in 1678 and moved with him to Springfield Township, Burlington County, New Jersey. She died on 26 April 1714 and is buried at Jobstown.
kv: 26 Apr 1714, Springfield Twp., Burlington Co., N.J.
Mehitable (b. c.1685), wife of Thomas Staples
P.title: A Quaker wedding at Sandwich, 1678
P.hook: Hananiah Gaunt posted his marriage intention on 3 May 1678 and the next day traded his Cape Cod land for acres in New Jersey.
body: Hananiah Gaunt posted his intention of marriage at the Sandwich Friends Meeting on 3 May 1678 to Dorothy Butler, daughter of Thomas Butler of Sandwich. On 4 May he and his brother Israel exchanged their Sandwich land for land in New Jersey. Hananiah and Dorothy married on 10 May.

They lived at Dartmouth, Massachusetts, until as late as 1685, when Hananiah took up 500 acres at a place he named Hananicon in Springfield Township, Burlington County, New Jersey. Dorothy died there on 26 April 1714.

Their daughter Mehitable (born about 1685) married Thomas Staples, and Mehitable's daughter Ann Staples, born in 1714, married Thomas Rogers in 1736. Hananiah's will of 17 July 1720, proved 17 November 1721, names Mehitable Staples among his children.
P.src: WikiTree Gaunt-14 and Butler-294, citing McLean (NGSQ 1974), Sandwich Friends records and the Calendar of New Jersey Wills
P.note: The Quaker marriage record names her father; the 1720 will names her daughter. Evidence: probable (the marriage record is cited only through WikiTree and McLean).

P.name: Peter & Lydia Gaunt
P.place: Peter Gaunt was baptized at St Peter at Gowts, Lincoln, on 29 June 1610 (WikiTree: 'almost certainly' the emigrant), settled at Sandwich on Cape Cod in Plymouth Colony, and became a Quaker. He died there on 10 May 1678, and Lydia in April 1692. Their sons included Israel and Hananiah, who moved to New Jersey.
kv: 29 Jun 1610, St Peter at Gowts, Lincoln (inferred)
McLean, 'Peter Gaunt of Sandwich, Mass.', NGSQ 62:4 (1974); Anderson, Great Migration Directory p. 128
P.src: WikiTree Gaunt-5 and Gaunt-14, citing McLean (NGSQ 1974), the Great Migration Directory and brother Israel's will (1698); WikiTree Gaunt-202 and Bate-1462
P.note: Evidence: probable (Plymouth court books name Peter Gaunt at Sandwich, 1654-61). The Lincoln baptism is an inference. Peter's parents (a Thomas Gaunt who left a 1621 will) are a lead only. Trees date his death to 10 May 1678, the same day as his son Hananiah's wedding at the Sandwich meeting, so one of the two dates is probably wrong.
body: Peter's parents, Thomas Gaunt and Susan Bate, married at Rotherham on 28 August 1609; Peter was born at Lincoln in June 1610, and Susan's will calls him her only son.

The Plymouth Colony court books follow Peter Gaunt from 1655 to 1661: questioned for not attending public worship ("hee knew noc publicke vizable worship now in the world"), fined for keeping his hat on before the court in 1658, robbed of seven cows and heifers, two steers and seven and a half bushels of peas for a 24-pound fine in 1660, and listed in 1661 among those who "entertained two forraigne Quakers." It is told under "No publicke vizable worship now in the world."

quotes.t: Peter Gaunt entertained two forraigne Quakers.
quotes.c: Plymouth Colony Records, vol. 3, court of May 1661, p. 213

P.name: Thomas & Dorothy Butler
P.place: Thomas Butler was at Sandwich, Plymouth Colony, soon after the town was founded in 1637. His wife Dorothy died there on 9 August 1675 and was buried the next day; Thomas died on 12 March 1690. Their daughter Dorothy married Hananiah Gaunt. Thomas's origin is not known.
kv: Brownson, 'Thomas Butler of Sandwich', NEHGR; Anderson, Great Migration Directory p. 53
P.src: WikiTree Butler-289, citing Sandwich town records and Brownson in the New England Historical and Genealogical Register
P.note: Evidence: probable. Dorothy's maiden name is not known; 'Howes' is a guess.
body: In June 1660 the Plymouth Colony court had their son Daniel Butler publicly whipped for rescuing a "Strang Quaker" from the Sandwich marshal and fined Thomas and Dorothy forty shillings for "turbulent cariages the same night that theire son Daniell was serched for att theire house." In 1667 the court granted Thomas a neck of land called Tassacausett that he had bought from an Indian called Charles, alias Pampmumitt, for a yoke of oxen. Both are told under "Daniel Butler's whipping, June 1660."

P.name: Thomas & Susan (Bate) Gaunt
P.place: Rotherham, Norton and Lincoln, England. Peter Gaunt, who crossed to Sandwich in Plymouth Colony, was the only son of their 1609 marriage.
kv: Baptized 22 Jul 1571 Silkstone, Yorkshire; buried 14 Apr 1621 Lincoln
Baptized 23 Sep 1571, St James, Norton, daughter of James Bate; buried Feb 1626 Lincoln
Peter Gaunt, b. 29 Jun 1610, Lincoln; d. 10 May 1678, Sandwich, Mass.
P.src: FamilySearch Yorkshire Bishop's Transcripts 1547-1957 (marriage of Thomas Gaunt and Susan Bat[e], Rotherham, 1609; Blagg, Yorkshire Marriage Registers, West Riding, vol. 1, p. 50); Simpson, Parish Registers of S. James' Church, Norton, vol. 1 (1908), p. 8; wills of Thomas Gaunt (1621) and Susan Gaunt, Lincoln, as cited on WikiTree Gaunt-202 (https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Gaunt-202) and WikiTree Bate-1462 (https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Bate-1462)
P.title: A Lincoln husband, a Sheffield-side bride and one surviving son
P.hook: Peter Gaunt's parents married at Rotherham in 1609; she was 38, he already had grown children, and she said in her will that Peter was her only son.
body: Thomas Gaunt was baptized at Silkstone in the West Riding on 22 July 1571, though the register does not name his parents. On 28 August 1609 he married Susan Bate at Rotherham, about thirteen miles from Silkstone and ten from her home parish of Norton, south of Sheffield. Susan had been baptized at St James, Norton, on 23 September 1571, the daughter of James Bate, which made her 38 at the wedding.

Thomas was almost certainly marrying for the second time. His will of 1621 names children George, James, Anne and 'Dynes' as well as Peter, and Susan's own will says Peter was her only son. Peter was born at Lincoln on 29 June 1610, the year after the wedding. The family lived in Lincoln, where Thomas was buried on 14 April 1621; Susan was buried there in February 1626, leaving a will that also names her brothers and sister, Thomas, Adam and Alice Bate.

WikiTree separates this Thomas Gaunt from a Thomas Gaunt of Pinchbeck, Lincolnshire, who married Isabel Wheelwright in 1602, and it removes an older, unsourced pair of parents (Thomas Gaunt and Elizabeth Wheelwright) that online trees had given him. His own parents are not known.
P.note: The marriage, Susan's baptism and both wills are record-based. The link from Peter Gaunt of Sandwich to this Lincoln couple rests on the wills naming Peter, as summarized on WikiTree; Thomas's parents are not known.

P.name: James & Dorothy (Harrison) Bate
P.place: Jordanthorpe, in the parish of Norton just south of Sheffield, on the Yorkshire and Derbyshire border.
P.src: Simpson, Parish Registers of S. James' Church, Norton, vol. 1 (1908); FamilySearch England, Yorkshire Parish Registers 1538-2016; as cited on WikiTree Bate-357 (https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Bate-357) and WikiTree Bate-1462 (https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Bate-1462)
P.title: The Bates of Jordanthorpe
P.hook: Susan Bate's father James is known only from the Norton baptisms of his children; where he came from is not recorded.
body: James Bate and Dorothy Harrison married in 1569, and their children were baptized at St James, Norton, a mile north of the hamlet of Jordanthorpe: William in 1570, Susan in September 1571, Jane in 1576. James is called 'of Jordanthorpe' at the marriage of his daughter Elizabeth and at his own death in March 1608. Dorothy outlived him by four years.

WikiTree says plainly that James Bate's origins are not known. A baptism for a James 'Batty', son of Robert, at Kirkburton about twenty-five miles away in January 1547/8 fits his estimated birth year, but the name is too common to claim him.
Susan carried the Bate name to Lincoln when she married Thomas Gaunt in 1609, and she remembered her brothers Thomas and Adam and her sister Alice in her will.
P.note: Parish registers name James as father of Susan; his own parents are unknown. Dorothy's parents are not given.

P.name: William & Elizabeth (Hayhurst) Croasdale
P.place: Newhey (Newah) in the Forest of Bowland, Yorkshire. Quakers of Settle Monthly Meeting; buried at Settle Meeting, Newton.
kv: Died 29th of 11th month 1666; buried 31st, Settle Meeting, Newton
Died 18th of 4th month 1672; buried 20th beside him
Thomas Croasdale, b. 20 May 1644, Waddington; emigrated 1682
P.src: McCracken, Welcome Claimants Proved, Disproved and Doubtful, vol. 2; Patterson, Quaker Emigrants to America (Swarthmore); Cleaver, Ancestry of Allenn Grinnell Cleaver and Martha Irene Jessup, 1989, pp. 328-9; as cited on WikiTree Croasdale-17 (https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Croasdale-17)
P.title: Friends of Newhey, and the son who sailed on the Lamb
P.hook: Thomas Croasdale's parents are buried side by side at Settle Meeting; the authors call it 'highly probable' that they are the parents of the emigrant.
body: William Croasdale of Newhey in the Forest of Bowland died on the 29th day of the 11th month 1666 and was buried on the 31st at the Friends' burial ground at Settle Meeting, Newton. His wife Elizabeth died in the 4th month of 1672 and was buried next to him.

The Welcome Society's reference work and Patterson's list of Quaker emigrants both place a Thomas, son of William and Elizabeth, at Settle. Cleaver, the family genealogist cited on WikiTree, calls it 'highly probable' that William and Elizabeth were the parents of the Thomas who crossed on the Lamb in 1682, while noting that other parentage has been suggested. In every proposed line, Henry Croasdale of Newhey is the common ancestor.
Elizabeth's surname Hayhurst is taken from the same compiled sources; her WikiTree profile cites no original record.
P.note: Burial dates come from the Settle Meeting register as abstracted by the cited authors; the parent link to Thomas is secondary-source probable, and Elizabeth's surname is unconfirmed.

P.name: Henry & Janet (Harrison) Croasdale
P.place: Newhey in the Forest of Bowland, parish of Waddington, Yorkshire.
kv: Dated 21 Sep 1652, Henrie Croasdale, yeoman, of Newhay; administrator William Croasdale, son
Elizabeth (buried 1 Jun 1616), Edward (bapt. 13 Jan 1617/8), William (bapt. 24 Oct 1621)
P.src: Waddington parish register (FreeREG; Ancestry Yorkshire Parish Records 1599-1812); FamilySearch England Births and Christenings; YAS Record Series; as cited on WikiTree Croasdale-34 (https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Croasdale-34)
P.title: Henry Croasdale of Newhey, yeoman
P.hook: A Bowland yeoman made his will in September 1652 and was buried at Waddington three weeks later, naming his son William as administrator.
body: Henry Croasdale lived at Newhey in the Forest of Bowland, within the parish of Waddington. The register records three of his children between 1616 and 1621: Elizabeth, buried 1 June 1616; Edward, baptized 13 January 1617/8; and William, baptized 24 October 1621.

His burial reads 'Henry Croasdell buried Oct: 10' (1652). He had made his will the month before, on 21 September 1652, as 'Henrie Croasdale, yeoman; Newhay within Bolannd', with his son William as administrator; it was registered in 1654.

WikiTree makes this Henry the grandfather of the Thomas Croasdale who emigrated in 1682. That step is a family-history inference: the William baptized in 1621 would have been 23 at Thomas's birth in 1644, and some published lines give a different Henry (died 1595).

quotes.t: Henry Croasdell buried Oct: 10
quotes.c: Waddington register, 1652, as quoted on WikiTree Croasdale-34

P.note: Henry's will and burial are record-based; whether this Henry is the emigrant's grandfather is not proven. The baptism of William in 1621 does not match the c.1618 birth year used on WikiTree.

P.name: William & Elizabeth Hawthornthwaite
P.place: Tatham (Tethem) parish, on the Yorkshire and Lancashire border. His daughter Agnes married Thomas Croasdale and sailed to Pennsylvania in 1682.
kv: Born 1607, Tatham parish; died and buried 1633, Lancashire, age 26
Agnes, b. 13 Jul 1633; d. 20 Oct 1686, Neshaminy, Bucks Co., Pa.
P.src: Ancestry Lancashire, England, Baptisms, Marriages and Burials 1538-1812; England, Select Deaths and Burials 1538-1991, as cited on WikiTree Hawthornthwaite-8 (https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Hawthornthwaite-8) and WikiTree Hawthornewaite-1 (https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Hawthornewaite-1)
P.title: A father who died the year his daughter was born
P.hook: Agnes Hawthornthwaite was baptized in 1633, the year her father William died at 26.
body: WikiTree gives Agnes Hawthornthwaite, later wife of Thomas Croasdale, a birth on 13 July 1633 in Tatham parish. Her father William Hawthornthwaite, born in 1607, is said to have married Elizabeth in Lancashire in 1631 and to have died in 1633, aged 26.

The profile's sources are database indexes of Lancashire parish registers and burials, not images of the register entries, and it does not say how Agnes is tied to William beyond the dates. The link stays a lead until the Tatham register is read.
Agnes came to Pennsylvania with the Settle Friends in 1682 and died at Neshaminy in 1686.
P.note: Index-level sourcing only; the parent link to Agnes is not shown from a register entry.

P.name: Anthony & Ann (Pitts) Chamness of London
P.place: East Smithfield and Wapping, London. If the link holds, they are the grandparents of Anthony Chamness, who was sent to America as a boy and settled at Cane Creek.
kv: 23 Sep 1686, St James, Duke's Place, London (FamilySearch)
John Chamness, b. c.1681, bapt. 19 Nov 1682, St Saviour, Southwark; d. 1716 London
Born c.1665; said to have died 1745 at Tedburn St Mary, Devon
P.src: FamilySearch England Marriages 1538-1973 (FHL film 374448, NV29-23V), as cited on WikiTree Chamness-43 (https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Chamness-43); WikiTree Chamness-8 (https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Chamness-8)
P.title: A 1686 marriage in Duke's Place
P.hook: A London record shows an Anthony Champneys marrying Anne Pitts in 1686, but their son John was baptized four years earlier.
body: WikiTree makes John Chamness, who married Ann Wearey at St John's, Wapping, in 1704, the son of Anthony Chamness and Ann Pitts. The only document cited for the parents is the marriage of Anthony 'Champneys' and Anne Pitts at St James, Duke's Place, on 23 September 1686.

That date is four years after John's baptism, which WikiTree places in November 1682 at St Saviour's in Southwark. The profile says there is 'no geographical or chronological reason to dispute' the link; the order of dates is a reason to be careful. John could have been baptized before his parents formally married, or the baptism belongs to another family.
WikiTree also says Anthony 'appears to be' the son of a John Chamness of Stansted Mountfitchet, Essex, and his wife Mary Reffell. Those Essex generations are not added here.
P.note: Marriage record exists; nothing cited ties John Chamness (b. c.1681) to this couple as their son.

P.name: John Rogers & Mary (Groom) Rogers of Burlington
P.place: Quakers of Nottingham township, Burlington County, New Jersey. John is said to have come from Rotherham, Yorkshire, on the ship Kent in 1677.
kv: Born c.1656 Rotherham; d. 1699 Burlington Co., N.J.
Born c.1665 Byberry, Pa.; d. 13 Feb 1693, Burlington Co.
P.src: U.S., Quaker Meeting Records 1681-1935 (Chesterfield Monthly Meeting birth record, 1687), as cited on WikiTree Rogers-3993 (https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Rogers-3993) and WikiTree Rogers-3994 (https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Rogers-3994)
P.title: A Quaker family on the Kent
P.hook: A Chesterfield Meeting birth record gives a John Rogers born in 1687 to John and Mary; whether he is the John Rogers whose son Thomas married Ann Staples is not settled.
body: The Burlington County Quaker John Rogers, born about 1656 at Rotherham, is said to have crossed with Friends on the Kent, which loaded at London in March 1677 and landed at the Delaware in 1678. He married Mary Groom, who died on 13 February 1693, and the couple had at least five children.

WikiTree attaches this family to the John Rogers born 'the 5th day of the 1st month 1687' at Nottingham, Burlington County, on the strength of the Chesterfield Monthly Meeting birth record, and gives that John a wife Martha Middleton, whose mother's 1712 will names a 'son-in-law John Rogers' - a fact already in this tree.

The trouble is the John Rodgers whose will was proved in 1767 and who left his son Thomas one-fifth of the residue. WikiTree's John Rogers has ten children and a will of 1769 proved in 1776 at Windsor, which does not match. The two may be different men.
P.note: Parentage from a Quaker birth record is solid for the 1687 John; that he is our Thomas Rogers's father conflicts with the dates of our John Rodgers's will (proved 1767).

P.name: Henry & Ann (Curlett) Stevenson
P.place: Downpatrick and Belfast, County Antrim, Ireland. If the line is right, they are the parents of the Scots-Irish James Stevenson who died in Iredell County, North Carolina, in 1820.
kv: 2 Jun 1720, Saul parish, Downpatrick, Co. Down
Baptized 27 May 1698, Braddan, Isle of Man, daughter of William Curlett; d. c.1735
Said to be born at Ricalton, Oxnam, Roxburghshire; d. c.1743 Belfast
P.src: Ireland, Select Marriages 1619-1898 and Irish Records Extraction Database (marriage of Henry Stevenson and Ann Curlett, 1720), via WikiTree Stevenson-754 (https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Stevenson-754) and WikiTree Curlett-6 (https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Curlett-6); Raleigh Star, 29 Mar 1820 (obituary of James Stevenson sen.)
P.title: From the Isle of Man to Belfast to Iredell
P.hook: A 1720 marriage record at Downpatrick is the only solid piece in the chain behind James Stevenson of Iredell County.
body: WikiTree records Henry Stevenson's marriage to Ann Curlett on 2 June 1720 at Saul parish, Downpatrick, in two Irish marriage indexes. Ann had been baptized on 27 May 1698 at Braddan on the Isle of Man, a daughter of William Curlett. The couple's children, listed from family trees, include a James born about March 1721 at Belfast.

That James is the James Stevenson who died on 5 March 1820 in Iredell County, North Carolina, and whose obituary in the Raleigh Star calls him a native of Ireland, nearly 90 years old, married 65 years, with 208 descendants. His estate was probated in Iredell in 1820.

Henry's own birthplace and his parents (given as William Stevenson and Katherine Alison) have no cited source. Whether this James is the father of the James Stevenson (1746-1828) in the Stevenson line here is itself only a lead.
P.note: Marriage indexes are solid; the children are attached from family-tree compilations, and the obituary does not name Henry or Ann.

Elmore of Louisa Co. 11-19-1759' and 'Robert and Virginia Johnson rec. on cert. from Cedar Creek M.M., Va., dated 1766-3-29'. Both were buried at Springfield Meeting in North Carolina. Robert's estate file was opened in Stokes County in 1808.
Robert was born 8 February 1738 in New Kent County, a son of Ashley Johnson and Martha Woody. Virginia, born at Black Creek in 1737, was a daughter of Thomas Elmore and Cecilia Ellyson.

A GEDCOM import on WikiTree, with no sources, lists Martha Johnson, born 28 August 1766 at Deep River, who married Aden Nordyke in 1787, among their children. The Quaker minutes support the couple but do not themselves name Martha.

P.title: A gift of everything for 'love and affection'
P.hook: In 1794 Ashley Johnson deeded his whole estate to his son Elijah in return for keeping him and Martha for the rest of their lives.
body: Ashley Johnson was born about 1710 in St Peter's Parish, New Kent County, and married Martha Woody in Henrico or New Kent County; the sources give 12 December 1734 and 10 or 12 October 1735. They raised at least eight sons and five daughters, including Robert, born February 1738.

Two Louisa County deeds fill in the later years. On 9 November 1778 Ashley gave his son Elijah 241 acres on Chamberlain's Creek. On 3 February 1794 he gave Elijah all his estate, real and personal, 'for love and affection and maintenance of the said Ashley Johnson and Martha his wife during their natural lives', except 210 acres jointly to David and James, with a feather bed and furniture each for Martha, Elizabeth and David.
Martha died on 6 September 1802 and Ashley about 1803, aged about 93; both are buried at Roundabout Castle Cemetery in Louisa County.

P.title: A land grant for five transported servants
P.hook: WikiTree flags John Johnson's parentage and his first wife as disputed; the land papers, though, are plain.
body: John Johnson first appears in the records of St Peter's Parish on 22 November 1702, when his son John was baptized. On 2 November 1705 he was granted 252 acres on Black Creek, land formerly patented by Thomas Reynolds and then abandoned; the grant was earned by transporting five people into the colony.

On 9 February 1727/8 he was granted 200 acres on the south side of Chickahominy Swamp in Henrico County, and he and his wife Elizabeth sold it on 1 November 1736. He died on 5 September 1737 in St Paul's Parish, Hanover County.

Hinshaw's Quaker abstract names Ashley Johnson's mother as Lucretia Massie, but WikiTree notes that Friends' records call John's wife Elizabeth and treats Lucretia as 'purported' and unsourced; her claimed Massie parentage rests on uncited published histories. John's own parents are also marked disputed.
P.note: Land records are original; the first wife and John's parents are unresolved on WikiTree.

body: John Paine was born in Drysdale Parish, King and Queen County, in 1705, a son of Barnett Paine. He witnessed a Spotsylvania County deed in 1740 and died there between the date of his will, 25 July 1764, and the executors' bond of 20 September 1770. The will names his wife Frances and sons John (eldest), Thomas, Barnett, William, Robert and George.

Frances is thought to be a daughter of Robert and Mary (Clayton) Coleman, but WikiTree says the choice among Coleman families is the subject of 'considerable disagreement'. A 1750 will reportedly calls her 'Francis Pain'.

The link to the Stevensons is by way of Rev. Elam Stevenson's wife Lydia Payne, whose father William Paine (1754-1807, Burke County, N.C.) WikiTree lists as one of John's sons. That William is attached to Lydia only through a Find a Grave memorial, and two men named William Paine have been merged on Catherine Arnold's profile, so the whole link is a lead.
P.note: The will is a real record; whether William Paine of Burke County is John's son, and Lydia his daughter, is unproven.

body: Hezekiah Alexander was born on 13 January 1728 at New Munster in Cecil County, Maryland, and settled in the Sugaw Creek congregation in Mecklenburg County, North Carolina. He married Mary Sample, a daughter of William Sample Sr. and Esther Garrison, and they raised eleven children. He is a DAR-recognized patriot ancestor, and his homesite in Charlotte is kept as a museum.

Their daughter Esther, born 28 September 1762, appears in the lists of his children on WikiTree. She is the wife of Samuel Garrison, whose son John Milton Garrison lived in Allen County, Kentucky, but her own profile cites no record, so the tie from Hezekiah to our Garrison family is a lead.
P.note: Hezekiah and Mary are well documented; that Esther (Alexander) Garrison is their daughter, and mother of John Milton Garrison, rests on compiled lists only.

He signed a will on 26 January 1769 and died that same month; his wife Esther Garrison signed her own will the same day. The loose estate papers name five children: William, John, Joseph, Mary and Agnes.
Their daughter Mary, born 31 January 1734, married Hezekiah Alexander in 1752. Esther's parentage is not carried further here.

body: James Alexander was born between 1690 and 1695 at Manokin in Somerset County, Maryland, and married Margaret McKnitt (1693-1736). A family list gives twelve children by her, including Hezekiah in 1722. After her death he married her sister Abigail and had five more.

Three separate marriage-record compilations give his birth as 1690, and DAR recognizes him as a patriot ancestor. He died in Cecil County on 31 May 1779 and was buried at the Head of Christiana Church cemetery near Newark, Delaware.
This is as far as the Alexander line goes in print: WikiTree itself warns that its sketches of the 'Seven Brothers' Alexanders from Donegal are 'speculative' and not primary sources.

P.hook: Samuel Garrison's name rests on a DAR number and an unsourced profile, so he is entered as a lead.
body: WikiTree gives Samuel Garrison a birth on 24 August 1762 in Halifax County, North Carolina, a Revolutionary service as a private in the Continental Line, and a burial in Old Scottsville Cemetery in Kentucky. His wife Esther Alexander was born in Mecklenburg County in 1762, but her place of death is given as Coles County, Illinois, which does not fit a husband buried in Kentucky.

John Milton Garrison's WikiTree profile says he came from Mecklenburg County to Warren, later Allen, County, Kentucky, with his parents before 1809, which matches Samuel's move. No cited record names John Milton as Samuel's son. Samuel's father, John Garrison of Salem, New Jersey, has no source at all on WikiTree.
P.note: Plausible and consistent with the move to Allen County, but no cited record names John Milton as Samuel's son.

EXTRA.name: Judge Edward Ward Tims

imgs.cap: 1896 Choctaw census: brothers Vinson and Edward Tims's households, Towson County
Dawes Card 1238: Columbus Tims, son of E. W. and Polly Tims

EXTRA.title: Postmaster and judge of Doaksville
EXTRA.hook: Vinson's brother was a Towson County judge, Doaksville's postmaster, and once talked of for Principal Chief.
body: Doaksville was the capital of the Choctaw Nation from 1858 to 1863. By 1850 it was the largest town in Indian Territory, and in 1860 a convention there adopted the constitution that governed the Choctaw Nation until 1906. At the end of the Civil War there were two surrenders at Doaksville: Principal Chief Peter Pitchlynn surrendered the Choctaw forces on 19 June 1865, and General Stand Watie surrendered his Cherokee, Creek, Seminole and Osage troops on 23 June, the last Confederate general to lay down arms.

Edward Ward Tims, Choctaw by Blood No. 4009, served as District Trustee of Apukshunnubbee District in the early 1880s and for many years as County Judge of Towson County. On 24 October 1887 he was appointed postmaster at Doaksville, succeeding James T. Fleming; the office closed in 1903, when the name changed to Fort Towson.

On 29 April 1888 in Towson County he married Willie Jane Maxwell of Arkansas. After statehood he retired to his allotment southeast of Hugo. He died on 7 February 1923, four months after Willie Jane, and is buried in Springs Chapel Cemetery near Hugo.

His second wife, Willie Jane, was born on 27 July 1870 and died on 8 October 1922, four months before him. Their children were Lucy Ann (1889-1970), Minnie (1891-1930), Edmond (1893-1918), Benjamin (1897-1969), Myrtle (1899-1988), Abel (1901-1966) and Nora (1906-1977). By his first wife Polly, a full-blood Choctaw, he had a son, Columbus, born on Christmas Day 1860, who died on 21 October 1918 and is also buried at Springs Chapel.

In January 1940 the Paris News reported that his old log house, a quarter mile northeast of Fort Towson, had been proposed as a museum, and wrote that Tims was 'once county judge of Towson County' and was 'once considered for the position as principal chief of the Choctaw Nation.' The house was said to have been the setting for talk of the 1860 Council and the 1837 treaty. That detail is local lore, not a record. Joel Thompson remembered him simply as the man 'who was post master and Judge at Doaksville for so many years.'

His own Dawes card is 1437, applied for on 8 May 1899, post office Doaksville. It lists "Tims, Edward W.," age 58, one-half blood, Roll No. 4009, with parents "Vincent B. Tims," dead, a non-citizen, and "Betsy Tims," dead, of Towson County. Edward's son Columbus, born in 1860, is on Card 1238 as "Tims, Columbus," 40, three-quarter blood, Roll No. 3355, with parents "E. W. Tims" and "Polly Tims," the latter dead.

The jacket for Card 1437 has the details of his second marriage. The Commission's decision gives the wedding as 29 April 1888, and a copy of the certificate, signed by R. S. Frazier, reads the same; family summaries that give 19 April are a few days off. Their youngest child on the card, Abel E., was born on 14 December 1901. The card also includes a ward, Adam Nanomantubbe, whom O. W. Seay of Oscar called Edward's orphan grandson in a letter of 1903.

quotes.t: My grandfather, Vinson Tims, was a brother to Judge Edward Ward Tims, who was post master and Judge at Doaksville for so many years.
quotes.c: Joel J. Thompson, 1937

quotes.t: Tims, a prominent Choctaw citizen, was once county judge of Towson County, I. T. and was once considered for the position as principal chief of the Choctaw Nation.

EXTRA.name: Pvt. Edmond Tims

imgs.cap: 142nd Infantry report, January 1919: "In the first action of the 142nd Infantry at St Etienne…" describing the Choctaw code
Soldiers of the Great War, vol. 3 (1920), Oklahoma, killed in action: "TIMS, Edmond, Hugo." (public domain)

EXTRA.title: Killed in France, 1918
EXTRA.hook: A runner in the Choctaw Code Talkers' regiment, awarded the Croix de Guerre.
body: Judge Tims's son by Willie Jane Maxwell, enrolled Choctaw by Blood No. 4012 and listed as "Edmund, 3" in the 1896 Choctaw census. He served first in Co. L, 1st Oklahoma Infantry, then as a company runner in Co. D, 142nd Infantry, 36th Division. On 9 October 1918, near St. Étienne, France, a fellow runner spoke with him at 8 a.m. and an hour later found him killed by shrapnel.

He was posthumously awarded the French Croix de Guerre with Palm and lies in the Meuse-Argonne American Cemetery. The 142nd was the regiment of the Choctaw Code Talkers. The report pictured here, written by the regiment's commander, describes how Choctaw speakers were first used to send messages in this same St. Étienne fighting. Edmond is not listed as a code talker, but he served alongside them.

Two books printed in 1920 carry his name. Capt. Ben H. Chastaine of the 142d Infantry, in Story of the 36th: The Experiences of the 36th Division in the World War (Oklahoma City, Harlow Publishing Company), closes with an Honor Roll of the division's dead. Under "142d Infantry" it lists "TIMS, EDMOND, Private, Co. D," with the date October 8, 1918 (p. 287). The same year the War Department's casualty lists were printed state by state in Soldiers of the Great War, vol. 3. In the Oklahoma section, among the privates killed in action, the entry reads "TIMS, Edmond, Hugo" (p. 31).

The Honor Roll gives 8 October 1918 where the company runner's account in the regiment's report puts his death on the morning of the 9th. The two dates fall within the same two days, 8 and 9 October 1918, of the 142d Infantry's fighting at St. Étienne.

Chastaine's narrative of the morning of 8 October gives Edmond's battalion a hard start. The First Battalion lost its commander, Capt. Charles Kuhlman, and "half of the battalion headquarters group, including several runners," to a single shell before the jump-off, and Company D "wandered into the French sector to the left" and stayed there. The longer account is told under "The runner's morning: Company D at St. Etienne."
EXTRA.src: Choctaw Nation veterans file for Edmond Tims; 1896 Choctaw census, Towson County; 142nd Infantry report, 23 January 1919. Dawes final roll index (NARA M1186); Ben H. Chastaine, Story of the 36th: The Experiences of the 36th Division in the World War (Oklahoma City: Harlow, 1920), p. 287; Soldiers of the Great War, vol. 3 (Washington: Soldiers Record Publishing Association, 1920), Oklahoma, p. 31.
EXTRA.note: His division's records give his death as 8 October 1918; the burial-case statements give 9 October.

EXTRA.name: The Mississippi-born ancestors

imgs.cap: Their grandchildren on the Dawes rolls seventy years later

EXTRA.title: The Choctaw removal
EXTRA.hook: Several ancestors were born in the old Choctaw Nation in Mississippi before the Trail of Tears.
body: Our tree lists Pisachubbe "Wilson" (born 1807), Nancy Te-hol-ba-ta-bi (born 1825), Jackson Gardner (born about 1820) and O-we-na as born in the old Choctaw Nation in Mississippi. The Choctaw were the first nation removed under the Indian Removal Act, walking and riding west in 1831–1833.
These families settled in the Kiamitia, Blue and Towson districts of the new Choctaw Nation, where their grandchildren were enrolled by the Dawes Commission seventy years later.

A 1937 newspaper account of the Pisachubbe family says they came from Mississippi with the first group of exiles in 1832 and settled first at Fort Coffee, near present-day Spiro. At Doaksville, the trading firm of Doak & Tims, Vincent Tims's partnership, held the contract to feed arriving families at 13 cents a ration.

Two cautions on the Mississippi-born names. None of them has yet been found on the Armstrong Roll or another removal-era list. And the tree's link between Joseph Pisachubbe and Nancy Te-hol-ba-ta-bi as mother and son does not fit her age on the Dawes roll.

Dawes Card 1278 names a full-blood Nancy Pisachubbi, 69, whose father was Te-hol-ba-ta-bi, dead, and whose mother, Malindy, was dead and listed under Mississippi. She appears to be the tree's Nancy Te-hol-ba-ta-bi, though the card does not say whose mother she was.

The best-documented part of the removal's first winter is the stretch from the Mississippi to the Red River. About 18,880 Choctaws were counted in Major Francis Armstrong's census of 1831; by the first week of November four thousand were on the road, and between 26 November and 8 December about 2,500 were landed at Arkansas Post in a blizzard. A Choctaw letter of February 1833 shows Doaksville already a place where annuities were issued and 'a small town' of white traders stood below the Kiamichi. These are told under 'With the first group of exiles' and 'Doaksville before the store.'
EXTRA.note: These individuals have not yet been found on a removal-era roll such as the 1831 Armstrong Roll.
EXTRA.src: Family tree records; Dawes enrollment cards for their descendants; Hugo Daily News, 11 May 1937; Hughes, 'Trader V. B. Tims of Doaksville' (2020); Dawes Card 1278; Thoburn and Wright, Oklahoma: A History of the State and Its People (1929), vol. 1, pp. 165-70; Senate Doc. 512 (1835), vol. 4

EXTRA.name: Two households in 1940
EXTRA.title: The Depression, house by house
EXTRA.hook: The 1940 census caught both of Dad's and Mom's families at the bottom of the hard years.
body: In April 1940 the census takers wrote down how many weeks each man had worked the year before. Grady Moffitt in Hugo: 12 weeks, $100, unemployed 50 weeks, eight children at home in a rented house. Oscar Hulsey at South Fork, Arkansas: 16 weeks on a government relief job, $140, unemployed 48 weeks, five children in a house worth $2. Simon Thompson at Jeter: 52 weeks on his own farm, worth $400, feeding twelve people, including his in-laws and their nieces and nephews.
Within a few years John Moffitt was in the Navy, the Hulseys had moved to the Oklahoma lumber towns, and the three families' children would meet and marry in Hugo.
EXTRA.src: 1940 U.S. Census: Hugo and Jeter, Choctaw County, Okla.; South Fork, Montgomery County, Ark.

EXTRA.name: Spencer Academy
EXTRA.title: The school where 'Swing Low' was written down
EXTRA.hook: Joseph Thompson's boarding school north of Doaksville gave the world a famous spiritual.
body: Spencer Academy was the first school created under the Choctaw Council's school law of 1842. It opened on 1 February 1844, a quarter mile north of present-day Spencerville on the old Fort Smith–Fort Towson military road, and was named for Secretary of War John C. Spencer, who gave it a 250-pound bell. Presbyterian missionaries ran it from 1846. Its three two-story halls had long porches, and the dining room served tanfula, a Choctaw crushed-corn dish.

The school closed in 1861. During the Civil War its buildings served as a Confederate hospital and sheltered homeless Choctaw families. It reopened in 1871 and ran until 1881, when a new Spencer Academy opened at Nelson, near Antlers. Joseph Thompson, born in 1861, was of school age during the reopened years. Among Spencer's earlier students was Allen Wright, later Principal Chief, who gave Oklahoma its name.

Before the war, Wallace and Minerva Willis, enslaved people hired out to the academy, sang their songs at their cabin door. Superintendent Alexander Reid wrote them down, and in 1871 he spent a day in Brooklyn teaching them to the Fisk Jubilee Singers: 'Steal Away to Jesus,' 'I'm a Rolling,' and 'Swing Low, Sweet Chariot.' Whether Wallace Willis composed the songs himself is debated.
EXTRA.src: National Register of Historic Places nomination, Spencer Academy (NRIS 75001562); Robert E. Flickinger, The Choctaw Freedmen and the Story of Oak Hill Industrial Academy (1914); O'Beirne, Leaders and Leading Men of the Indian Territory (1891).

EXTRA.name: Court day at Sulphur Springs
EXTRA.title: Court day at Sulphur Springs
EXTRA.hook: A log courthouse, a whipping post, and a justice system built on keeping your word.

imgs.cap: Joel Thompson's 1937 interview about his father

body: Cedar County was created by the Choctaw Nation's Doaksville Constitution of 1860 and lasted until statehood in 1907. Each county elected a judge for a two-year term to oversee county business, a sheriff, who collected taxes and took the census, and a ranger, who sold stray livestock. When an arrest or a sentence had to be carried out, the sheriff called on the district Lighthorsemen.

The Cedar County court met at Sulphur Springs, near present-day Rattan, on the first Monday of each month, in "a large log house, constructed of long, straight logs" that also served as a Choctaw Methodist church. Families camped at the springs on court days. A stump from the tree used as the whipping post is kept by the Pushmataha County Historical Society in Antlers.

Choctaw law punished crimes such as theft with lashes, fifty for a first offense and one hundred for a second. H. B. Cushman, who knew the Nation, described what came after: the whole crowd shook hands with the man who had been whipped, and the matter was never spoken of again.

From 1866 the Nation's death penalty was carried out by rifle. By custom a condemned man went home to plant and harvest his crop and came back on the appointed day, often choosing a friend or relative to fire the shot so no one would seek revenge. Capital cases went to the district court, not the county judge, so when Joel said his father "could have sentenced criminals to be shot," the whippings are the part that fits a county judge.

quotes.t: ...the whole assembly came out and shook hands with the 'Fummah' (whipped), thus reinstating him to his former position in society, and the subject was then and there dropped, never to be mentioned again.
quotes.c: H. B. Cushman, 1899

quotes.t: Never was a full-blood Choctaw known to evade the death penalty ... by flight.
quotes.c: H. B. Cushman, 1899

Cushman, History of the Choctaw, Chickasaw and Natchez Indians (1899), pp. 218–23; Choctaw Nation, Iti Fabvssa (Oct. 2016, Feb. 2017); WPA interview #7418 (Joel J. Thompson).

EXTRA.name: Dois L. Moffitt
EXTRA.title: Home from the Navy, lost in the Red River
EXTRA.hook: John's older brother cooked for the Navy through the war, then died two summers after coming home.
body: Dois was the "Dais, 19" of the 1940 census, born 16 February 1921, the third of Grady and Mary's sons. He joined the U.S. Navy on 3 September 1942 and served as a Ship's Cook until 27 January 1946, the same years his younger brother John spent as a corpsman in the Pacific.

On Thursday afternoon, 21 August 1947, he dove into shallow water in the Red River at Arthur City and broke his neck. A companion, Mac Davidson, pulled him out, and an ambulance took him to the Sanitarium of Paris. He died days later, at 26.
His funeral was at Grant Baptist Church, and he is buried at Shoat Springs Cemetery near Hugo. In October 1947 his father Grady signed the application for his military headstone.

His Texas death certificate lists him as single, 26 years, 6 months, 9 days old, a discharged U.S. Navy man, born in Choctaw County, Oklahoma, and living at Grant. It gives the cause as a fracture of the fifth cervical vertebra with a severed spinal cord, from an accident on 21 August at the Red River bridge north of Paris, and he lived four days. His father Grady Moffitt signed as informant and the certificate gives his mother's maiden name as Mary Shackelford, born in Alabama.
The Shoat Springs listing gives his rating as SC1C, Ship's Cook First Class, U.S. Naval Reserve, and the date 25 August 1947 that appears on his death certificate.
EXTRA.note: The newspaper places the accident on 21 August; his grave memorial gives his death as 25 August 1947.

EXTRA.name: Doaksville
EXTRA.title: Doaksville: the biggest town in Indian Territory
EXTRA.hook: A trading post by the Kiamichi grew into the busiest town in the Choctaw Nation, then faded within a lifetime.
body: Doaksville took its name from Josiah Stuart Doak, co-owner of a trading post. He and his brother first set up at the mouth of the Kiamichi River, then moved about a mile west after the U.S. Army founded Fort Towson in 1824. Choctaw people relocated from Mississippi settled here, and steamboat access on the Red River made it a principal town of the Nation.

By 1840 it had several stores, a gristmill, a blacksmith and a hotel. In 1842 the Indian agent William Armstrong called it one of the most orderly and quiet towns in the West. A post office opened in 1847, and by 1850 it was the largest town in Indian Territory, with more than thirty buildings and two newspapers, one printed in Choctaw.

The Army left Fort Towson in 1854 and the town's importance began to slip. The Civil War wrecked the plantation economy around it, an 1870 railroad bypassed it, and most businesses moved to Fort Towson. The post office closed in 1903. Only the Fort Towson-Doaksville Cemetery remains; the Oklahoma Historical Society acquired the site in 1960 and it was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on May 29, 1975.
This is the town and neighborhood of the Cedar, Towson and Kiamitia county families, framed here as the place they lived near, not as a record of any one relative.

quotes.t: one of the most orderly and quiet towns that you will find in the west
quotes.c: Agent William Armstrong, 1842, as quoted in Wikipedia, Doaksville, Choctaw Nation

EXTRA.note: Place history from secondary sources; not tied to a named relative.
EXTRA.src: Wikipedia, Doaksville, Choctaw Nation; Oklahoma Historical Society, Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture (Fort Towson, Choctaw County)

EXTRA.name: Doaksville Constitution
EXTRA.title: The 1860 constitution written at Doaksville
EXTRA.hook: A convention at Doaksville set the framework that governed the Choctaw Nation until its government ended in 1906.
body: In 1860 a convention at Doaksville ratified the Doaksville Constitution, which guided the Choctaw Nation until 1906. Doaksville served as the capital in this period; sources differ on the exact dates, and the capital later moved to Chahta Tamaha in 1863.

The constitution created Cedar County and others in the Nation's district system. Each county elected members to the National Council and also a county judge, a sheriff and a ranger to two-year terms. The judge ran county administration, the sheriff collected taxes, watched for intruders and took the census, and the ranger advertised and sold stray livestock.
For families in the Kiamichi country this was everyday government: the people holding these offices were their neighbors.
EXTRA.note: Capital dates are inconsistent between sources; stated loosely on purpose.
EXTRA.src: Wikipedia, Doaksville, Choctaw Nation; Wikipedia, Cedar County, Choctaw Nation

EXTRA.name: Doaksville, June 1865
EXTRA.title: The last Confederate general lays down arms near Fort Towson
EXTRA.hook: The Civil War ended in Indian Territory in the Choctaw Nation, a few miles from where these families lived.
body: After the Army abandoned Fort Towson in 1854, the post saw a brief resurgence during the Civil War when Gen. Samuel Bell Maxey chose it as headquarters for Confederate forces in Indian Territory.

On June 23, 1865, Cherokee Brig. Gen. Stand Watie surrendered his First Indian Brigade at Doaksville, near the fort, signing with two Union commissioners. He is generally called the last Confederate general officer to surrender. Some sources place the signing at Fort Towson itself; the date is consistent.

The war had wrecked the plantation economy around Doaksville, and the town never recovered. For Choctaw families of the area the surrender was the end of four years in which their homeland was a Confederate district.
EXTRA.note: Place and event history; no specific family member is documented here. Whether a relative served is a lead to check in Confederate Choctaw rolls.
EXTRA.src: Oklahoma Historical Society, Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture, Fort Towson entry; Wikipedia, Doaksville, Choctaw Nation

EXTRA.name: Fort Towson
EXTRA.title: Fort Towson: the army post built to receive the Choctaw
EXTRA.hook: The fort existed before the Choctaw arrived, to be a buffer for people still in Mississippi.
body: In May 1824 a company of the Seventh Infantry camped on Gates Creek near the Kiamichi and Red rivers. The outpost, Cantonment Towson, was named for Gen. Nathan Towson.

It was abandoned in 1829. After the Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek it reopened in 1830 as Camp Phoenix and was soon renamed Fort Towson. The Oklahoma Historical Society says the fort was meant as a buffer for the Choctaw slated for removal to the area, and it later served as a terminal on the Choctaw Trail of Tears.
Troops left for good in 1854. The state acquired the property in 1967 and a visitor center and sutler's store are open to the public.
EXTRA.note: Institution history only.
EXTRA.src: Oklahoma Historical Society, Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture, Fort Towson (FO044)

EXTRA.name: Atoka Agreement
EXTRA.title: The Atoka Agreement and the end of Choctaw common land
EXTRA.hook: The 1897 deal that turned shared tribal land into individual allotments is why the Dawes rolls exist.
body: The Atoka Agreement was signed April 23, 1897 by representatives of the Choctaw and Chickasaw Nations and the Dawes Commission. Common tribal land was to be divided into household allotments for certified citizens, with surplus land sold to non-Natives. Coal and asphalt lands were reserved and sold or leased for the tribes' benefit.

Tribal governments were to end on March 4, 1906. Both nations ratified it in November 1897, but Chickasaw voters rejected it under Chickasaw law. The Curtis Act of 1898 required resubmission, and approval came in a joint election on August 24, 1898.
Enrolling for an allotment is the reason a family like this appears on the Dawes cards between 1898 and 1906.
EXTRA.note: Background to the Dawes enrollment; connection to specific cards is covered by existing stories.
EXTRA.src: Wikipedia, Atoka Agreement

EXTRA.name: Butler County, Kentucky
EXTRA.place: Morgantown, Butler County, KY
EXTRA.title: A monument for both armies
EXTRA.hook: On the courthouse lawn in Morgantown stands a Civil War monument that honors soldiers from both sides.
body: Butler County, Kentucky, was created by the General Assembly on January 18, 1810, from parts of Logan and Ohio counties, and named for Major General Richard Butler, who died at the Battle of the Wabash in 1791.

Kentucky stayed in the Union but sent men to both armies, and Butler County felt it directly. Fighting broke out near Morgantown on October 29, 1861, and a skirmish followed the next day where Confederate forces were encamped. The war slowed the county's growth.

In 1907 the Confederate-Union Veterans' Monument was dedicated on the courthouse lawn. It is described as one of only two Kentucky Civil War monuments honoring soldiers from both sides, a sign of how neighbors and kin had been divided and then lived side by side.
EXTRA.note: Place story. It describes the county where Smith and Satterfield kin lived. It does not claim a named ancestor served in either army.
EXTRA.src: Butler County, Kentucky, Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Butler_County,_Kentucky)

EXTRA.name: Scottsville, Allen County, KY
EXTRA.place: Scottsville, Allen County, KY
EXTRA.title: Allen County and its county seat
EXTRA.hook: Allen County was cut out of Barren and Warren counties in 1815 and named for a colonel killed in the War of 1812.
body: Allen County was established in 1815 from parts of Barren and Warren counties. It honors Colonel John Allen, a state senator and soldier killed at the Battle of Frenchtown in Michigan during the War of 1812.

The county seat began as a settlement on Bays Fork in 1797 that grew into a stagecoach station. The town was laid off in 1816, established in 1817 and named for Charles Scott, Kentucky's fourth governor. Early on it was also called Allen Court House and Scottville. It was incorporated in 1860.
A fire at the courthouse in 1902 destroyed some county records, which is why some Allen County families are hard to trace in local papers.
EXTRA.note: Place story. The 1902 fire is a fact about the county, not a record of a particular family.

EXTRA.name: Hagansport, Franklin County, TX
EXTRA.place: Hagansport, Franklin County, TX
EXTRA.title: A crossing on the Sulphur River
EXTRA.hook: Hagansport began as a river crossing, and its post office came and went over 70 years.
body: Hagansport grew up at a Sulphur River crossing called Hagan's Port, named for an early settler. The spelling Hagansport was in use by 1857, when F. M. Sims was postmaster. The post office closed in 1866, reopened in 1876, and closed for good in 1929.
By 1884 the community had about 150 people, four churches, a school, a mill and a cotton gin. In 1896 its one-room school had 69 pupils.
By the 1930s the center had moved south to Farm Road 71 and later shifted again to its present spot. About 40 people lived there in 1985, and about 40 still in 2000.
EXTRA.note: Place story. Complements the neighbors story already in the app.
EXTRA.src: Handbook of Texas, Hagansport (https://www.tshaonline.org/handbook/entries/hagansport-tx)

EXTRA.name: Franklin County, TX
EXTRA.place: Franklin County, TX
EXTRA.title: Cotton, rails and tenant farms in Franklin County
EXTRA.hook: Between 1879 and 1929 the county's cotton acreage grew more than fourfold while yields fell by more than half.
body: Franklin County was created in March 1875 and named for Benjamin C. Franklin. White settlers had come from the late 1830s, mostly from Tennessee and the upper South. The St. Louis, Arkansas and Texas Railway crossed the county in 1887 and became the main route to market.
In 1879, 706 farms planted 8,660 acres of cotton. By 1929, 1,678 farms planted 37,969 acres. Yields fell from about half a bale per acre to about one-fifth.

Tenants were 34 percent of farmers in 1880 and 62 percent in 1930. The county's population peaked at 9,331 in 1910, then declined as the Depression and the shift to livestock took hold. Cotton fell to 16,582 acres by 1940.
EXTRA.note: Context for families who moved from Kentucky to Franklin County around 1900-1910. It does not say any named ancestor was a tenant or an owner.
EXTRA.src: Handbook of Texas, Franklin County (https://www.tshaonline.org/handbook/entries/franklin-county)

EXTRA.name: Grant, Choctaw Nation
EXTRA.place: Grant, Choctaw County, OK
EXTRA.title: Grant began as a railroad stop in the Choctaw Nation
EXTRA.hook: Grant was born in 1887 as a station on the Frisco line, when the land was still part of the Choctaw Nation.
body: Grant was founded as a station stop on the St. Louis and San Francisco Railroad, which opened through Indian Territory in June 1887. It was named for President Ulysses S. Grant.
A post office opened at Grant, Indian Territory, on January 31, 1889. At its founding the town lay in Kiamitia County, part of the Apukshunnubbee District of the Choctaw Nation.
The town counted 289 people in 2010 and 190 in 2020.

Charles Oscar and Artie Smith are buried at Grant Cemetery. Grant began about 1885 with Basil Gooding's store. A Red River ferry six miles south connected residents with Texas markets, and when the Arkansas & Choctaw laid its track five miles north, business drifted to Hugo. Grant had 416 people in 1910 and 296 in 1930, with a cotton gin, bank, hotel and a newspaper, the Grant Graphic. By 1930, 73 percent of Choctaw County's farmers were tenants.
EXTRA.note: Place story. It does not claim a Choctaw citizenship record for a named ancestor.
EXTRA.src: Grant, Oklahoma, Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grant,_Oklahoma)

EXTRA.name: 42nd Indiana Infantry
EXTRA.rel: Regiment of Daniel O'Neal (already in the app)
EXTRA.title: From Evansville to Perryville and Stones River
EXTRA.hook: Raised in October 1861 from six southwestern Indiana counties, the 42nd was in the field at Perryville within a year and at Stones River by New Year's.
body: The 42nd Indiana Infantry was organized at Evansville and mustered in for three years on October 9, 1861, under Colonel James Garrard Jones. Its men came from six counties of southwestern Indiana.

In the autumn of 1862 the regiment moved into Kentucky, pursued Bragg's army from October 1 to 15, and fought at the Battle of Perryville on October 8. One of its lieutenant colonels, Charles Harvey Denby, left after Perryville to command the 80th Indiana.

The regiment then returned to Nashville and advanced on Murfreesboro on December 30, 1862. At Stones River (December 30, 1862 to January 3, 1863) Lieutenant Colonel James M. Shanklin commanded and was surrounded and captured on 3 January 1863.
From January 1863 the regiment belonged to the XIV Corps, Army of the Cumberland.

Horrall gives the Perryville losses plainly. On the morning of 8 October 1862 the regiment "numbered less than five hundred effective men. The entire loss, officers and men, killed, wounded and missing, was 166, or fully one-third of the entire command." Company G, one of the largest, had 52 rank and file in the fight and lost 22 killed and wounded. The regiment's actual fighting, the book says, "was not to exceed two hours." Horrall writes that this was "the first general engagement the regiment was in, and its loss was by far the greatest of any of the succeeding ones."

At Stones River, on the morning of 31 December 1862, the regiment fought in the cedar woods beside the 15th Kentucky, whose colonel was killed. Company F's captain, William M. Cockrum, was wounded in the right shoulder, and his company's part in the day is told under "Captain Cockrum: Stones River to Libby Prison."
EXTRA.note: Regimental facts are documented. The connection to this family rests on Daniel O'Neal's service in the 42nd, covered in his own story.
EXTRA.src: Wikipedia, 42nd Indiana Infantry Regiment (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/42nd_Indiana_Infantry_Regiment); NPS Stones River people page (https://www.nps.gov/people/guest-joseph.htm); Horrall, History of the Forty-second Indiana (1892), pp. 153–154 (Perryville), 167–168 and 178–179 (Stones River)

EXTRA.name: 42nd Indiana Infantry
EXTRA.rel: Regiment of Daniel O'Neal (already in the app)
EXTRA.title: Chickamauga, reenlistment, and the road through Atlanta
EXTRA.hook: After Chickamauga and Missionary Ridge the regiment reenlisted and fought on to Atlanta, Savannah and Bentonville, losing 310 men in all.
body: At Chickamauga (September 19-21, 1863) the regiment was commanded by Lieutenant Colonel William T. B. McIntire. In November 1863 it fought at Lookout Mountain and Missionary Ridge.

The 42nd reenlisted on January 1, 1864, and served in the Atlanta Campaign from May 1 to September 8, 1864: Resaca (May 14-15), Kennesaw Mountain, Peachtree Creek (July 19-20), the Siege of Atlanta (July 22 to August 25) and Jonesboro (August 31 to September 1).

It went on to the March to the Sea, the siege of Savannah and the Carolinas, fighting at Bentonville March 19-21, 1865, and marched in the Grand Review at Washington on May 24, 1865. It mustered out at Louisville on July 21, 1865.
Total losses were 310: 113 killed or mortally wounded, and 197 dead of disease.

At Chickamauga the regiment lost "eight killed, fifty-three wounded, and thirty-two missing, making a total of ninety-three," nearly all the missing taken prisoner; Company F's captain was among them. Horrall describes the reenlistment that followed: the government "offered inducements to the men to re-enlist, or veteranize, on the first day of January, 1864," and "there were but few in the 42d Indiana who did not re-enlist." The regiment reached Indianapolis on 28 January 1864, where Governor Morton and others addressed a public reception, and the soldiers "became recruiting officers" to fill the ranks.

Company F paid for the Atlanta campaign in names: David W. Johnson (killed 14 August 1864), John Warick (7 August 1864) and David W. Wallam (31 May 1864, at Altoona or Allatoona). Horrall adds that he could not give the regiment's losses by name for the campaign, because "the day's and month's losses were reported in the aggregate, and not in detail." The last of Company F's dead, Lt. John Q. A. Steele, fell at Bentonville on 19 March 1865. See "Company F: the men around Daniel O'Neal."
EXTRA.note: Regimental history is documented. Daniel O'Neal's own dates of service should be checked against it.

EXTRA.name: Wright City, McCurtain County, Oklahoma
EXTRA.title: A company town built around a sawmill
EXTRA.hook: Wright City began about 1909 as a Dierks lumber company town, with the mill, houses, stores, bank and hotel all owned by the company.
body: The Choctaw Lumber Company, a subsidiary of Dierks Lumber and Coal, founded the town about 1909 beside a large timber-processing plant. Its first log was cut July 13, 1910, and a post office was chartered March 24, 1910. Renamed Wright City on May 18, 1920, it honors William Wiley Wright, the county's first war casualty.

The company supplied a sawmill, planer, railroad shops, housing, stores, a bank, a hotel, an ice factory and fire and police protection, and donated land for a school and churches. A company railroad ran from Valliant to De Queen, Arkansas.
Together the Wright City and Broken Bow mills could cut nearly 250,000 board feet of pine and 60,000 of hardwood a day. Workers struck for two months in 1947 and won an eight-cent hourly raise.
Weyerhaeuser bought the Dierks holdings in 1969, and the town incorporated in 1966. Its Little Cheyenne Rodeo dates to 1933.
EXTRA.note: Place history for the family's McCurtain County years. No record here names an ancestor who worked in the mills.

EXTRA.name: Families of the Regulators
EXTRA.title: The Oath, the Burned Fields, and the Road West
EXTRA.hook: For the families who stood at Alamance, the battle lasted an afternoon. What came after lasted years.
body: Governor William Tryon's militia of about 1,000 won the field on May 16, 1771. Casualty figures are disputed: 9 to 27 government dead, and perhaps 100 or more Regulators.

James Few was executed at the camp the next day. Twelve more prisoners were tried and sentenced to hang; six were pardoned at the last minute, and six were hanged at Hillsborough on June 19, 1771, among them Benjamin Merrill, Robert Matear, James Pugh and Captain Robert Messer.
Tryon then marched across Regulator country, burning homes and destroying crops. Residents were made to sign oaths of allegiance and surrender their firearms.

Many Regulators and their families moved west. Some went to Tennessee, where the Watauga Association formed in 1772 and the State of Franklin in 1784. Later study found that of 883 known Regulators only 34 became Loyalists, while 289 were Whigs.

quotes.t: Many Regulators and their families migrated westward, beyond North Carolina.
quotes.c: Summary of the aftermath of Alamance

EXTRA.note: Frames the westward chain the family followed. Whether a specific Moffitt signed the oath should be checked against the 1771 oath lists.
EXTRA.src: Wikipedia, Battle of Alamance; Wikipedia, Regulator Movement

EXTRA.name: Hugo, Choctaw Nation
EXTRA.rel: Choctaw County Oklahoma home area (place story)
EXTRA.title: A Town Born at a Railroad Crossing
EXTRA.hook: Hugo did not grow from a farm or a fort. It sprang up where two railroad lines crossed in the Choctaw Nation.
body: The Frisco built a north-south line through the area in 1887. In 1902 the St. Louis, San Francisco and New Orleans Railroad built a line from Hope, Arkansas, to Ardmore. The territorial town that sprang up at the crossing became Hugo.

It was founded in 1901 in Kiamitia County, part of the Pushmataha District of the Choctaw Nation, and named for the French novelist Victor Hugo. The name was suggested by the wife of surveyor W. H. Darrough, a fan of his books.
Agriculture, timber and ranching have been mainstays of the local economy since the start, which fits the family's timber work in Choctaw County.
In 1941 the Al G. Kelly and Miller Brothers Circus relocated to Hugo from Kansas, and for decades about twenty circuses at times wintered there.
EXTRA.note: Place story. Grady and the timber work are already in the app; this gives the town's setting. No specific mill is tied to our family here.

EXTRA.name: Etowah County, Alabama
EXTRA.title: The County That Had Two Names
EXTRA.hook: Etowah County was created under one name and renamed two years later, so records from the late 1860s can sit under either.
body: Before 1866 the area was split mainly between DeKalb and Cherokee counties.
On December 7, 1866, the first postwar legislature created Baine County, named for David W. Baine, a politician and Confederate officer who died in battle in 1862. Gadsden was made the county seat.
On December 1, 1868, after the 1868 constitutional convention abolished Baine County, the same boundaries became Etowah County, from a Cherokee-language word.
Anyone searching for family records of the period should look under DeKalb or Cherokee before 1866, Baine from 1866 to 1868, and Etowah afterward.
EXTRA.note: Place story with a practical research tip for the family; no named ancestor is tied to it here.
EXTRA.src: Wikipedia, Etowah County, Alabama (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etowah_County,_Alabama)

EXTRA.name: William Moffitt
EXTRA.title: Four documents, one name: William Moffitt in 1768
EXTRA.hook: In a single spring and autumn, William Moffitt's name went onto a petition, a committee list and the Governor's list of men too dangerous to pardon.
body: The Regulators kept their papers, and so did the royal government. William's year can be followed in print. On 30 April 1768 the Regulators issued their eighth Advertisement, and "William Maffet" is among the signers, alongside nearly the whole leadership. The meeting agreed to "send 12 men that we have chosen to meet on the said 11th day of May at Thomas Lindley's," the mill on Cane Creek.

The ninth Advertisement, the petition on public fees, carries roughly 450 names. "Wm Moffit" signs on page 734; a "James Moffitt" signs on page 737, probably a relative. Then on 21 May 1768, at George Sally's house, the Regulators chose a committee to collect their grievances and carry them to the Governor. The list begins "Wm Maffit." His name is first.

The Governor's answer came on 3 October 1768 at Hillsborough. His proclamation pardoned the insurgents except thirteen men, and "William Moffitt" is on the Council's list between Malachi Fyke and Christopher Nation. A general pardon of 9 September 1769 covered "all persons concerned in the said late Insurrection" and listed no exceptions; the pardon text does not say outright that it reached the thirteen.

His name does not appear in 1771. The reward proclamation outlawed only four men, and the sixteen men excepted from the June 1771 pardon include no Moffitt. Whether he stood on the field at Alamance on 16 May 1771 is not recorded.
In 1901 the boys' novel The Boy Spies with the Regulators printed Tryon's list, with "William Moffat" on it, as the names of "the patriots of upper Carolina in the opinion of William Tryon."

quotes.c: Regulators' Advertisement No. 10, 21 May 1768

EXTRA.name: William Moffitt
EXTRA.title: What William did after Alamance
EXTRA.hook: The records leave William out of the 1771 outlaw lists, and family accounts say he fed the Patriots rather than fought in the Revolution.
body: After the Regulators were beaten at Alamance in May 1771, the Governor outlawed four leaders and named sixteen more for exception from pardon. William is on neither list. He went home to the farm on Richland Creek.

A family history says he took the oath that followed Alamance, never to bear arms against the King, and stayed neutral in the Revolution because of it. No militia service record for him has been found. Instead, the family account and the Alamance Battleground Book of Remembrance both say he supplied provisions to the Patriots, and one compiled record cites a North Carolina pay voucher (no. 156) for provisions furnished.

The mill is where the sources disagree. The community of Moffitt, North Carolina, takes its name from the mill on Richland Creek, and a post office called Moffitt's Mills ran from 1823 to 1935. The state gazetteer credits Hugh Moffitt, William's probable brother, with the first mill. Family histories say William and Hugh built it together, and a Patriot record credits a James Moffitt of Brush Creek with "supplied sundries to the militia; ran Moffitt's Mill." That is likely another brother, and the vouchers have not been checked for the payee's name.
Be careful with the Roberts. A Patriot named Robert Moffitt, born 1762 of Brush Creek, is a different man, and his service should not be credited to William's son Robert.

A county history of Randolph County, 1779–1979, records the militia's first court meeting on 16 September 1801. Governor Caswell commissioned John Collier, Richard Owen and Joseph Shepherd as the regiment's officers, and the nine company captains were Shubal York, Joseph Smith, Dobson Burrow, Robert Redding, Samuel Moffitt, Colon Steed, John Brown, Charles Duncan and John Craven. A Samuel Moffitt among them is a lead only: no record seen ties him to William and Mary's household or to Hugh Moffitt's.
kv: Said by family history to have sworn after 1771; not seen in a record
EXTRA.note: The provisions claim rests on a family account and a compiled record; the voucher itself has not been seen. Whether William or Hugh or James ran the mill is unsettled. The Alamance book's statements about his birth in Donegal and burial at Richland Creek carry no citation.
