EXTRA.name: William and Mary (Davies) Moffitt
EXTRA.title: A wagon, a still and 250 acres: two Moffitt wills
EXTRA.hook: William's will of 1796 and Mary's of 1820 show a working farm: a wagon, a still, a new field on the river, and eight grown or growing children.
body: William's will begins "I William Moffitt of Randolph County in the province of North Carolina, being weak in body." He gave his sons Robert, William and David land, and his daughters Naomi (Neomi Macky), Catharine Cox, Hannah Cox, Mary Wilkinson and Margaret £3 each, with Margaret also getting cows, sheep and a bed.

Robert received the 250 acres William had bought of William Cox, except "the new field that is cleared upon the River," which his mother kept for life. William got the 225-acre plantation where his father lived, with a share reserved for Mary while she was a widow. David, who was clearly under age, got land on Tibs Run, wagon iron "brought from Pig River," and a quarter of a lot in Campbelltown in Cumberland County. If David died young, his brothers inherited and each sister would get £15.

"My Loveing Wife Mary Moffitt" received the wagon, the still, the plantation tools and the stock, and was named executrix with "my son Robart Moffitt" as executor. The witnesses were Hugh Moffitt and Charles Moffitt.

Mary outlived him by more than twenty years. She dated her own will "the 23rd day of the 9th month, 1820," in the Quaker style, naming the same five daughters and "my three sons," Robert, William and David. Her daughter Margaret was executrix and David executor, and William Cox and Stephen Cox witnessed. It was filed in 1822. Robert, her son and our ancestor, was alive in 1820.

quotes.t: my Loveing Wife Mary Moffitt Executrix & my son Robart Moffitt Executor
quotes.c: Will of William Moffitt, Randolph Co., N.C.

EXTRA.note: The last digit of William's will date is faint: one reading gives 1790, but the 1796 reading fits Robert as executor. Online trees give his death as 10 August 1797 or 1799; no record settles it. Mary's death is given as February 1822.
EXTRA.src: Will of William Moffitt (1796), Randolph Co. Will Book 2, pp. 30-31 (FamilySearch film 007640058); will of Mary Moffitt (1820, filed 1822)

EXTRA.name: Chamness, Norton, Moffitt and Davies
EXTRA.title: Two weddings at Cane Creek, sixteen days apart
EXTRA.hook: In the spring of 1763 the Cane Creek meetinghouse saw Joseph Chamness marry Margaret Norton and William Moffitt marry Mary Davies. Their children would marry each other in 1797.
body: Cane Creek Monthly Meeting was organized in 1751, with Anthony Chamness named its overseer. By 1763 the Chamnesses had been in North Carolina for fourteen years, since a transfer from Monocacy in Maryland to Carver's Creek Meeting in 1749, followed by a 490-acre grant on Cane Creek dated 24 June 1751.

On 17 March 1763 Anthony's son Joseph, born in Baltimore County, Maryland, married Margaret Norton, daughter of Edward and Elizabeth Norton, who had arrived from Virginia in 1762. Joseph became the meeting's recorder of marriage certificates. Margaret bore eleven children and died in 1784.

Sixteen days later, on 2 April 1763, William Moffitt, 23, married Mary Davies, 22, at the same meeting. Her father Charles Davies had crossed the Atlantic as a bound youth, married Hannah Matson of Merion in Pennsylvania in 1732 or 1733, and followed the Quaker migration south. He was recorded as a minister at Cane Creek in 1761 and was disowned by the meeting five years later, after complaining that the women's minutes were "mixed with an untruth." He bought 187 acres in Orange County on 2 August 1758 and died on 13 May 1801; Hannah died on 25 October 1812.

Margaret's daughter Martha was born in 1778. On 20 September 1797 she married Mary's son Robert at Centre Meeting, and the Chamness and Moffitt lines joined. Their son Nathan carried the Moffitt name to Arkansas.

The Chamness-Norton certificate itself is printed in Zimri Hanson's History and Genealogy of the American Descendants of John and Ann Chamness (1922, pp. 17-18). It reads: "Whereas, Joseph Chamness, son of Anthony Chamness and Sarah, his wife, of Orange County, in the Province of North Carolina, and Margaret Norton, daughter of Edward Norton and Elizabeth, his wife, of Rowan County; and Province aforesaid; having declared their intentions of Marriage with each other before several Monthly Meetings of the people called Quakers, held at Cane Creek, in Orange County, and Province aforesaid, according to the good order used amongst them, and having consent of parents, or parties concerned, their said proposals of marriage were allowed by said meeting." The day was "the Seventeenth day of the Third Month in the Year of Our Lord One Thousand Seven Hundred and Sixty-three," when the two stood up "in a public meeting of the said people, held at their meeting house at Cane Creek" and each promised "with Divine Assistance" to be a faithful and loving spouse until death.

Beneath the signatures of "Joseph Chamness" and "Margaret Chamness," twelve witnesses signed: "John Marshall, Joseph Pike, William Piggott, John Stout, John Davis, William Marshall," and, in the second column, "Thomas Branson, Anthony Chamness, Edward Norton, Sarah Chamness, Elizabeth Norton, Elizabeth Chamness." Hanson comments: "We note, also, the parents of Joseph and Margaret and his oldest sister all signed the certificate." So the page carries the names of all four grandparents of Martha Chamness, who would marry Robert Moffitt in 1797: Anthony and Sarah Chamness, and Edward and Elizabeth Norton. Hanson adds that Joseph was made recorder of marriage certificates in 1764 and that the meeting's records from then until 1769, when he moved into Providence Meeting in Randolph County, "must be" in his writing.

EXTRA.name: Robert Moffitt and Martha Chamness
EXTRA.title: Robert and Martha: nine children in Randolph County
EXTRA.hook: Married at Centre Meeting in 1797, Robert and Martha Moffitt raised nine children in Randolph County, and two of them left North Carolina for Missouri.
body: Robert Moffitt's marriage is in the Quaker record as "1797, 9, 20. Robert, s William & Mary, Randolph Co., m Martha Chamness." Martha, born 6 October 1778 in Guilford County, was the daughter of Joseph Chamness and Margaret Norton and the granddaughter of Anthony Chamness.

Robert had been named executor of his father William's will the year before and inherited the 250 acres his father had bought of William Cox. He was alive when his mother made her will in 1820, and appears in the 1830 and 1840 censuses of Randolph County.

Their children, all born in Randolph County, were Naomi (1800), Sarah (1801), David (1802), William C. (1803), Aaron (1805), Hannah, Lydia (1811), Nathan (1814) and Robert (1815). Robert, the youngest, died at Hutton Valley, Howell County, Missouri, in 1872. Sarah died at Lorimor, Iowa, in 1860, so Nathan was not the only child to leave. Martha lived to 1865.
kv: Naomi, Sarah, David, William C., Aaron, Hannah, Lydia, Nathan, Robert
EXTRA.note: The marriage and Robert's parentage come from the Quaker record. The children's list and Martha's parents come from compiled Quaker abstracts. Online memorials give Robert's birth as 6 October 1778 and his death as 6 October 1844, which is Martha's birth date copied over; as executor in 1796 he was probably born by about 1775. Martha's death is given as 11 October or 11 November 1865. Two other Robert Moffitts lived nearby and are not him.
EXTRA.src: Hinshaw, Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy, vol. 1 (Centre MM); wills of William (1796) and Mary Moffitt (1820); 1830 and 1840 U.S. Censuses, Randolph Co., N.C.; WikiTree Moffitt-108 and Chamness-49

EXTRA.name: Nathan H. Moffitt
EXTRA.title: Nathan the wheelwright, and a son in blue
EXTRA.hook: Nathan's census trail runs from Randolph County to Arkansas to Missouri, and one of his sons served as a Union cavalryman while the Moffitts' own Ozark neighbors were choosing sides.
body: Nathan married Rebecca Williams on 13 October 1835 in Randolph County, North Carolina, and he is in the 1840 census of the county's South Division. A son, Calvin, was born there on 4 December 1841. By 1850 the family was farming in Strawberry Township, Lawrence County, Arkansas.

Lawrence County in the 1850s was a mix of small farms, a county seat at Smithville, and 494 enslaved people among 8,875 white residents in 1860. By then Nathan was a wheelwright with $1,200 in land. Patrick was born in May 1853 and Henry in 1855. The war brought jayhawkers and bushwhackers to the county, though no major battle. Some residents joined the Federal side, and Nathan's son Calvin V. Moffitt did: the National Park Service database lists him as a private in Company L, 4th Arkansas Cavalry (Union). He was later at Duncan, Oklahoma, where he died on 13 February 1913.

By 1870 Nathan and Rebecca were in Dent County, Missouri, farming with no land of their own. Oregon County, where they next lived, was largely pro-Southern and suffered raids; its Alton courthouse burned in October 1863, and the historical marker adds that Lee's surrender "did not end the Civil War in Oregon County." Rebecca died there in 1871. That year Nathan married a widow, Nancy (Rowe) Cole.
Nathan died on 23 December 1873 in Oregon County. That August his son Patrick had married Alice Ann Cole there. A photograph labeled "Nathan Moffitt," shown with children, is kept in the family tree.

Nathan's brothers and sisters spread widely: Sarah and Naomi to Iowa, Robert to Strawberry Township and then Howell County, Missouri, and Hannah, Lydia, Aaron and William C. stayed in Randolph County. Aaron's son Veno Moffitt died in 1864 as a Confederate prisoner at Elmira.

Calvin's regiment, the 4th Arkansas Cavalry (Union), was organized at Little Rock in December 1863, and Company L, the company the NPS database gives him, was made up in Montgomery County, far from Lawrence County. Whether the National Park Service entry belongs to this Calvin remains a lead. Company L's petition of March 1864 and the regiment's scouts are told under "The 4th Arkansas Cavalry: Union men from the Ouachita hills."
EXTRA.note: Calvin's service is proved by the NPS soldier record; that he is Nathan's son comes from a family-tree profile. Patrick is given as born 11 May 1853 at Sylamore and as dying on 20 December 1905 at Mountain View in one source, and as dying in November 1904 and buried at Sallisaw in another. Who burned the Alton courthouse is disputed: the marker says Union troops, a 2024 survey says Southern partisans.
EXTRA.src: 1840 U.S. Census, Randolph Co., N.C.; 1850 and 1860 Censuses, Lawrence Co., Ark.; 1870 Census, Dent Co., Mo.; NC Marriages, Randolph Co. (1835); Missouri Marriages (1871); NPS Civil War Soldiers database; Encyclopedia of Arkansas, 'Lawrence County'; Alton marker (HMDB 179894); WikiTree Moffitt-107, Moffitt-400

EXTRA.name: Henry and Hannah (Grimes) Moffitt
EXTRA.title: 1901: a death in Mountain View and 22 years of widowhood
EXTRA.hook: Henry died at 46 in the Stone County hills. Hannah, who could not read or write, kept the family together for another two decades.
body: Stone County was only 28 years old when Henry died. It was created in 1873, and Mountain View, its seat, had 99 residents in 1880, was incorporated on 14 August 1890, and got its first wooden courthouse in 1888. Henry, a farmer who owned his land free and clear in the 1900 census, died there in 1901 at 46. Family records give the date as 9 September. No grave has been found and he has no memorial anywhere; Arkansas did not register deaths in Stone County until 1914.
The same spring, on 26 May 1901, Henry's brother Patrick lost his wife, Alice Ann (Cole) Moffitt, who is buried at Levisy Flat Cemetery in Stone County.

Hannah stayed. In 1910 she was renting a house in Franklin Township with Tom, who worked as a railroad section hand, and Grady, who made barrel staves. She had borne seven children and six were living: among them Josephine, Jesse, Gimsa, Bertha, Tom and Grady. Jesse Gee Moffitt went to Texas and died in Amarillo in 1957; Tom died in Paris, Texas, in 1953.

She spent her last years at Herpel, a Rocky Bayou community six miles east of Mountain View with a grist mill, cotton gin, stave mill and sawmill by the early 1900s. Its post office opened in 1907, and the Herpel Missionary Baptist Church laid its cornerstone on 5 March 1923. Hannah died there on 4 April 1923, about a month later, and is buried in Herpel Cemetery, where her stone reads "Wife of Henry H Moffitt."
kv: Hannah, Herpel Cemetery; Henry's grave not found
EXTRA.note: Henry's exact death date comes from family records and no original has been seen. The Stone County Record newspapers for September 1901 would be the likeliest check. Bertha May Moffitt Barham (1888-1930), buried at Herpel, may be a daughter but is not proved.
EXTRA.src: 1900 and 1910 U.S. Censuses, Franklin Twp., Stone Co., Ark.; Find a Grave (Hannah Moffitt, Herpel Cemetery; Alice Ann Moffitt, Levisy Flat; Jesse Gee and Thomas Berry Moffitt); Encyclopedia of Arkansas, 'Stone County' and 'Herpel'

EXTRA.name: Grady and Mary Moffitt
EXTRA.title: Nine children, a timber camp and a rented house in Hugo
EXTRA.hook: Grady and Mary raised nine children through Ervin, Wilson, West Texas and Hugo, and buried three of them.
body: Grady and Mary married about 1914. Their first son, Alvin, was born in September 1915. In 1917 Grady's draft card puts him at Ervin, Oklahoma, a place that existed only from 1904 to 1922, as a timberman for C. D. Neese. Which sawmill that was is not recorded. The county's biggest one was the Pine Belt Lumber Company at Fort Towson, begun in 1902.

Hugo was a young town. It was founded in 1901 where the Frisco's north-south line crossed the Arkansas & Choctaw, and the Frisco depot went up in 1914. Grady's family rented there at 411 North H Street by 1940.

The children, with the dates family trees give, were Alvin B. (1915-1994, U.S. Army Air Corps in World War II), Odas Eugene (1918-1995; "Odis" in the census, and "Ottis" in 1920), Dois L. (1921-1947), Jimmie Gaynell (1923-1926), John Winfred (1925-1990), the twins Alton V. (1928-1975) and Eldon Herman (1928-2014), Donald K. (1931-2014) and Henry Wayne (1934-1937). The two toddlers who died were three years old.

In 1930, with six boys, they were living with Mary's parents, John Morgan and Lizzie Shackleford, in Martin County, Texas. That is the county where Mary's father is buried. In 1940 Grady, 48, had been out of work for 50 weeks and earned $100.

Grady's brother Tom farmed beside him in 1920 and later lived in Paris, Texas, where he died in 1953, with a stone marked WW I and WW II. Their brother Jesse is buried at Tahoka, Texas. Grady and Mary lie at Shoat Springs Cemetery near Hugo.
The Shoat Springs transcription confirms the full dates for the two children who died young: Jimmie Gaynell, 17 January 1923 to 26 October 1926, and Henry Wayne, 13 January 1934 to 12 May 1937.
kv: Dois L. 1921-1947; Jimmie Gaynell 17 Jan 1923 - 26 Oct 1926; Henry Wayne 13 Jan 1934 - 12 May 1937; Grady and Mary 1891-1972 and 1895-1962

In the 1940 household, Alton and Eldon are both born in 1928, which fits the twins aged 11 shown there. Hugo's founding and the Frisco depot date are from the Oklahoma Historical Society; Grady's own connection to any particular mill is unknown.

EXTRA.name: John Morgan and Lizzie (Newton) Shackleford
EXTRA.title: Mary's people: from Etowah County to Texas and Oklahoma
EXTRA.hook: Mary Tinsley Shackleford's parents married in Etowah County, Alabama, in 1889, and their six living children scattered from West Texas to California.
body: John Morgan Shackleford was born on 30 September 1862 in Alabama and married Catherine Elizabeth "Lizzie" Newton on 1 December 1889 in Etowah County. Etowah County had been created only 21 years before, and for two of those years, 1866 to 1868, it was called Baine County. In the 1900 census at Gilbert, John was 37 and Elizabeth 28, with five living children. Mary, born 4 June 1895, was the "May, 5."

Her siblings were Balis Anthony (1892-1982, who died in Los Angeles County), Robert Yates (1897-1961), John Newton (1906-2002), Hazel Marzee King (1908-1980), Edward Richard (1910-1988) and Helen Elizabeth Josey (1915-1997). Their son John Newton's name confirms the mother's maiden name.

By 1930 John Morgan was in Martin County, Texas, with his wife and children; Grady and Mary and their six boys were living with them. John died on 22 May 1930 and is buried at Evergreen Cemetery in Stanton. Lizzie died on 8 November 1951 and is buried at Fairview Cemetery, Apache, Caddo County, Oklahoma.

The Shackelfords of Virginia trace to an immigrant, Roger, who received a grant in Gloucester County in 1658. A Shackleford family history of 1940 says the family had no coat of arms, and Mary's descent from Roger is not proved.

The 1900 census household at Gilbert lists John, 37, Elizabeth, 28, and five children: "Balous" 8, Myrtle 6, May 5, Robert 3 and Eddie 8 months. Two later obituaries (Chico Enterprise-Record, 23 June 1961; Lamar County Echo, 1 January 1981) name sisters Josephine Haskell, Eulah Tillman and Beulah Hutchins who do not fit that list. Hazel was born at Rattan in Delta County, Texas, so the family was in northeast Texas about 1908 before reaching Martin County.

EXTRA.name: John Winfred Moffitt
EXTRA.title: ARD-19: the drydock that could not sail
EXTRA.hook: John's first ship had no engines, was 488 feet long, and was hit by a Japanese fighter while it held a damaged destroyer.
body: ARD-19 was a floating drydock built by the Pacific Bridge Company at Alameda, California, in 1943-44. It was about 488 feet long, 81 feet wide and 5,200 tons, with two 40 mm and two 20 mm gun mounts. It had no engines, so it was towed. Its work was to lift destroyers, minesweepers and landing ships out of the water at forward bases so their hulls could be repaired close to the fighting.

It was commissioned on 22 March 1944, the day John's muster rolls begin. It was towed across the Pacific in stages to join Service Squadron 10, the Navy's mobile base force, and reached Seeadler Harbor at Manus in the Admiralty Islands at the end of August 1944. In November it moved up to San Pedro Bay, Leyte.

The destroyer USS Ross had hit two Japanese mines off Dinagat and Homonhon on 19 October 1944, killing three men and leaving twenty missing. She was docked in ARD-19 on 24 November. Shortly before noon on 27 or 28 November (the two ship histories differ), a Japanese Army fighter crashed into the dock, starting gasoline fires that spread to Ross. Gunfire from ARD-19, Ross and LST-556 shot down a second fighter that was strafing them. The damage was heavy but kept the dock busy with its own repairs "for only a brief time." ARD-19 earned one battle star for Leyte, for 10-29 November 1944.

ARD-19 then carried on repair work at Subic Bay on Luzon "until after the end of World War II." Later its life was long: it was recommissioned in 1963 as USS Oak Ridge to dock ballistic-missile submarines and served until 2001.

On a crew of about 130 there was usually no doctor, and one or two corpsmen ran sick call. On a repair dock that meant burns, crushed hands and welding-flash eye injuries. That is general practice for such ships, and John's exact rate and duties are not recorded; his service file would give them.

EXTRA.name: John Winfred Moffitt
EXTRA.title: USS Chief: minesweepers, Nagoya and home
EXTRA.hook: John's second ship had already swept the mines ahead of Saipan, then spent the first postwar winter keeping Japanese waters clear.
body: USS Chief (AM-315) was an 890-ton Auk-class minesweeper commissioned on 9 October 1943. In June 1944 she swept mines ahead of the Saipan and Tinian landings. She was at Okinawa from late May to late August 1945. In September she swept minefields at Wakayama, Japan, ahead of the occupation forces and helped salvage the minesweeper YMS-418.

John's muster rolls on Chief begin on 1 December 1945 or 1 January 1946, so he joined her after the war, on occupation duty at Nagoya and Sasebo, which lasted until March 1946. Where he joined her is unknown; he may have come aboard in the Philippines or in Japan.

In March 1946 Chief sailed for San Francisco and arrived in April. John was discharged on 9 May 1946, and the rolls run to 31 May, a gap that is probably just how the muster index records report dates. In 1947 he married Faye Smith, on 12 June at Paris, Texas.
Chief went out of commission in reserve at San Pedro on 17 March 1947, was recommissioned for the Korean War, and was sold to Mexico in 1973 as ARM Jesus Gonzalez Ortega.
EXTRA.note: The muster index labels this ship MCM 14, which is a 1990s ship named after her; a 1946 roll can only be AM-315. The photograph is the ship in 1952, not in John's time.

EXTRA.name: John C. and Samantha (Johnson) Satterfield
EXTRA.title: From Morgantown to Soper: the Satterfield road
EXTRA.hook: Samantha Johnson married a widower with three children at about 20, raised eight more, moved the family to Texas, and ended her life in Choctaw County, Oklahoma.
body: Samantha D. "Mantha" Johnson was born on 28 March 1872 in Kentucky, a daughter of Melvina (Clark) Johnson. In 1892 she married John C. Satterfield, a widower with three children: Henry B. (born May 1883), Martha A. (August 1884) and John W. (January 1887).

The first six of their eight children were born in Kentucky. Wavey Lincoln arrived at Morgantown, in Butler County, on 28 December 1895 by his draft cards (his stone says 9 January 1896); Artie Pearl followed in August 1898. In 1900 they were farming at Horse Mill,. Joseph, an early son, died before 1910.

About 1907 the family moved to Franklin County, Texas. In April 1910 John, 46, was renting a farm at Hagansport with Wavey, Pearl, James, Ira and Stella, and a last child was born there in 1912. John died in Franklin County between 1912 and 1916; there is no grave record.

On 28 July 1917 Samantha married Bird Alexander "Alex" Stephens, a widower, at Mount Vernon, Texas, and they crossed the Red River into Choctaw County, Oklahoma. Wavey Lincoln served as a private in the Army in the first World War and died at Soper in 1952. Samantha died on 1 October 1928 and is buried as Samantha D. Stephens at Soper Cemetery. Her daughter Artie Pearl married Charles Oscar Smith in 1914, and they lie at Grant Cemetery.
kv: About 1907, Butler Co., Ky. to Franklin Co., Tex.
EXTRA.note: John's death is given as 1919 in family trees but a family biography places it between 1912 and 1916, and he is absent by Samantha's 1917 remarriage. Most details about Samantha come from a Find a Grave biography written by a Stephens family member; the 1892 marriage record itself has not been seen.

EXTRA.name: Joel J. Thompson
EXTRA.title: Joel Thompson tells it in Hugo, 1937
EXTRA.hook: At 45, Joel Thompson sat down with a WPA interviewer and described the log house, the deer, the court and the schools of his boyhood.
body: On 28 August 1937 a field worker named Hazel B. Greene took down Joel Thompson's story at his home, 508 North G Street in Hugo, for the Works Progress Administration's Indian-Pioneer History project. Joel was born on 29 January 1892, 'about 2 miles west of High Hill Methodist Church,' the son of Joseph P. Thompson and Betsy Tims. The form notes that his father 'was second of nine children.'

He named the brothers and sisters who lived to be grown: Alex B., then himself, Peter Pitchlyn, Simon W., Joseph W., Jincy, who married Wilson Aaron, a full-blood Choctaw, and Marietta, who married Stephen Caldwell, also a full-blood. The family also raised an orphan boy, Wister Davis, from the time he was twelve. Our Simon is the fourth name on that list.

His picture of the place is plain and specific. The family finished school and Sunday school in the High Hill church house, and Joel got through the seventh grade there. The 1901 house had chimneys at each end, made of 'mudcats, or stick and dirt above the fireplaces which were made of native rocks.' Doaksville, where they got their mail and did their trading, was eight miles south by a very sandy road. Corinne was three miles north 'over the mountain,' which was easier once a store opened there.

He also remembered what his people did when someone was sick. Before white doctors came, and sometimes after, the family used Choctaw healers, who boiled tobacco in a pot set in a hole, spread a sheet over it, and laid the patient across the steam with the aching place directly above the pot.

Joel was 45 and said plainly what he could not recall, such as the maiden names of his grandmothers. Where his account can be checked against the Dawes cards and other records, it mostly holds up. Where it cannot (his father's years as judge and senator, the Massachusetts college), it is still the only account.

EXTRA.name: The Thompson allotments
EXTRA.title: Choosing the land, 1903
EXTRA.hook: Joseph Thompson went to Atoka in 1903 and picked out the family's homesteads, including a 160-acre quarter for his four-year-old son Simon.
body: The family applied for Choctaw enrollment on 1 May 1899 and the Secretary of the Interior approved it on 12 December 1902. The next step was land. In the fall of 1903 Joseph P. Thompson gave testimony at Atoka, where the Commission to the Five Civilized Tribes took the selections, naming tracts for his wife and children.

For Betsy he selected a homestead of Lots 3 and 4 and the south half of the northwest quarter of Section 4, Township 5 South, Range 19 East, about 160 acres valued at $519.71. In November 1903 he added the northwest quarter of Section 9 in the same township, another 160 acres valued at $520. Her Certificate of Allotment is No. 4179.

Simon, then four years old, received his homestead on 2 October 1903: the northeast quarter of Section 11, Township 5 South, Range 19 East, 160 acres valued at $520. Further tracts were selected for him in November 1903, March 1904 and October 1907, and his citizenship certificate was issued at Hugo on 6 December 1907. A younger child enrolled as a 'new born' under the Act of 3 March 1905 has a separate card, No. 1410. Ella, who died in May 1899, was dismissed from the roll and received no land.

Allotments were held under federal restrictions, so the owners had to ask permission to sell or free their land. Joseph's petition was filed on 27 August 1908, when he was at Fort Towson. He filed again from Corinne on 10 September 1915, and the Secretary of the Interior approved removal of restrictions on 28 March 1916. Betsy's report was filed on 29 March 1920 from 'R.F.D. #1, Box 45, Corinne'; it was approved on 30 April and the order removing restrictions was mailed to her on 11 May 1920.

EXTRA.name: Ella N. Thompson
EXTRA.title: Three weeks in the spring of 1899
EXTRA.hook: The family applied for enrollment on 1 May 1899. Simon was born on 4 May and his five-year-old sister Ella died on 22 May.
body: Ella was the third child of Joseph and Betsy Thompson to be listed on the Choctaw rolls. She appears on the 1896 census of Cedar County as 'Ella,' and on Dawes Card 1283 as 'Thompson, Ella N.,' a daughter, age 5, three-quarter blood.

The family made its application on 1 May 1899. Three days later Betsy gave birth to Simon, with her mother Emeline as midwife. On 22 May, Ella died. The card says so in plain words: 'No. 5 Died May 22, 1899.' The evidence of her death was not filed until 18 April 1901.

Because she had died before the enrollment was approved, her name was struck. A purple stamp on the card reads that 'No. 5 hereon dismissed under order of the Commission to the Five Civilized Tribes of March 31, 1905.' She received no allotment, but she is on the card with her parents and brothers.

The affidavits about her death are in the jacket. On 13 April 1901 at Doaksville, Joseph P. Thompson, then 39, swore that he was the father of "Ella N. Thompson" and that she "died on 22 day of May 1899." A second affidavit, as an acquaintance, was sworn the same day by Robert Tims, 26, her mother's brother; both were sworn before the notary R. L. Carter of Doaksville. The Commission had written to Joseph on 9 March 1901 that it "has information of the death of your daughter" and sent a blank form, and on 18 April it acknowledged "your affidavit and that of Robert Tims, relative to the death of your daughter, Ella N. Thompson, which occurred May 22, 1899."

EXTRA.name: James Brown "Jimmie" Tims
EXTRA.title: Betsy's brother on Merchants Row
EXTRA.hook: Betsy's brother sat in the Choctaw Council, and in 1937 he described his grandfather's store at Doaksville, in front of the old rock jail.
body: James Brown Tims, called Jimmie, was a son of Vinson and Emeline Tims and Betsy's elder brother. Joel Thompson remembered that when his father Joseph served as county judge and then senator, 'James Brown Tims was a Representative in the Choctaw Council.' Joel said the Tims family was 'quite prominent in public affairs.'

Jimmie gave an Indian-Pioneer interview in 1937, the same year as his nephew Joel. A local history of the Tims family says he described his parents, Vinson and Emeline, and the stand of V. B. Tims on Merchants Row in Doaksville, in front of the old rock jail, whose foundations can still be seen. (The history does not say whether he meant his grandfather Vincent or his father Vinson.) An article on Cedar County's Choctaw name, Chuala, 'cedar,' from Big Cedar Creek, also cites his interview.

The jail is still there in outline. Visitors to the Doaksville site today walk past capped stone wells, a few foundations and the outlines of three jail cells. His brother Mitchell Tims (1869-1950) is buried at High Hill Cemetery near the old home place. By 1910 a James Tims household, probably his, was among the Thompsons' nearest neighbors in Wilson Township.

In September 1941 the Methodist Indian Mission of Oklahoma printed his memoir in the minutes of its annual session at Ware's Chapel, near Anadarko, and it supplies what no other record does: "James Brown Tims was born eight miles north of Ft. Towson, in what was then known as Doaksville, Indian Territory, on June 25, 1864. He was seventy-seven years of age at the time of his departure." That puts his death between 25 June and the conference of 12-14 September 1941. The memoir was signed by the Rev. Johnson W. Bobb, superintendent of the Choctaw District.

"Brother Tims was better known among the Choctaws as J. B. Tims. Of him it can be said: He loved everybody and everybody loved him." He began as a class leader and later became a local deacon in the Methodist Church, "preached to and led his people in the Christian way for about forty-five years," and served the Antlers Circuit for eleven of them. "Very influential among his people, Brother Tims always stood for right living and for Christian Education. At one time he was a member of the Choctaw Council." That last line is the same office his nephew Joel Thompson gave him in 1937.

The conference rolls show him at work. 'James B. Tims' is on the list of local deacons of the Choctaw District in 1934, 1935 and 1936, and the 1940 session at Hampton's Chapel lists "Tims, J. B., L.D., Rt. 1, Ft. Towson." A memorial roll printed in later minutes puts his name under 1940, but its own footnote warns that it contains errors, and the memoir's age of 77 fits 1941.

The Dawes cards give Jimmie's household in 1899. Card 510 lists "Tims, James B.," age 36, one-half Choctaw, Roll No. 1035, of Towson County, post office Alikchi. His parents are written as "Vinson W. Tims," dead, and "Emeline Tims," and the card notes that he was on the 1896 roll as "Jas. B. Tims." His wife, "Mary J.," 31, full-blood, is the daughter of Dixon Willis and Elizabeth Willis, both dead. Their children on the card are Evelyn, Dixon and Rufus (Rufus an infant of five months when they applied on 18 April 1899).

Twins followed. On 27 August 1901 the Commission wrote that it had the application for "Lewie Tims and Lula Tims, twin children of James B. and Mary J. Tims, born July 19, 1901," and sent two forms because each child needed a separate application. Lula died on 19 January 1902 at about six months. On 30 October 1902 the Commission acknowledged "your affidavit and that of Mary J. Tims relative to the death of your minor daughter, Lula Tims," and the card carries a red-ink note that her enrollment was cancelled in 1904. Lowie was enrolled as Roll No. 1041.

A Methodist missions catalogue of 1919 lists him among the Indian pastors the Southern church helped to support. In the Board of Missions' appeal, "J. B. Tims, Bruno Circuit (part support)" appears with a grant of $40 a year, in a list that also includes Wewoka, Chickasaw, Jesse, LeFlore and McCurtain circuits. The memoir of 1941 says he later spent eleven years on the Antlers Circuit.

EXTRA.name: Doaksville to Corinne
EXTRA.title: Where the Thompsons got their mail
EXTRA.hook: Joseph and Betsy's addresses on the records move from Doaksville to Fort Towson to Corinne as the post offices changed around them.
body: On the 1899 enrollment card the family's post office is Doaksville, Indian Territory, in Cedar County. Joel Thompson said Doaksville was about eight miles south of the home place, and that the family did 'all of our trading' there. A faint pencil note added in April 1905 changes it to 'Ft. Towson, I.T.' The Doaksville post office had closed in 1903, when the name became Fort Towson.

Corinne, three miles north 'over the mountain,' was more convenient. Its post office opened on 24 August 1904 and ran until 1958; it was named for Corinne Estill Lesueur, the daughter of a Confederate officer who later became Missouri's secretary of state. By September 1915 Joseph was writing from Corinne. In September 1918 Simon, 19, gave his work on his draft card as farmer for his father at Corinne. In 1920 Betsy's address was 'R.F.D. #1, Box 45, Corinne.'

In the 1910 census the family is recorded in Wilson Township of Choctaw County, which was formed at statehood in 1907 from parts of Cedar, Towson and other old counties. They had not moved far; the county and post office names changed around them.

EXTRA.name: Peter Pitchlynn Thompson
EXTRA.title: Peter, the brother just older than Simon
EXTRA.hook: Joel's interview lists his brother as 'Peter Pitchlyn,' the same name as a famous Choctaw principal chief.
body: Joel Thompson's list of his brothers includes 'Peter Pitchlyn,' and Dawes Card 1283 lists the boy as 'Peter P.,' roll No. 3491, age 2 in 1899, three-quarter blood. On the 1896 census he was entered as 'Peter B.,' probably a clerk's slip. He was the brother just older than Simon.
The name matches Peter Pitchlynn, a principal chief of the Choctaw Nation during Joseph's boyhood. The interview does not say whether the boy was named for him.
Peter P. Thompson (1896-1979) is listed in the High Hill Cemetery transcription, near the church where the family worshipped and went to school.

The Methodist Indian Mission's conference minutes follow a Peter Thompson of Fort Towson for nearly thirty years. In 1938 the list of church school superintendents for the Choctaw District includes "Peter Thompson, Ft. Towson, Okla." and, a line below, "Mitchell Tims, Ft. Towson, Okla.," Peter's uncle. In 1940 Peter Thompson is a lay delegate for the Rufe Circuit, and the lists for 1947 and 1948 read "High Hill . . . Pete Thompson, Fort Towson." Pete Thompson of the Rufe Circuit is still named as a lay delegate in 1952, 1955 and 1965.
The minutes give no middle initial, so this is probably, not certainly, Joseph and Betsy's son. The Fort Towson address, the High Hill church and his burial at High Hill all point to him.

EXTRA.name: High Hill
EXTRA.rel: The Thompsons' church, school and cemetery
EXTRA.title: High Hill: church, school and cemetery
EXTRA.hook: Betsy's parents are remembered at the old place, the Thompsons went to church and school in the High Hill church house, and several of the family are listed in the cemetery.
body: Joel Thompson remembered High Hill as a Methodist church where 'they had school in the church house for many years.' His father sat on the school board and the children went to school and Sunday school there 'all of our lives.' The 1901 house stood within 300 yards, and in camp-meeting weeks the Thompsons had 'lots of company,' with whole deer, hogs and turkeys barbecued for the crowd.

Betsy was married at her parents' home about four miles north and a little west of Doaksville, in Towson County, the place later known as the Charley Blankenship place. Joel said his grandparents Vinson and Emeline Tims were 'buried there at the old place.' The cemetery roster for High Hill, three miles east of the junction of the Spencerville Road and State Highway 147 and half a mile south, lists Peter P. Thompson (1896-1979), Mitchell Tims (1869-1950), and Emeline Steadman Tims (1842-1918). Vinson's marker there is a cenotaph.

The name is a puzzle. No outside source has been found that names a 'High Hill Methodist Church' in Choctaw County, and another High Hill, two miles south of Alderson in Pittsburg County, appears in a different WPA interview, so the two should not be confused. For this family, High Hill rests on Joel's memory, the cemetery roster and the Find a Grave memorials for Emeline, Vinson and Peter.

High Hill was a church of the Methodist Indian Mission of Oklahoma, on the Rufe Circuit. The 1941 report of the Choctaw District lists the churches "in Choctaw county: High Hill, Hampton Chapel, Honey Spring, Pecan Groves, Kullichito," and the church school superintendents' lists from 1942 to 1948 give High Hill first to Willie S. Tims and then to Pete Thompson, both of Fort Towson. The 1943 minutes call the burying ground the "High Hill Indian Cemetery, north of Fort Towson."

Its neighbor, Hampton's Chapel, which the minutes call "the Church in the Wild Woods," ten miles north of Fort Towson, hosted the whole conference on 13-15 September 1940, with the Rev. Edgar Tims as host pastor. The same book lists Betsy's brother Mitchell Tims of Fort Towson among the Choctaw District's church school superintendents, as the 1938 and 1939 lists do, and puts Betsy's brothers J. B. Tims and Robert J. Tims on the roll of local deacons.

EXTRA.name: The Choctaw names on the cards
EXTRA.title: Names on the cards
EXTRA.hook: Ata-sa-ha-bi, Lotima, O-we-na, Te-hol-ba-ta-bi, Brazil and Siney appear on the Dawes cards as the parents of our enrolled ancestors.
body: The Dawes cards name parents who did not themselves enroll, because they were dead by 1899. Card 1363 gives Legion Austin's father as Ata-sa-ha-bi and his mother as Lotima, both dead and both of Towson County. It gives Molsey Austin's parents as Brazil and Siney, both dead, of Red River. Emeline Tims's mother, O-we-na, was Choctaw of Towson County, and Nancy Te-hol-ba-ta-bi is the Mississippi-born name on another line of the family.

The names tell something about the Choctaw naming practice. A linguist, Ovid Vickers, wrote that in old Mississippi names were 'nearly always connotative,' earned by deeds, and that 'a great proportion of those who had earned second names as a result of participation in a war were given names carrying the termination abi signifying killer.' Surnames such as Thompson, Austin and Gardner were adopted after 1830, often from the given name of a respected white man.

Pisachubbe, Te-hol-ba-ta-bi and Ata-sa-ha-bi all look like names of this kind, ending in the war-name element. Their exact meanings are not recorded, and the Choctaw Nation's language staff cautions against reading the ending 'killer.' O-we-na is a Choctaw given name, meaning unknown. Joel Thompson said his father's mother's family 'had some sort of a Choctaw name' and 'never adopted a white man's name,' the same pattern from another line.

EXTRA.name: William Moffitt
EXTRA.title: The Act nobody could find
EXTRA.hook: In the Regulators' own account of how their movement began, William Moffit is the man who went through the laws and found no such Act as the deputy sheriff claimed.
body: In May 1768 the Regulators' committee wrote out a plain account of their quarrel with the Orange County officers, to carry to the Governor with their petition. In the Colonial Records it is Regulators' Advertisement No. 11, and it runs from page 759 to page 766 of volume 7. Midway through comes a scene at a tax meeting on Deep River, William Moffitt's own neighborhood.

The High Sheriff, Mr. Harris, had published an advertisement citing an Act of the Assembly as the authority for the tax, and many paid but disputed the authority of the Act. At the meeting, the committee wrote, Deputy Sheriff John Wood, "being questioned about the Act confidently persisted in the affirmative. Upon which William Moffit on examining the Laws, no such Act could be found, Wood now finding his knavery was detected, no less confidently denied the Advertisement to be Harris's." The sentence is clumsy in print, but its sense is plain: William looked through the laws, the Act was not there, and the deputy then denied that the advertisement was the sheriff's at all.

The committee drew its own moral. "This unprecedented Effrontery, convinced the Spectators that there was Knavery, and Collusion," and, judging the whole business of a piece, they "formed themselves into Bodies under the denomination of Regulators." By the committee's account, it was this scene that led the neighborhood to organize.

William's name is at the foot of the document. It closes "Signed in behalf and by Order of the Regulators by us the Committee," over eight names: John Low, James Hunter, Rednap Howell, Harmon Cox, John Marshel, W. Cox, W. Moffitt and George Hendry. A second paper, dated at Thomas Cox's mill on Monday 30 May 1768, orders the narrative carried to the Governor and Council by James Hunter and Rednap Howell, and William Moffitt signs that one too (pages 766-767).

He had known the Cox family on Deep River for years. A Cox family history, citing Orange County court records, says William Moffitt proved a deed from Thomas Cox to Jacob Grigg for 179 acres in May 1765, and that he witnessed the will of William Cox, dated "the 20th Day of the first month 1767," together with John Cox and John Allen. When the Orange County court sat at Hillsborough in February 1767, the clerk recorded that "this Will was Exhibited in Open Court & Duly proved by the Oaths of William Moffitt, & John Allen." Years later two of his daughters, Catharine and Hannah, are named in the family wills as Cox wives, and the 250 acres he left his son Robert were land he had bought of William Cox.

The Colonial Records spell the name Maffet, Moffit and Moffitt for the same man. The 1765 deed and the 1767 will come through the Cox family history rather than from the court books themselves, so those two dates rest on that book.

EXTRA.name: William Moffitt
EXTRA.title: September 1768: a letter, an address and an indictment
EXTRA.hook: As Tryon's troops closed on Hillsborough, William Moffitt signed a letter to the Governor, headed the signers of the Regulators' plea for pardon, and was named in a riot indictment the court threw out.
body: In 1768, while the Governor's troops were on the march from Salisbury to Hillsborough, James Hunter delivered a letter to Tryon signed for the Regulators by four men: Peter Julian, James Evans, Abraham Teague and William Moffitt. It protests loyalty, saying the Regulators "will when occasion requires fight for and defend him to the last drop of blood" for King George, and that they bear "no ill-will to any but our cruel Oppressors from which number we exclude your Excellency." It then turns: "But will nothing propitiate but our blood, we are determined at all events to fall like men, and sell our lives at the very dearest rate." The last line is a plea: "We beseech you Sir not to drive us to despair." (Vol. 7, pp. 811-812.)

When the Regulators were assembled at Hillsborough, they sent "The humble Address of the Inhabitants of several Counties called Regulators." They were "desirous to submit ourselves to the clemency of your Excellency, and to lay aside all method of redress of our grievances, but by a due course of Law," and they begged that the Governor "will forgive all our past offences by your gracious Proclamation." It is "Signed in behalf of the said Counties," and the first name in the list of twenty-two signers is William Moffitt's, ahead of Peter Julian, Lewis Lowry, Christopher Nation, Samuel Low, John Marshill and the rest (pages 812-813).

The court minutes of the same month show the other side. At the Hillsborough Superior Court on Thursday the 29th, the clerk wrote: "The indictment preferred against James Hunter, Ninion Hamilton, Isaac Jackson, John Philip Hartso, William Moffitt, John Pile & Francis Dossett, for a Rout, having been returned by the Grand Jury 'a true bill as to all except John Pile,' it is ordered by the Court that the bill be Quashed, by reason of the irregularity of the return, and that the Attorney General prepare a new bill." Two more bills against other Regulators were quashed the same day (pages 844-845).

So within a few weeks William was a signer of letters for the Regulators, the first name on their plea for pardon, a man indicted for riot whose bill failed on a technicality, and then, on 3 October, one of the thirteen named in the Governor's proclamation as excepted from pardon. No later bill against him appears in the volume.

quotes.t: We beseech you Sir not to drive us to despair.

EXTRA.name: Vincent B. Tims
EXTRA.title: A postmaster's letters, August to November 1864
EXTRA.hook: The Confederate Post Office Department's surviving papers include letters signed by V. B. Tims, postmaster at Doaksville, and the last is dated 1 November 1864.
body: In 1963 George H. Shirk, president of the Oklahoma Historical Society, printed the surviving records of the Confederate postal system in Indian Territory in The Chronicles of Oklahoma (vol. 41, no. 2, pp. 160-219). Doaksville was the end of two mail routes, Nos. 409 and 410, and in 1862 and 1863 its postmaster was J. P. Kingsbury. By 1864 the office was in the hands of V. B. Tims.

On 16 August 1864 he wrote to Dr. James H. Starr, the Post Office Department's agent at Marshall, Texas, that he had advertised for bids to carry the mail on Route 410 from Doaksville to Fort Washita, "the time having expired, I have now to inform you that there was but one bid given in and that was by Thomas M. Arnett." On 9 September, signing himself in full as "Vincent B. Tims, P. M.," he sent back the contract and oath executed by Arnett, with the news that Arnett's application for exemption from army service had been refused by the district headquarters at Fort Towson, so he could not start work. The contract then went to the second-best bidder, and an October letter from Tims reports the new contractor, James M. Nunn, at work on the route.

The last letter is the plainest. "Doaksville C. N., Nov 1st 1864," it begins: "I herewith enclose you my accounts current from January 1st to Sept. 30th 1864 inclusive which shows a balance of Twenty cents due to you. I herewith enclose you Ten Dollars new issue from which please deduct my account and send the balance in postage stamps." It is signed "V. B. Tims P. M." His accounts for the first nine months of 1864 left a balance of twenty cents. Of the office's 1862 and 1863 accounts, Shirk remarks that the volume of mail handled at Doaksville "was quite small."

These letters bear on the date of his death. The family accounts give 14 or 17 June 1864, and his grandson Joel Thompson remembered him as the first postmaster at Doaksville. But the postmaster who signed in September and November 1864, with the same name and initials he used on the Chickasaw treaty of 1837, was alive and in office months after that date. The June 1864 date cannot stand, and the 1871 postmaster-roll entry for a 'V. B. Tims,' which seemed to conflict with it, may simply be Vincent himself.

One more signature is on a petition of 1 July 1864 from the postmasters along the Washington-to-Doaksville mail route, who complained that since the army courier line had stopped "we are deprived of all means of hearing from our friends and relatives in the army." It was signed by R. D. Wright of Netra Bok, Arkansas, William K. McKean of Ultima Thule, Arkansas, P. P. Pitchlynn at Eagle Town and "V. B. Tims, P. M., Doaksville, C. N." General Maxey forwarded it from Fort Towson on 30 July, and on 8 August Dr. Starr replied that the contractors had been ordered to resume service or the route would be readvertised.

EXTRA.name: Rev. Elam Stevenson
EXTRA.title: In his own words, 1869
EXTRA.hook: At 81, too old and nervous to write, the Rev. Elam Stevenson dictated his memories of early Methodism in Giles County to his son Augustus, and a church historian printed them.
body: In 1869 the Methodist historian John B. McFerrin asked old Elam Stephenson (McFerrin's spelling) for what he remembered of the first Methodists in Giles and Lincoln counties. The answer is dated "Elkton, Giles county, Tennessee, July 28, 1869." It came through Elam's son John, and was written down by another son, Augustus, "as I am too old and nervous to write now." McFerrin printed it in his History of Methodism in Tennessee (vol. 2, 1871, pp. 178-190).

Elam is frank about his health. "My memory is failing me, and I am much afflicted with asthma, and I am not able to be out of my bed more than half my time. I have come down to the edge of the last river, and expect soon to cross over and join those who have gone on before." Of the people who came to the country when he did, "not one is now left; they are all gone, and I am left with only my wife as survivors of a past generation." He lived six more years, and Lydia three.

He remembers the move in 1813. The preacher Philip Bruce, he says, "came to my house and asked me to bring a part of his books in my wagon, as he had no conveyance but a one-horse sulky. I agreed to do so, and accordingly brought the books." Bruce's brother had married a sister of Elam's wife, and Bruce "made our neighborhood his home, after coming to Tennessee." This is Elam's own word on the journey, and it speaks of a wagon, which sits badly with the family story of a pack-horse crossing because there were no wagon roads.

He writes about his church as someone who helped build it. "Our Church at Bee Spring (so named because it was famous as a place for coursing wild bees, in the early settlement of the country) was organized in 1814. The society now numbers about two hundred, and worships in a large frame-church, and is in a prosperous condition. The present is the fourth house of worship we have had." In 1814, he adds, "Brothers Coleman Harwell, Meshach Boyce, and myself, began to preach in Lincoln county, in what is now called the Shiloh neighborhood, in private houses," and in 1815 the first society there was formed at the house of Seaborn Bruce.

McFerrin follows the letter with a short sketch of the writer: "Elam was the third son, and the first of the family to join the Methodist Church. He professed religion in 1804, and joined the Church in 1806. He was much opposed by his parents, who were Presbyterians... He was licensed to preach in 1813, and the same year removed to Tennessee." His house "was a welcome home" to every preacher on the Richland Circuit. "All his children are members of the Church, and four of his sons are preachers of the gospel; one of them, the Rev. J. B. Stephenson, once of the Tennessee, but now of the North Alabama Conference, is an itinerant." The sketch also calls his father James "a Captain in the Revolutionary war," a title the family later repeated and the militia record does not support.

EXTRA.name: Rev. Elam Stevenson and his sons
EXTRA.title: The Stevensons in the Pulaski Citizen
EXTRA.hook: A weekly Giles County newspaper printed Elam Stevenson's death notice in 1875 and kept naming his preaching sons for the next ten years, including one who talked of moving to Texas.
body: Giles County, Tennessee, had a weekly paper, the Pulaski Citizen, and its neighborhood columns noted who was preaching where, who was sick and who had come home. The Stevenson preachers turn up in it again and again between 1875 and 1885.

On 18 March 1875 the Citizen printed a death notice: "Died, at the residence of W. M. Stevenson, near Bethany, on the 13th inst., Rev. Elam Stevenson, in his 88th year." It called him "this venerable minister of God," who "died as he had lived, with perfect Christian resignation," and said he left "a large line of descendants—children, grand children, and great-grand children, who will ever revere his memory." The 13th of March matches the date on the family's own record of his death. The W. M. Stevenson whose house it was is most likely his son Willis M., who is on the family roll of Elam's eleven children.

Three years later a writer visiting Bee Spring church walked through its graveyard and wrote: "Here repose the sacred dust of old Father Stevenson and his beloved consort, and many others, the founders and upholders of Methodism at Bee Spring." No first name is given, but Bee Spring was the church Elam founded in 1815, and Elam and Lydia were its founders.

Elam's son Abner appears as a working circuit preacher. When the Mt. Pisgah circuit preachers published their monthly appointments on 21 November 1878, the list read "Blooming Grove, 4th Sunday, 11 a. m., Abner Stevenson." In February 1878 a neighborhood correspondent, after listing the sick of the community, added: "We are informed that Rev. Abner Stevenson has a cancer cure. If true, come over." In August 1879 the paper's account of a revival at Bee Spring, where 41 people professed faith in seven days, listed him among the ministers who "aided in other services." In May 1884 a column reported: "We had two sermons at Rocky Point last Sunday, one by Abner Stevenson and one by W. H. Dixon," and said the fourth Sunday in June was his.

Texas comes into the story in 1881. On 27 January the Friendship column reported: "Rev. Abner Stevenson has abandoned the idea of going to Texas and will remain where he is now living." On 5 May the Bee Spring column added: "Judge Geo. Stevenson, son of Rev. A. Stevenson, returned from Texas last week." The 1870 census shows a George W., the same age as Gilbert, in Abner's household, so this is probably that son; the paper does not say why he went or how long he stayed. Abner stayed in Giles County, and it was his son Gilbert, later known as Frank, who later took a preacher's family west. The 1910 census lists Frank's seven children as born in Indiana, Texas, Oklahoma and Arkansas.

One more brother is in the paper. On 20 August 1885 the county correspondent wrote of visiting "our old friends, Rev. and Mrs. Jas. C. Stevenson of near Bryson," who "speak of celebrating their golden wedding in October." James C. is the third child on the family roll of Elam's children, and the family letter of 1932 remembers "Uncle Jimmie" as having preached 63 years.

EXTRA.name: Rev. Robert James Tims
EXTRA.title: A circuit preacher near Idabel
EXTRA.hook: Betsy's brother preached for forty years in the Choctaw country, and a memoir written by his nephew in 1944 names his parents as Vincent and Emiline Tims.
body: Robert James Tims was a brother of Betsy (Tims) Thompson. The Methodist Indian Mission of Oklahoma printed his memoir in the minutes of its September 1944 session at Salt Creek Church, near Holdenville, signed by his nephew, the Rev. Edgar Tims. It begins: "Robert James Tims was born six miles north of Fort Towson, Oklahoma, being the son of Vincent and Emiline Tims."

He stayed in the Fort Towson community until he entered Spencer Academy and finished his schooling there, and "upon leaving school it was his good fortune to meet Fannie Weesley, and they were married." The marriage lasted 48 years, until she died a few months before him. They had no children, "but a mighty host of friends."

In 1904, the memoir says, he was converted and licensed to preach, and he was later ordained a deacon. He was pastor of the Rufe Circuit, whose churches in the 1940s included High Hill and Hampton Chapel, for two years, and then of the Idabel Circuit for six, until failing health made him retire to a home five miles west of Idabel. The conference rolls follow him: he is among the clerical members in 1934 and 1935, is listed as pastor of the Idabel Circuit in 1936, and appears in 1940 as "Tims, Robert J., L.D., Idabel."

"He preached his last sermon at Thomas Chapel on Sunday just before his triumphant passing on Tuesday." He died on Tuesday, 12 September 1944, and was buried in the Idabel cemetery. The memoir closes: "The name of Robert Tims will always be affectionately mentioned in the churches where he ministered."

Robert's own Dawes card is No. 816, filled out at Doaksville on 25 April 1899 for Cedar County. It lists "Tims, Robert," age 25, three-quarter blood, Roll No. 2085, with his wife "Fannie," 18, Roll No. 2086. His parents are written as "Vincent Tims," dead, and "Emiline Tims," and hers as "John Wesley," dead, and "Winnie Wesley," both of Cedar County. The memoir spells her family name Weesley. In April 1901, aged 26, he swore the affidavit as an acquaintance on his niece Ella's death for the Dawes Commission, signing his name "Robert Tims."

quotes.c: Memoir by Edgar Tims, Minutes of the Indian Mission of Oklahoma, 1944, p. 31

EXTRA.name: Noble Shaw
EXTRA.title: Noble Shaw's land, advertised at Oak Ridge in 1857
EXTRA.hook: In the spring of 1857 Sicily Shaw and J. H. Leak put Noble Shaw's 268-acre farm up for sale in the Greensboro newspaper.
body: The Times of Greensboro, North Carolina, for Thursday, 26 March 1857, carries a notice headed "Land Sale." It reads: "Having qualified as Administrators on the Estate of Noble Shaw, deceased, with a will annexed, at the dwelling of said deceased, we will expose to public vendure on the 16th April next, a tract of land, consisting of 268 acres, well timbered and well watered, convenient to the Oak Ridge Institute, and on the direct road from Danville, Va., to Salisbury. The land will be sold on a credit." It is signed "J. H. Leak, Sicily Shaw, Administrators," at "Oak Ridge, P. O., March 24th, 1857." The same notice ran again in the issue of 2 April 1857.

"With a will annexed" is the old legal phrase for administrators who carry out a written will when the executor it names cannot or does not act. So the notice tells us two things: Noble left a will, and Sicily, then 66, was one of the two people the court trusted to settle his estate and sell his land.

The farm lay near the Oak Ridge Institute, the academy in northwestern Guilford County, on the road that runs from Danville, Virginia, down to Salisbury. That fits the Guilford County home the Quaker records give the Shaw and Nordyke families. Noble was born on 22 April 1787 and Sicily on 2 August 1790; she outlived the sale by four years.

EXTRA.name: Dennis Garrett
EXTRA.title: "The jurors doe present John Oldton": the death of Dennis Garrett
EXTRA.hook: A 1921 article on Baltimore County's frontier rangers prints the court's indictment word for word, with Dennis's son-in-law John Cole and his widow Barbara among the witnesses.
body: Dennis Garrett of Baltimore County died on 2 September 1691, weeks after a sword blow to the forehead. William B. Marye, writing on the county's frontier "Garrison" and its first captain, John Oldton, in the Maryland Historical Magazine for June 1921, prints the Provincial Court's record of the case from "Provincial Court Proceedings Judgments," Liber D. S. No. C, 1692-1693, folio 15: "The jurors . . . doe present John Oldton late of Baltemore County taylor for that he the said John Oldton the 31st of July 1691 at Baltemore County . . . with force and armes in and upon the body of one Dennis Garrett then and there . . . an assault did make and him the said Dennis with one sword of the value of twenty shillings being the proper sword of the said John Ouldton upon the forehead of the said Dennis one blow did give of which said blow the said Dennis immediately from the 30th day of July aforesaid till the 2nd day of September did languish on which 2nd day of September in the year and at the place aforesaid the said Dennis Garrett of the said blow did dye."

The witnesses were "Philip Roper, Nicholas Hale, John Cole (son-in-law of the deceased), Thomas Stone, Abraham Vaughan and Barbara Garrett (the widow)." John Cole is the husband of Dennis's daughter Johanna, and Barbara is the widow who later deeded land to her grandson Dennis Garrett Cole. Oldton "was condemned to be hanged; but 'afterwards the said John Oulton was graciously pardoned by their Majesties pardon in usuall forme.'" Marye's text puts it more briefly: Oldton "was found guilty of the murder of Dennis Garrett of Baltimore County, and was condemned to be hanged, but received a royal pardon in time to save his life."

The Governor and Council of Maryland, meeting at St. Mary's on 11 April 1692, had already ordered the same stay of execution for "One John Olton a Taylor convict and under Sentence of Death for Murder" that they gave another condemned prisoner that day (Archives of Maryland, vol. 8, p. 314). Oldton went on to be appointed captain of the county's rangers in 1694/5, and Marye remarks that "the onus of a verdict of murder in the first degree" did not stop him from "guarding the frontiers of a province."

In a note to the same record Marye also describes Dennis himself: "Dennis Garrett, an early settler on the site of Baltimore, has many descendants through the Cole, Gorsuch and Ensor families. With Thomas Stone he purchased 'Long Island Point,' a tract surveyed for William Poultney on the site of Fell's Point. His widow, Barbara Garrett, married (2nd) Thomas Broad." Other records give her second husband's name as John Broad.

A Virginia Magazine of History and Biography article on the Gorsuch and Lovelace families (October 1916) tells the same story from the same record. Oldton, it says, "got into serious trouble as the result of an affray with Dennis Garrett, a prominent planter, which caused Garrett's death. . . . The occurrence took place July 31, 1691, and Garrett languished away, dying Sept. 2" (p. 438).

EXTRA.name: John Cole
EXTRA.title: Cole's Choice, Cole's Addition and Cole's Adventure
EXTRA.hook: Three Baltimore County tracts surveyed for John Cole between 1694 and 1706 are described in the 1921 magazine article, and in March 1737/8 he stood on the ground himself and gave his age as about 67.
body: William B. Marye's study of the old Baltimore County rangers' roads, in the Maryland Historical Magazine for 1921, keeps running into the Cole tracts, because they lay along the roads he was tracing. "Coles Choice" was "surveyed for John Cole July 28th, 1694, but never patented" and was later taken up again under the name "Orange"; the same survey appears again as "Cole's Chance," with a deed from John Cole to Robert Green dated 1702 (pp. 118, 242). "A tract of 67 acres called 'Cole's Addition' surveyed for John Cole May 29th, 1698," lay "on the north side of Patapsco River in the woods," beside the path called Darley Path, where Chase Street and the Bel Air Road now cross in Baltimore (p. 118).

"Cole's Adventure" was "surveyed for John Cole in the year 1706" and sat "on a run called Gwins Run." When Thomas Demmett held a land commission on it in March 1737/8, a note records that "John Cole, Senior, aged about 67 years, testified before the same commission that the beginning tree of 'Cole's Adventure' stood about a hundred yards to the eastward of Gwinn's Run" (p. 218, note 15). An age of about 67 in 1738 puts his birth around 1670.

A second land commission, held in August 1750 on Cole's Addition, took the depositions of men who had known him. John Ensor, Sr., aged 55, said that "about eighteen years ago the aforesaid John Cole (referred to elsewhere in the same deposition as the deponent's father-in-law) came with him this deponent to the place where he now stands" and showed him where the boundary oak of Cole's Addition must stand. William Green, aged 58, told the same story, "the aforesaid John Cole said there should have been a bounded tree of Coles Addition." Ensor was born about 1695, and Marye's note on the Garrett trial lists the Ensor family among the descendants of Dennis Garrett, John Cole's father-in-law (pp. 118-119).
The tracts lay north of the Patapsco on ground that is now in and around Baltimore, a generation before the town was laid out in 1729.

EXTRA.name: Vincent B. Tims
EXTRA.title: Thirteen cents a ration: the Doak & Tims contracts, 1838-1839
EXTRA.hook: A House report of 1843 prints the army's signed contracts with Doak & Tims to feed Chickasaw emigrants at Doaksville, at thirteen cents a ration.
body: The Doaksville trading firm of Josiah Doak and Vincent B. Tims shows up in the government's own paper in a report to the House of Representatives dated 25 February 1843 (27th Congress, 3d Session, Report No. 271, "Frauds upon Indians"). The report reproduced a run of army subsistence contracts from the removal years, and four of them are with "Doak & Tims." The report charges the firm with nothing; the contracts are printed as exhibits among those of other suppliers.

No. 41 is "an extract from a contract made January 1, 1838, between Captain R. D. C. Collins, United States army, and Doak & Tims." It reads: "That the said Doak & Tims shall furnish complete rations to a party of about two hundred Chickasaw emigrants, and all such of said tribe who may join said party, to be supplied at this place from time to time . . . for the term of twelve months from the date of this contract; the ration to consist of one pound of beef or pork, or three-quarters of a pound of salt pork or bacon, a pint and a half of corn meal, and one gallon of salt to the hundred rations." For each ration "the said Doak & Tims shall receive from the United States the sum of thirteen cents" (p. 86).

No. 42, of the same date, has them feed up to two hundred horses belonging to the emigrants, "one gallon of good sound merchantable corn" a ration, again at thirteen cents. No. 44 renews the arrangement on 1 January 1839: "the said Doak & Tims shall furnish and deliver, to the Chickasaw Indians, at the depot at Doaksville, Choctaw nation, west, all rations of subsistence that shall be required at said depot, be the same more or less, for one year from the date hereof," at "thirteen cents" a full ration (p. 87).

Elsewhere in the report, the notes to a witness summary say the Fort Towson issues for the twelve months "appear to have been made by David Folsom and Doak & Tims"; the witness, the Chickasaw interpreter Stone Love, "thinks satisfactory" those twelve months' issues (p. 56). A letter from the officer settling the Chickasaw accounts mentions "a small party subsisting for the year, by Doak & Tims, under a contract with Captain Collins" (p. 84). Another contract, between the removal contractors Glasgow & Harrison and the army, carves out "the party of emigrants now at 'Doaksville,' and being subsisted by Doak & Tims" (p. 75).

These are the contracts behind the thirteen cents a ration that a missionary later remembered for the Doaksville trading establishment of Doak and Tims. They put the firm at Doaksville, feeding Chickasaw families as they arrived from Mississippi, at the start of 1838, before the town had a post office.

EXTRA.name: Vincent B. Tims
EXTRA.title: "Mr. Tims one of the men I am living with": a clerk's letters from Doaksville, 1841 and 1843
EXTRA.hook: A young Connecticut clerk at the Doaksville trading house wrote his mother that Mr. Tims was in New York buying goods; two years later Tims was still making the trip for him.
body: In "Tryphena," published in the Chronicles of Oklahoma for June 1931, Muriel H. Wright printed two letters from Charles Fanning Stewart of Connecticut to his mother. Stewart, born in 1814, had gone west "after having been engaged to clerk in a trading establishment at Doaksville, a thriving village in the Red River region of the Choctaw Nation." His letter of 17 April 1841 is headed "Doaks Ville, Choctaw Nation West." It describes the place: "Doaks Ville is some sixty miles west of the Boundary line between the United States and the Indian country. It is six miles north of the Red River which forms the line between us and Texas. Fort Towson is only half a mile from us . . . Our trade which is verry extencive is confined to the Red Men of the forrest."

Tims comes in near the end. "Mr. Tims one of the men I am living with is now in New York purchasing a stock of goods," Stewart tells his mother. He had sent fifty dollars with him to leave with her friends in New York, and asked him to collect fifty more that was owed him in New Orleans. Stewart had meant to come home that summer, "but Mr. Tims trip to New York prevented it" (Chronicles, vol. 9, p. 184).

Stewart married Tryphena Wall on 9 May 1842 and opened his own store at Mayhew, on the road between Fort Towson and Fort Washita, with goods bought from his old employer in New Orleans. On 19 April 1843 he wrote that the stock he had brought the previous spring was sold and that he had "sent by my friend Mr. Tims last week for another stock of goods he will be in New York sometime in May." So Tims made the buying trip east in the spring of 1841 and again in 1843, and Stewart, who had clerked in his house, still trusted him to carry his orders and money (p. 186).

Stewart does not give the firm's name or Tims's first name. The Mr. Tims of the Doaksville trading house in those years is almost certainly Vincent B. Tims of Doak & Tims, whose partnership with Josiah Doak was dissolved in February 1844.

EXTRA.name: Rev. Elam Stevenson
EXTRA.title: "A Methodist preacher all his life": a neighbor remembers Elam Stevenson, 1884
EXTRA.hook: In September 1884 the Pulaski Citizen printed a boyhood neighbor's recollection of Elam Stevenson settling near Bee Spring church, and of his sons and the families they married into.
body: On 25 September 1884 the front page of The Pulaski Citizen carried a column headed "Old Times in Giles," signed "By F. T. M'Laurine." The writer walks through the families who settled his neighborhood on Little Bradshaw Creek, naming each in turn, the teachers he went to school to at Bee Spring, and the preachers who held the community together. One paragraph is about the Stevensons.

"Elam Stevenson and family settled 1½ miles south of us near Bee Spring church in 1815 or 1816; he soon after obtained license to preach and was a Methodist preacher all his life; died a few years since a very old man. He had one daughter, Catharine, who married a Mr. Hamilton. His sons were William, James, Coleman, John and others; James and John and one other were Methodist preachers, all good, industrious citizens. William married a Miss Malinda Rowe, a daughter of Joseph Rowe who lived near by. She was a beautiful young lady. James married a daughter of Mr. Duncan Brown, sister of ex-Gov. N. S. and J. C. Brown. John is a noted Methodist preacher."

The Browns he names are Neill S. Brown, governor of Tennessee from 1847 to 1849, and John C. Brown, governor from 1871 to 1875, both Giles County men. So the Rev. James Stevenson of this paragraph married into the family of two governors. The unnamed "one other" preacher among the brothers fits Abner.

The memory is a neighbor's, written seventy years on, and it differs in detail from the family's own record. Elam's 1869 letter says Bee Spring church was organized in 1814, and the Goodspeed sketch of his grandson says the family came to Giles County about 1813, a little earlier than the 1815 or 1816 given here. Goodspeed's list of the children has a daughter Katherine, which matches Catharine, but no son Coleman; William P., James C., Abner A., Willis M., John B., Thomas C., Elam A. and Gilbert are the sons it names. What the column adds is how the family looked from the next farm: a settled preaching family, with a license to preach early and a long ministry, whose sons married local daughters and, in three cases, took up the pulpit too.

EXTRA.name: Willie Jane (Maxwell) Tims
EXTRA.rel: 3rd great-grandaunt by marriage (wife of Judge Edward Ward Tims)
EXTRA.title: Sworn at Tuskahoma: Willie Tims on her marriage, 1902
EXTRA.hook: In December 1902 Willie J. Tims told the Dawes Commission she had lived sixteen years in the Choctaw Nation and had married Edward Tims near Doaksville in 1888.
body: On 8 December 1902 the Dawes Commission took testimony at Tuskahoma from "Willie J. Tims," who gave her age as thirty-two and her post office as Grant, Indian Territory. She was a white woman, born Willie Jane Maxwell, and she was asking to be enrolled as a citizen by intermarriage through her husband, Judge Edward Ward Tims of Doaksville. The Commission asked her the plain questions the law required: how long she had lived in the Nation, whether her husband was enrolled, when and where they married, and who had been married before.

Her answers put the marriage in 1888, "Close to Doaksville," performed by a minister named Frazier, without a license. Edward had been married once before, to a woman whose "given name was Polly," and Polly was dead by then. Willie said the two had lived together continuously, "No" separation, abandonment or divorce, as residents of the Nation.

The Commission's written decision, dated 9 December 1903, gave the date of the wedding as 29 April 1888. A certified copy of the marriage certificate is in the same jacket, written in the Choctaw Nation's own court style: "Tonson County C. N. April 29th A. D. 1888." It is signed by R. S. Frazier, who wrote that he had that day "Joined the holy Estate of Matrimony, Hon. E. W. Tims and Mifs Wille Maxful all of Tonson County C. N." The clerk copying it in December 1906 kept the old spelling.

Card 1437 lists her as Roll No. 635, "Willie J.," age 29, an intermarried white citizen; her father, Maxwell, is marked dead and a non-citizen. Beneath her on the card are her children with Edward: Lucy, Minnie J., Edmond, Benjamin W., Mertle (a baby of two months when the family applied on 8 May 1899) and Abel E., born 14 December 1901 and enrolled on 14 February 1902. The card also carries Adam Nanomantubbe, a boy listed as Edward's ward, whose dead parents are written as Tobias and Susan Nanomantubbe. In July 1903 the Commission answered a neighbor from Oscar, O. W. Seay, who had written that "Mr. Tims has a grandson named Adam Nonomatubi who is an orphan," and told him the boy was already enrolled with the family; the Secretary of the Interior had approved the whole group on 12 December 1902.
Willie Jane Tims was born on 27 July 1870 and died on 8 October 1922, four months before her husband. She is the mother of Private Edmond Tims, killed in France in 1918.

EXTRA.name: Mitchell Tims
EXTRA.title: Mitchell and Mildred Tims: a card with a red line
EXTRA.hook: Betsy's brother Mitchell and his full-blood wife Mildred are on Dawes Card 850, where a red line runs through the name of their baby daughter Else.
body: Dawes Card 850 was filled out on 25 April 1899 for Towson County, post office Doaksville. Its first line is "Tims, Mitchell," age 30, one-half Choctaw, Roll No. 2201. In the columns for his parents the clerk wrote "Benson Tims," dead, of Towson County, and "Emiline Tims," still living on the 1896 census. It is one of seven cards on which Emeline Tims is enrolled or named as mother; her husband's first name is spelled Vinson, Vincent and, here, Benson, but the family is the same.

Line 2 is his wife Mildred, 19, full-blood, who is noted as having been on the 1896 roll as "Mildred Billy." The card names her parents as "Nuck-a-masha" and "Me-ley," both dead, of Jacks Fork County.

Their first daughter, Else, was born on 9 November 1899, after the application, and was transferred onto the card on 11 July 1902. She had already died. On 5 December 1902 the Commission wrote to Mitchell at Doaksville acknowledging "your affidavit and that of James Wilson relative to the death of your daughter, Else Tims," which "occurred November 25, 1900." The family tree gives the name James Wilson for the husband of Mitchell's sister Rosie. The card marks Else's line with a red rule and the note that her enrollment was cancelled on 8 July 1904, because she had died before the roll was made.

A second daughter, Agnes E., was born on 21 December 1901 and enrolled on 3 January 1902 as Roll No. 2203. A son, Vincenta W. Tims, was born on 28 July 1904. On 25 April 1905 the Commission wrote to Mitchell at Fort Towson that it had received "the affidavits of Mildred and Emeline Tims to the birth of Vincenta W. Tims," so his own mother, Emeline, again vouched for a grandchild's birth, as she did for Betsy's children. Two months later Mitchell wrote to ask whether the birth certificate had arrived, and the Commission confirmed it. The boy was entered as Roll No. 1045 on the roll of newborn children (Card 1170).

Mitchell Tims is buried at High Hill Cemetery. In 1938 the Methodist Indian Mission lists Mitchell Tims of Fort Towson, with his nephew Peter Thompson, among the Choctaw District's church school superintendents.

The James Wilson who swore with Mitchell in 1902 is probably his brother-in-law: Mitchell's sister Rosanna married a James Wilson of Cedar County, whose Card 1281 sits among the cards filed at Doaksville on 1 May 1899.

quotes.t: Receipt is hereby acknowledged of the affidavits of Mildred and Emeline Tims to the birth of Vincenta W. Tims, son of Mitchell and Mildred Tims, July 28, 1904, and the same have been filed with our records as an application for the enrollment of said child.
