EXTRA.name: Willie Tims and Mary (Lewis) Tims
EXTRA.title: A letter to the Principal Chief about a baby who had died
EXTRA.hook: Willie Tims, Betsy's brother, was enrolled with his wife Mary and a baby son in 1901; in 1905 he had to correct the rolls for a second baby who had died.
body: Dawes Card 1268, filled out on 1 May 1899, lists "Tims, Willie," age 23, three-quarter Choctaw, Roll No. 3441, of Towson County, post office Doaksville. The card names his parents as "Vincent Tims," dead, and "Emiline Tims," living on the 1896 census, the same pair named on Betsy Thompson's card. His wife Mary, 21, full-blood, was on the 1896 roll as "Mawey Lewis"; her parents are "King Lewis" and "Nancy Lewis." Their first son, Roberson, was born on 18 February 1901 and enrolled on 17 May 1901.

The jacket then follows the family for years. A second son, Wilson Tims, was born on 11 May 1904 and was entered as Roll No. 1101 when the Secretary of the Interior approved the roll of newborn children on 22 July 1905. But the child had died before the cutoff date of 4 March 1905, and the affidavit had said he was living. In September 1905 Green McCurtain, Principal Chief of the Choctaw Nation, wrote to the Commission from Kinta that "Willis Tims," of Fort Towson, had told him the child "was at that time deceased" and wanted the name struck from the rolls. The Commission wrote on to the land office to stop any allotment for the dead child.

A daughter, Etline Tims, was born on 6 July 1905. On 19 May 1906 the Commission acknowledged "the affidavits of Mary Tims and Nancy Lewis," her mother and grandmother, to her birth. She appears as Roll No. 214 on the roll of minor children (Card 274), a girl of seven-eighths Choctaw blood.
A Willie Tims of Fort Towson later appears in Methodist Indian Mission minutes as a church officer at High Hill, but the minutes do not say whether he is this Willie.

quotes.t: when in truth and in fact said child Wilson Tims, was at that time deceased, and that he made this mistake in the affidavit ignorantly
quotes.c: Green McCurtain, Principal Chief of the Choctaw Nation, to the Commission to the Five Civilized Tribes, Kinta, 25 September 1905 (Choctaw New Born 1424)

EXTRA.name: Henry W. Thompson
EXTRA.rel: Neighbor on the Dawes rolls (no recorded kinship)
EXTRA.title: The man on the card before Joseph's: Henry W. Thompson
EXTRA.hook: Dawes Card 1282 is Henry W. Thompson's, filed the same day as Joseph P. Thompson's Card 1283. It names his parents as Simon and Lucy Thompson.
body: Henry W. Thompson and Joseph P. Thompson both applied for Choctaw enrollment on 1 May 1899, and their cards are numbered 1282 and 1283. They lived in Cedar County with the same post office, Doaksville. In the 1910 census a Henry W. Thompson is among the Thompsons' nearest neighbors in Wilson Township.

Card 1282 lists "Thompson, Henry W.," age 25, full-blood, Roll No. 3486, with his parents written as "Simon Thompson" and "Lucy Thompson," both dead, of Cedar County. Joseph's card, by contrast, names his parents as John and Betsy Thompson. On the Dawes record Henry is not Joseph's brother.

A note on the card says he was "now the husband of Illie Thompson on Choctaw Card #1288," with evidence of marriage filed on 16 July 1902. In 1903 the Commission returned to him at Doaksville the "certificate of marriage of Henry Thompson and Mrs. Eli Pesahombi, dated July 11, 1900." Card 1288 carries Illie, 18, and a one-year-old son, Hampton Thompson, born on 12 November 1901, along with a Pisahambe youth and the Aaron family. When the baby's application reached the Commission through a notary at Doaksville in February 1902, it was sent back with a request for the mother's maiden name, since no one of her name had been listed.

EXTRA.name: Joseph W. Thompson
EXTRA.title: Joseph W.: a sworn birth in 1905, and Emeline the midwife again
EXTRA.hook: Joseph and Betsy's son Joseph W. was born on 5 March 1903 and enrolled under the 1905 act; his grandmother Emeline Tims swore to his birth, as she had for Simon.
body: Joel Thompson's list of his brothers includes Joseph W. The Dawes jacket shows how he got on the roll. The Act of Congress of 3 March 1905 allowed children born after September 1902 and living on 4 March 1905 to be enrolled, so the family had to swear to his birth and to the fact that he was alive on that date.

On a birth affidavit sworn at the Central District on 29 April 1905, "Betsy Thompson," of Fort Towson, said she was the lawful wife of Joseph P. Thompson, "who is a citizen, by Blood, of the Choctaw Nation," and that a male child "born to me on 5th day of March 1903" had been named "Joseph W. Thompson" and "was living March 4, 1905." On the same page, as "midwife," Emeline Tims swore that she had attended Betsy on the same day and that the child was living on the cutoff date. The notary for both was Thomas Fennell. It is the same arrangement as in 1899, when Emeline attended Simon's birth and swore to it.
He is entered on Choctaw Newborn Card 1410, and a note on the family's own Card 1283 points to it: "For child of nos 1 & 2 see NB (March 3, 1905) #1410."

EXTRA.name: William Harrison Pisachubbe
EXTRA.title: One man, two names: William Harrison Pisachubbe enrolled twice
EXTRA.hook: A boys' school list in 1899 put "Harrison Pisachubbe" on the Choctaw rolls, and he was already there as William H. In 1911 the Interior Department sorted it out.
body: On Dawes Card 1580, filled out on 10 May 1899 for Kiamitia County with the post office Goodland, line 2 is "William H.," son of the widow Eunice Pisachubbe, 16 years old and full-blood, Roll No. 4466. A note on the card says he had been on the 1896 roll as "William Harrison." His father, Joseph Pisachubbe, is written as dead.

Three months later, on 22 August 1899, a list of students at Armstrong Academy, a Choctaw school, was sent to the Commission, and it included "Harrison Pisachubbe." That name was also put on the final roll as No. 10559, approved on 4 February 1903. In the meantime William H. had received a complete allotment under his first number, and in 1905 the Commission, not knowing about the doubling, made a second, arbitrary allotment in the name of Harrison. The certificates were mailed to Academy, Oklahoma, and came back marked "unclaimed."

On 2 August 1909 William H. testified at Hugo that he had told the postmaster to send the certificates back, as he already had his allotment as William H. Pisachubbe. Eunice, Harrison Nohio and Thomas Hunter also gave testimony. On 1 August 1911 the Commissioner at Muskogee wrote to the Secretary of the Interior that it showed "that Harrison Pisachubbe, Choctaw by Blood Roll No. 10559, is a duplicate enrollment of William H. Pisachubbe, No. 4466 on the same roll." The Secretary's office approved a notation on the roll on 16 August 1911: "Duplicate enrollment of No. 4466; not entitled to land or money under this number."

William H. had a son, Colbert, born on 26 June 1906 at Hugo, whose mother Mamie signed her application with a mark and whose birth was attended by a midwife, Cassie Davis. His enrollment was refused: the Commissioner decided on 27 November 1906 that, because Colbert "was not living March 4, 1906," the cutoff in the Act of 26 April 1906, he had no authority to consider it, and the Secretary affirmed on 26 February 1907. Mamie is called a non-citizen in the decision.
William Harrison Pisachubbe died in May 1937; his obituary in the Hugo Daily News is the source of the family's account of the removal from Mississippi in 1832.

EXTRA.name: Edward Pisachubbe
EXTRA.rel: Ward of Eunice Pisachubbe, listed with Robert and William H. on Card 1580
EXTRA.title: Edward Pisachubbi's land letter, 1903
EXTRA.hook: Edward, listed as Eunice's ward on Card 1580, wrote to the Commission in January 1903 about land he had picked for himself and his wife Frances.
body: Line 4 of Eunice Pisachubbe's card is not one of her sons. "Edward," 17, full-blood, Roll No. 4468, is written as her ward, and the card gives his dead parents as "Simpson Pisachubbe" and "Sallie Pisachubbe," of Jackson County. A note says he was the husband of Frances Byington, whose own card is No. 956.

On 31 January 1903 the Commission wrote to him at Hugo, answering his letter of 16 January, "in which you state that you have selected certain lands for the allotments of yourself and your wife, Frances Pisachubbi." He had added that part of the land he described was claimed by another citizen. The Commission told him it had "no means of recording the selections of citizens" and could not settle disputes about possession; the matter would be heard when land offices opened in the Nation, which it expected between the first of March and the first of April. A follow-up letter said admission to the land office would be by tickets handed out on or after 16 April 1903.
His letters show how the land was chosen in the Choctaw Nation in 1903: families walked the ground first and wrote to the Commission, and then had to apply in person at the land office.

quotes.t: in which you state that you have selected certain lands for the allotments of yourself and your wife, Frances Pisachubbi.
quotes.c: Commission to the Five Civilized Tribes to Edward Pisachubbi, Hugo, 31 January 1903 (Choctaw 7-956, 7-1580)

EXTRA.name: Vincent B. Tims
EXTRA.title: Doak & Tims in the Texas Supreme Court, 1849
EXTRA.hook: A Doaksville store's unpaid account from 1840 to 1844 ended up before the Supreme Court of Texas, in a case titled Love v. Doak & Tims.
body: Doak & Tims, the Doaksville trading firm of Josiah L. Doak and Vincent B. Tims, appears in the law reports of Texas. The case, Love v. Doak & Tims, was decided at the December 1849 term and printed in volume 5 of the Texas Reports, at page 343.

The court summarized the suit this way: it "was brought in the names of the appellees as copartners, trading as merchants, for the use and benefit of Josiah L. Doak, one of the said copartners." It was an action on a store account against a man named Love who lived across the Red River in the Choctaw Nation. The first item in the account was dated 1840 and the last 30 July 1844; the suit was begun in Grayson County, Texas, on 24 January 1848. A witness testified that he had sold Love goods up to 28 August 1840, "that at the time said account was made the defendant was a resident of Mississippi," and that Love "did remove in 1841" to the Choctaw Nation. A second witness said that in 1844 he had presented the account for payment and asked Love for an order on a Colonel Upshaw, or his note, and Love said he would settle it himself.

The trial jury found for Doak & Tims. On appeal, Chief Justice Hemphill reversed and dismissed the case on the law of limitations: the debt was more than two years old, and nothing in writing acknowledged it. The partnership is the one the family's Doaksville records describe, from the army ration contracts of 1838 and 1839 through the store letters of 1841; the suit of 1848 came four years after the partners dissolved their business by mutual agreement in 1844, and it is brought for the use and benefit of Doak alone.
The account shows the store selling goods on credit over four years, with the bill pursued years later in a Texas court.

quotes.t: brought in the names of the appellees as copartners, trading as merchants, for the use and benefit of Josiah L. Doak, one of the said copartners.
quotes.c: Love v. Doak & Tims, 5 Tex. 343 (Supreme Court of Texas, December 1849), statement of the case

EXTRA.name: Judge Edward Ward Tims
EXTRA.title: Edward Tims on the ballot for Principal Chief, August 1886
EXTRA.hook: A New York Times wire from Little Rock on 5 August 1886 names Edward Tims among four candidates for Principal Chief of the Choctaw Nation.
body: The Paris (Texas) News said in 1940 that Judge Tims was "once considered for the position as principal chief of the Choctaw Nation." A newspaper from the time shows how far it went. On 6 August 1886 the New York Times printed a short dispatch headed "Choctaws Hold an Election," dated Little Rock, Ark., 5 August: "The election for principal chief of the Choctaw Nation was held yesterday." It names four men: Ben Smallwood, Thompson McKinney, J. P. Folsom (printed Fulsom) and Edward Tims. It adds that a large vote was cast and that unofficial returns pointed to the election of McKinney.

Edward Tims was then in his mid-forties, a county judge of Towson County and, since the early 1880s, a trustee of Apukshunnubbee District. The Doaksville post office came to him the next year. The dispatch gives no vote totals; Thompson McKinney went on to serve as Principal Chief, so Edward Tims was a losing candidate in a four-man race for the highest office in the Nation.
He is the same Edward Tims whose 1888 marriage near Doaksville is on the Dawes jacket, and whose enrollment card names his father as Vincent B. Tims.

quotes.t: The election for principal chief of the Choctaw Nation was held yesterday.
quotes.c: "Choctaws Hold an Election," The New York Times, 6 August 1886, dispatch from Little Rock, Ark., 5 August

quotes.c: The Paris (Texas) News, January 1940

EXTRA.name: Nancy Pisachubbi (daughter of Te-hol-ba-ta-bi)
EXTRA.rel: A Pisachubbi woman named in the family tree (her tie to Joseph Pisachubbe is not recorded)
EXTRA.title: Nancy Pisachubbi: a card that names her father, Te-hol-ba-ta-bi
EXTRA.hook: The family tree gives a Nancy Te-hol-ba-ta-bi. Dawes Card 1278 is a Nancy Pisachubbi, a full-blood widow of about 69 whose father was Te-hol-ba-ta-bi.
body: Dawes Card 1278 was made out in May 1899 for "Pisachubbi, Nancy," age 69, a full-blood woman of Eagle County, post office Luk-fa-tah, Indian Territory, Roll No. 3474. She is alone on the card, and her enrollment was approved on 12 December 1902.

The columns for her parents give two names: her father was "Te-hol-ba-ta-bi," dead, of Eagle County, and her mother was "Malindy," dead, with Mississippi written as her county. At 69 Nancy would have been born about 1830, in the old Choctaw Nation in Mississippi, before the removal.

The family tree has a Nancy Te-hol-ba-ta-bi, born in 1825 in Mississippi. The card suggests that this is the same woman, recorded under her father's name, and that she later carried her husband's name, Pisachubbi. The card does not list any children or a husband, and nothing on it links her to Joseph Pisachubbe, the father of William H. and Robert, so the tie remains a lead. A Case Pisachubbi on the neighboring Card 1277 is a younger man of Eagle County whose father was also called Pisachubbi, and whose mother was "Noise," not Nancy.

EXTRA.name: Rosanna "Rosie" (Tims) Wilson
EXTRA.title: "Rosey Ann Tims": a notary's letter and a grandmother who delivered the babies
EXTRA.hook: Betsy's sister Rosie married James Wilson. In October 1900 a Doaksville notary wrote to the Dawes Commission to say who she was, and her mother Emeline attended her children's births.
body: Rosie does not appear under the Tims name on the roll. She was enrolled on 24 April 1899 on her mother's Card 778 as "Rosanna Tims," and when she married James Wilson she was moved to his card. Dawes Card 1281, filled out on 1 May 1899 at Doaksville (the same day as Henry W. Thompson's Card 1282 and Joseph P. Thompson's Card 1283), lists "Wilson, James," age 24, full-blood, of Cedar County, with parents "Simon Wilson" and "Melissie Wilson," both dead; his wife "Rosanna," 18, three-quarter blood, with her parents written "Benson Tims," dead, and "Emiline Tims," of Towson County; and a baby son. A note on the card says Rosanna was "transferred to this card with her husband, Oct. 26, 1900."

How she was found is in the jacket. In September 1900 the notary R. L. Carter of Doaksville sent in an application for the baby, Islam Wilson, born on 10 August 1900. The Commission sent it back because it could not identify the mother, who gave her age as eighteen and had clearly been married since she was listed. On 19 October 1900 Carter replied: "Rosey Wilson the wife of James Wilson was registered as Rosey Ann Tims and has been married since she was registered. Her mother name is Emaline Times her father died before he was registered." The Commission wrote back on 27 October that it had identified her as "Rosanna Tims the daughter of Emiline Tims, who was listed for enrollment April 24th, 1899." It still wanted the marriage certificate, and on 19 August 1902 acknowledged one between "James Wilson and Rosa Tims."

Two more children are on the jacket. A son was born on 23 March 1903, and Rosanna swore the birth affidavit on 25 March 1905 with her mark, her husband James Wilson and John Aaron as witnesses. The midwife's affidavit, sworn on 19 April 1905, is signed "Emeline Tims," Rosanna's mother, who swore the same kind of affidavit for her grandson Joseph W. Thompson ten days later. A daughter, Candace, was born on 16 June 1905; in May 1906 the Commission acknowledged "the affidavits of Rosanna Wilson and Emeline Tims to the birth of Candace Wilson."
Rosie's husband is probably the James Wilson who swore with her brother Mitchell Tims in 1902 to the death of Mitchell's baby daughter.

EXTRA.name: James Austin
EXTRA.place: Fowlerville, Towson County, Choctaw Nation
EXTRA.src: Dawes Card 1363 (front and back) and jacket 7-1363, NARA Dawes Enrollment Jackets (Choctaw by Blood)
EXTRA.title: The boy who died before the roll was taken
EXTRA.hook: Born 15 November 1898, dead by April 1899, and still on a federal roll until 1904 when the Department struck him off.
body: James Austin was the second child on his parents' card. His father Legion swore at Fowlerville in early May 1899 that the boy was born on 15 November 1898 and was "now living." The card gave his age as 1 and entered him as No. 3739, with a note: "No. 4 died April 1899."

The boy's birth proof is as plain as such papers get. The form's printed "Affidavit of Mother" is crossed out and "Father" written over it, and Legion signed by mark as a 33-year-old citizen by blood. The second affidavit, normally for a doctor or nurse, was sworn by a neighbor, Leonidas Willis, who "knew" of the birth and also made his mark.

Proof of the death reached the Commission on 2 December 1902. The Secretary of the Interior approved the other four on 12 December 1902; the card stamps James "Died prior to September 25, 1902" and runs a red rule through his line. The Department did not cancel his enrollment until 16 September 1904.

quotes.t: No. 4 died April 1899: Enrollment cancelled by Department Sept. 16, 1904

EXTRA.name: Adline (Austin) Pisachubbe
EXTRA.place: Fowlerville, then Speer, Choctaw County
kv: Choctaw by Blood No. 3740, Card 1363, enrolled 4 June 1901
EXTRA.src: Dawes Card 1363 and jacket 7-1363 (letters of 9 Oct. 1900 and 5 June 1901; birth affidavit of 19 Apr. 1901); 1940 U.S. census.
EXTRA.title: A baby on a card that was nearly closed
EXTRA.hook: Born 5 August 1900, a year after her family applied, and added by a letter and an affidavit signed with two marks.
body: Adline was born on 5 August 1900, a year after her parents' application and two years before the roll was approved. Her father wrote to the Commission from Garvin that October; on 9 October the Commission replied with a blank infant application and the instruction that if the mother or the midwife could not write, two disinterested witnesses must attest each mark.

Her mother, "Mulcy Austin," swore on 19 April 1901 that she was 25, a citizen by blood and "the lawful wife of Leageon Austin," and that a girl was born 5 August 1900 and named Adline Austin. The midwife, Sinie Hall, swore the same. Both signed with a mark before the notary William Swink at Fowlerville, with two witnesses, one of them Sallie Johnson.

The Commission acknowledged it on 5 June 1901, "the same being in proper form," and listed the child as Choctaw by Blood No. 3740. The roll was approved on 12 December 1902. Adline later married William Harrison Pisachubbe, whose younger brother Robert had married her sister Lizzie, and died at Speer in 1929.

EXTRA.name: Towson, Red River, Blue and Kiamitia
EXTRA.place: Choctaw Nation, Indian Territory
kv: Legion and Molsey Austin, Emeline Tims; 1896 census Nos. 199-201, 12116
EXTRA.src: Dawes Cards 778, 1363, 1580; Constitution and Laws of the Choctaw Nation (1894), archive.org constitutionand00watkgoog.
EXTRA.title: Four counties on three cards
EXTRA.hook: The grandparents' counties were Choctaw counties, not Oklahoma ones, and the 1896 census numbers show which was which.
body: The Dawes clerks recorded where each person was counted in 1896, and where their dead parents had lived. On the three cards for this line the answers are four Choctaw Nation counties: Towson for Legion and Molsey Austin and for Emeline Tims; Kiamitia for Eunice Pisachubbe, her sons and the ward Edward; Blue for her parents Jackson and Viney Gardner; and Red River for Molsey's parents Brazil and Siney.

Under the Choctaw constitution and its acts, as printed in 1894, Towson belonged to the Apukshunnubbee District, while Blue and Kiamichi were counties of the Pushmataha District, each sending one senator. In 1886 the Council cut Jackson County out of Kiamitia, Blue and Atoka, which is why Edward Pisachubbe's dead parents, Simpson and Sallie, are written as of Jackson County in 1899 while he was counted in Kiamitia.

The cards give both a county and a post office. The Austins were Towson County people with a Fowlerville post office, renamed Valliant in 1902, and Eunice was a Kiamitia County woman at Goodland. The old counties vanished at statehood in 1907, and the families that had been counted in four of them came together in Choctaw County, Oklahoma, where Simon and Frances settled at Jeter.

EXTRA.name: Calvin Vestal Moffitt
EXTRA.place: Born in Randolph County, N.C.; raised in Lawrence County, Ark.; died at Duncan, Stephens County, Okla.
kv: Widowed head of household, Reyno, Randolph Co., Ark.
EXTRA.title: The brother in blue who ended up in Oklahoma
EXTRA.hook: Henry's oldest brother wore Union blue from the Arkansas hills, buried a wife and three children, and died at Duncan, Oklahoma, in 1913.
body: Calvin was the oldest of Nathan and Rebecca Moffitt's sons known by name, born 4 December 1841 in Randolph County, North Carolina, and eight years old when the family was counted at Strawberry Township, Lawrence County, Arkansas, in 1850. He was still in the same township in 1860, a year after his parents' twin daughters were born, and when Henry was a child of four.

A soldier index lists "Calvin V. Moffitt" (also written Moffett) as a private in Company L of the 4th Arkansas Cavalry, a Union regiment, and a Federal service record from 1864 gives his age as 22. The 1870 census has him married and living at Lebanon Township, Sharp County, Arkansas. His wife was Matilda Dailey (born 23 January 1849 in Polk County, Missouri).

The family tree names six children. Andrew Webster was born in Sharp County on 17 January 1869 and died 24 December 1899. Sarah A. (born 1874 in Missouri) died 11 September 1883, and John W. (born 1877 in Missouri) died 7 February 1885, both as children. Milburn Green (1880-1956) lived and died in Arkansas. Wilson Cornelius, born at Golden City, Missouri, on 14 January 1889, farmed in Stephens County, Oklahoma, later lived in Johnson County, Arkansas, and died at Norco, California, in 1971.

The last child, Girdy Emalah, is shown as born and dying on 19 July 1891. Matilda died the next day, 20 July 1891, at New Pocahontas, Arkansas. In 1900 Calvin, a widower, was head of a household at Reyno, Randolph County. By 1910 he was at King Township, Stephens County, Oklahoma, near his son Wilson, and he died in nearby Duncan on 13 February 1913. A Civil War pension index entry was filed from Oklahoma.
EXTRA.src: WikiTree profiles (api.wikitree.com, 2026): Moffitt-400 (Calvin Vestal Moffitt), citing 1850, 1860, 1870, 1900, 1910 U.S. censuses, Arkansas Union soldier service records (M399) and NPS Soldiers and Sailors database; Moffitt-450, -401, -460; Dailey-682
EXTRA.note: Calvin's service is documented in the NPS soldier record; his link to Nathan rests on WikiTree/family-tree profiles and the shared Strawberry Township household in 1850 and 1860. The dates of Matilda's and the infant's deaths come from a tree import and no certificate has been seen. A 1880 census entry at Janes Creek, Randolph County, attached to him in that profile does not fit his children being born in Missouri through 1889, so it is not used here.

EXTRA.name: Patrick Green Moffitt
EXTRA.place: Born at Sylamore, Ark.; married in Oregon County, Mo.; lived and died at Mountain View, Stone County, Ark.
kv: Aug 1873, Oregon Co., Mo., to Alice Ann Cole (1857-1901)
20 Dec 1905, Mountain View (one source: Nov 1904, buried Sallisaw)
EXTRA.title: Patrick: the brother who stayed in Stone County
EXTRA.hook: Patrick married in Missouri the year his father died, then lived on in Mountain View, where Henry settled, and buried his wife four months before Henry died.
body: Patrick Green Moffitt was born on 11 May 1853 at Sylamore, in the Ozark hills along the White River. He was two years older than Henry. After the family went north into Dent and Oregon counties, Missouri, he married Alice Ann Cole there in August 1873, four months before Nathan's death on 23 December.

Alice Ann was born on 18 December 1857 in Missouri. Nathan's second wife was a widow, Nancy (Rowe) Cole, whom he married in 1871. It is likely, though unproved, that Alice was a Cole child of that household, which would make Patrick's bride his stepsister.

The couple returned to Arkansas and settled at Mountain View, where Henry's family was by 1889. Their daughter Lillian was born in 1894 and died in 1988. Alice Ann died on 26 May 1901 and is buried at Levisy Flat Cemetery; Henry died that September.

Patrick's own death is recorded two ways: WikiTree has 20 December 1905 at Mountain View, and another tree has November 1904 with burial at Sallisaw, Oklahoma. The 1905 date is the more widely repeated.
EXTRA.src: WikiTree profiles (api.wikitree.com, 2026): Moffitt-106 (Patrick Green Moffitt), Cole-3005 (Alice Cole), Moffitt-105 (Lillian); Missouri marriages 1750-1920 index entry for Nathan Mofit, 1871; Find a Grave (Levisy Flat Cemetery)
EXTRA.note: Alice as Nancy Cole's daughter is a guess from the surname; no record names her parents.

EXTRA.name: Robert Moffitt (Nathan's youngest brother)
EXTRA.place: Born in Randolph County, N.C.; farmed in Henderson County, Tenn., and Strawberry Township, Lawrence County, Ark.; died at Hutton Valley, Howell County, Mo.
kv: 9 Nov 1872, Hutton Valley, Howell Co., Mo.
EXTRA.title: Uncle Robert, one house over in Strawberry Township
EXTRA.hook: Nathan's youngest brother followed him to Strawberry Township, Arkansas, by 1860, buried most of his early children, and ended up in the Missouri Ozarks.
body: Robert was the youngest of Robert and Martha (Chamness) Moffitt's nine children, born 19 June 1815, a year after Nathan. He married Cynthia Gardner, born in North Carolina on 29 April 1815, and in the 1850 census they were in District 17 of Henderson County, Tennessee, with seven children: John 17, Mary Ann 12, Malcy 10, Alzia 8, Henry P. 6, James H. 3 and Martha E., a baby.

By the 1860 census Robert, 45, and Cynthia, 45, were in Strawberry Township, Lawrence County, Arkansas (page 224), where his brother Nathan was a wheelwright. The household had shrunk to Alzira 18, Parker 15, James 13, Martha 10, Jane 8 and Franklin 5. John, Mary Ann and Malcy do not appear again in any record found, and Parker is last seen in 1860.

The family moved on into Missouri. Robert died on 9 November 1872 at Hutton Valley, Howell County, and was buried in what is now called Moffitt Cemetery near Willow Springs. Cynthia lived until 9 October 1895.

Three of the children have traceable lives. Alzira Adelaide (1842-1923) married James Thomas Loving in 1867, bore seven children and is buried at Willow Springs. James Henderson Moffitt (1848-1916) became a physician at Redford, Reynolds County; the Ellington Press of 20 January 1916 reported, "We were greatly pained to hear of the death of Dr. Moffitt which occurred at Redford the evening of the 7th." Martha Elizabeth (1850-1931) died at Springfield and Margaret Jane (1852-1923) at Montier, Missouri.
EXTRA.src: WikiTree profiles (api.wikitree.com, 2026): Moffitt-1932 (Robert Moffitt), Moffitt-1957, -1965, -1964, -1963, Gardner-25214; 1850 U.S. Census, Dist. 17, Henderson Co., Tenn.; 1860 U.S. Census, Strawberry Twp., Lawrence Co., Ark., p. 224; Ellington Press (Ellington, Mo.), 20 Jan 1916, p. 4; Missouri death certificate for J. H. Moffitt, 1916

quotes.t: We were greatly pained to hear of the death of Dr. Moffitt which occurred at Redford the evening of the 7th.
quotes.c: The Ellington Press, Ellington, Mo., 20 Jan 1916, p. 4 (as transcribed on WikiTree)

EXTRA.note: The census citations are given in the WikiTree profile; the census pages themselves were not viewed. Cynthia Gardner is from North Carolina and no link to the Choctaw Gardner family on the maternal side has been found.

EXTRA.name: Veno (Zeno) Moffitt
EXTRA.rel: Cousin of the 2nd great-grandfather (nephew of Nathan)
EXTRA.place: Randolph County, N.C.; died as a Confederate prisoner at Elmira, N.Y.
kv: Aaron C. Moffitt and Mary "Polly" Brady
Co. F, 24th N.C. Infantry (CSA), enlisted 8 Apr 1863
EXTRA.title: Nathan's nephew, who died in the Elmira prison camp
EXTRA.hook: While his uncle Nathan's boys wore Union blue in Arkansas, cousin Veno from Randolph County, North Carolina, was captured in Virginia and died at Elmira.
body: Nathan's older brother Aaron C. Moffitt (6 December 1805 to 20 June 1877) stayed in Randolph County, North Carolina. He married Mary "Polly" Brady on 7 August 1827 and is in the 1850 and 1870 censuses with her. Their son Veno, called Zeno in the 1860 census, was born about 1828.

Veno married Charlotte L. "Lottie" Gardner (1824-1904), and they had Mary Jane (1860-1920) and the Rev. James Alfred Moffitt (1864-1926). At 34 he enlisted in the Confederate army on 8 April 1863 and joined Company F, 24th North Carolina Infantry.

The roll of honor card says that he was captured near Drewry's Bluff, Virginia, on 16 May 1864. He was sent to the prison camp at Elmira, New York, where he died of chronic diarrhea on 11 October 1864. He is buried in Woodlawn National Cemetery at Elmira.
The Moffitts were split by the war. Veno's cousin Calvin served the Union in the Arkansas cavalry, and Lydia Moffitt Rains lost two sons in the war in North Carolina.
EXTRA.src: WikiTree profiles (api.wikitree.com, 2026): Moffitt-1958 (Veno Moffitt), Moffitt-1959 (Aaron C. Moffitt), Gardner-25498; 1860 U.S. Census (Zeno Moffitt); U.S. Register of Confederates and Civilians Who Died in the North, 1861-1865; Find a Grave memorial 66301062 (Woodlawn National Cemetery)
EXTRA.note: The prison record and burial are from the cards cited on WikiTree and Find a Grave; the originals were not viewed.

EXTRA.name: William Cornelius Moffitt
EXTRA.place: Randolph County, N.C.
kv: Thalitha Williams (m. 7 Aug 1827); Elizabeth Fesmire (m. 1866); Araminta Hicks (m. 1873)
Milo, Dennis, Reuben, Mahala, Marshall, Mary Delphina, John Tyler; Hannah V., William Dufoe
EXTRA.title: William C. and his three Randolph County wives
EXTRA.hook: Nathan's brother stayed in North Carolina, married three times, and lost two sons by 1873; his first wife was a Williams, like Nathan's.
body: William Cornelius Moffitt, born about 1802, married Thalitha (Aletha) Williams on 7 August 1827, the same day Aaron, his brother, married Polly Brady. Thalitha was born 16 September 1804 at Deep River, Randolph County, and died before 1866. The 1850 and 1860 censuses show them with children.

Their children were Milo (1828-1881, died in Chatham County), Dennis (1830-1886), Reuben Elwood (1833-1915), Mahala Adeline (1835-1903), Marshall (1839-1863), Mary Delphina (1842-1898, died at Decatur, Indiana) and John Tyler (1843-1873). Marshall died in 1863, which fits the Civil War, but no record of his service has been seen.

William married Elizabeth Fesmire on 2 September 1866; she appears in the 1870 census and died about 1873. On 7 October 1873 he married Araminta Hicks (1844-1932), and the 1880 census shows them with two young children, Hannah V. (born 1875) and William Dufoe (born 1876). He died in 1884 aged about 82; the birth date on his Find a Grave memorial is regarded as doubtful.

Nathan's wife was Rebecca Williams, also from Randolph County. Whether Rebecca and Thalitha were sisters is not shown by any record; it is a lead worth checking in the Randolph County Williams families.
EXTRA.src: WikiTree profiles (api.wikitree.com, 2026): Moffitt-922 (William Cornelius Moffitt), Williams-38370, Fesmire-258, Hicks-22845; North Carolina county marriages, Randolph Co., 7 Aug 1827 (FHL film 418,149); 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880 U.S. censuses
EXTRA.note: The Williams sister idea is only a lead.

EXTRA.name: Sarah and Naomi (Moffitt) Barker
EXTRA.place: Randolph County, N.C.; Union County, Iowa
kv: 21 Apr 1800 - 18 Dec 1860, Lorimor, Iowa; m. 1821 Rev. Beeson Barker (1802-1873)
b. c.1800; m. 5 Mar 1822 Robert Barker
Groesbeck Cemetery, Lorimor, Union Co., Iowa
EXTRA.title: Two sisters who went to Iowa with their Barker husbands
EXTRA.hook: Nathan went west to Arkansas; his sisters Sarah and Naomi married two Barkers and settled in Iowa, where Sarah died on a sled being hauled home.
body: Sarah and Naomi were the oldest of Robert and Martha Moffitt's children. Naomi married Robert Barker on 5 March 1822, and Sarah married the Rev. Beeson Barker in 1821. Both families left Randolph County for Union County, Iowa.

Sarah's WikiTree profile preserves a family memory of her death: "Mrs. Beeson Barker was born in 1800 and died in 1860 in the early winter. She took sick at the home of her son, Jerry, in Winterset. She wanted to come home so Marion Carey took a yoke of oxen hitched to a pin sled with a wagon box on it and putting a feather bed in it, brought her home. She lived only a few days. This broke up the active home of Rev. Barker." She is buried at Groesbeck Cemetery, Lorimor.

Sarah and Beeson had eight children: Aaron Dennis (1824-1881), Jeremiah Harmon (1826-1885), Robert Moffitt (1830-1834), Martha Jane (1831-1838), David Pearce (1834-1918), Mary Rahab (1838-1891), Sarah Ann (1841-1850) and William Beeson (1842-1926).

Naomi and Robert Barker's daughters Mary D. (1823-1899) and Deborah L. (1824-1907) both married their Moffitt cousins, Solomon C. and Stancil, sons of Charles Moffitt and Mary Beeson, and both died in Union County, Iowa.
EXTRA.src: WikiTree profiles (api.wikitree.com, 2026): Moffitt-1914 (Sarah Mary Moffitt Barker), Moffitt-1915 (Naomi Moffitt), Barker-20885, Barker-20899, -20900, -20901; NC marriages 1759-1979; 1850 and 1860 U.S. censuses; Find a Grave memorial 9344842 (Groesbeck Cemetery)

quotes.t: She wanted to come home so Marion Carey took a yoke of oxen hitched to a pin sled with a wagon box on it and putting a feather bed in it, brought her home.
quotes.c: Family account quoted on WikiTree, Moffitt-1914

EXTRA.note: The deathbed account is an undated family account; the census and burial records are as cited on WikiTree.

EXTRA.name: Lydia (Moffitt) Rains and Hannah (Moffitt) Craven
EXTRA.place: Randolph County, N.C. (Coleridge and Ramseur)
kv: 11 Dec 1806 - 24 Jan 1888; m. Isaiah Craven (1799-1885); Concord Cemetery, Coleridge
18 Jun 1811 - 2 Mar 1885; m. 29 Jun 1833 Alfred Rains (1811-1888)
Nathan (1834), Mary, Susannah, William Anderson (1841), Alfred Evans, Daniel, Robert Monroe
EXTRA.title: The sisters who never left: Hannah and Lydia
EXTRA.hook: Nathan's sisters Hannah and Lydia stayed in Randolph County, and Lydia lost two sons in the Civil War.
body: Hannah Moffitt, born 11 December 1806, married Isaiah Craven and in 1850 lived in his household in Randolph County. They had at least Hiram Peter (1835-1900), Peter W. (1837-1861), Molcy, and Lewis Pickett (1846-1924). Hannah died on 24 January 1888 and is buried at Concord Cemetery, Coleridge.

Lydia, born 18 June 1811, married Alford Rains on 29 June 1833 and appears in the censuses of 1850 through 1880. Her seven children were Nathan (born 1834), Mary (1836), Susannah (1838, died young), William Anderson (1841), Alfred Evans (1844), Daniel (1845) and Robert Monroe (1853). WikiTree records that Nathan and William Anderson "died in the Civil War."
Lydia died on 2 March 1885 and is buried in the Rains-Caveness family cemetery at Ramseur. Her brother Nathan, far away in Missouri, had died twelve years earlier.
EXTRA.src: WikiTree profiles (api.wikitree.com, 2026): Moffitt-1398 (Hannah Moffitt Craven), Moffitt-1913 (Lydia Moffitt Rains), Craven-2765, Rains-1897; NC marriages (Alford Rains and Lydia Moffitt, 29 Jun 1833); 1850-1880 U.S. censuses; Find a Grave memorials 29673064 and 133480891
EXTRA.note: The sons' deaths are a one-line statement on WikiTree; the units were not checked.

EXTRA.name: Thomas Berry "Tom" Moffitt
EXTRA.place: Born at St. James, Stone County, Ark.; farmed beside Grady in Choctaw County, Okla.; died at Paris, Texas.
kv: 17 Feb 1889, St. James, Stone Co., Ark.
Farming next to Grady, Wilson Twp., Choctaw Co.
21 Mar 1953, Paris, Texas; stone marked WW I and WW II
EXTRA.title: Tom, the brother next door
EXTRA.hook: Tom was born at the old Buck Horn settlement, worked the railroad, and followed his brother Grady to Choctaw County.
body: Thomas Berry Moffitt was born on 17 February 1889 at St. James in Stone County, Arkansas, the first of Henry and Hannah's children known to be born in Stone County. In the 1910 census he was living with his widowed mother in Franklin Township and working as a railroad section hand.

By 1920 he was farming next door to Grady in Wilson Township, Choctaw County, Oklahoma. His wife, Vesta, was born in Arkansas on 2 March 1892 and died at Holdenville, Hughes County, Oklahoma, on 15 October 1930.

Tom later lived at Paris, Texas, where he died on 21 March 1953. His grave marker is carved with World War I and World War II service, and WikiTree gives him as the son of Henry H. Moffitt and Hannah Grimes and the brother of Grady.
EXTRA.src: WikiTree profiles (api.wikitree.com, 2026): Moffitt-1137 (Thomas Berry Moffitt), Moffitt-1138, Grimes-4049; 1910 U.S. Census, Franklin Twp., Stone Co., Ark.; 1920 U.S. Census, Wilson Twp., Choctaw Co., Okla.; Find a Grave (Thomas Berry Moffitt)
EXTRA.note: The WikiTree profile does not give his military record; the marker wording is from Find a Grave. Henry's death date appears on WikiTree as 9 September 1901.

EXTRA.name: Josephine, Jesse Gee, Gimsa and Bertha Moffitt
EXTRA.place: Randolph and Stone counties, Ark.; West Texas
kv: Born about 1877; age 3 in Janes Creek Twp., Randolph Co., 1880
At home in Franklin Twp., Stone Co., 1900
At home in 1900; Bertha May Moffitt Barham (1888-1930) is possibly the same
EXTRA.title: Grady's older brothers and sisters
EXTRA.hook: Four of Henry and Hannah's seven children are known only by a census line or a gravestone, and one of them went to the Texas plains.
body: The 1880 census at Janes Creek Township, Randolph County, lists Henry and Hannah with Josephine, 3, and Jesse, 1. Hannah told the 1910 census taker that she had borne seven children and six were still living, so one died young and has left no record.

Jesse Gee Moffitt (1879-1957) went to the Texas plains; he is buried at Tahoka in Lynn County, and family notes place his death at Amarillo. Josephine, Gimsa and Bertha are with their parents in the 1900 census at Franklin Township, Stone County, along with Tom and Woodford (Grady).
A Bertha May Moffitt Barham (1888-1930) is buried at Herpel Cemetery, near her mother, and may be the Bertha of the census. That is not proved.
EXTRA.src: 1880 U.S. Census, Janes Creek Twp., Randolph Co., Ark.; 1900 and 1910 U.S. Censuses, Franklin Twp., Stone Co., Ark.; Find a Grave (Jesse Gee Moffitt; Bertha May Barham, Herpel Cemetery)
EXTRA.note: Little is recorded for these siblings. Gimsa is the spelling transcribed from the 1900 census and may be a misreading of a given name.

EXTRA.name: Alvin, Odas, Alton, Eldon and Donald Moffitt
EXTRA.place: Choctaw County, Okla.; Paris, Texas
kv: Twins born 1928; Alton d. 1975, Eldon d. 2014
EXTRA.title: Nine children, three lost: the rest of Grady's boys
EXTRA.hook: Grady and Mary raised five more sons to adulthood beside John and Dois, and lost two toddlers and Dois himself.
body: Alvin B., born in September 1915, was the first of Grady and Mary's children. He served in the U.S. Army Air Corps in World War II and died in 1994.
Odas Eugene (1918-1995) was "Odis, 21" in the 1940 census and "Ottis" in 1920. The twins Alton V. and Eldon Herman were born in 1928 and were 11 in 1940; Donald K., born in 1931, was 8.

Two children died at three years old: Jimmie Gaynell in 1926 and Henry Wayne in 1937. With Dois, who died after breaking his neck in the Red River in 1947, that makes three of the nine buried before their parents.
EXTRA.src: 1920, 1930 and 1940 U.S. censuses (Choctaw Co., Okla.; Martin Co., Tex.; Hugo); Find a Grave family links (Shoat Springs Cemetery); family-tree dates
EXTRA.note: Dates are the ones family trees give; they repeat what the Grady and Mary entry already says, with names added.

EXTRA.name: John Grimes and Penelope "Penny" Blackshear
EXTRA.place: Williamson County, then Wayne County, Tenn. (Hardin Creek, near Waynesboro)
kv: Born c.1775 in South Carolina; died 14 Jun 1844, Wayne Co., Tenn.; buried Haggard Farm
Born 6 Jun 1789, Jones Co., N.C.; living after 1850 (one list: after 1864)
James B., Elisha S., John Anderson, William Jasper, and probably David H.
EXTRA.title: The Grimes farm on Hardin Creek
EXTRA.hook: A Blackshear daughter from Jones County, North Carolina, married a South Carolina Grimes and raised a family at the Haggard farm near Waynesboro, where David H. Grimes was born.
body: John Grimes was born in South Carolina about 1775. Penelope, called Penny, was the daughter of Jesse and Hannah (Huggins) Blackshear of Jones County, North Carolina, and she was born there on 6 June 1789. Jesse took his family to Williamson County, Tennessee, between 1800 and 1810. John and Penelope's first known child, James B., was born in Williamson County about 1807.

In October 1814 the Williamson County court settled the estate of Jesse Blackshare, deceased: his widow had remarried as Hannah Mairs, and the balance was due to "Penny Blackshare and James Blackshare" and the other heirs. The Grimes site dates Penelope's first child to about 1807, so she was already married by then; the court may simply have used her maiden name for the share due to her.

The Grimes family later moved to Wayne County. John died there on 14 June 1844 and was buried on the Haggard farm. The Grimes family website lists their children as James B. (about 1807), a daughter (1810-1815), Elisha S. (about 1817), a daughter (1820-1825), John Anderson (born October 1823), an unnamed son (1825-1829) and William Jasper (born 1826). David H. Grimes, born in 1829 in Wayne County, fits the unnamed son, and a family tree names a John Grimes as his father.
A 1954 Blackshear genealogy lists "A dau., m. Grimes" as the first child of Jesse Blackshear of Jones County and Williamson County. Penelope is shown still living after 1850.
EXTRA.src: Grimes Family Genealogy, "Our Grimes Line" (descendants of John Grimes and Penelope Blackshear); Genealogy.com Grimes forum, Pamela Bryant, 17 July 2003; Williamson Co., Tenn., Probate Court Wills vol. 2, p. 109 (Oct. 1814), as cited on WikiTree Blackshear-160; P. L. Blackshear, Blacksheariana (1954); Ancestry family tree for David H. Grimes
EXTRA.note: David H. Grimes is not named in the Grimes family website; he fits the unnamed son of 1825-1829. The tree that names John Grimes as his father calls him "John Jasper" born 1784, which does not match the site's John, born about 1775. WikiTree gives Penelope an 1814 death date that cannot be right if she was living in 1850 or 1864.

EXTRA.name: William Jasper, John Anderson and the other Grimes brothers
EXTRA.place: Wayne County, Tenn.
kv: Born 1826; will probated 1 Jul 1872; wives Malaha Keaton, Tennessee Ann McClanahan
Born Oct 1823; wife Mary C. Arnett; 1860 farmer worth $4,000 land and $3,500 personal
Born c.1817, Williamson Co.; Haggard Farm
EXTRA.title: "John A. Grimes, my brother, as executor"
EXTRA.hook: In 1872 William Jasper Grimes made a will leaving his land to his second family and his first wife's children, and named his brother John executor.
body: John Anderson Grimes, born in October 1823 in Wayne County, married Mary C. Arnett about 1852. In the 1860 census he was a farmer, 37, with $4,000 in land and $3,500 in personal property, with Mary, 27, and children Nancy E., 7, George (Kearney), 5, Sarah F., 3, and John, 1. They are still on the family farm in the 1900 census, run by their son George.

William Jasper Grimes was born in 1826. He married first Malaha Keaton and had twelve children between 1844 and 1868, among them Sarah J., Margaret G., John Q. A., Lucinda, Mary P., William Jasper K., Sevilla, Nancy C., Jasper Wayne, Benjamin Stout (a Blackshear name), Fannie and Mahulda Vista. His second wife was Tennessee Ann McClanahan.

His will was probated on 1 July 1872. It leaves his wife Tennessee Ann the home farm for her life and the land bought from John H. Cole, requires that "each of our children at the age of 21 years or at marriage" receive "one good horse, Bridle and Saddle, one cow and calf, one bed, bedstead and furniture," gives his two sons John A. and W. J. Grimes the tract bought from John B. Rutledge, and ends: "I nominate and appoint John A. Grimes, my brother, as executor to this my will."
James B. (born about 1807) and Elisha S. (born about 1817) both lived in Wayne County, Elisha on the Haggard farm.
EXTRA.src: Genealogy.com Grimes forum: "Will Abstract of William Jasper Grimes, Wayne Co. Tennessee" (P. Bryant, 16 Oct 2002); "Grimes in Wayne Co., Tn. 1860 census" (17 July 2003); Grimes Family Genealogy, Our Grimes Line

quotes.t: I nominate and appoint John A. Grimes, my brother, as executor to this my will.
quotes.c: Will of W. J. Grimes, Wayne Co., Tenn., probated 1 July 1872 (transcription by Pamela Bryant)

EXTRA.note: The will is a modern transcription from a poor photocopy. The brothers are tied to David H. only through the unproved link to John and Penelope Grimes.

EXTRA.name: Jesse Blackshear and the 1814 heirs
EXTRA.place: Jones County, N.C.; Williamson County, Tenn.
kv: About 1767, Jones (or Craven) Co., N.C.; father Elisha Stout Blackshear
Williamson Co., Tenn.; WikiTree gives 26 Jul 1803
Ezekiel, Elisha, Luke, David, Elijah, Jacob, Jesse, Penny and James
EXTRA.title: A Williamson County estate and a daughter named Penny
EXTRA.hook: The 1814 court order dividing Jesse Blackshear's estate is the paper that names Penny Blackshear, who married John Grimes.
body: Jesse Blackshear was born about 1767 in Jones County, North Carolina, son of Susannah and Elisha Stout Blackshear. He moved to Williamson County, Tennessee, between 1800 and 1810; two of his sons remained in North Carolina until after 1810.

In October 1814 the Williamson County court heard the settlement of "Jesse Blackshare, Dec'd." Hannah, his widow and administrator, was by then "Hannah Mairs, wife of Isaac Mairs," and the "balance of $227.30" was divided between "Penny Blackshare and James Blackshare and the above named Legatees," Ezekiel, Elisha, Luke, David, Elijah, Jacob and Jesse. Hannah died on 4 June 1829 and is buried in Brown Cemetery, Wayne County.

The 1954 Blacksheariana traces the sons. Ezekiel (born 13 July 1792) lived in Williamson County in 1820, in Haywood County in 1830, and died at Brownsville on 23 April 1837; his widow, Isabella Dobson, was "bur. in the Ozarks" in 1882. Elisha (about 1794) farmed in Marshall County in 1840. Jacob (born 26 January 1802) moved to McNairy and Obion counties. The first child in the book is "A dau., m. Grimes."
EXTRA.src: Tennessee Probate Court Books, Williamson Co., Wills 1812-1819, vol. 2, p. 109 (Oct. 1814), as cited on WikiTree Blackshear-160 and Blackshear-2; P. L. Blackshear, Blacksheariana (1954), entries for Jesse, Ezekiel, Elisha, Jacob; WikiTree Huggins-10
EXTRA.note: WikiTree gives Jesse's death as 1803, which does not fit an estate settled in 1814 with a guardian; the settlement could follow years after his death. Penelope's place as the "dau., m. Grimes" rests on the name Penny and the Grimes family site.

EXTRA.name: Elijah Blackshear of Waynesboro
EXTRA.rel: 3rd great-granduncle (probable brother of David H. Grimes's mother)
EXTRA.place: Waynesboro, Wayne County, Tenn.
kv: 29 Mar 1830, before Isaac G. Grimes, J.P.
EXTRA.title: A militia oath before a Grimes justice of the peace
EXTRA.hook: Penelope's brother Elijah swore never to fight a duel, in front of a Wayne County Grimes.
body: Elijah Blackshear was born on 9 June 1800, the son of Jesse Blackshear. He lived in Waynesboro, Tennessee, and married Dicena McMahon about 1820. Their children were Lucinda (1823), the twins Jesse Marion and James Newton (1826), and Hannah Permelia. James Newton married a Grimes, Elizabeth Anne, daughter of Isaac G. Grimes, on 11 April 1847.

The Blacksheariana prints two oaths Elijah signed on 29 March 1830: "I do solemnly swear that I will support the Constitution of the U. S., and the State of Tenn.," and "I, Elijah Blackshear do solemnly swear that I will not give or accept a challenge either written or verbal to fight a duel, nor will I be the bearer of a challenge for such purpose." Both were sworn before Isaac G. Grimes, J.P., the same man who is the father of his son's later wife.
Isaac G. Grimes's relationship to John Grimes has not been traced.
EXTRA.src: P. L. Blackshear, Blacksheariana (1954), entries for Elijah and James Newton Blackshear (archive.org blackshearianage00blac)

quotes.t: I do solemnly swear that I will not give or accept a challenge either written or verbal to fight a duel.

EXTRA.name: William Roy Hulsey
kv: George Washington Hulsey and Sarah Rebecca Graves
Roy Hulsey, 34, to Bonnie Meredith, 15, Montgomery Co., Ark., 22 Jan 1938 (Bk J, p. 635)
EXTRA.src: 1910 U.S. Census, Mountain Twp, Garland Co., Ark.; 1920 U.S. Census, Sulphur Twp, McCurtain Co., Okla.; 1930 U.S. Census near Wright City, McCurtain Co., Okla. (as summarized in the Rev. George Washington Hulsey entry); Graves Family Association, Gen. 242 (https://www.graves-fa.org/gen-histories/gens/gen242.html); McCurtain Gazette, 20 Jun 1982, obituary of Oscar Franklin Hulsey (survived by two sisters and four brothers).
EXTRA.title: The oldest of the ten Hulsey children
EXTRA.hook: Eldest of ten, he was about six at the 1910 census and about thirty when his father died.
body: William Roy was the eldest of the ten children, born in 1904, three years after his parents married on 22 December 1901. By the April 1910 census he was about five or six and the family was in Mountain Township, Garland County, Arkansas, listed with his parents and two younger brothers, John W. and Noah, before Oscar was born in October of that year at Hot Springs.

He was the child who saw the whole move. His father was a laborer on the Camp Pike construction job near Little Rock in September 1918 and living at Story in Montgomery County; by the 1920 census the household was in Sulphur Township, McCurtain County, Oklahoma, farming as tenants, and in 1930 it was near Wright City. When his father died on 5 August 1935 William Roy was about 30 or 31, the oldest of the nine surviving children (the youngest, George Paul, was 9 or 10).

Oscar's 1982 obituary says he was survived by four brothers, so at least two of the eight siblings had died by then. Whether William Roy was one of them, whom he married and where he lived as an adult are still open (lead). A Roy Hulsey, 34, married Bonnie Meredith, 15, in Montgomery County, Arkansas on 22 Jan 1938 (marriage index, Montgomery Co., book J, p. 635); that age fits William Roy (b. 1904) but is only a lead until checked against a record that names his parents.
EXTRA.note: The birth year and parentage come from the family listing of the ten children; the dates of death, marriages and later homes have not been confirmed from a certificate or census page and are marked lead where given.

EXTRA.title: John Wesley, the second son
EXTRA.hook: The second son, three years old at the 1910 census in Garland County.
body: John Wesley, called John W. on the 1910 census, was born in 1906 and was the second son. In April 1910 he was three or four years old in the Mountain Township, Garland County household with his father George, mother Rebecca and brothers William R. and Noah. His father, then farming in Garland County, was also a preacher.

He was twelve when his father registered for the draft at Story in September 1918, and about fourteen when the family moved west over the line to McCurtain County, Oklahoma, a county then filling with sawmill and railroad work. His brother Oscar later worked government relief jobs and lumber towns in the same corner of the state.
His marriage, children, death and burial are not yet traced (lead). Oscar's 1982 obituary lists four brothers living, and he may or may not be one of them.
EXTRA.note: The birth year and parentage come from the family listing of the ten children; the dates of death, marriages and later homes have not been confirmed from a certificate or census page and are marked lead where given.

EXTRA.hook: Third of ten, born 1908, the baby of the 1910 census household.
body: Noah was born in 1908, two years before Oscar and the third of the ten. He is the youngest child named in the April 1910 census household in Mountain Township, Garland County, where he would have been one or two years old beside William R. and John W.
He grew up as the family moved from Garland to Montgomery County, Arkansas (where his father was working on Camp Pike in 1918) and on to McCurtain County, Oklahoma.
Noah's adult life, spouse and death are not yet found in any record seen (lead).

EXTRA.title: Fred, the brother born in 1913
EXTRA.hook: Born in 1913, he was seven when the family counted six children at home in Oklahoma.
body: Fred was born in 1913, three years after Oscar, and was five years old when his father registered for the draft at Story in September 1918.

He was about seven at the 1920 census, the year the household was recorded as tenant farmers in Sulphur Township, McCurtain County, Oklahoma with six children at home. By the 1930 census, when the household of ten was renting a farm near Wright City, he was about sixteen or seventeen.
Fred's marriage, military record and death are not yet found (lead). A WWII draft registration would be expected, since he was 27 at the first call-up in October 1940, but no card has been matched.

EXTRA.title: Ruby Ellen, who became a Stipe
EXTRA.hook: The first Hulsey daughter, born 1915 and married to a Stipe.
body: Ruby Ellen was the first daughter after five sons, born in 1915 when her mother Rebecca was about thirty. She married a Stipe, and that is how she is recorded in the family list; Oscar's 1982 obituary says he was survived by two sisters, so she was either one of them or had died before him.
She was a girl of five at the 1920 census in McCurtain County, Oklahoma, and fourteen or fifteen in 1930 near Wright City. She was about twenty when her father died in August 1935.
Her husband's first name, the date and place of the marriage and her death are not yet found (lead).

EXTRA.title: Grady, born the year of the draft card
EXTRA.hook: Born in 1918, the year his father was building Camp Pike.
body: Grady was born in 1918, the year his father registered for the draft at Story, Montgomery County, while working for Stewart-McGehee on Camp Pike. He was the seventh child and probably the last born in Arkansas (lead).

He was about two at the 1920 census in Sulphur Township, McCurtain County, and about twelve in 1930. He was about seventeen when his father died in 1935, and in 1940, at 21 or 22, he was old enough for the first peacetime draft registration of 16 October 1940.
His registration card, marriage and death are not yet found (lead).

EXTRA.title: Louis Daniel, the Oklahoma-born brother
EXTRA.hook: Born 1920, probably in Oklahoma, where the family had just moved.
body: Louis Daniel was born in 1920, most likely in McCurtain County, Oklahoma, since the family was settled there by the census of that year (lead). He was the eighth child.

He was ten at the 1930 census near Wright City, and fifteen when his father died. His eldest brother Oscar married Katie Stevenson when Louis was seven. Born in 1920, he reached draft age in the early years of the Second World War.
No marriage, draft card or death record for him has been matched (lead).

EXTRA.title: Grace Irene, who became a Dunagan
EXTRA.hook: Born 1923 and married a Dunagan; one of the two sisters in her brother's 1982 obituary, unless she had died.
body: Grace Irene was born in 1923, the ninth child and second daughter, when her mother was about 39. She married a Dunagan, and the family list records her under that name.

She was about seven in 1930 in the renting household of ten near Wright City, and about twelve when her father died in August 1935. Her mother, Sarah Rebecca, later left Oklahoma and died at Bandon, Coos County, Oregon on 23 December 1972; whether Grace lived near her in Oregon is not known (lead).

Her husband's first name, her marriage and her death are not yet found (lead). With Ruby Stipe she is one of the two sisters Oscar's 1982 obituary names as surviving, unless one of them had died before him.

EXTRA.title: George Paul, the last child
EXTRA.hook: The youngest of the ten, nine or ten when his father died.
body: George Paul was the youngest, born in 1925 when his father was 48 or 49 and his mother Rebecca 41. He shared his first name with his father, George Washington Hulsey.

He was four or five at the 1930 census near Wright City and nine or ten when his father died on 5 August 1935 and was buried at Breashears Cemetery near Story. At seventeen, in 1942, he would have been of age for the draft within the following year, in the middle of the Second World War.
No record of his adult life has been matched (lead).

EXTRA.name: Margaret (Cornett) Crumpton Graves
EXTRA.place: Garland Co., Arkansas
kv: John Speer and Elizabeth Mason, or Edward Cornett and Rebecca (the genealogy gives both)
5 May 1884, Little Rock or Cedar Glades, at the birth of her child
EXTRA.src: Graves Family Association, Gen. 242 (https://www.graves-fa.org/gen-histories/gens/gen242.html), Jesse S. Graves (no. 14), citing family records and the 1880 census, Garland Co., Ark.
EXTRA.title: She died the day her daughter was born
EXTRA.hook: Margaret Crumpton married Jesse Graves on 31 January 1884 and died on 5 May, the day Sarah Rebecca was born.
body: Margaret was born about 1855 in Arkansas. The Graves genealogy names her as Margaret (Speer or Cornett) Crumpton, and gives two sets of parents for her: John Speer and Elizabeth Mason, or Edward Cornett and a Rebecca. The surname Crumpton is from an earlier marriage to a man of that name, who had died by 1880.

The 1880 census of Garland County has her as "Margaret Crumpton living with her mother Rebecca Cornett and her two Crumpton sons." The sons are named as John and Henry Crumpton, who became Jesse Graves's stepsons.
She married Jesse S. Graves in Garland County on 31 January 1884. She was a widow with two sons; he was about 29, and his first wife Emma is last recorded in the 1880 census.

Margaret died on 5 May 1884, at the birth of the child who became Sarah Rebecca (Graves) Hulsey, the grandmother of the Hulsey children of McCurtain County. The genealogy gives her place of death as Little Rock, or Cedar Glades in Garland County. Her grave is not recorded in that source (lead).

quotes.t: Margaret Crumpton living with her mother Rebecca Cornett and her two Crumpton sons
quotes.c: Graves Family Association, Gen. 242, on the 1880 census, Garland Co., Ark.

EXTRA.note: The mother's maiden name is Speer or Cornett in the source itself. Her mother is called Rebecca Cornett in the 1880 census entry, which favors Cornett, and may be the origin of the name Rebecca for her daughter (lead).

EXTRA.title: Married at fifteen in a neighbor's house
EXTRA.hook: Jesse Graves's first wife was 15 when they married at Jack Phillips's house in 1871.
body: Emma Fisher was the daughter of Nicholas Fisher and Sarah L. (Garrett) Gray Kirkland. Her mother had a hard run of husbands: Gray, Kirkland, Fisher and then Jack Zacharia Phillips, whose home in Mountain Township, Montgomery County, hosted the wedding.
The marriage record, Book A, page 278, is quoted in the Graves genealogy: Jesse was "18 years old and Emma was 15." They married on 2 April 1871 at the residence of Jack Phillips.

They lived in Garland County, and the family was recorded there on the census of 11 June 1880 with four children, Abraham Nicholas (b. 7 Jan 1874), Catherine Eunice (b. 9 Mar 1876), Greenbury H. (b. Jan 1880) and Vestal (b. 21 Mar 1881, so added after the census). Emma is not recorded after that census; by January 1884 Jesse had married Margaret Crumpton (lead as to what became of Emma).

quotes.t: Jesse was 18 years old and Emma was 15
quotes.c: Marriage Record Bk. A, p. 278, Montgomery Co., Ark., as quoted in Graves Family Association, Gen. 242

EXTRA.note: Vestal's birth date (21 Mar 1881) is after the 1880 census date, so the census household listed Abraham, Catherine and Greenbury only.

EXTRA.name: Nancy (Wilborn) Kyle Cuttler Graves
EXTRA.place: Garland Co., Arkansas
kv: John B. Kyle; Samuel B. Cuttler; Jesse S. Graves (19 Sep 1889)
20 Nov 1932; buried McGill Cemetery, Garland Co.
Lucinda, William Vestal, Pearl Mae, Cora Ellen
EXTRA.src: Graves Family Association, Gen. 242 (https://www.graves-fa.org/gen-histories/gens/gen242.html), Jesse S. Graves (no. 14) and nos. 67-70.
EXTRA.title: The stepmother of the Graves children
EXTRA.hook: Nancy Wilborn married Jesse Graves when his motherless daughter Sarah Rebecca was five, and was still in Garland County in 1930.
body: Nancy Wilborn married first John B. Kyle, and their son Isaac was born on 15 December 1879. She next married Samuel B. Cuttler and had a son, Prince Sylvester Cuttler, in 1882. The genealogy also lists a Cindy Sutton, about Sarah Rebecca's age, among her children.

On 19 September 1889 she married Jesse Graves. Sarah Rebecca, then five, had lost her mother Margaret on the day she was born, and Nancy became her stepmother. Nancy and Jesse had four children of their own: Lucinda (b. 8 Jun 1889), William Vestal (b. 22 Apr 1892), Pearl Mae (b. 24 May 1895) and Cora Ellen (b. 1 Jul 1898).

Jesse died in 1910 and was buried in the yard of the old home on Walnut Valley Road. Nancy was on the 1920 census in Garland County with her daughter Lucinda and son-in-law Benjamin Hogue, and in 1930 she lived in Hot Springs with her widowed son William. She died on 20 November 1932 and was buried in McGill Cemetery.
EXTRA.note: The genealogy gives her second husband's surname as Cuttler and alternatively Sutton; one step-child is named Cindy Sutton.

EXTRA.name: Robert R. Hulsey
EXTRA.rel: Likely brother of Benjamin Franklin Hulsey (lead)
EXTRA.place: Union Co., Georgia; Hempstead Co., Arkansas
kv: Age 17, Union Co., Ga., in the household of Salathiel Hulsey (as transcribed)
Robert R. Hulsey, 27, Hempstead Co., Ark., with Sarah A., 20, born Miss., and a son Salathel G., 1, born Ark.
EXTRA.src: 1850 U.S. Census, Union Co., Ga., and 1860 U.S. Census, Hempstead Co., Ark., as transcribed in San Diego Genealogical Society Families: Hulsey (archive.org item sdgsfamilies64)
EXTRA.title: The brother who went to Arkansas first
EXTRA.hook: A son of Salathiel Hulsey is in southwest Arkansas by 1860, with a baby named for his father.
body: The 1850 Union County, Georgia transcription lists Salathiel Hulsey, 43, born Georgia, with Elizabeth, 35, and children Maryann 19, Robert R. 17, Elizabeth 12, Jesse 10, Jennings 8, Benjamin 6, Lillean 3 and Nancy 1, with Arminda Burnet 20 and J. C. Bell 23 in the house.

Robert R. Hulsey, age 27, is in the 1860 Hempstead County, Arkansas census with Sarah A., 20, born Mississippi, and a son Salathel G., 1, born Arkansas. The son's name, Salathel, matches his probable father's, and the 1860 age fits Robert R. of 1850.

If this is the same man, he was in Arkansas several years before Benjamin F. Hulsey first appears there, on the 1864 Union roster, and may be one reason Benjamin came to Arkansas. That is lead only: no record says the two Roberts are one man, and only the shared 1850 household suggests he was Benjamin's brother.
EXTRA.note: In this transcription Benjamin is 6 in 1850, which gives a birth about 1844; the family record and the entry for Benjamin say 2 February 1847, and the census would then have said 3.

EXTRA.name: Samuel and Sarah Graves's children
EXTRA.place: Montgomery Co., Arkansas
EXTRA.src: Graves Family Association, Gen. 242 (https://www.graves-fa.org/gen-histories/gens/gen242.html), Gilliam Graves (no. 1), citing the 1853-1861 Montgomery Co. tax and guardianship records and the 1860 census.
EXTRA.title: Gilliam Graves and the orphans of Samuel and Sarah
EXTRA.hook: In 1854 Gilliam Graves was named guardian of the children of Samuel and Sarah Graves; one of them, William Riley, died without a will in 1861.
body: In January 1854 Gilliam Graves was appointed guardian for the children of Samuel and Sarah Graves of Montgomery County, Arkansas. The Graves genealogy suggests the parents are Samuel Graves and Sarah Cole, who were married on 30 March 1837 in Randolph County, North Carolina, by Moore Graves.

Gillum and Moor Graves are both on the 1840 census of Cherokee County, Georgia, and "it is believed that Moore Graves died in the 1840s." The widow Sarah appears on the Montgomery County tax lists from 1851 and bought a 40-acre tract, the NW SE of section 11.

The 1860 census lists the children as a household of their own: William (Riley), 22, farmer, and Alley, 17, Ursa, 15, Alison, 14 and Madison, 11, all born North Carolina. In April 1861 Gilliam is again named guardian for the minor heirs Alley, Ultha, Alison and Madison. William Riley died intestate on 1 November 1861.
How these children were related to Gilliam, whether nephews and nieces or otherwise, is not established (lead).

quotes.t: It is believed that Moore Graves died in the 1840s.
quotes.c: Graves Family Association, Gen. 242

EXTRA.note: Names are spelled Alley, Ursa, Alison, Madison in the 1860 census and Alley, Ultha, Alison, Madison in the 1861 guardianship; Ursa and Ultha are probably the same child.

EXTRA.name: Mary (Polly) Gray Washburn Graves
EXTRA.rel: Third wife of Gilliam Graves, stepmother of Jesse Graves
EXTRA.place: Hot Spring Co. and Cedar Glades, Arkansas
kv: William Andrew Gray and Sarah L. Garrett
Franklin W. Washburn, 1 Feb 1859, Hot Spring Co.
c.1879, Cedar Glades; buried beside Gilliam, Mountain Valley Cemetery
EXTRA.src: Graves Family Association, Gen. 242 (https://www.graves-fa.org/gen-histories/gens/gen242.html), Gilliam Graves (no. 1) and children by Mary Gray (nos. 16 ff.).
EXTRA.title: Married at nineteen, then to a man twice her age
EXTRA.hook: Polly Gray was 19 when she married Franklin Washburn in 1859; by 1864 she had a daughter by Gilliam Graves.
body: Polly Gray was the daughter of William Andrew Gray and Sarah L. Garrett, a woman who married four times (Gray, Kirkland, Fisher and Phillips). She was born about 1840 in Hot Spring County and, on 1 February 1859, married Franklin W. Washburn: the record lists him as 21 and her as 19.

By 1864 she was Gilliam Graves's wife, and their daughter Mary Elizabeth was born on 13 August 1864, two months before Gilliam deserted from the Union army (12 October 1864) and returned on Christmas Day. The 1880 census shows the Graves children by Polly living with Andrew Washburn, her son by Franklin, and his wife Amanda.
Polly died about 1879 at Cedar Glades. Gilliam, who is supposed to have been killed by robbers in January 1876, is buried next to Polly in Mountain Valley Cemetery, once called Mt. Pleasant Cemetery.
EXTRA.note: The genealogy gives the 1859 ages as 21 for Washburn and 19 for her. The date of her death is given only as about 1879.

EXTRA.name: Sylvania Partin and Lucy Lee Morgan Hulsey
EXTRA.place: Montgomery Co., Arkansas
kv: 1849-1889, married 1868; likely mother of George Washington Hulsey (lead)
EXTRA.src: Find a Grave memorials and Montgomery Co., Ark. marriage records as cited in the Benjamin Franklin Hulsey entry.
EXTRA.title: Two wives, thirty years apart in age
EXTRA.hook: Benjamin Hulsey married Sylvania Partin in 1868 and, four years after she died, a woman 31 years younger than himself.
body: Sylvania Susane Partin was born in 1849, two years after Benjamin, and they married in 1868. She died in 1889, aged about 40, and is the likely mother of George Washington Hulsey, born in December 1876 (lead; no record yet names her as his mother).
On 25 September 1893 Benjamin, then 46, married Lucy Lee Morgan in Montgomery County. She was born in 1878, so was 15, and she lived until 1947, 23 years longer than he did.
Benjamin died at Story on 16 December 1924.
EXTRA.note: The marriage dates and birth years are taken from the entry for Benjamin F. Hulsey; the ages here are arithmetic from those years and are not stated in any record seen.

EXTRA.name: Cedar Glades, Montgomery County
EXTRA.rel: Place the family lived (home of Gilliam Graves, 4th great-grandfather)
EXTRA.place: Cedar Glades, Montgomery County, Arkansas
EXTRA.title: "Dr. Brown, of Cedar Glades, was shot down": a Union petition, March 1864
EXTRA.hook: Weeks after Gilliam Graves joined the Union cavalry at Cedar Glades, Union men from the same county begged the army for help against murder and plunder.
body: Gilliam Graves, 45, volunteered for the Union 4th Arkansas Cavalry at Cedar Glades on 14 January 1864. Less than two months later, on 10 March 1864, a letter went from Little Rock to Col. C. C. Andrews, who commanded the post. It was signed by Oliver Adair "and others" who called themselves "citizens of Montgomery County, Ark., and members of Company L, Fourth Arkansas Cavalry." The printed letter reads Company L, which may be a misprint for D, the company raised at Cedar Glades; the family's own man is on the roster of Company D.

The men wrote that "Deeds of cruelty and barbarity that would shame Indians are of daily occurrence." They gave three cases from a single day: "On the 1st instant the wife of Mr. James Dosier was shot through the shoulders, and her child (one year old) shot through the arms. On the same day Dr. Brown, of Cedar Glades, was shot down, mortally wounded, and his brains then blown out. William Gray (citizen) was shot in a brutal and cowardly manner on same day."

They added that "the plundering of houses, breaking and burning of cotton cards, wheels, &c., belonging to Union citizens is of common occurrence," and asked that about 100 cavalry be sent into the county, where forage and mills were plentiful. Because "our company is not armed," they suggested that guides be taken from among themselves. The army's own list of operations for March 1864 has a "Skirmish at Cedar Glade, Ark." on 1 March, the same day as the shootings, with the note that no circumstantial reports are on file.

The letter does not name Gilliam Graves, and nothing seen says he or any Hulsey signed it. What it shows is the neighborhood he enlisted from: Union families in the Ouachita hills in the winter of 1864, with their cavalry company still unarmed while their neighbors were being shot at home. Gilliam's later death, "supposedly killed by robbers" in Garland County in 1876, came in the same kind of country.
EXTRA.src: The War of the Rebellion: Official Records, Series I, vol. 34, part 2 (1891), p. 631, Oliver Adair and others to Col. C. C. Andrews, Little Rock, 10 March 1864; vol. 34, part 1, p. 3 and Index (Skirmish at Cedar Glade, Ark., 1 March 1864). archive.org full text of vol. 34.

quotes.t: Deeds of cruelty and barbarity that would shame Indians are of daily occurrence.
quotes.c: Oliver Adair and others, Montgomery County, 10 March 1864

quotes.t: On the same day Dr. Brown, of Cedar Glades, was shot down, mortally wounded, and his brains then blown out.
quotes.c: Official Records, vol. 34, pt. 2, p. 631

EXTRA.note: The event and the petition are proven by the printed Official Records. That Gilliam Graves or B. F. Hulsey took part in it is not shown; the OCR text reads "Company L".

EXTRA.name: The 4th Arkansas Cavalry in Montgomery and Hot Springs counties
EXTRA.rel: Place and regiment of Gilliam Graves and B. F. Hulsey
EXTRA.place: Montgomery County, Arkansas
EXTRA.title: Scouts "to secure all guerrillas and bushwhackers," 1864
EXTRA.hook: The orders and reports that sent the 4th Arkansas Cavalry back through Montgomery County in 1864, with the wounded and missing it cost.
body: A Union company recruited at Cedar Glades had to be used somewhere, and the army's papers show where. On 11 April 1864 Col. A. H. Ryan, commanding the 4th Arkansas Cavalry at Lewisburg, was ordered to send 2nd Lt. John N. Jones with 75 men to Hot Springs County. The general "wishes the detail to start at the earliest practicable moment. He orders that no houses be burnt by them and no property destroyed, but he wishes them to secure all guerrillas and bushwhackers who may fall in their way."

On 11 June 1864 an expedition was organized "to make a scout in Saline, Hot Springs, Montgomery, and Perry Counties," with 100 men of the 4th Arkansas Cavalry, four companies of the 3rd U.S. Cavalry and part of Merrill's Horse, under Maj. G. Harker, "to be gone six or eight days." Fifteen days later, on 26 June, Capt. Joel Brown of Company A wrote General Steele about the loyal families crowded into Dardanelle: "mostly soldiers' families," "without medical aid, and not enough of men in town to bury the dead."

The army's monthly summary for August 1864 records the result: "14th, a battalion of the Fourth Arkansas Cavalry returned from scout through Saline, Hot Springs, and Montgomery Counties. Fought with small bands of the enemy daily until arriving at Farr's Mill. Captain Green, with twenty-five men of this battalion, engaged Cook's and Crawford's companies, numbering about 100 men, drove them and killed 4 and wounded 6 of the enemy." The battalion itself lost "1 private killed, Captain Quin and Lieutenant Spiva and 6 privates wounded, and 3 men missing."

None of these papers names Gilliam Graves or Benjamin Hulsey. They show the war they were in: a cavalry that was short of arms and horses, scouting the hills it came from, with soldiers' wives sheltered in river towns and bushwhackers threatening to burn out Union households. Deserters were a constant trouble for the regiment; in the fall a scout at Helena arrested one Company I man at his home. Gilliam's own absence from 12 October to 25 December 1864 fits that same autumn, but the reason for it is not recorded.
