EXTRA.name: Company F, 42nd Indiana: the eleven who starved at Andersonville
EXTRA.rel: Comrades of Daniel W. O'Neal (3rd great-grandfather)
EXTRA.place: Oakland City, Gibson County, Indiana
EXTRA.title: "Starved to death at Andersonville": the Company F monument, 1893
EXTRA.hook: Daniel O'Neal's company raised its own limestone shaft at Oakland City and carved on it the names of eleven men who died as prisoners.
body: The monument stands on a small triangle of ground beside the railroad in Oakland City. Gil. R. Stormont's 1913 booklet says it was put up by the surviving members of Company F, 42nd Indiana, "as a loving tribute to the memory of their comrades who gave up their lives in defense of the flag." It was built in the summer of 1893 and dedicated that September, with an address by Capt. A. J. McCutchan of Company A.

A committee of Col. W. M. Cockrum, John W. Corder, James T. Bell, John P. Simpson and Washington Strickland raised the money, and Cockrum deeded the lot to the county. The contract went to William Kelley of Oakland City for nearly $1,000. The shaft is of oolitic limestone, twenty-eight feet tall, with a carved soldier on top. "On the several sides of the dies are the names of all the original members of the company and the recruits, 143 in number." That should include Daniel W. O'Neal, who is on the company roll, but the stone has not been read for his name.

On one side is a scroll reading "Starved to death at Andersonville," and beneath it eleven names: Chesterfield P. Dill, Alford Farmer, J. M. Hunter, H. H. Hunter, John H. Martin, Adam Canon, Wm. A. Reavis, W. W. Oliver, A. H. Mariner, Jacob Strickland and A. C. Coleman. Stormont adds: "These all were taken prisoners at the battle of Chickamauga and died at Andersonville." Most can be matched on Horrall's roll of Company F, though spelled a little differently: Christfield P. Dill, Alfred Farmer, Henry H. Hunter, Adam Cannon, William A. Revis, William W. Oliver, Adolphus H. Marriner and Andrew C. Coleman.

The shaft also lists the company's battles: Perryville, Stone's River, Stevenson, Flint River, Chickamauga, Lookout Mountain, Mission Ridge, Ringgold, Buzzard Roost, Big Shanty, Snake Creek Gap, Chattahoochee River and Bentonville. Whether Daniel was present for all of them or left in March 1862 is the open question about his service; the men who built this stone, his neighbors from the same few townships, would have known.
EXTRA.src: Gil. R. Stormont, Gibson County in the Civil War (Princeton, 1913), "Co. F, 42nd Indiana Monument" (archive.org, gibsoncountyinci00stor); S. F. Horrall, History of the Forty-second Indiana (1892), roll of Company F, pp. 64-67.

quotes.t: Starved to death at Andersonville.
quotes.c: Inscription on the Company F monument, Oakland City, 1893

EXTRA.note: That Daniel W. O'Neal is among the 143 names has not been confirmed by a reading of the stone.

EXTRA.name: The first legal hanging in Gibson County
EXTRA.rel: Place the O'Neal family lived (Gibson County, Indiana)
EXTRA.place: Princeton and Haubstadt, Gibson County, Indiana
EXTRA.title: William Thomas Camp, hanged at Princeton, 22 November 1872
EXTRA.hook: A murder over a $75 note ended with Gibson County's first execution, while Daniel and Vashti O'Neal were raising their young family in the county.
body: The 1884 History of Gibson County calls it "the first legal execution in this county." William Thomas Camp and J. R. Bilderback, both of Pike County, walked and rode to Haubstadt on 31 July 1871 and, finding no lodging, lay down to sleep in a piece of woods near the village. Camp had picked up a hickory club to use as a cane. As Bilderback slept "with his head on the roots of a tree," Camp "struck him on the head several times and killed him."

"There had been no grudge or quarrel between them, but the motive for the crime was shown by the larceny of a note for seventy-five dollars which Bilderback held on Camp." Camp threw the body into a fallen treetop, took some of the dead man's clothes and rode his horse to New Harmony, where the dead man's brother William had him arrested. Back at Haubstadt he showed where the body lay; a coroner's jury found it "horribly mangled by hogs," and Camp confessed under oath.

Jailed at Princeton, he escaped before trial and hid near his mother's home, was later picked up in Kentucky for horse-stealing and jailed at Owensboro, and was brought back. He was convicted of first-degree murder in July 1872 and sentenced to hang on 4 October. Gov. Baker gave him a respite until Friday, 22 November 1872, "when, at 2 o'clock p.m. of that day, he was executed by Sheriff F. W. Hauss." His lawyers were Col. Charles Denby, who had left the 42nd Indiana to become colonel of another regiment, and C. A. Buskirk.

Daniel O'Neal's household was then on its farm in Columbia Township, with Parsis (born 1868) a small child; the case was the talk of the county but is a place story, not a family one. No O'Neal is named in the account.
EXTRA.src: History of Gibson County, Indiana (Chicago, 1884), "First Legal Hanging," in the chapter on the county courts (archive.org, historyofgibsonc0000jast).

EXTRA.name: The Princeton cyclone
EXTRA.rel: Place the O'Neal family lived (Gibson County, Indiana)
EXTRA.place: Princeton, Gibson County, Indiana
EXTRA.title: A Sunday-evening cyclone, 27 February 1876
EXTRA.hook: The worst storm in Gibson County history took the roof off a church at "church time" and carried a house thirteen feet.
body: The county history of 1884 says that "on Sunday evening, Feb. 27, 1876, the most severe cyclone which ever passed over Gibson County struck Princeton." It came from the southwest and "destroyed almost the entire southern part of Princeton, doing damage to the extent of over fifty thousand dollars." It "happened about church time and few of the people were at their homes." The roof and steeple of the C. P. Church were taken off.

The Sutton family's two-story frame house was "large," "comparatively new." "The wind lifted the house and it came down over the fence, distant thirteen feet from the foundation," breaking it "into three parts, one part going north, another east and another west." Ten persons were inside, "Mrs. Sutton and seven children, a son-in-law and his children." A two-year-old was found "hanging by its hands to a rafter on top of the fallen house"; a nine-year-old blown out of an upstairs window walked about four hundred feet to a neighbor's door and knocked, "remarking 'his house was blowed.'" Eight of the family were found huddled in a space about ten feet square, saved by a bureau, and "crawled out" through a hole sixteen inches across.

Parsis O'Neal, Katie Stevenson's mother, had been born at Princeton in 1868, and the family's farm was in Columbia Township a few miles south. The history does not mention any O'Neal in connection with the storm; it is told here as the county's worst disaster of the years they lived there.
EXTRA.src: History of Gibson County, Indiana (Chicago, 1884), chapter on climate and natural events ("Cyclones") (archive.org, historyofgibsonc0000jast).

quotes.t: It happened about church time and few of the people were at their homes.
quotes.c: History of Gibson County, 1884

EXTRA.note: The O'Neal link to this storm is by place only. The text says the storm "passed out northeast of Oakland" in the OCR, which may be misread.

EXTRA.name: Coleman L. Stevenson (b. 1832)
EXTRA.rel: First cousin of Frank Stevenson (2nd great-grandfather)
EXTRA.place: Ninth District, Giles County, Tennessee
EXTRA.title: A Stevenson cousin in the 32nd Tennessee, 1862-1865
EXTRA.hook: While Daniel O'Neal wore Union blue in Indiana, a first cousin of his future son-in-law wore Confederate gray from Giles County.
body: Goodspeed's 1886 History of Tennessee prints the sketch of Coleman L. Stevenson, "a first-class farmer and stock-raiser" of the Ninth Civil District of Giles County, born 26 December 1832. He was the eldest son of William P. Stevenson, a brother of Rev. Abner A. Stevenson, and so a first cousin of Frank Stevenson.

Goodspeed says: "In 1862 Mr. Stevenson enlisted in the Thirty-second Tennessee Regiment of Volunteers, and served until the close of the war. He participated in most of the principal battles, and was a brave and gallant soldier." The 32nd was a Confederate regiment. His family was large: two wives, who were sisters (Louisa and Dorcas Jackson), his own children, and "three orphan children to raise," Martha V., Nancy M. and Mary J. Jackson, daughters of his wife's dead brother and sister-in-law.

The same sketch is where the family's own roll of Rev. Elam Stevenson's children is printed, and it records that William P. "has four brothers who are ministers of the gospel." Coleman held 265 acres at home and 400 more elsewhere in Giles County in 1886, was a Democrat, and belonged, like his uncles, to the Methodist Episcopal Church South.
The Stevensons were Giles County people, and Frank's O'Neal in-laws were Indiana Unionists, so the two sides of the family met only after the war, in Frank's marriage to Parsis O'Neal.
EXTRA.src: Goodspeed Publishing Co., History of Tennessee (1886), Giles County Biographical Appendix, sketch of Coleman L. Stevenson, p. 871-872 (archive.org, historyoftenness00good).

quotes.t: In 1862 Mr. Stevenson enlisted in the Thirty-second Tennessee Regiment of Volunteers, and served until the close of the war.
quotes.c: Goodspeed, History of Tennessee, 1886

EXTRA.note: Goodspeed does not say the 32nd was Confederate; that is from the regiment itself. Whether Abner or his own sons served is not known.

EXTRA.name: Rev. Philip Bruce (1765-1825)
EXTRA.rel: Preacher who made his home with the family of Rev. Elam Stevenson (4th great-grandfather)
EXTRA.place: Bee Spring, Giles County, Tennessee
EXTRA.title: "I saw him die, and closed his eyes": Elam Stevenson and Philip Bruce
EXTRA.hook: The old itinerant whose books Elam hauled in his wagon died among the Stevensons' neighbors, and Elam shaved and shrouded him.
body: In 1869 Elam Stevenson, then 81 and housebound, dictated to the Methodist historian John B. McFerrin his memories of the preacher Philip Bruce, who came to Giles County in 1813 and "made our neighborhood his home." Bruce, in Elam's telling, was a Virginia Conference man who never married, who had once been offered a rich young Charleston woman's plantation and declined it ("he thought she had about money enough to send him to ruin"), and who after his health failed lived with his brother Joel and taught a day school for the neighborhood's children, giving to the poor every dollar the Conference sent him.

Elam was at the deathbed. "I saw him die, and closed his eyes, shaved him, and assisted in shrouding him. His death was calm and peaceful; there was not a struggle nor a groan. He did not move a muscle, only a slight quiver of the upper lip when the last breath left the body." A few days earlier the circuit preacher had preached to him: "It was a high day with him. He was very happy, and spoke in raptures of heaven." Bruce died in May 1825.

He was buried in the country graveyard "about two miles distant from our church (Bee Spring), by the side of his sainted mother and two of his brothers." His stone, Elam says, was put up by the Virginia Conference and reads: "To the memory of the Rev. Philip Bruce, an itinerant Methodist preacher nearly fifty years. He was born December 25, 1765, and died May, 1825. He loved God and the souls of mankind, many of whom became seals to his ministry."

The same letter records the cost of the Civil War to Elam's church. The first Methodist church in Giles County, Rehoboth, was replaced "by a large frame-church, which was destroyed by the Federal soldiers during the late war." It also tells of Meshach Boyce's son William, who "went to Arkansas at an early day as a missionary, and was drowned in a small stream, the second year of his labors."
EXTRA.src: John B. McFerrin, History of Methodism in Tennessee, vol. 2 (Nashville, 1871), pp. 180-190, letter of Rev. Elam Stephenson, Elkton, 28 July 1869 (archive.org, historymethodis00mcfegoog).

quotes.t: I saw him die, and closed his eyes, shaved him, and assisted in shrouding him.
quotes.c: Rev. Elam Stevenson, 1869

quotes.c: Rev. Elam Stevenson on Rehoboth church, 1869

EXTRA.name: Salathiel Hulsey's household in 1850
EXTRA.place: Union County, Georgia
EXTRA.title: Ten Hulseys in one house: Union County, Georgia, 1850
EXTRA.hook: A compiled Hulsey census list names Benjamin's brothers and sisters, and puts Benjamin at 6 instead of 3.
body: A volume of Hulsey census extracts compiled for the San Diego Genealogical Society copies the 1850 census of Union County, Georgia, for the household of "Salatheil Hulsey 43 GA": Elizabeth, 35; Maryann, 19; Robert R., 17; Elizabeth, 12; Jesse, 10; Jennings, 8; Benjamin, 6; Lillean, 3; and Nancy, 1. Listed in the same dwelling are Arminda Burnet, 20, and J. C. Bell, 23.

The ages matter. The wife Elizabeth is 35, only sixteen years older than the eldest daughter Maryann, so Maryann may be an older stepchild, or one of the ages is off. And Benjamin is 6, which would put his birth about 1844, not the 2 February 1847 on his grave memorial. The existing note that he was "3" in 1850 does not match this transcription; one of the two readings, or the grave date, needs checking against the film.

The compiler added a note to the eldest son: "Robert R. Hulsey, age 27, is in 1860 Hempstead Co., AR" with "Sarah A. 20 MS, & Salathel G. 1, AR." So an older brother of Benjamin was also in Arkansas by 1860, and he named a son for the father, as Benjamin did with Martin Salatheil.
In 1840 Salathiel was counted in Hall County, and in the 1830 Hall County Hulsey list he is one of seventeen men named Hulsey, living among the Hulseys of Charles and Adler.
EXTRA.src: San Diego Genealogical Society, Hulsey Families (2000), "1850 Union Co., GA" and "1860 Hempstead Co., AR" census extracts (archive.org, sdgsfamilies64); 1850 U.S. Census, Union Co., Ga.
EXTRA.note: This is a transcription of a transcription; the original census page has not been seen. The ages of Benjamin disagree with the grave and with the earlier text.

EXTRA.name: The Hulsey cluster of Hall County, Georgia
EXTRA.rel: Possible kin of Salathiel Hulsey (4th great-grandfather)
EXTRA.place: Hall County, Georgia
EXTRA.title: Seventeen Hulsey households in Hall County, 1830
EXTRA.hook: Salathiel Hulsey was one of a whole neighborhood of South Carolina-born Hulseys; his place in that family is the open question.
body: The 1830 census of Hall County, Georgia, a county formed in 1818 from the Cherokee cession, lists seventeen heads of household named Hulsey, among them Charles, Adler Jr., Joel, Elija, Demsey, William, Sarah, Pleasant, James, Adler Sr., Armistead, Hiram, Micajah, Jesse, Salathiel, Charles F. and Vincent. Printed lists of the 1832 Cherokee land lottery also carry Hall County names such as Pleasant T. Hulsey, James Halsey and Alder Halsey Jr., all in Hall County districts.

A 1997 newsletter article, drawing on The Hulsey Book by Lou Pero, traces the senior line: Charles Hulsey and his wife Hannah, married about 1752, lived in Pittsylvania County, Virginia, in the 1770s, near the North Carolina line, then in Greenville County, South Carolina. A Greenville deed of 1792 names their sons "James, Charles, Jesse, Adonijah and Adler." The article says the family name was spelled "interchangeably Huddlesy, Hulsey, Huldsey."

Where Salathiel fits is unknown. Online trees give him a father Jesse Hamilton Hulsey and a mother Mary Tharp, but no record has been found; the Hall County Jesse of 1830, and the Jesse among Charles's sons, are both possible fathers by name alone. Salathiel was born about 1807 in Georgia, which puts a South Carolina-born parent in Hall County at the right time.

The 1850 Hall County census, which the compiler calls "a very hard to read film," still shows a Charles Hulsey, 55, farmer, real estate $2,000, born in South Carolina, with Hannah, 52, also born in South Carolina, and a widow, Sally Hulsey, 33, with children. None of this ties to Salathiel, but it is the neighborhood he came from.
EXTRA.src: San Diego Genealogical Society, Hulsey Families (2000), 1830 and 1850 Hall Co., Ga. extracts and "Extended Branches" Nos. 12-13 (1997), quoting Lou Pero, The Hulsey Book; J. T. Smith, Cherokee Land Lottery (1838), lists for Hall County (archive.org).
EXTRA.note: A lead only. Salathiel's parentage is not established.

EXTRA.name: 4th Arkansas Cavalry (Union)
EXTRA.rel: Regiment of Benjamin F. Hulsey and Gilliam Graves (3rd and 4th great-grandfathers); Calvin Moffitt's regiment (2nd great-granduncle)
EXTRA.place: Montgomery County and Little Rock, Arkansas
EXTRA.title: The 4th Arkansas Cavalry: Union men from the Ouachita hills
EXTRA.hook: Hulsey, Graves and a Moffitt cousin all turn up in a Union regiment that spent the war at Little Rock and chasing guerrillas through Montgomery County.
body: The 4th Regiment Arkansas Volunteer Cavalry (Union) was organized at Little Rock in December 1863 and, by Dyer's Compendium, mustered out on 30 June 1865. Its companies were raised among Arkansas Unionists. Company D was recruited in Montgomery County in the winter of 1863–64, and on 14 January 1864 Gilliam Graves volunteered at Cedar Glades, at 45, a farmer, five feet ten inches tall with black eyes. The roster of the same company has a private "Hulsey, Benjamin F.", who would have been 16 or 17. The National Park Service database puts Calvin V. Moffitt, the son of Nathan Moffitt, the wheelwright, in Company L.

Dyer's list of the regiment's actions reads like a calendar of small, hard marches. A skirmish on the Saline River on 15 February 1864. A move to Cedar Glade on 1 March, which the Official Records index also lists as a skirmish that day (no report was filed). A scout from Little Rock to Benton on 27–31 March, led by Capt. E. H. Vance, who arrested three women hauling cotton for guerrillas and wrote that "the bushwhackers made a desperate rally to get the captured wagon and their fair friends, but they failed to get either." Mount Elba on 30 March. Then the Camden expedition of April 1864, in which Dyer lists Jenkins' Ferry. In mid-May the regiment was at Dardanelle, and from 25 September to 13 October it took part in an expedition from Little Rock to Fort Smith.

The regiment's own story had darker edges. Union men in Montgomery County were hunted by neighbors, and the March 1864 petition from Company L, told under "Union families of Montgomery County ask for cavalry," names a wife and child shot and a doctor killed at Cedar Glades. In September 1864 a detachment out of Helena went looking for "deserters from the Fourth Arkansas Cavalry" and took one, Benjamin Davis of Company I. Gilliam Graves's own roll entry reads that he "deserted on 12 October 1864 and returned on 25 December 1864." The roll gives no reason, and no record seen places Company D on any particular march that month.

In November 1864, Maj. Harris S. Greeno led 130 men of the regiment out of Devall's Bluff, where the regiment had its cavalry depot, toward Batesville and Searcy and reported that Price's army had been "badly whipped at every point." The regiment finished the war at Little Rock, scouting to the Saline River and Bayou Metoe in April and May 1865, and was mustered out on 30 June.

EXTRA.name: Buck Horn, Stone County
EXTRA.rel: Place the family lived (Henry and Hannah Moffitt's Stone County, Arkansas)
EXTRA.place: Buck Horn, Stone County, Arkansas
EXTRA.title: Buck Horn in the Official Records, March 1864
EXTRA.hook: Two Union reports name Buck Horn: one orders cavalry to "kill, capture, and destroy" a camp there, the other says the farmers wanted "peace on any terms."
body: Buck Horn, in what is now Stone County, Arkansas, is the old settlement near St. James where Henry and Hannah Moffitt's son Tom was born in 1889. Twenty-five years earlier it appears twice in the Union record of the war. On 14 March 1864 the district headquarters at Batesville wrote to Lt. Col. William Baumer, First Nebraska Cavalry, to take men across White River at Ramsay's Ferry and go to Round Bottom, near Sylamore, for forage, protecting the steam transport Miller. The order goes on: "You will endeavor to hunt up the enemy reported to be in camp at McDermott's, near Buck Horn, and kill, capture, and destroy them."

The order shows the care its writer thought necessary. Baumer was to recapture any mules taken from the Union train that he found with local people, "leaving the women and children of the family undisturbed and in possession of their household goods and such work-cattle as they need to cultivate their farms." He was told to be "kind and courteous in your dealings with the defenseless citizens," to give receipts for everything he took, and to "prevent your men from entering houses, pillaging, or burning any houses or fence rails." "Incendiarism or unnecessary severity," the order says, "you are strictly charged to prevent."

A week later Maj. Lewis C. Pace of the Eleventh Missouri Cavalry reported from Batesville on a seven-day scout of 206 miles (15–21 March 1864) after a Confederate force under Rutherford. On the last day he marched "down the river through Buck Horn. Here I could gain no information of Rutherford." His men were out of rations and many horses barefooted. He added a note on the country that fits the hills the Moffitts later farmed: "a rough, rocky, and mountainous country, destitute of forage excepting in the valleys and coves of the mountains," where "the farmers generally are busily engaged preparing their ground for planting, and express a great desire for peace on any terms."

These are two glimpses, not the story of a battle. The county's bloodiest fight of the war came at Buck Horn in May 1864, when Jo Shelby's Confederates attacked a band of bushwhackers; that is told under Henry and Hannah in the Ozarks.

EXTRA.name: Company D, 142d Infantry, 8 October 1918
EXTRA.rel: Edmond Tims's company (cousin of Judge Edward Tims's line)
EXTRA.place: St. Etienne-a-Arnes, Champagne, France
EXTRA.title: The runner's morning: Company D at St. Etienne
EXTRA.hook: Edmond Tims's company got lost in the French sector that day, but his battalion lost its commander and half its runners to a single shell.
body: The 36th Division's book of 1920, Story of the 36th, describes the morning of 8 October 1918 from the front. The 142d Infantry was ordered forward at 5:15 a.m. to take the village of St. Etienne-a-Arnes, in Champagne, after the Marines in the 2d Division had taken the ridge. The Second Battalion jumped off from Hill 140 and went through machine-gun fire. The First Battalion, Companies A through D, followed in support. Companies A and B were in the first wave and C and D in the second.

To reach the jumping-off place, Chastaine writes, the men of the First Battalion had to pass "in squad columns, or single file, through the trees down the northern slope of Blanc Mont and through the barrage placed by the enemy's batteries to cut off the supporting troops from the fight." They suffered heavy casualties from shell fire and lost their commanding officer, Capt. Charles Kuhlman: "The burst of a shell wounded half of the battalion headquarters group, including several runners." Edmond Tims was a company runner, and a company runner's job was to carry messages between the company and the battalion.

Company D's morning went wrong in a different way. "In this advance the men of Company D failed to follow the wake of Company B and wandered into the French sector to the left, where they remained through the balance of the day." Captain Kuhlman was so badly hurt that his loss "did not become known to his company commanders until the middle of the afternoon." The high-explosive shells were mixed with gas, and many gas casualties followed later in the day. Company B, whose wake Company D had been told to follow, lost its first lieutenant, Arthur J. Matheny, "killed instantly just after he had crossed the last belt of wire," and the second lieutenant, Thomas F. Collins; "more than thirty men in Company B had been killed and more than fifty wounded."

The Honor Roll printed at the back of the book lists "TIMS, EDMOND, Private, Co. D," with the date 8 October 1918. The regiment's own report, written in January 1919 and quoted in Edmond's own story, says a fellow runner spoke to him at 8 a.m. on the 9th and found him killed an hour later. The two dates are a day apart and both fall inside the 142d's fighting at St. Etienne. Before the war he had served in Company L of the First Oklahoma Infantry, the National Guard regiment that Chastaine says was assembled at Fort Sill in the spring of 1917, after months of border duty the year before.

quotes.c: Ben H. Chastaine, Story of the 36th (Oklahoma City, 1920), p. 117

EXTRA.name: Camp Pike, September 1918
EXTRA.rel: Place Rev. George W. Hulsey worked in 1918 (2nd great-grandfather)
EXTRA.place: Camp Pike, near Little Rock, Arkansas
EXTRA.title: The camp where George Hulsey was working when the influenza came
EXTRA.hook: George W. Hulsey signed his draft card on 12 September 1918 as a laborer at Camp Pike, and eleven days later the camp's base hospital admitted 214 influenza cases in a day.
body: On 12 September 1918 George Washington Hulsey, 42, filled out his draft card at Story in Montgomery County. It gave his employer as the Stewart-McGehee Construction Company at Camp Pike, the Army training camp near Little Rock. The camp had been established on 18 July 1917 and was the mobilization point for the 87th Division.

The Army's medical commission that studied pneumonia and influenza in the camps reached Camp Pike on 5 September 1918. Its report says the camp's death rate from lobar pneumonia, over its whole history, was third among the 32 camps in the country, and from bronchopneumonia fourth. The report adds that "beginning September 1 there had been a gradual increase of the number of patients admitted with the diagnosis of acute bronchitis." On 23 September, 214 cases of influenza were admitted to the base hospital in a single day, and that is the day the commission dates the epidemic.

"The epidemic was at its height from September 27 to October 3, during which period there were in the neighborhood of 1,000 new cases daily." By 31 October it was over, and a second, milder wave came at the end of November. Counting from 1 September to 31 October, the commission recorded 12,393 men reporting sick with influenza and 1,499 cases of pneumonia, with 466 deaths. These are figures for soldiers; the report says nothing about the civilian construction crews working on the camp.

Nothing seen says whether George Hulsey was working at Camp Pike during those weeks, or whether he was ill. His draft card is the only record that puts him there. By the 1920 census he was a tenant farmer in Sulphur Township, McCurtain County, Oklahoma.

quotes.t: The epidemic was at its height from September 27 to October 3, during which period there were in the neighborhood of 1,000 new cases daily.
quotes.c: Opie, Freeman, Blake, Small and Rivers, Epidemic Respiratory Disease (St. Louis, 1921), p. 52

EXTRA.name: Draft registration days, 1917–1942
EXTRA.rel: The men of the family at four registrations (Grady Moffitt, Simon Thompson, Oscar Hulsey, Charles Oscar Smith)
EXTRA.place: Choctaw, Montgomery and Pushmataha counties
EXTRA.title: Four registration days and the men who signed
EXTRA.hook: On 5 June 1917, 12 September 1918, 16 October 1940 and 27 April 1942, the family's men lined up to give a clerk their name, age and employer.
body: The first World War registration was on 5 June 1917 for men aged 21 to 30. Grady Moffitt was 25, a timberman at Ervin, Oklahoma, married and supporting his wife, his mother and a child; the card describes him as tall and stout, with gray eyes and dark hair. Robert Pisachubbe, 28, farmed for himself at Speer, black eyes, black hair, medium height, slender. By age Joel Thompson (b. 29 January 1892), Peter P. Thompson (b. about 1896), Wavey Lincoln Satterfield (b. 28 December 1895, at Morgantown, Kentucky) and Edmond Tims (b. about 1893) all fell into the same registration. No card has been seen for Joel or Peter, and nothing seen shows that either was inducted. Wavey served as a private in the Army, and Edmond served first in Company L, First Oklahoma Infantry.

The third and widest registration, on 12 September 1918, took in men aged 18 through 45. Simon Thompson, 19, signed as a farmer working for his father at Corinne. George Washington Hulsey, 42, signed at Story, Arkansas, as a laborer at Camp Pike. Edmond Tims died on the fields of St. Etienne less than a month later.

The World War II draft began on 16 October 1940 with men aged 21 to 35. Oscar Franklin Hulsey, 30, registered that day at Mount Ida, Montgomery County. When the war began, Congress required all men aged 18 through 64 to register. The fourth registration, on 27 April 1942, was for men 45 to 64, and was nicknamed "The Old Man's Draft." Its purpose was an inventory of skills and available labor; those men were not liable for service. Charles Oscar Smith, 52, signed as "Charlie Oscar Smith" of Forney, Choctaw County, working on a farm, with mail at Hugo Route 1, naming "Mrs. Pearl Smith" as the person who would always know his address. Robert Pisachubbe, 53, signed at Speer, naming his wife Lizzie.

Their sons went in different ways. Dois Moffitt enlisted in the U.S. Navy on 3 September 1942, aged 21, and served as a ship's cook until 27 January 1946. John Winfred Moffitt enlisted on 17 December 1943, at 18, and served as a corpsman. No record seen gives service dates for their older brothers Alvin and Odis, or for the Hulsey brothers of Oscar's generation.

EXTRA.name: James H. Satterfield and the 9th Kentucky
EXTRA.place: Allen and Butler counties, Kentucky
EXTRA.title: Three months in the 9th Kentucky
EXTRA.hook: James Satterfield joined the Union army in 1861 and left after three months; the regiment he joined lost 357 men, 250 of them to disease.
body: James H. Satterfield told the authors of Kentucky: A History of the State in 1885 that "in 1861 he enlisted in the Ninth Kentucky (Federal) Infantry, remaining in the field but three months, after which he was engaged in the recruiting service." He was 23, a young farmer in Allen County, and his father, Henry, died that same year.

The 9th Kentucky Infantry was organized at Camp Boyle, Adair County, and mustered in for three years on 20 November 1861. Its first winter was spent in camp at Columbia, Kentucky, until February 1862. If James joined in the autumn of 1861, the three months he describes would have ended about the time the regiment marched to Bowling Green and then Nashville, leaving camp on 15 February. His own account does not say whether he was discharged, detailed or transferred, and the roll that would show it has not been seen.

The regiment was in the rest of the war. Dyer lists it at Shiloh on 7 April 1862, the siege of Corinth, Perryville (in reserve), Stones River, Chickamauga, Missionary Ridge, the Atlanta campaign and Jonesboro. It mustered out on 15 December 1864. Its dead number 357: 8 officers and 96 enlisted men killed or mortally wounded, and 3 officers and 250 enlisted men dead of disease. In the 9th Kentucky, disease killed more than twice as many men as the enemy.
Butler County, where James settled in 1876, put up a veterans' monument in 1907 on the courthouse lawn to the soldiers of both armies. It is described as one of two such Kentucky monuments.

quotes.t: In 1861 he enlisted in the Ninth Kentucky (Federal) Infantry, remaining in the field but three months, after which he was engaged in the recruiting service.
quotes.c: Battle, Perrin and Kniffin, Kentucky: A History of the State (1885), sketch of James H. Satterfield, Butler County

EXTRA.name: Sidney Rufus Satterfield & Eliza "Ancie" (Johnson)
EXTRA.rel: 2nd great-granduncle (brother of John C. Satterfield) and his wife, Samantha's first cousin
EXTRA.place: Butler County, Kentucky; buried at Satterfield Cemetery, Jetson
EXTRA.title: Two brothers' wives from one Clark family
EXTRA.hook: John C. Satterfield's brother Sidney married a Johnson girl whose mother was a sister of Samantha Johnson's mother.
body: Sidney Rufus Satterfield was born on 2 September 1865 in Kentucky, the second son named in his father's 1885 biography ("Henry W., John C., Sidney R., James D., Martha A. and Mary C."). Find a Grave gives his parents as James Henry Satterfield and Malissa A. Gibson, so he was John C. Satterfield's full brother. He died on 19 November 1949 at Richardsville, Warren County, and was buried at Satterfield Cemetery, near Jetson in Butler County.

His wife was Eliza "Ancie" Johnson, born 19 July 1871, died 27 December 1951. Her parents were James P. Johnson (1840-1884) and Martha J. Clark (1839-1923), and Martha J. was an older sister of Melvina (Clark) Johnson, the mother of Samantha "Mantha" Johnson. That makes Ancie a first cousin of the woman who married Sidney's brother John C. in 1892. Two Satterfield brothers married into the same Clark-Johnson family.

Sidney and Ancie had at least three children: Walter, born and died in 1890; Mary Cecil (Woosley), 1891-1989; and Lillie (Embry), 1893-1946. All of them are shown on Find a Grave with the Satterfield Cemetery burials.
kv: Satterfield Cemetery, Jetson, Butler Co., Ky.
Walter (1890), Mary Cecil Woosley (1891-1989), Lillie Embry (1893-1946)

EXTRA.name: James Doiser Satterfield
EXTRA.place: Born in Allen County, Kentucky; died at Hickoria, Clay County, Arkansas
EXTRA.title: The brother who went to Arkansas
EXTRA.hook: James D. Satterfield, born in Allen County just before the family left for Minnesota, ended up in Clay County, Arkansas.
body: James Doiser Satterfield was born in February 1867 in Allen County, Kentucky, a son of James Henry Satterfield and Malissa Gibson. The 1885 county history lists him as "James D." among the six children of the first marriage. He was born the year his father says the family "removed to Dakota County, Minn."

On Find a Grave he is shown as married in 1889 to a wife recorded as Iverson Embry Satterfield (1871-1926), with five children: Laura Myrtle Hooper (1890-1951), Juvanda McKinney (1892-1922), Claud Edward (1899-1963), Fannie Esther Dobbins Tisdal (1902-1977) and James Ralph (1909-1983).

He died on 10 July 1929 at Hickoria, Clay County, Arkansas, and is buried at Redenbo Cemetery in that county. That is a different part of the Mid-South from his half-brothers at Texarkana, and from John C., who went to Franklin County, Texas.
EXTRA.src: Find a Grave memorial 126103925 (James Doiser Satterfield); Kentucky: A History of the State (1885), Butler County, p. 676
EXTRA.note: The wife's name as given on Find a Grave looks like a transcription of a maiden name (Embry); not checked.

EXTRA.name: A. M. (Satterfield) Coots
EXTRA.place: Born in Minnesota; buried at Butler Phelps Cemetery, Butler County, Kentucky
EXTRA.title: A daughter born in Minnesota, dead at twenty-one
EXTRA.hook: One Satterfield child was born during the eight years the family spent in Dakota County, Minnesota, and came home to Kentucky to die a year after her wedding.
body: James H. Satterfield's 1885 biography says that "in 1867 he removed to Dakota County, Minn., and in 1875 he returned to Kentucky." A Find a Grave memorial supplies the only child known to have been born there. A. M. Satterfield was born on 23 July 1870 in Minnesota, a daughter of James Henry Satterfield and Malissa Gibson and a full sister of John C. Satterfield.

She married Calvin H. Coots (1869-1932) in 1891 and died on 25 May 1892, aged 21. She is buried at Butler Phelps Cemetery in Butler County. Her mother had died in 1877, soon after the move back, and her father had remarried in 1878 to Lucinda Belle Phelps, a Butler County woman.
Her Minnesota birth is a small piece of independent support for the Minnesota years in the 1885 sketch, which no other record seen so far confirms.
kv: Butler Phelps Cemetery, Butler Co., Ky.
EXTRA.src: Find a Grave memorial 112297434 (A. M. Satterfield Coots); Kentucky: A History of the State (1885), Butler County, p. 676

EXTRA.name: Lucinda Belle (Phelps) Satterfield and her nine children
EXTRA.rel: Step-3rd-great-grandmother; her children are half-siblings of John C. Satterfield
EXTRA.place: Butler County, Kentucky, then Bowie County, Texas
EXTRA.title: James Satterfield's second family
EXTRA.hook: After Melissa died in 1877 James H. Satterfield married a 21-year-old neighbor and had nine more children, most of whom ended up around Texarkana.
body: Lucinda Belle Phelps was born on 30 May 1857 in Butler County, a daughter of Solomon Phelps and Sarah J. (Deweese). She married James H. Satterfield on 2 June 1878, a year after Melissa Gibson's death. A Bowie County family group sheet, which says the compiler holds a copy of the marriage bond, lists nine children: Martha Belle (born Nov 1879), Alonzo Thomas (1882), Minnie E. (1884), Joe Griffin (1886), Laura E. (1887), Charles J. (1890), George Franklin (1892), Grover C. (1894) and Effie J. (1899). Find a Grave gives Lucinda's death as 5 June 1917.

By 1909 the grown children were marrying in Bowie County, Texas, or across the Arkansas line: Charles J. to Alma Morgan on 5 December 1909; Alonzo to Zoda Mae Slader Reed in September 1914; Grover to Norah Walker on 28 May 1917 at Maud; Joe Griffin to Lennia Champion on 11 November 1917; George to Eula Viola Martin on 2 September 1917 at Hatfield, Polk County, Arkansas. Laura married a Douglas Henry and died in October 1975.
The sheet shows Minnie E. married to a "(?) Smith." That could be a coincidence of a common name, and nothing links her husband to Charles Oscar Smith's family.

James himself died in Bowie County on 28 November 1922 (Find a Grave; the group sheet says 24 November 1922 or 1924) and is buried at Reed Cemetery. His 1885 biography already credits him with 1,340 acres in Butler County and another 425 acres in Tennessee.

EXTRA.name: George Franklin Satterfield
EXTRA.place: Born at Brooklyn, Butler County, Kentucky; died at Texarkana; buried at Lockesburg, Arkansas
EXTRA.title: A corporal in the Arkansas training regiment
EXTRA.hook: John C.'s half-brother George, born at Brooklyn, Kentucky, served as a corporal in 1917-18 and married in Polk County, Arkansas, five months after the United States entered the war.
body: George Franklin Satterfield was born on 10 May 1892 at Brooklyn in Butler County, a son of James H. Satterfield and Lucinda Belle Phelps. His father died in Bowie County, Texas, in 1922.

On 2 September 1917, according to the Bowie County family sheet, he married Eula Viola Martin at Hatfield, Polk County, Arkansas. His headstone is marked "ARKANSAS CPL CO E 3 TRAINING REGT WORLD WAR I."
He died on 4 January 1958 at Texarkana and was buried at Odd Fellows Cemetery, Lockesburg, Sevier County, Arkansas.

EXTRA.name: Alonzo Thomas and Grover Cleveland Satterfield
EXTRA.place: Born in Butler County, Kentucky; lived in Bowie County, Texas
EXTRA.title: Two brothers at Maud, Texas
EXTRA.hook: Two sons of James H. Satterfield's second marriage lived out their lives near Texarkana, one marrying in 1914 and one in 1917.
body: Alonzo Thomas Satterfield was born on 6 June 1882 in Butler County, one of the three children named in his father's 1885 biography. In September 1914 he married Zoda Mae Slader Reed in Bowie County, Texas. He died there on 18 December 1950.
Grover Cleveland Satterfield was born on 5 April 1894 in Butler County. He married Norah Walker at Maud, Bowie County, on 28 May 1917, and died at Maud on 13 December 1966.
Both brothers appear as children on the Find a Grave memorial of their half-brother Sidney Rufus Satterfield, and in the Bowie County family sheet.

EXTRA.name: Wavey Lincoln Satterfield
EXTRA.place: Born at Morgantown, Butler County, Kentucky; died at Soper, Choctaw County, Oklahoma
EXTRA.title: A headstone that gets the birthday wrong
EXTRA.hook: Artie Pearl's older brother was a private in the Army in the First World War; his Oklahoma stone and his draft cards disagree about his birth date.
body: Wavey Lincoln Satterfield was the oldest surviving child of John C. and Samantha Satterfield. His stone at Soper Cemetery gives his birth as 9 January 1896, but the Find a Grave memorial says his World War I and World War II draft registrations both give 28 December 1895 at Morgan Town, Butler County, Kentucky. The memorial treats the stone as the error.

The stone is marked "TEXAS PVT. U.S. ARMY World War I." That fits the family's move to Franklin County, Texas, about 1907. In 1925 he married Jewel Dale Weems (1908-1984), and they later lived in Choctaw County, Oklahoma, where Samantha and her second husband had settled.
He died at Soper on 24 March 1952, aged 56, and is buried there in plot E4, the same plot as his mother Samantha.
kv: 28 Dec 1895, Morgantown, Ky. (draft cards); stone says 9 Jan 1896

EXTRA.name: James Bethel Satterfield
EXTRA.place: Born in Kentucky; died at Paris, Lamar County, Texas; buried at Soper, Oklahoma
EXTRA.title: The brother who married a Riddle
EXTRA.hook: James Bethel Satterfield and his sister Stella both married into the Riddle family.
body: James Bethel Satterfield was born on 12 May 1901 in Butler County, Kentucky, and was about six when the family moved to Franklin County, Texas. He married Alice Elizabeth Riddle (1900-1976), and Find a Grave shows seven children born between 1922 and 1940, one of whom, Charlie, died in 1940 at about ten.
His sister Stella had married Clifford Calvin Riddle (1898-1975). Whether Alice and Clifford were brother and sister is not shown in the records seen, so the two marriages are a lead only.
James died on 7 December 1964 at Paris, Texas, and is buried at Soper Cemetery in Choctaw County, Oklahoma, near his mother.
EXTRA.src: Find a Grave memorial 16723739 (James Bethel Satterfield)
EXTRA.note: Whether the two Riddle spouses were related is unchecked (lead).

EXTRA.name: Stella (Satterfield) Riddle
EXTRA.place: Born in Franklin County, Texas; buried at Chillicothe, Hardeman County, Texas
EXTRA.title: Stella, dead at seventeen
EXTRA.hook: Artie Pearl's youngest sister married a Riddle and died at 17.
body: Stella B. Satterfield was born on 6 October 1907 and was one of the two children John C. and Samantha had after the move to Texas (the 1910 census shows her at about two). Her mother married again in 1917 and moved with Stephens to Oklahoma.

She married Clifford Calvin Riddle (1898-1975). She died on 25 January 1925, aged 17, and is buried at Chillicothe Cemetery, Hardeman County, Texas, far from Soper and Hugo where her mother and sister lie. No cause of death is given.
The Hagansport household of April 1910 lists her as "little Stella."
EXTRA.src: Find a Grave memorial 166737339 (Stella Satterfield Riddle); 1910 U.S. Census, Hagansport, Franklin Co., Tex.

EXTRA.name: Ira L. and Jewel Thompson Satterfield
EXTRA.place: Ira born in Kentucky; Jewel born at Talco, Titus County, Texas; both ended in Choctaw County, Oklahoma
EXTRA.title: The two youngest Satterfield boys
EXTRA.hook: Ira served in the Army in the Second World War; Jewel was born at Talco, Texas, five years before his mother remarried.
body: Ira L. Satterfield was born in 1905 in Kentucky and was five in the April 1910 census at Hagansport. He is buried at Grant Cemetery, the same cemetery as his sister Artie Pearl and Charles Oscar Smith, in plot B2, with a stone marked "AMRY WWII." He died in 1977.

Jewel Thompson Satterfield, the last child, was born on 3 May 1912 at Talco in Titus County, Texas. He married Marie Nabors in 1929, when he was 17, and had five children. He died at Hugo on 13 January 1995 and is buried at Mount Olivet Cemetery there.
EXTRA.src: Find a Grave memorial 37721080 (Ira L. Satterfield) and 31608133 (Jewel Thompson Satterfield)

EXTRA.name: Bird Alexander "Alex" Stephens
EXTRA.place: Born in Tennessee; Oaks Township, Choctaw County, Oklahoma, in 1920; buried at Mount Pleasant, Texas
EXTRA.title: The widower Samantha married in 1917
EXTRA.hook: Samantha Satterfield's second husband was a 59-year-old widower whose first wife was part Choctaw and who went back to Texas after Samantha died.
body: Billy Alexander "Bird" Stephens was born on 16 February 1858 in Tennessee, a son of Calaway "Cal" Stephens (1824-1863) and Sarah Ann Little (1822-1913). He appears in Find a Grave as the youngest of six children.

The biography on Samantha's memorial says he married Martha Adeline Liles in Newton County, Arkansas, on 28 March 1878, and that she was one-quarter Choctaw. She died in 1916 and is buried at Old Saltillo Cemetery in Hopkins County, Texas. The memorial gives them eight children, of whom seven are linked: John Harvey, Nancy Ann (Brown), Mary Adeline (Simmons), Joseph Carroll, Wiley Alexander, Francis Henry and Tomie Delmane, who died at 10 in 1907.

On 28 July 1917 at Mount Vernon, Franklin County, the 59-year-old widower married 44-year-old Mrs. M. D. Satterfield. They moved to Oaks Township, Choctaw County, and were there in the 1920 census. After Samantha died in October 1928 he went back to Titus County, Texas, and died at Mount Pleasant on 23 January 1944. He is buried at Bridges Chapel Cemetery.
kv: 28 Jul 1917, Mount Vernon, Franklin Co., Tex.
EXTRA.src: Find a Grave memorial 25283760 (Billy Alexander Bird Stephens) and 82285257 (Samantha D. Johnson Stephens, biography by William Gorman)
EXTRA.note: The Choctaw detail about his first wife is from a family biography and has not been checked against a roll or record (lead).

EXTRA.name: Newton Jasper Clark & Mary Dunn "Polly" (Elms)
EXTRA.place: Brooklyn, Butler County, Kentucky
EXTRA.title: The Clarks of Brooklyn, Kentucky
EXTRA.hook: Melvina's parents married in Butler County in January 1839 and are buried at a family cemetery that bears their name.
body: Newton Jasper Clark was born on 6 August 1817 and died on 3 April 1878 in Butler County. His parents were William Clark (1785-1856), born in Granville County, North Carolina, and Levina Willis (1785-1877). WikiTree credits William with service in the War of 1812; that is not checked.

He married Mary Dunn "Polly" Elms, born in 1818 in Ohio County, Kentucky, on 20 January 1839 (the Butler County marriage register is on FHL film 928,314 per WikiTree). In 1850 they were in Butler County and in 1860 in Edmonson County.

Newton died in 1878 and is buried at Newton Clark Cemetery, Brooklyn, in Butler County. Polly died on 16 February 1888 and is buried at Clark Cemetery, Morgantown. Four children are linked: Martha J. (1839-1923), Stanford C. (1844-1913), Beverly L. "Belva" (1850-1939) and Melvina (1851-1929).
kv: 6 Aug 1817 (Pulaski Co. per Find a Grave)
