EXTRA.name: Stanford C. Clark
EXTRA.place: Butler County, Kentucky
EXTRA.title: A Union cavalry private
EXTRA.hook: Samantha Johnson's uncle Stanford Clark rode with the 12th Kentucky Cavalry.
body: Stanford C. Clark was born on 6 June 1844 in Kentucky, a son of Newton Jasper Clark and Polly Elms. His headstone at Belmont General Baptist Church Cemetery, Morgantown, is marked "PVT TRP A 12 REGT KY CAV CIVIL WAR." The 12th Kentucky Cavalry was a Union regiment.

On 9 February 1867 he married Serenia Hunt (1851-1918) in Butler County. He died on 12 June 1913 at age 69. By then his niece Samantha and her husband John C. Satterfield had left Butler County for Texas.
EXTRA.src: Find a Grave memorial 161043736 (Stanford C. Clark)
EXTRA.note: Service is from the headstone inscription; no muster roll seen.

EXTRA.name: Beverly L. "Belva" Clark
EXTRA.place: Born in Butler County, Kentucky; died at Cushing, Payne County, Oklahoma
EXTRA.title: The Clark brother who went to Oklahoma
EXTRA.hook: Melvina's youngest brother Belva Clark died at Cushing, Oklahoma, at 88, with eight children behind him.
body: Beverly L. "Belva" Clark was born on 2 October 1850 in Butler County, Kentucky, a son of Newton Jasper Clark and Polly Elms. In 1877 he married Margaret Ann Coots (1861-1944).

Find a Grave lists eight children: Palvena (Smith), Sardena (Flener), William Pearl, Fannie Ellen (Coots), Purnie Dee (Noteware), Carrie (born and died in 1891), Martha D. (Fulkerson) and David Carl. Most were born in Kentucky; the Clark family was in Oklahoma by the time he died.
He died on 18 February 1939 at Cushing in Payne County, Oklahoma, and is buried at Fairlawn Cemetery there.
EXTRA.src: Find a Grave memorial 63240768 (Beverly L. Clark)
EXTRA.note: The date the Clarks reached Oklahoma is not given on the memorial.

EXTRA.name: Martha J. (Clark) Johnson & James P. Johnson
EXTRA.place: Butler County, Kentucky; buried at Satterfield Cemetery, Jetson
EXTRA.title: Melvina's older sister
EXTRA.hook: Martha Clark married James P. Johnson; their daughter Ancie married a Satterfield and is buried at the cemetery that carries the Satterfield name.
body: Martha J. Clark was born on 1 February 1839 in Butler County, the eldest child of Newton Jasper Clark and Polly Elms. She married James P. Johnson (7 January 1840 - 30 June 1884). Find a Grave names three of their children: Mary Isabella "Isey" (Phelps), 1868-1936; Eliza "Ancie" (Satterfield), 1871-1951; and William Miligan Johnson, 1875-1950. The memorial notes two more, Oliver P. and Drucilla.
James died in 1884 and Martha lived on as a widow for 39 years. She died on 13 February 1923 in Butler County. Both are buried at Satterfield Cemetery near Jetson.
James P. and Melvina's husband, who is not named in the records seen, shared the surname Johnson. Whether the two husbands were brothers or cousins is unchecked.
EXTRA.src: Find a Grave memorial 19786592 (Martha J. Clark Johnson) and 19786602 (James P. Johnson)
EXTRA.note: Relationship of the two Johnson husbands is a lead.

EXTRA.name: Charlie Johnson
EXTRA.place: Born at Brooklyn, Butler County, Kentucky; died at Welchs Creek, Butler County
EXTRA.title: Samantha's brother who stayed
EXTRA.hook: Samantha went to Texas and Oklahoma; her brother Charlie lived and died within a few miles of where they were born.
body: Charlie Johnson was born on 27 April 1885 at Brooklyn in Butler County, a son of Melvina Clark Johnson, 13 years after his sister Samantha. He died on 14 February 1959 at Welchs Creek, Butler County, and is buried at Clark Cemetery, Morgantown, with his mother's Clark family.

He had two wives. The first was Martha Alice Satterfield (27 August 1886 - 22 July 1918), buried at Clark Cemetery; she died at Riverside, Warren County, aged 31. The second was Pernie Brooks (1905-1944). Find a Grave lists eight children, among them Carlie, Cooper F., James Wallace, Artie Mae Roberts, Cevil, Golda Marie Hunt, Chester and Cova Myrl Felty.
Martha Alice's parents are not named, so whether she belonged to the same Satterfield family as her husband's brother-in-law John C. is unknown.
kv: 14 Feb 1959, Welchs Creek, Butler Co., Ky.
EXTRA.src: Find a Grave memorial 200863883 (Charlie Johnson) and 200880527 (Martha Alice Satterfield Johnson)
EXTRA.note: Martha Alice Satterfield's parentage is a lead.

EXTRA.name: Hazel Marzee (Shackleford) King
EXTRA.rel: Great-grandaunt (sister of Mary Tinsley Shackleford Moffitt)
EXTRA.place: Born at Rattan, Delta County, Texas; died at Paris, Texas
EXTRA.title: Hazel's 1981 obituary names all her sisters
EXTRA.hook: A Paris, Texas, newspaper listed Mary's sisters and brothers by their married names, and her Moffitt nephews carried the casket.
body: Hazel Marzee Shackleford was born in 1908 at Rattan in Delta County, Texas, and died on 22 December 1980 at Paris, Lamar County. The Lamar County Echo of 1 January 1981 printed: "Mrs. King was born in the Rattan community of Delta County, a daughter of John Morgan Shackleford and Kathryn Elizabeth Newton. She attended schools in Delta County and married John Wesley King who preceded her in death in 1968."

The paper named her brothers and sisters: "four sisters, Mrs. Joe Haskell, Mrs. Beula [sic] Hutchings and Mrs. Helen Josey, all of Apache, OK, and Mrs. Eular Tillman of Lawton, OK; three brothers, Balis Shackleford of CA, John S. Shackleford and Edward Shackleford, both of Apache, OK." Mary Moffitt had died in 1962, and Robert Yates in 1961.

The pallbearers were "Loyd Mathews, Roy Chadwick, Bill Halliday Sr., Donald Moffitt, Odis Moffitt and Tommy Moffitt." The three Moffitts are very likely sons of Grady and Mary, which would make them Hazel's nephews, but the paper does not say so. She is buried at Meadowbrook Memorial Park, Paris.

quotes.t: Mrs. King was born in the Rattan community of Delta County, a daughter of John Morgan Shackleford and Kathryn Elizabeth Newton.
quotes.c: The Lamar County Echo, 1 January 1981 (transcribed on Find a Grave memorial 200655081)

EXTRA.src: The Lamar County Echo, 1 Jan 1981, as transcribed on Find a Grave memorial 200655081 (Hazel Marzee Shackleford King)
EXTRA.note: The Moffitt pallbearers are an inference from the surname; the obituary does not name Mary or Grady.

EXTRA.name: Balis Anthony Shackleford
EXTRA.place: Born in Alabama; died in Los Angeles County, California
EXTRA.title: Mary's oldest brother, who went to California
EXTRA.hook: The 1900 census lists the Shackleford children at Gilbert, Alabama; Balis, the oldest, spent his last decades in Los Angeles County.
body: Balis Anthony Shackleford was born on 5 February 1892 in Alabama. The 1900 census at Gilbert, Etowah County, as transcribed on his Find a Grave page, lists "John Shackleford 37, Sep 1862, married 10 yrs, b. AL, parent GA" and wife Elizabeth, 28, "5 children born, 5 living," with "Balous" 8; Myrtle, 6 (Aug 1893); May, 5 (Jun 1894); Robert, 3 (Oct 1896); and Eddie, 8 months (Sep 1899).

That list holds two children not in the later obituaries. Myrtle (born Aug 1893) and Eddie (born Sep 1899) do not appear among the survivors named in 1961 and 1981. They may have died young or may be known by other names; unchecked. The Edward Richard Shackelford who lived to 1988 was born in 1910, a different child.

Balis married Bertha Mae Fox (1895-1970); a daughter, Jewell Irene Denman, lived 1914-1978. He died on 9 January 1982 in Los Angeles County and was buried on 2 February at Green Hills Memorial Park, Rancho Palos Verdes. The California death record gives his name as Balis Anthony Shackelford.
kv: Green Hills Memorial Park, Rancho Palos Verdes
EXTRA.src: 1900 U.S. Census, Gilbert, Etowah Co., Ala., as transcribed on Find a Grave memorial 72144106; California Death Records
EXTRA.note: Myrtle and Eddie appear only in the 1900 census transcription (lead).

EXTRA.name: Robert Yates Shackleford
EXTRA.place: Born at Gadsden, Etowah County, Alabama; died at Oroville, California
EXTRA.title: An obituary from a California paper
EXTRA.hook: The Chico Enterprise-Record named all his brothers and sisters, including 'Mamie Moffett' of Oklahoma.
body: Robert Yates Shackleford was born on 25 October 1897 at Gadsden, Etowah County. The Chico Enterprise-Record of 23 June 1961, page 3, said: "Robert Y. Shackleford died early this morning in an Oroville Hospital. He was 63. Born in Alabama, he was a resided of Gridley for 10 years... He was a veteran of World War I."

The survivors section reads: "three brothers. Bayles of Los Angeles and Ed and John of Oklahoma; six sisters, Mrs. Josephine Haskell, Mrs. Helen Josey, Eulah Tillman and Mamie Moffett, all of Oklahoma; Beulah Hutchins and Mrs. Hazel King, both of Texas, and 16 grandchildren." Mamie Moffett is Mary Tinsley Shackleford Moffitt, who died the next year. His widow was Mae and he had eight children.
He is buried at Gridley-Biggs Cemetery in Butte County, California; the stone carries a World War II marker, while the paper says World War I.

quotes.t: six sisters, Mrs. Josephine Haskell, Mrs. Helen Josey, Eulah Tillman and Mamie Moffett, all of Oklahoma; Beulah Hutchins and Mrs. Hazel King, both of Texas
quotes.c: The Chico Enterprise-Record, 23 June 1961, p. 3 (transcribed on Find a Grave memorial 162164634)

EXTRA.src: The Chico Enterprise-Record (Chico, Calif.), 23 Jun 1961, p. 3, as transcribed on Find a Grave memorial 162164634
EXTRA.note: Josephine Haskell, Eulah Tillman and Beulah Hutchins are not yet tied to a birth year or place.

EXTRA.name: Josephine Haskell, Eulah Tillman and Beulah Hutchins
EXTRA.rel: Great-grandaunts (sisters of Mary Tinsley Shackleford Moffitt), lead
EXTRA.place: Oklahoma and Texas
EXTRA.title: Three sisters known only by married names
EXTRA.hook: Two obituaries from 1961 and 1981 list sisters of Mary Moffitt who do not appear in the 1900 census household.
body: The Chico paper of 1961 and the Paris, Texas, paper of 1981 together name three sisters of Mary Shackleford Moffitt who are not in the earlier list of siblings: Mrs. Josephine (Mrs. Joe) Haskell, Eulah (Eular) Tillman of Lawton, Oklahoma, and Beulah (Beula) Hutchins (Hutchings). Both papers also name Helen Josey and Hazel King, whose Find a Grave pages are linked as John Morgan Shackleford's children.

The 1900 census lists John and Elizabeth with five children, the youngest born in 1899. Josephine, Eulah and Beulah were therefore born after 1900, between about 1901 and 1915, or Myrtle (born 1893) may be one of them under another name. Without a birth record this cannot be settled.
The family lived in Delta County, Texas, around 1908, in Martin County, Texas, by 1930, and later in Caddo County, Oklahoma, where Lizzie is buried at Fairview Cemetery, Apache.
kv: Chico Enterprise-Record 23 Jun 1961; Lamar County Echo 1 Jan 1981
EXTRA.src: The Chico Enterprise-Record, 23 Jun 1961, p. 3; The Lamar County Echo, 1 Jan 1981 (both as transcribed on Find a Grave)
EXTRA.note: Lead: no vital record seen for any of the three.

EXTRA.name: Hagansport Cemetery
EXTRA.place: Hagansport, Franklin County, Texas
EXTRA.title: Where Hagansport buried its dead
EXTRA.hook: The cemetery where John B. Smith and Emma Langley lie holds about 250 graves, begun in the 1880s.
body: Historical Records of Franklin County, Texas, compiled by B. F. Hicks and Doris Meek between 1967 and 1972 and reproduced by the county's TXGenWeb page, describes the cemetery: "Hagansport Cemetery is in the Hagansport Community and has around 250 graves. Burials probably started in the 1880's. The people of the community had probably used the Pierces Chapel Cemetery previous to the start of Hagansport Cemetery."

The earliest marked grave is Laura Terry's, born 13 June 1870 and died 13 October 1876. Smaller family burying places nearby, now lost, include the Cannon cemetery two miles south of Hagansport and the Singleton cemetery two miles northeast, where "there were once about ten wooden stakes marking gravesites."

Emma Langley Smith, who died on 15 March 1905, and John B. Smith, who died in 1918 and whose grave was marked with a wooden stob, were buried here. Some of John B. and Emma's children also grew up here: Charles Oscar Smith and his sisters Vera, Luina, Lona and Allie and brother Jimmie are the children recorded in 1900.
EXTRA.src: Historical Records of Franklin County, Texas (B. F. Hicks and Doris Meek, 1967-72), cemetery descriptions at https://www.txgenwebcounties.net/franklin/cemetery.htm; 1900 U.S. Census, Franklin Co., Tex.

EXTRA.name: Satterfield Cemetery, Jetson
EXTRA.place: Jetson, Butler County, Kentucky
EXTRA.title: A Butler County burying ground with the family's name
EXTRA.hook: At least five of the Satterfield and Johnson kin are buried at Satterfield Cemetery near Jetson, Kentucky.
body: Find a Grave places Satterfield Cemetery at Jetson, Butler County, at 37.2579 N, 86.5703 W. Among those memorialized there are Sidney Rufus Satterfield (1865-1949), his wife Eliza "Ancie" Johnson (1871-1951), their infant Walter (1890), Ancie's father James P. Johnson (1840-1884) and her mother Martha J. Clark Johnson (1839-1923).

The cemetery is the burial place of those who stayed. John C. and Samantha moved to Texas about 1907; Sidney and Ancie stayed on the farm country of Butler and Warren counties, and Sidney died at Richardsville, Warren County, in 1949.
The Satterfields buried here are the sons and daughters of James H. Satterfield, who farmed in Butler County from 1876 and, by his own 1885 account, owned 1,340 acres there.
kv: Sidney R. and Ancie Satterfield; James P. and Martha J. Johnson; Walter Satterfield
EXTRA.src: Find a Grave memorial 19774914, 19774910, 19786592 and 19786602; Kentucky: A History of the State (1885), p. 676

EXTRA.name: Wheelock Cemetery, Millerton
EXTRA.rel: Place the family buried Oscar Hulsey
EXTRA.place: Wheelock, near Millerton, McCurtain County, Oklahoma, the old Choctaw mission ground where Oscar Franklin Hulsey was buried in June 1982.
kv: Wheelock mission ground, 2 miles northeast of Millerton, McCurtain Co., Okla.
Oscar Franklin Hulsey, funeral at 2 p.m. on the Sunday, reported in the McCurtain Gazette of 20 Jun 1982
No Wheelock transcription is posted in the McCurtain County USGenWeb cemetery files, so Oscar's stone is not confirmed by a published listing
Missionaries of the 1830s-1850s, e.g. Rev. Alfred Wright, d. 31 March 1853
EXTRA.src: R. E. Flickinger, The Choctaw Freedmen and the Story of Oak Hill Industrial Academy (1914), p. 22 (archive.org/details/choctawfreed00flick); Chronicles of Oklahoma 25:3 (Autumn 1947) and 26:3 (Autumn 1948); McCurtain Gazette, 20 June 1982 (obituary of Oscar Hulsey, quoted in his entry); McCurtain County cemetery files, USGenWeb Archives (files.usgwarchives.net/ok/mccurtain/cemeteries/, no Wheelock file)
EXTRA.title: Buried among the missionaries at Wheelock
EXTRA.hook: Oscar Hulsey's funeral in 1982 was held at a mission graveyard where stones from the 1850s still stand.
body: Wheelock was a Presbyterian mission to the Choctaws. Its church was organized in December 1832 by Rev. Alfred Wright, who removed to the Choctaws' new land in October 1832, and the buildings stood about two miles northeast of the later town of Millerton. A 1914 book on the neighborhood says what remained: 'the two mission school buildings, a strongly built stone church 30 by 50 feet, a two story parsonage and cemetery.'

The same book copies one stone from the graveyard: 'Sacred to the memory of the Rev. Alfred Wright who entered into his heavenly rest March 31, 1853, age 65 years. Born in Columbia, Connecticut, March 1, 1788. Appointed Missionary to the Choctaws 1820. Removed to this land October, 1832. Organized Wheelock Church December, 1832. Received to its fellowship 570 members.' In 1947 the Oklahoma Historical Society's journal listed Wheelock among the state's 'historic old cemeteries ... that offer much fine material.'

Oscar Franklin Hulsey died at his home at Holly Creek on 17 June 1982, at 71. His funeral, according to the McCurtain Gazette of 20 June, was held at 2 p.m. at Wheelock Cemetery with Rev. Bob Lewis officiating. He was laid there in a graveyard where, a teacher at the mission school wrote of a three-year-old's burial there in the 1890s, the child was placed 'beside missionaries who had passed away half a century before.'

No transcription of Wheelock is posted among the McCurtain County cemetery files, so the family's information for Oscar rests on the newspaper notice and on the memorial listing already cited in his entry, not on a published list of stones. His wife Katie is buried at Mount Olivet in Hugo.

EXTRA.name: Mount Olivet Cemetery, Hugo
EXTRA.rel: Place the family buried Frank, Parsis and Katie
EXTRA.place: Hugo, Choctaw County, Oklahoma, where Frank and Parsis Jane Stevenson and their daughter Katie Hulsey are buried.
kv: 1907, as Burgoyne Cemetery (Choctaw County cemetery list; Association for Gravestone Studies newsletter)
Main entrance at 8th Street and Trice, Hugo; Sec. 29, T6S, R17E
STEVENSON Frank N. 1860-1950; STEVENSON Parsis Jane 1887-1956, Block 2
Buried here after services 2 Feb 2009; too recent for the 2000 canvass
EXTRA.src: Choctaw County, Oklahoma, Mount Olivet Cemetery, Block 2 (Upper and Lower), canvassed 2000 by Ron Henson (USGenWeb Archives, files.usgwarchives.net/ok/choctaw/cemeteries/mtolivet/block2.txt); Cemeteries of Choctaw County Oklahoma, Ron Henson, USGenWeb Archives (files.usgwarchives.net/ok/choctaw/cemeteries/cemchoc.txt); Newsletter of the Association for Gravestone Studies (Showmen's Rest article), archive.org/details/newsletterofasso1422asso; obituary of Katie Hulsey, 2009
EXTRA.title: Two Stevenson stones in Block 2
EXTRA.hook: A year-2000 canvass of Hugo's Mount Olivet lists Frank and Parsis Stevenson side by side, with one birth year that cannot be right.
body: Mount Olivet is Hugo's old municipal cemetery. The county list calls it 'Originally called Burgoyne Cemetery,' and a gravestone-studies newsletter dates it to 1907, 'very nearly to the town's beginning.' It is better known as the home of Showmen's Rest, the circus performers' section dedicated in 1961, with its granite dancing elephant at the entrance.

In 2000 Ron Henson canvassed Block 2 and posted 652 names. Two lines read: 'Stevenson  Frank N.  1860  1950' and 'Stevenson  Parsis Jane  1887  1956.' This is the only transcription found that confirms a stone for Gilbert Franklin 'Frank' Stevenson, who died at Hugo on 9 May 1950, and for his wife Parsis Jane.

Two points need care. Frank's stone gives birth as 1860 while his family record has 17 November 1861; the 1870 and 1880 censuses fit either year, and the middle initial N is not in his known name. Parsis Jane's death year, 1956, matches the family record, but a birth in 1887 is impossible for the mother of children born from 1884; her birth was 1868, so the listed 1887 is a misreading or a carving error. The transcription gives no inscriptions beyond names and years.
Their daughter Katie Cornelia Hulsey died on 30 January 2009, with burial at Mount Olivet. That is nine years after the canvass, so her stone is not in this listing.

EXTRA.name: Shoat Springs Cemetery: the Moffitt graves
EXTRA.rel: Place where Grady and Mary Moffitt and three of their sons are buried
EXTRA.place: South of Hugo, Choctaw County, Oklahoma (3 miles east of SH 93 on US 70, then 2.75 miles south on Fallon Road).
kv: Feb 16, 1921 - Aug 25, 1947; OK SC1C USNR WWII
EXTRA.src: Shoat Springs Cemetery, Choctaw County, Oklahoma, transcription by Tammy Sharp and Karla K. Willis Sharp (USGenWeb Archives, files.usgwarchives.net/ok/choctaw/cemeteries/shoatesprings.txt); Cemeteries of Choctaw County Oklahoma, Ron Henson, USGenWeb Archives (files.usgwarchives.net/ok/choctaw/cemeteries/cemchoc.txt)
EXTRA.title: Five Moffitt stones at Shoat Springs
EXTRA.hook: The cemetery list confirms the dates of Grady, Mary and three of the boys they buried.
body: The Shoat Springs transcription lists five Moffitt entries in a row: 'Moffitt, Dois L. -- Feb 16, 1921 - Aug 25, 1947; OK SC1C USNR WWII', 'Moffitt, Jimmie Gaynell -- Jan 17, 1923 - Oct 26, 1926', 'Moffitt, Henry Wayne -- Jan 13, 1934 - May 12, 1937', and 'Moffitt, Woodford Grady -- Nov 6, 1891 - Jun 21, 1972; Mary Tinsley -- Jun 4, 1895 - Aug 26, 1962.'

These match the dates already in the family record. Dois's date of 25 August 1947 is the date on his Texas death certificate, four days after the Red River accident of 21 August. The rating on his stone, SC1C, is Ship's Cook First Class in the U.S. Naval Reserve, the job he held through the war.
Jimmie Gaynell and Henry Wayne were each three; their parents joined them in 1962 and 1972. The county list places the cemetery in the community of Hugo, in section 4, T7S R18E.
The transcription gives names and dates only, with no epitaphs, so the wording on the stones is not recorded.

EXTRA.name: Cane Creek Friends burial ground
EXTRA.rel: Place the Chamness and Moffitt Quaker ancestors worshipped
EXTRA.place: Cane Creek Meeting, Snow Camp, Alamance County, North Carolina.
kv: 26 acres and a house, 14 Feb 1764, 'for the use and benefit of Cane Creek Meeting' (trustees Peter Stout, Jeremiah and Benjamin Piggott, David Vestal)
Large stone placed 1975 for Anthony and Sarah Chamness
Not individually confirmed: early Friends graves were unmarked and no grave list for William Moffitt, Mary Davies or Sarah Cole appears in this source
EXTRA.src: From Whence We Came: Cane Creek Meeting Sesquibicentennial Reunion (Snow Camp, N.C., c. 2000), archive.org/details/fromwhencewecame00cane
EXTRA.title: The meeting ground where the Chamness stone stands
EXTRA.hook: Anthony Chamness has a 1975 memorial in the Cane Creek cemetery, placed by descendants, not a stone of his own day.
body: The Cane Creek Meeting history records that on 14 February 1764 William Marshall transferred 26 acres on Cane Creek, next to Simon Dixon's mill dam, to the trustees Peter Stout, Jeremiah Piggott, Benjamin Piggott and David Vestal 'for the use and benefit of Cane Creek Meeting.' It adds: 'This is the property where the Meeting House and burial grounds are presently located.' A separate Marshall account says William and Rebecca Marshall gave the 26 acres and the house on it.

Of Anthony Chamness the book says: 'In 1975 friends and family erected a large stone in the Cane Creek Meeting's cemetery to commemorate these early pioneers and their devoted service to the Cane Creek congregation.' It dates him 'circa 1713-1777,' says he and Sarah Cole 'were among the first overseers of the Cane Creek Meeting,' and notes that his will was made on 24 November 1776. 'Chamness descendants still come yearly to stroll between the quiet graves.'
The same book says British troops took over the meeting-house during the Revolution and 'some English soldiers are buried in the cemetery.'

The memorial stone is a modern commemoration. This source does not say where Anthony, Sarah, William Moffitt or Mary Davies lie, and Quaker burials of that time were commonly unmarked, so those graves remain unlocated.

EXTRA.name: Breashears Cemetery, Story
EXTRA.rel: Place the family buried Rev. G. W. Hulsey
EXTRA.place: 1.25 miles east of Story, Montgomery County, Arkansas, on Red Ridge Road, a quarter mile off Highway 298.
kv: 1.25 miles east of Story on Red Ridge Road, in a fenced field
Online list (2008, 139 names); Montgomery County Cemetery Records (1986, 117 names; 1998 edition); 106 graves unmarked
Four Hulsey headstones counted; the posted photo study does not list which
EXTRA.src: Montgomery County ARGenWeb, 'Breashears Cemetery, Story' (argenweb.net/montgomery/breashears_cemetery.htm; photo study, June 2020); Find a Grave index (Breashears Cemetery), as cited in the entries for Benjamin F. and G. W. Hulsey
EXTRA.title: A small graveyard with four Hulsey stones
EXTRA.hook: Both Benjamin and George Washington Hulsey are said to rest at Breashears, but the public list names only the surname count.
body: Breashears Cemetery lies east of the Montgomery County town of Story, in a field off a gravel road, 'fenced, with a bench under the shade of an old tree.' The ARGenWeb page says it has been transcribed at least three times: online in 2008 with 139 names, and in the county's published cemetery books of 1986 and 1998, which recorded 117 names and 106 unmarked graves.

The surname count in that page is 'Breashears (15), ... Holmes (7), Hulsey (4), ... Kilby (10), Lamb (12), Lenderman (9) ...,' with the majority of the stones belonging to eight families. The Hulsey stones are not itemized: the page is a photo study of selected stones, not a transcription.

Rev. George Washington Hulsey (d. 5 August 1935, age 58) and his father Benjamin Franklin Hulsey (d. 16 December 1924) are the two Hulseys the family has placed here. The four-stone count is consistent with that, but the page does not confirm either name. Other burials listed there show the kind of neighbors who surround them: Rev. H. H. Holmes (July 2, 1863 - May 15, 1935, 'The Lord is my shepherd'), M. R. Lenderman (1858-1935) and Gertrude A. Breashears (1881-1952, 'Mother is Resting').
Nothing posted names a church for the cemetery, which has no stated affiliation.

EXTRA.name: Bee Spring church-yard, Giles County
EXTRA.rel: Place the Stevenson preachers were buried
EXTRA.place: Bee Spring Methodist church, about 3 miles northeast of Bryson and 15 miles southeast of Pulaski, Tennessee.
kv: 1815 by Rev. Elam Stevenson, with Stephen Loyd, Meshack Boice and James McCowan
1855, a frame church 36x50 ft; building committee included J. G. Stevenson
Night of 29 April 1909 by a tornado
'All that remains of this today is the cemetery, sadly neglected'
None found online for Bee Spring; Giles County USGenWeb lists Campbell, Diana, Doster and Shane only
EXTRA.src: History of Methodist Churches and Institutions in Middle Tennessee, 1787-1956 (1956), 'Bee Spring Memorial' by Sterling E. Stovall, historian (archive.org/details/historyofmethodi00cart); Rev. Elam Stevenson in McFerrin, History of Methodism in Tennessee, vol. 2 (1871), account of Bee Spring (archive.org/details/historymethodis00mcfegoog); Giles County Archives index (usgwarchives.net/tn/giles/gilcems.html)
EXTRA.title: What is left of Bee Spring is the graveyard
EXTRA.hook: The church where Elam Stevenson preached for decades was blown down in 1909; by 1956 only the cemetery survived, neglected.
body: The Methodist history of middle Tennessee says the original Bee Spring church 'was organized in 1815 by Rev. Elam Stevenson,' son of a Revolutionary captain, who 'professed religion in 1804,' united with the church in 1806, was licensed to preach in 1813 and 'the same year moved to Tennessee.' The first house was logs; a larger log church followed in 1822 or 1823, and a frame church in 1855 whose building committee included J. G. Stevenson. Its members were 'largely the families of the McClaurines, Loyds, McGuires, Sherrills, Moseleys, Bruces, Rowes, and Stevensons.'

Elam's own 1869 account mentions the church-yard: Rev. Meshach Boyce, who helped build the first house, 'died in the faith, and his dust now sleeps in our church-yard at Bee Spring.' A visitor in 1878 wrote that 'here repose the sacred dust of old Father Stevenson and his beloved consort,' which is the newspaper item already cited for Elam and Lydia.

'On the night of April 29, 1909, the Bee Springs Memorial Methodist Church was totally destroyed by the memorable and terrible tornado which passed through this section of Giles and Lincoln Counties.' The congregation rebuilt at Bryson, three miles away. Of the old site the 1956 history says: 'All that remains of this today is the cemetery, sadly neglected.'

No transcription of the Bee Spring graves appears in the Giles County cemetery archives, so the stones of Elam, Rev. Abner A. Stevenson (d. 1896) and Martha Still Watson (d. 12 July 1887) are known only from the family's memorial listing and the 1878 newspaper.

EXTRA.name: Robert and Margaret (Stuart) Moffitt's sons
EXTRA.rel: The family 5th great-grandfather William Moffitt came from
EXTRA.place: Donegal, Ireland; Philadelphia; Chatham and Randolph counties, North Carolina
EXTRA.title: Six brothers and the road from Donegal
EXTRA.hook: Two family records agree that Moffitt sons left Donegal for Philadelphia and went on to the North Carolina Piedmont, and they disagree about which brother came first.
body: Two family accounts tell the Moffitt crossing, and they do not match in every detail. The Bible Record of Abijah Moffitt, quoted on WikiTree, says Robert Moffitt was born in Scotland, went to Ireland when young, and married Margaret Stuart there. It names eleven children: James, Charles, William, Adam, Margaret, Mary, Catheren, Robert, Hugh, John and Patrick. In that record John crossed first, went back to Ireland, and returned to Philadelphia with five brothers.

The 1928 Moffitt Genealogy, compiled by Frank Moffitt for the descendants of Silas Moffitt of Hamilton County, Indiana, has the wedding of "Robert Moffat to Margaret Stuart at Moffat Wells, Scotland" about 1750, and then: "After their marriage, Robert and Margaret migrated to Donegal County, Ireland." It names the same eleven children and says "all but Catharine and Patrick emigrated to America." On the crossing it gives a different brother: "According to tradition, William came first, alone, and went back. Being pleased with the country, he and five other brothers afterward came to Philadelphia and remained there for some time. Later they went to Chatham or Randolph County, N. C."

The Donegal end has no parish or townland. The one piece of background that fits a bride named Stuart is a line in Hanna's 1902 history, which says that in "eastern Donegal" the Cunninghams and the Stewarts "settled" colonists "from Ayrshire and Galloway." That places Scots-Irish Presbyterians of her surname in the county; it does not place Margaret's own family.

The Carolina end is on record. At Cane Creek Meeting in 1763 William married Mary Davies and, in the family's account, his brother Hugh married her sister Hannah, which shows the brothers had joined the Quaker neighborhood of Charles Davies rather than a Presbyterian one. The counties give a sense of how little the family needed to move. The North Carolina Historical Commission's county-formation volume says Orange was formed in 1752 from Johnston, Bladen and Granville; Chatham in 1770 from Orange; Guilford in 1770 from Rowan and Orange; and Randolph in 1779 from Guilford. A household on one stretch of the upper Deep River could have been written into the Orange court records in 1765, the Chatham records in the 1770s and the Randolph records in 1796, the year William made his will, without anyone leaving home, if the family stayed put.

The surname spelling is the family's own explanation. The 1928 book says the brothers agreed to end the name in -itt so that kin could recognize each other wherever it turned up. North Carolina papers of the 1760s write Maffet, Moffit and Moffitt interchangeably, so the story is tradition, not record.
EXTRA.src: Bible Record of Abijah Moffitt (quoted on WikiTree, Moffitt-65); Frank Moffitt, Moffitt Genealogy: Silas Moffitt and Hannah Wilkinson Moffitt (1928), pp. 1-3, archive.org/details/moffittgenealogy00moff; J. A. Hanna, The Scotch-Irish (1902), archive.org/details/scotchirishorsco01hann_0; D. L. Corbitt, The Formation of the North Carolina Counties 1663-1943, archive.org/details/formationofnorth00corb (Orange, Chatham, Guilford, Randolph entries)

quotes.t: According to tradition, William came first, alone, and went back. Being pleased with the country, he and five other brothers afterward came to Philadelphia and remained there for some time. Later they went to Chatham or Randolph County, N. C.
quotes.c: Moffitt Genealogy (1928), p. 2-3

quotes.t: Randolph was formed in 1779 from Guilford.
quotes.c: Corbitt, Formation of the North Carolina Counties

EXTRA.note: The two family accounts disagree on who crossed first (John in the Bible Record, William in the 1928 book) and on whether Robert's wife was Margaret or, in the Alamance Battleground book, Martha. No Donegal parish record has been seen.

EXTRA.name: Hugh Moffitt
EXTRA.place: Cane Creek, North Carolina to the Scioto River near Chillicothe, Ohio
EXTRA.title: Hugh Moffitt goes to the Scioto, 1798
EXTRA.hook: William's brother Hugh went to Ohio in 1798 or 1799 and was dead near Chillicothe by about 1800, five years before the Carolina Quaker wave reached the same country.
body: Hugh is the brother who married into the Davies family. The Bible Record of Abijah Moffitt says "William and Hugh married Davis daughters of North Carolina," and the 1928 Moffitt Genealogy names the two wives as Mary and Hannah, daughters of Charles Davis. On Hugh's own end the Bible Record is short: he "went to Ohio in 1798 or 1799 and died near Chillicothe about 1800."

The date matters because it is early. Weeks's 1896 study of Southern Quakers says the first certificates from Cane Creek Monthly Meeting to Ohio were granted in 1804, when five went to Miami; seven followed in 1806 and sixteen in 1807. Before that the only westward door was Tennessee. But in 1798, the same year Hugh is said to have left, Weeks reports that Westfield Monthly Meeting in Guilford County "requests advice on the removal of some of its members to the Scioto River 'or thereaway,'" and that the committee it asked "wisely left Friends to do as they thought best." The Scioto is the river Chillicothe stands on. Hugh's removal looks like part of that first, unorganized probe rather than of the Quaker wave that followed.

The same town turns up in a later Moffitt-kin story. When Micajah Nordyke, a son of our Abraham Nordyke, settled near what is now New Vienna, Ohio, in the winter of 1805, the family history says he "had to go to Chillicothe, forty miles distant, to get flour and sugar." Hugh, if the family record is right, had died in that country five years earlier.

Nothing else is known of Hugh in Ohio: no land entry, will or burial has been seen, and the Bible Record does not say whether his wife and children went with him. The year, the place and the death near Chillicothe rest on that one family record.
EXTRA.src: Bible Record of Abijah Moffitt (WikiTree Moffitt-65); Moffitt Genealogy (1928), p. 3; S. B. Weeks, Southern Quakers and Slavery (1896), pp. 256 and 265, archive.org/details/southernquakerss00week; C. Clayton Terrell, Terrell-Nordyke Genealogy (1960), p. 14, archive.org/details/terrellnordykege00terr
EXTRA.note: Single family record. Hugh's wife is given as Hannah Davies by the 1928 book; whether she and their children went to Ohio is not stated.

EXTRA.name: Silas and Hannah (Wilkinson) Moffitt
EXTRA.rel: Cousin of 4th great-grandfather Robert Moffitt; Hannah was Robert's niece
EXTRA.place: Randolph County, North Carolina to Hamilton County, Indiana
EXTRA.title: Silas Moffitt's wagon: Randolph County to Hamilton County, October 1823
EXTRA.hook: A first cousin of our Robert Moffitt rode ahead to Indiana in 1822, built a cabin, and brought his wife and two children north in a single wagon in the fall of 1823.
body: Silas Moffitt (1794-1873) was the son of Charles Moffitt, one of William Moffitt's brothers, and Mary Cox; our Robert Moffitt was William's son, so the two were first cousins. Silas married Hannah Wilkinson (1799-1886) in Randolph County, North Carolina, on 4 May 1820. Hannah was the daughter of William Wilkinson, an Englishman, and Mary Moffitt, William Moffitt's daughter, who married on the 26th day of the 3rd month, 1795 by the family's papers. That makes Hannah Robert's niece, and Silas her first cousin once removed.

The 1928 genealogy says the son-in-law and father-in-law "both seemed to think the Northwest Territory offered them better opportunities, so two years after the wedding they started for Indiana on horseback in quest of their future homes." The land "was bought direct from the government, and so far as is known, most of it was bought in Wilkinson's name." They built "rude cabins" and went back for the families. Wilkinson, "unable to return the following year," died in Carolina before he could make the trip, and his family left soon after.

Silas and Hannah, "with their two children Mary and Charles, along with another family whose names have been lost, made the trip in the early fall and reached the site of their future home on the 8th day of the golden month of October, 1823." The book quotes Haines's history of Hamilton County: "The family made the trip from North Carolina with a four-horse team and all their possessions in one wagon." Their eldest son Charles W. was born in North Carolina only weeks before they started.

They lived in the log cabin for three years. Then Silas built a brick house out of brick he made himself, the second brick house in the township. When he died on 28 August 1873, nearly 79 and a few weeks short of fifty years on the place, he owned several hundred acres and had served as county commissioner and for two terms as treasurer of the township trustees. The book says he "lived and labored for half a century on the old Moffitt homestead." He and Hannah are buried in Carmel Cemetery. The Wilkinsons owned land, slaves and a tan yard, and the family left a slaveholding county for a free state, the same road Weeks documents for hundreds of Carolina Quaker families.
EXTRA.src: Moffitt Genealogy: Silas Moffitt and Hannah Wilkinson Moffitt (1928), pp. 3-5, quoting Haines, History of Hamilton County, Indiana, archive.org/details/moffittgenealogy00moff; S. B. Weeks, Southern Quakers and Slavery (1896)

quotes.t: The family made the trip from North Carolina with a four-horse team and all their possessions in one wagon.
quotes.c: Haines, Hamilton County history, quoted in the Moffitt Genealogy (1928)

EXTRA.note: Compiled 1928 family book quoting a county history; no North Carolina or Indiana deed has been checked.

EXTRA.name: Charles and Hannah (Matson) Davies; Edward and Elizabeth (Brown) Norton
EXTRA.rel: 6th great-grandparents (Mary Davies Moffitt's parents) and 6th great-grandparents (Margaret Norton Chamness's parents)
EXTRA.place: Radnor and Goshen, Pennsylvania; Hopewell and Fairfax, Virginia; Cane Creek, North Carolina
EXTRA.title: Two Quaker families, one road: Davies and Norton to Cane Creek
EXTRA.hook: A Welsh-named indentured servant and an Irish Quaker's son took the same Pennsylvania-Virginia-Carolina road, twelve years apart.
body: Charles Davies and Hannah Matson were married at Radnor Meeting, Pennsylvania, in the twelfth month (February) of 1732/3. The Davis family book of 1985, whose title names "Charles Davies, the immigrant to Pennsylvania about 1725, from there to North Carolina," gives the marriage. Hannah was "daughter of John Matson of Merion"; the family's own note in the back of the Cane Creek minute book says Charles "was brought over the ocean and sold to pay his passage." The Davies surname, with its alternate spelling Davis, is Welsh, and Radnor and Merion were Welsh townships in the Quaker settlement west of Philadelphia.

From Pennsylvania the couple went to Virginia. The same family book quotes a minute that a certificate "having been made for Charles Davis and Hannah, his wife to Hopewell Monthly Meeting, therefore this meeting [appoints]," and says the early Hopewell minutes were burned, so the exact year of the move is lost. It says Charles and Hannah were charter members of Cane Creek Monthly Meeting and moved "in or before 1750." Cane Creek was set up in the tenth month of 1751; Orange County, in which the land fell, was cut from Johnston, Bladen and Granville in 1752. Charles bought 187 acres from Henry McCullogh on 2 August 1758 and died in 1801.

Edward Norton's son, also Edward, was the other traveler. His 1739 marriage record at West Nottingham Meeting calls his father "Edward Norton, dec., of the County & Parish of Armagh, in the Kingdome of Ireland." The Nortons are said to have moved to Hopewell in Virginia, then to Fairfax, and reached Cane Creek in 1762, the year before their daughter Margaret married Joseph Chamness. Weeks's survey of the Southern meetings describes exactly this stream: in 1754, the first year of New Garden Monthly Meeting, "we have settlers coming in from Pennsylvania, from Hopewell and Fairfax meetings, Virginia," and he concludes that "the large settlement of Friends in Alamance, Chatham, Guilford, Randolph and Surry counties was formed by Quaker immigrants, not by the expansion of the native element."

Those two sentences are the family's story in small. The Davieses reached Cane Creek about 1750, the Chamnesses in 1749-51, and the Nortons in 1762. By 1763 the three families met at the meetinghouse for two weddings, sixteen days apart: Joseph Chamness and Margaret Norton on 17 March, William Moffitt and Mary Davies on 2 April.
EXTRA.src: Davis: A Quaker Family: Charles Davies, the immigrant to Pennsylvania about 1725 ... (1985), archive.org/details/davisquakerfamil00davi (text excerpts via archive.org full-text search); S. B. Weeks, Southern Quakers and Slavery (1896), pp. 101-103, archive.org/details/southernquakerss00week; Corbitt, Formation of the North Carolina Counties; Cane Creek and West Nottingham Quaker records as quoted in the tree entries for Charles Davies and Edward Norton

quotes.t: we have settlers coming in from Pennsylvania, from Hopewell and Fairfax meetings, Virginia.
quotes.c: Weeks, Southern Quakers and Slavery, on New Garden Monthly Meeting, 1754

quotes.t: Charles was brought over the ocean and sold to pay his passage.

EXTRA.note: The exact year Charles and Hannah left Hopewell is not recorded because the early minutes burned. The Norton route to Cane Creek rests on the tree's reading of West Nottingham, Hopewell and Fairfax records.

EXTRA.name: Anthony Chamness and his descendants
EXTRA.rel: 6th great-grandfather; the line to Martha Chamness, who married Robert Moffitt
EXTRA.place: Whitechapel, London; Baltimore County, Maryland; Monocacy; Carver's Creek and Cane Creek, North Carolina
EXTRA.title: From Whitechapel to Cane Creek in four moves
EXTRA.hook: A fifteen-year-old London apprentice bound for Maryland in 1725 left a line that stayed in Randolph County for a hundred and forty years.
body: Anthony Chamness was baptized at St John's, Wapping, in February 1713, the son of John Chamness and Ann Weary, who had married there on 4 January 1704. The parish clerk wrote the name "Chamniss." Cane Creek Meeting later wrote him down as "Anthony Chamness, s. John & Ann, b. about 2 mo. 1713, Est. Smithfield, London." On 9 February 1724/5, giving his age as 15 and his home as Whitechapel, he bound himself for seven years to John Cooke, a London victualler, for service in "Maryland (his Majesty's Plantation in America)."

He was out of his time by 1732. On 24 November 1735 he married Sarah Cole at St. Paul's Parish, Baltimore County, in the family of the Coles who had been in the county since the 1690s. They were Friends of Gunpowder Meeting. About 1741 they moved to Monocacy, then, in 1749, to Carver's Creek Meeting in North Carolina, and in June 1751 he took up 490 acres at Cane Creek. When Cane Creek Monthly Meeting was organized that autumn, Anthony was its overseer. Weeks writes that "the large settlement of Friends in Alamance, Chatham, Guilford, Randolph and Surry counties was formed by Quaker immigrants," and Anthony is one of them: an English servant boy who became a landowner and the officer of a meeting.

His son Joseph, born in Baltimore County in 1740, married Margaret Norton at Cane Creek on 17 March 1763 and became the meeting's recorder of marriage certificates. Their daughter Martha was born on 6 October 1778 at Centre, then in Guilford County; Randolph County was not cut from Guilford until 1779. She married Robert Moffitt there in 1797 and lived until 1865. Martha's son Nathan Moffitt, born in 1814, left Randolph County for Arkansas in the early 1840s rather than for Indiana.

The Chamness name did also leave by the Quaker road. In Weeks's appendix of removals, Dover Monthly Meeting's list of Friends who took certificates to Indiana between 1830 and 1860 includes "Camness," one more spelling of a name the Wapping clerk had written "Chamniss" a century earlier. The match is by surname only.
EXTRA.src: Cane Creek Meeting records and the London indenture, as quoted in the tree entry for Anthony Chamness; St John of Wapping registers (1704, 1713); S. B. Weeks, Southern Quakers and Slavery (1896), pp. 101 and 278; Corbitt, Formation of the North Carolina Counties (Randolph, 1779)
EXTRA.note: Martha's birthplace is given as Center, Guilford, in the tree; if Centre Meeting's neighborhood fell in Randolph County in 1778 the county named at birth would differ. The Dover 'Camness' is a surname match only.

EXTRA.name: Abraham and Mary (Rogers) Nordyke
EXTRA.place: Burlington County, New Jersey; Virginia; Georgia; Deep River, North Carolina; Lost Creek, Tennessee; East Fork, Ohio
EXTRA.title: Six homes in forty-four years: the Nordykes, 1761 to 1805
EXTRA.hook: From a New Jersey meeting to an Ohio farm by way of Virginia, Georgia, North Carolina and Tennessee, in time for a wolf-haunted winter in a one-sided shelter.
body: A Nordyke family history, the Terrell-Nordyke Genealogy of 1960, gives the stations of Abraham and Mary Nordyke in order. They married in 1761 and were Quakers "members of Chesterfield Monthly Meeting" in New Jersey. "In 1771, they moved to Virginia where they became members of Hopewell Monthly Meeting, which was located near Winchester. They then lived for eight years in Georgia. In 1788, we find them having transferred their membership to Deep River, Westfield Monthly Meeting in North Carolina. Then, in 1798, they moved again, this time to Lost Creek Monthly Meeting located near New Market, a few miles north of Knoxville, Tennessee. From there, in 1805, the family moved to Ohio."

Their son Micajah, the line the book follows, "was born in 1771 in Stafford County, Virginia. At the age of four, he, with the family, moved to Georgia where, because of imminent danger of an Indian invasion, he lay, secreted in a dense woods, through a whole night." Another son, our Aden, was shot in the arm in Georgia in an Indian attack, according to an Ohio county history. The book copies out the Quaker habit of recording the hour of birth: "Aden was born at 7:00 P.M.; Israel at 3:00 P.M.; Benajah at 9:00 P.M."

Lost Creek in 1798 was already a settlement with a history of trouble. Weeks reports that in 1787 Friends at Lost Creek, near the Holston River, asked New Garden Monthly Meeting for the right to hold meetings and were refused, because they had "settled on lands the title to which was still in dispute with the Indians," and were told to move off. The Western Quarterly Meeting added in 1792 that no Friend should "remove and settle out of the limits of a Monthly Meeting without first applying to and having consent." A meetinghouse went up at Lost Creek in 1796. The Nordykes reached it two years later, and it was from there that Weeks says many Tennessee Friends "drifted on, like Charles Osborn and William Williams, to the Northwest."

The last move, in 1805, put Micajah, then 34, his wife Charity, 26, with an infant in her arms and children of three, five and seven, and the "aging grandparents" on the road north. They bought land near what became New Vienna, Clinton County, Ohio, and "helped start a Friends Meeting which was called East Fork," on a lot that was part of the Nordyke farm. "Micajah had to go to Chillicothe, forty miles distant, to get flour and sugar," and Charity kept wolves off with brimstone on the fire. Mary died in 1814. Abraham's burial at East Fork was recorded in 1825, at 89; the tree gives 1822, so the death year is unsettled.
EXTRA.src: C. Clayton Terrell, Terrell-Nordyke Genealogy (1960), pp. 13-15, archive.org/details/terrellnordykege00terr; S. B. Weeks, Southern Quakers and Slavery (1896), pp. 251-54, archive.org/details/southernquakerss00week

quotes.t: In 1771, they moved to Virginia where they became members of Hopewell Monthly Meeting, which was located near Winchester. They then lived for eight years in Georgia.
quotes.c: Terrell-Nordyke Genealogy (1960), p. 13

EXTRA.note: Terrell dates the Ohio move to 1805 and Weeks's context supports Tennessee in 1798; the tree entry for Abraham gives Clinton County in 1806. The Georgia meeting is not named. A diary of the road from Tennessee to Ohio is quoted in the same book but is not attributed to the Nordykes.

EXTRA.name: Aden Nordyke, Sicily (Nordyke) Shaw and Parses (Shaw) O'Neal
EXTRA.rel: 5th great-grandfather Aden; 5th great-grandmother Sicily; Parses is the 4th great-grandmother
EXTRA.place: Deep River and Dover Meetings, Guilford County, North Carolina; Indiana; Gibson County, Indiana
EXTRA.title: Those who left and those who stayed: Aden Nordyke, Sicily Shaw and Parses
EXTRA.hook: Aden Nordyke died in Indiana in 1842, while his daughter Sicily and her husband Noble Shaw stayed in Guilford County; Parses Shaw turns up in Gibson County in 1839.
body: Aden Nordyke was born in Burlington County, New Jersey, in 1762, and came south with his parents. In the twelfth month of 1787 Deep River Monthly Meeting recorded the marriage intention of Adin Nordyke and Martha, and Hinshaw's index lists their daughter "Sicily b. 8-2-1790" first among their children. Aden's brother Micajah went to Ohio in 1805; Aden went on to Indiana, where trees give his death as 9 May 1842.

Sicily stayed. She married Noble Shaw, a member of Dover Monthly Meeting in Guilford County, whose register records him as born 22 April 1787 with children Aaron (16 December 1809), Parris (7 July 1817, died 30 May 1818) and Mary (17 November 1820). Noble died on 25 December 1855 and Sicily on 16 May 1861; in the spring of 1857 she and J. H. Leak advertised his 268-acre farm at Oak Ridge. Weeks's count for Dover Monthly Meeting is seventy-one certificates between 1816 and 1860, "nearly all" of them to Indiana; the Shaws were among the Friends who watched neighbors go and stayed behind.

Parses is the loose end. The 1884 History of Gibson County calls Mrs. Parsis Watt "a native of Lawrenceburg, Ohio," who "came to this county in 1839." Lawrenceburg, on the Ohio River near the mouth of the Great Miami, is in Dearborn County, Indiana, in the heart of the White Water country where Weeks says the Carolina Quakers headed. Parses was about 28 when she and Archibald O'Neal, a Tennessean, came to Gibson County; their son Daniel had been born in Tennessee in October 1838. Archibald died there on 25 April 1841 and she married the County Down Irishman Hugh Watt.

Whether Parses was a child of Noble and Sicily Shaw is not proven. The Dover register has a Parris who lived a year in 1817-18, and Parses, born about 1811, would have to be an earlier child missing from the page. The simplest reading is that her people belonged to the Shaw families who moved from North Carolina to the Ohio-Indiana line; no record has been seen naming her parents.
EXTRA.src: C. Clayton Terrell, Terrell-Nordyke Genealogy (1960); Hinshaw, Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy, vol. 1 (Nordyke and Shaw entries); Dover Monthly Meeting register; History of Gibson County, Indiana (1884), Columbia Township and directory, pp. 212 and 239; S. B. Weeks, Southern Quakers and Slavery (1896), pp. 264-65; The Times, Greensboro, 26 March 1857
EXTRA.note: Parses Shaw's parentage and the 'Ohio' of her birthplace (the town of that name is in Indiana) are unresolved. Aden Nordyke's Indiana death place comes from the tree and has not been checked against a record.

EXTRA.name: Salathiel Hulsey's household and the Hulseys of Hall County
EXTRA.rel: Possible 4th great-grandfather Salathiel Hulsey (link to Benjamin F. Hulsey not yet proven)
EXTRA.place: Virginia; South Carolina; Hall and Union counties, Georgia; Hempstead and Montgomery counties, Arkansas
EXTRA.title: Where the Hulseys came from, and how they got to Arkansas
EXTRA.hook: A Georgia memoir says the pioneer Hulsey came from England and a Virginia-born son went to South Carolina as a child; a Union County blacksmith's sons turn up in Arkansas by 1860.
body: The 1850 census for Union County in the north Georgia mountains, as transcribed in the San Diego Genealogical Society's Hulsey compilation, shows Salathiel Hulsey, 43, born in Georgia, with Elizabeth, 35, and children Mary Ann, Robert R., Elizabeth, Jesse, Jennings, Benjamin, Lillian and Nancy, with an Arminda Burnet, 20, in the house. An earlier reading of the same household gives Benjamin as 3; the transcription prints 6. This is the Salathiel the tree places as Benjamin Franklin Hulsey's father, a link not yet proved. He was in Hall County in 1840.

Hall County had Hulseys earlier. The Georgia land lottery of 1832, which gave away Cherokee land, lists "Charles Hulsy" of Hamilton's District, "Pleasant T. Hulsey" and "James Halsey," a soldier, of Dobbs's District, and "Alder Halsey, Jr.," of Hamilton's, all in Hall. Tax lists for Franklin County, Georgia, on 31 October 1820 name James Hulsey Sr., Joel Hulsey and Pleasant Hulsey. None of these has been tied to Salathiel.

The family's origin shows in a Georgia memoir quoted in the same compilation. The sketch of Col. William Hulsey, born in DeKalb County on 1 October 1839, says: "JENNINGS HULSEY, native of Virginia, immigrated to South Carolina with his parents while he was a child. Came to Georgia, married REBECCA PATE" and died in DeKalb County, and adds: "The pioneer Hulsey from England." So the best account of the surname is Virginia, then the South Carolina upcountry, then north Georgia, a path that matches the Hulseys of Franklin and Hall counties. Salathiel named a son Jennings, which may be a clue to a connection and is no more than that.

Arkansas came next. The compiler notes a Robert R. Hulsey, 27, in Hempstead County, Arkansas, in 1860, and a child named Salathel G. born in Arkansas, which may be Salathiel's son Robert and a grandson named for him. Benjamin F. Hulsey, then 16 or 17, is on the roster of Company D, 4th Arkansas Cavalry, a Union regiment raised in Montgomery County in the winter of 1863-64; so was Gilliam Graves, the grandfather of the woman Benjamin's son George Washington Hulsey would marry in 1901. Montgomery County had been organized on 9 December 1842, and the Ozark region history of 1894 says its settlers "came into the valleys of Montgomery in the thirties."
EXTRA.src: San Diego Genealogical Society, Families: Hulsey (2000), compiled census abstracts and Memoirs of Georgia (Southern Historical Association) extracts, archive.org/details/sdgsfamilies64; James F. Smith, The Cherokee Land Lottery (1838), archive.org/details/cherokeelandlott00smit; A Reminiscent History of the Ozark Region (1894), Montgomery County sketch, archive.org/details/reminiscenthisto00unse

quotes.t: JENNINGS HULSEY, native of Virginia, immigrated to South Carolina with his parents while he was a child. ... The pioneer Hulsey from England.
quotes.c: Memoirs of Georgia, as quoted in the SDGS Hulsey compilation

EXTRA.note: Salathiel's place in the line depends on Benjamin being G. W. Hulsey's father, and the Hall County Hulseys are not tied to Salathiel. The Memoirs' Jennings is the grandfather of a DeKalb County man, not a proven ancestor.

EXTRA.name: Gilliam Graves and his family
EXTRA.place: Toms Creek, Randolph County, North Carolina; Cherokee County, Georgia; Cedar Glades, Montgomery County, Arkansas; Garland County, Arkansas
EXTRA.title: Toms Creek to Cedar Glades: Gilliam Graves's three states
EXTRA.hook: He married in Randolph County in 1832, sat on Georgia juries in 1835 and 1838, and was farming in the Arkansas Ouachitas by 1853.
body: Gilliam Graves was born about 1813 on Toms Creek in Randolph County, North Carolina. He married Mary Tyler there on 18 August 1832. The county had been cut from Guilford in 1779, and his neighbors on the Deep River side included Friends whose meetings Weeks shows draining toward Indiana. Gilliam went south instead. By 1835 he was in Cherokee County, Georgia, where he served on county juries in December 1835 and again on 5 November 1838, and he is in Cherokee County in 1840.

By 1853 he was on the tax lists of Montgomery County, Arkansas, at Cedar Glades, and on 18 August 1845 he had married Delila Hawthorne there, so the move may be earlier than the tax list. The 1894 history of the Ozark region describes the county he came to: it "was organized December 9, 1842," its settlers "came into the valleys of Montgomery in the thirties," "in 1845 there were twenty-one slave-owners," and "the spinning-wheel and loom have not yet disappeared." Its seat is Mount Ida.

The Civil War put him in blue. On 14 January 1864, at 45, he volunteered at Cedar Glades for Company D, 4th Arkansas Cavalry, the same company that carried Benjamin F. Hulsey. He deserted on 12 October 1864 and came back on 25 December. His son Jesse is said to have been born about 1855 in Blount County, Alabama, which does not square with an Arkansas tax roll in 1853 and is unresolved.

Gilliam died in January 1876, supposedly killed by robbers, in Garland County, and is buried beside his third wife Polly in Mountain Valley Cemetery. Garland County was not yet three years old: the 1894 history says it "was established April 5, 1873," with Hot Springs the seat, and that "the greater part is mountainous, leaving only a small area worthy of the labor of the husbandman." Hot Springs is where G. W. Hulsey was born on 24 December 1876, and where Oscar Hulsey was born in 1910.
EXTRA.src: Tree entries for Gilliam and Jesse King Graves (Randolph Co., N.C., marriage 1832; Cherokee Co., Ga., jury lists 1835 and 1838; Montgomery Co., Ark., tax lists 1853; Union Army enlistment papers, 4th Arkansas Cavalry); A Reminiscent History of the Ozark Region (1894), Garland and Montgomery county sketches, archive.org/details/reminiscenthisto00unse; Corbitt, Formation of the North Carolina Counties (Randolph)
EXTRA.note: Jesse King Graves's Alabama birth conflicts with Gilliam's Arkansas tax record in 1853; the tree also gives different details for Gilliam's death.

EXTRA.name: The Satterfields and Garrisons: North Carolina to Kentucky to Texas
EXTRA.place: Orange County, North Carolina; South Carolina; Warren and Allen counties, Kentucky; Maury and Wilson counties, Tennessee; Butler County, Kentucky; Franklin County, Texas
EXTRA.title: Four families, two states and one county line: the Satterfield road
EXTRA.hook: From a Carolina Piedmont county to Warren County, Kentucky, with a detour through Tennessee and a widow of 77 who moved to Missouri.
body: John Satterfield was born about 1766 in Orange County, North Carolina, a county that had been formed in 1752 and has since been divided until the part he came from is Person County. He lived in South Carolina and settled in Warren County, Kentucky, where his will was proved on 10 November 1847 and names thirteen children, among them Ephraim. His son Ephraim, whom his grandson's 1885 sketch calls "a native of Virginia," married Ruth Knowles in Warren County on 12 November 1809. Ruth was born in Virginia about 1783; her father Joshua Knowles, born about 1747, was in Warren County in 1830, and his will of 11 November 1824 names a son John "of Franklin County, Virginia," and a daughter "Ruth Saterfield."

The second generation shows a Tennessee stop. The Butler County sketch of 1885 says Ephraim's son Henry Satterfield was "a native of Maury County, Tenn.; died in 1861, at the age of fifty years," so, if Henry is Ephraim and Ruth's son, as WikiTree has it, they were in Maury County about 1811, two years after their marriage. At the same moment another future ancestor was passing the same way: J. M. Garrison married Patsey Cannon, born in Mecklenburg County, North Carolina, at Wilson County, Tennessee, on 6 December 1809, and the couple settled in Warren County, Kentucky. In 1815 Allen County was cut from Warren and Barren, and the Garrisons found themselves in a new county. Their daughter Mary, born 17 October 1811, married Henry Satterfield. The Kentucky General Assembly dissolved the Garrisons' marriage by an act of its December 1847 session.

Ephraim died about 1850. His widow Ruth is in Allen County in 1850 with her daughter Elizabeth and in 1860, at about 77, in Gasconade County, Missouri, with Elizabeth and her husband Jesse Agee. She died there in 1864, a long way from Warren County.

Henry and Mary's son James H. Satterfield was born in Allen County on 14 April 1838 and married Melissa Gibson there on 17 September 1859. In 1867 he moved to Dakota County, Minnesota; in 1875 he returned to Kentucky and settled in Warren County, and in 1876 in Butler County, a county created on 18 January 1810 from Logan and Ohio. By 1885 he held 1,340 acres there and 425 acres in Tennessee. Melissa died in 1877, and in 1878 he married Lucinda Belle Phelps in Butler County. He died in Bowie County, Texas, on 24 November 1922. His son John C., born in 1864, farmed at Horse Mill in Butler County in 1900. About 1907 the family left for Franklin County, Texas; John died there between 1912 and 1916, and in 1917 his widow Samantha crossed the Red River into Choctaw County, Oklahoma. Their daughter Artie Pearl, born at Morgantown in Butler County on 13 August 1898, married Charles Oscar Smith in 1914.
EXTRA.src: Kentucky: A History of the State (1885), Butler County sketch of James H. Satterfield, p. 676; Warren County, Kentucky, Will Book D, p. 262 (John Satterfield, proved 10 Nov 1847); Joshua Knowles will, written 11 Nov 1824, proved Oct 1832; Wilson County, Tennessee, marriage 6 Dec 1809 (Garrison-Cannon); Acts of Kentucky General Assembly, Dec 1847; 1850 and 1860 censuses, Allen Co., Ky., and Gasconade Co., Mo.; Corbitt, Formation of the North Carolina Counties (Orange, 1752)
EXTRA.note: WikiTree gives Ephraim's birth as South Carolina in 1787, while the 1885 sketch says Virginia; the Maury County birthplace for Henry rests on the same sketch.

EXTRA.name: Nathan, Henry and Grady Moffitt
EXTRA.rel: 3rd great-grandfather Nathan; 2nd great-grandfather Henry; great-grandfather Grady
EXTRA.place: Lawrence County, Randolph County and Stone County, Arkansas; Choctaw County, Oklahoma; Martin County, Texas
EXTRA.title: Three Arkansas counties and a Red River crossing: the Moffitt road west
EXTRA.hook: The Moffitts did not come to Arkansas by way of Alabama; they came straight from the North Carolina Quaker country, and left it by the timber trade.
body: The family's Alabama link is a marriage, not a route. Nathan H. Moffitt, born in 1814 in Randolph County, North Carolina, a son of Robert Moffitt and Martha Chamness, grew up in the Centre meeting community; the North Carolina Manumission Society counted sixty-five members in its Centre branch in April 1819, and a New Garden member quoted by Weeks recalled that the little anti-slavery band there "continued to meet at New Garden until the majority of the members emigrated to the west, preferring to live in a free state." Nathan's own children's birthplaces tell the route: North Carolina up to about 1842, Arkansas from about 1843. In 1850 he was farming in Strawberry Township, Lawrence County. The mother county of northeast Arkansas, Lawrence was created in 1815, according to the county's own history.

His son Henry, born there in August 1855, was farming in Janes Creek Township, Randolph County, in June 1880, with his wife Hannah and two small children. By 1889 the family was in Stone County, where Tom was born at St. James. Stone County was brand new: the 1894 history says it "is one of the new divisions" organized "April 21, 1873," with Mountain View the county seat, and it counted 5,089 inhabitants in 1880 and 7,043 in 1890. Henry's youngest son Grady was born there on 6 November 1891, and Henry died at Mountain View in 1901 at 46.

Grady left the Ozarks in the timber trade. In June 1917 he was a timberman for C. D. Neese at Ervin, Oklahoma, a sawmill town that existed from 1904 to 1922; in 1920 he was a tenant farmer in Wilson Township, Choctaw County. He had married Mary Tinsley Shackleford about 1914, and her people had themselves moved west, from Gilbert in Etowah County, Alabama, in 1900, to Martin County, Texas, by 1930. So Alabama enters the Moffitt line through Mary, whose parents are on the 1900 census at Gilbert and the 1930 census at Stanton, Texas. In 1930 Grady, Mary and their six sons were living with her parents. By 1940 they rented a house at 411 North H Street in Hugo, in the Choctaw Nation, where Grady had been out of work for 50 weeks.

So a family that left Randolph County, North Carolina, for Arkansas in the early 1840s, and Arkansas for Oklahoma in the 1910s, finished its western moves a few miles from the Red River and the old Doaksville road, a few miles from where the Tims family had traded at Doaksville since the 1830s.

EXTRA.name: Rev. Gilbert Franklin 'Frank' Stevenson
EXTRA.place: Pulaski, Tennessee; Gibson County, Indiana; Texas; Oklahoma; Danville, Yell County, Arkansas; Valliant and Hugo, Oklahoma
EXTRA.title: Frank Stevenson's road: Pulaski to Indiana to Danville to Valliant
EXTRA.hook: His grandfather came to Giles County by pack horse in 1813; Frank spent seventy years going back west in short hops.
body: Giles County, Tennessee, where Frank was born on 17 November 1861 at Pulaski, was itself new when his grandfather Elam Stevenson came: it was formed in 1809 from Maury County, and Elam, licensed to preach in 1813, brought his wife Lydia Payne from Burke County, North Carolina, the same year. Elam's own letter of 1869 says Philip Bruce asked him to carry some of his books "in my wagon," which sits oddly with the family story that the move was made by pack horse. A neighbor remembered the family settling near Bee Spring church "in 1815 or 1816."

Frank is in his father Abner's household at Pulaski in 1870 and 1880. In January 1881 the Pulaski Citizen said his father had "abandoned the idea of going to Texas," and in May that his brother "Judge Geo. Stevenson" had "returned from Texas last week." Frank himself went north to Gibson County, Indiana, where his wife Parsis Jane O'Neal's family lived; her grandparents Archibald and Parses O'Neal had come to the county from Tennessee in 1839. Their first three children, Iva Myrtle (1884), Adison Galiton (1886) and Nellie Vashti (1889), were probably born there.

The 1910 census gives the rest of the order. Frank, 51, a clergyman, was renting at Danville in Yell County, Arkansas, married 25 years, with seven children "born in Indiana, Texas, Oklahoma and Arkansas." Yell County had been organized on 5 December 1840, and the 1894 Ozark history notes it had two county seats, Danville and Dardanelle. Katie Cornelia was born at Danville on 15 October 1910.

By January 1919 his mother-in-law Vashti's obituary placed her daughter at "Valiant, Oklahoma." In 1920 Frank farmed a rented place on South Millerton Road in McCurtain County; he died at Hugo on 9 May 1950 and is buried at Mount Olivet. Katie married Oscar Hulsey, born at Hot Springs, in 1927, and their daughter Mary Ellen (1938-2002) is buried at Hugo beside William Thompson Jr.

EXTRA.name: Joseph Pisachubbe's family and the first Choctaw exiles
EXTRA.rel: Frances (Pisachubbe) Thompson's grandfather Joseph and his people
EXTRA.place: Mississippi; Arkansas Post and Little Rock; the Arkansas River near Fort Smith and Fort Coffee
EXTRA.title: With 'the first group of exiles': what the winter of 1831-32 was like
EXTRA.hook: The Pisachubbes told their newspaper that they came west with the first group of exiles in 1832 and settled at Fort Coffee. The official record of that first winter, and of Fort Coffee, sets the story's dates.
body: When William Harrison Pisachubbe died in May 1937, the Hugo Daily News printed a family history from his relative Judge T. W. Hunter: the Pisachubbes "came from Mississippi with the first group of Choctaw exiles in 1832 and settled at Fort Coffee," near present-day Spiro. William Harrison and Robert were the sons of Joseph Pisachubbe, who is on Dawes Card 1580 only as a dead father. No roll of the removal has yet been seen that names him.

The record of the first removal fills in what that sentence meant. Major Francis W. Armstrong took the Choctaw census in the summer of 1831 and counted about 18,880 Choctaws. By the first week of November, Thoburn's history of Oklahoma says, "four thousand Choctaws, some in wagons, some on horseback, some on foot, were on their way to the Mississippi River": five hundred went north to Memphis and took steamboats for Arkansas Post, the rest to Vicksburg. A "fierce winter storm" followed. Between 26 November and 8 December about 2,500 were landed at Arkansas Post. "Few blankets and moccasins or shoes were seen among them; the women generally were barefoot and the young children naked, especially those from the extreme southern part of the nation in Mississippi." There were only forty government wagons for the 350 miles to the Kiamichi country, and the roads were frozen. More than a thousand others went by the Red and Ouachita rivers to Ecore de Fabre. The last parties of 1831 reached the Red River region "during the first week in March, 1832"; on 30 April 1832 Lieutenant Stephenson recorded 3,749 rations being issued at four stations on the Red River, and 536 near the Choctaw Agency by Fort Smith.

The ration was the one Doak & Tims would later be paid for. Thoburn's note gives it as "one and a half pounds of beef or pork, one pint of corn, or an equivalent of corn-meal or flour, with two quarts of salt to the hundred rations," with the corn raised to a quart a day in the fall of 1831.

A family that came "in 1832" is therefore either from the last of the 1831 parties, the winter exiles, or from the 1832-33 removals that the War Department reorganized in May 1832. Fort Coffee, however, was not there to settle at. The garrison at Fort Smith was moved twelve miles up the Arkansas to a new post called Fort Coffee only in June 1834, and the post was abandoned on 27 July 1838. The family's 1937 words most likely name the neighborhood where they put down roots by the agency and the later fort and Skullyville, not a place that existed in 1832. By 1899 the sons were in Kiamitia County, well over a hundred miles south, where Eunice Gardner Pisachubbe and her boys were enrolled at Goodland.

Wright, Oklahoma: A History of the State and Its People (1929), vol. 1, pp. 165-70 and note 17, archive.org/details/oklahomahistoryo01thob; Fort Coffee entry in the same volume's chapter on military posts

EXTRA.name: Doaksville in the removal papers, 1833
EXTRA.rel: Place where Vincent B. Tims, grandfather of Betsy (Tims) Thompson, traded and lived
EXTRA.place: Doaksville and the Kiamichi, Choctaw Nation
EXTRA.title: Doaksville before the store: 1833 in the removal papers
EXTRA.hook: A Choctaw district's letter of February 1833 complains of white traders in 'a small town below Kiametia' and names Doaksville as the place where annuities were received.
body: Doak & Tims is usually dated by its contracts of 1838-39. The removal correspondence puts Doaksville on the map five years earlier. In Senate Document 512, the printed correspondence on the emigration of the Indians, a letter dated at Horn Prairie on Red River on 6 February 1833 is signed by the treaty captains of Nittuckachee's district. They write that their people "are entirely satisfied with our new country" and ask that their annuity be delivered at Horn Prairie, because "at Doaksville, where we have generally received our arms and articles mentioned in the treaty, our horses have suffered much, as there is no winter range." There was a complaint too: "We have to inform you that we have too many white traders in our country, we wish you to have them removed. ... They have built a small town below Kiametia, consisting of white traders, with the exception of two." They would not object to "a few traders ... but we do not wish to be crowded."

The same volumes carry a smaller clue to the man the town was named for. In the account of Lieutenant J. R. Stephenson, the officer in charge of the subsistence depot at Fort Towson, a line lists Josiah S. Doak with "28 lbs. bacon and 4 lbs. sugar," for the first and third quarters of 1833. The printed columns are garbled in the scan, so what Doak was paid for is unclear, but it shows a Josiah S. Doak dealing with the removal's quartermasters on the Red River in the year of the letter.

Vincent B. Tims was a witness, with Doak, to the Treaty of Doaksville on 17 January 1837 and was feeding Chickasaw emigrants under contract by 1 January 1838, at thirteen cents a ration. His partnership with Doak was dissolved in 1844. A New Orleans advertisement in the Washington (Arkansas) Telegraph of 12 October 1845 lists references that begin with "Maj. Wm. Armstrong, Choctaw A[gency]" and include "Doak & Tims, Doaksville, C. Nation." Armstrong was the Choctaw agent, and his brother Francis had taken the 1831 census and run the removal; by 1845 the agent himself stood as a reference for the firm. The Oklahoma history of 1954 lists the Doak & Tims Mercantile Company among the stores of Doaksville, with a blacksmith shop and a hotel.

No document seen puts Tims himself at Doaksville in 1833. Family accounts say he was born in South Carolina in 1803 and had a Choctaw wife; his earliest record at Doaksville that has been seen is the January 1837 treaty. The 1833 letter shows what he walked into: a Red River town already built by white traders, already resented by the Choctaw districts around it, and already the place the government's goods and annuities were handed out.

EXTRA.name: Peter Gaunt
EXTRA.place: Sandwich, Plymouth Colony (Cape Cod)
EXTRA.title: "No publicke vizable worship now in the world": Peter Gaunt before the Plymouth court
EXTRA.hook: Between 1655 and 1661 the Plymouth Colony court questioned, fined and distrained Peter Gaunt of Sandwich, who told the magistrates he knew of no public worship in the world he could join.
body: Peter Gaunt lived at Sandwich, the Cape Cod town in Plymouth Colony, and the colony's court books follow him for six years. At the court of 6 March 1654/5 he was called in "to answare for neglecting to frequent the publick worship of God." Asked to speak to the charge, the record says, "Peter Gaunt affirmed hee knew noc publicke vizable worship now in the world, whereunto the said Ralph Allen assented, but Gorg Allen dissented; the case was left to further consideration." Within three years the same court was fining him for Quaker meetings.

On 2 March 1657/8 Gaunt, Daniel Wing, Ralph Allen Jr. and William Allin were summoned "for a tumultuose carriage att a meeting of the Quakers att Sandwich." The court cleared them of that charge, "notwithstanding, for theire vnreuerent carrying themselues before the Court, coming in before them with theire hatts on," it fined each of them twenty shillings. Thomas Butler, whose daughter Dorothy would marry Peter's son Hananiah in 1678, was summoned for the same disturbance and was "admonished and cleared."

The fines were collected in cattle. In June 1660 a note was entered in the court's record that Marshal George Barlow "tooke from Goodman Gaunt, for his fine of 24li, these particulares: seauen cowes & heifers, two steers, seauen bushells and an halfe of pease; and after, when one of the cowes died, hee tooke another liue one in stead therof, because Barlow had not the hide of the dead cow deliuered to him." Thomas Burgis Jr. owned in open court that he had made the report, and was himself fined thirty shillings for refusing to help the marshal. Joseph Besse's Sufferings of the People Called Quakers, in a list of goods taken from Plymouth Colony Friends about 1658, prints "Peter Gaunt 43 l. 14 s. 6 d."

The summonses kept coming. In October 1660 a long list of people "fined for being att Quakers meetings," ten shillings each, includes "Peter Gaunt, Dorithy Butler, Obadiah Butler." In February 1660/1 the Sandwich constable was ordered to bring Gaunt and nine others to Plymouth "to answare for theire tumultuouse carriages against the marshall and cunstable of Sandwich in the execution of theire offices in the cecuring of two Strang Quakers." A ten-shilling fine on Gaunt "was leuied vpon a mistake" and was given back. In 1661 a list given into the court of those who had sheltered visiting Friends reads: "Wiliam Allin entertained Christopher Holder. Wiliam Newland entertained one forraigne Quaker. Peter Gaunt entertained two forraigne Quakers."

Family trees date Peter's death at Sandwich to 10 May 1678, the same day as his son Hananiah's marriage to Dorothy Butler at the Friends meeting there, so one of the two dates is probably off. One entry in the same volume cannot be placed. In 1661 Thomas Burgis Jr. was whipped for "an act of vncleanes" with a Lydia Gaunt, and his wife was granted a divorce. Peter's wife was named Lydia, but the record does not say which Lydia Gaunt is meant, and the entry is not counted as evidence about this family.
