EXTRA.name: Thomas & Dorothy Butler
EXTRA.place: Sandwich, Plymouth Colony (Cape Cod)
EXTRA.title: Daniel Butler's whipping, June 1660
EXTRA.hook: Dorothy Butler's brother was whipped in 1660 for rescuing a "Strang Quaker" from the Sandwich marshal, and their parents were fined forty shillings for the night the officers searched the house.
body: The Plymouth Colony court in June 1660 passed two sentences on the Butler family of Sandwich. The first reads: "Daniell Butler, for rescuing a Strang Quaker, when apprehended by the marshall, Barlow, and for his breakeing away when taken p'soner, is sentanced to bee publickly whipt, which accordingly was pformed." The second follows it: "Thomas Butler, and Dorithy, his wife, for turbulent cariages the same night that theire son Daniell was serched for att theire house, fined forty shillings." Daniel was the son of Thomas and Dorothy and so the brother of the Dorothy Butler who married Hananiah Gaunt in 1678.

Thomas had been in trouble with the same marshal before. In 1658-9 he was fined ten shillings "for refusing to assist the marshall, Barlow, in the execution of his office." In 1659 he was fined fifty shillings "for refusing to serue in the office of a cunstable," and the next year the court ordered that "The fifty shillings fine amerced on Tho Butler, for refusing to serue in the office of cunstable, is assigned and disposed to Barlow", so the marshal who was seizing Quaker cattle was paid out of a Quaker's fine. In March 1657/8 Butler had been summoned with Peter Gaunt and others over the Quaker meeting at Sandwich and had been "admonished and cleared."

In October 1660 the court fined ten shillings each a long list of people "for being att Quakers meetings," and the list includes "Dorithy Butler" and "Obadiah Butler." Dorothy here is almost certainly the mother. Later the court gave back money taken from the family: "Twenty shillinges, that was leuied vpon Thomas Butler by the marshaU, Barlow, for a fine for his wife and son being att a Quakers meetings, was remitted and released to the said Thomas Butler againe."

Thomas was also a land-hunter. In 1665 the court sent Richard Bourne and William Bassett "to view and purchase some lands desired by Edmond Freeman and Thomas Butler lying towards Saconeesett," and when the Indians would not part with that parcel it gave them leave to buy other land for him. In 1667 the court granted Butler "a necke of land called Tassacausett, lying neare to Edmond Freemans land," which he had "bought ... of an Indian called Charles, alias Pampmumitt, for a yoake of oxen," provided the Indian returned three pounds to Butler.

Thomas's wife Dorothy died at Sandwich on 9 August 1675 and was buried the next day. Thomas died there on 12 March 1690. Their daughter Dorothy, born in January 1649/50, was ten years old in June 1660.

EXTRA.name: Sandwich, Plymouth Colony
EXTRA.rel: Place the Gaunt and Butler families lived
EXTRA.place: Sandwich, Cape Cod, Massachusetts
EXTRA.title: Thirty-five head of cattle: Sandwich in December 1658
EXTRA.hook: A magistrate's letter to a friend in London, printed by Joseph Besse, describes the town where the Gaunts and Butlers lived as nearly all Quaker and being stripped of its cows.
body: In December 1658 J. Cudworth (James Cudworth of Scituate), a Plymouth Colony magistrate who had lost his seat on the bench and his militia captaincy for "entertaining some of the Quakers at my House," wrote to a friend in London. Joseph Besse printed the letter in his Sufferings of the People Called Quakers. Of Sandwich, Cudworth said: "almost the whole Town of Sandwich is adhering towards them: And give me leave a little to acquaint you with their Sufferings, which is grievous unto, and saddens the Hearts of most of the precious Saints of God."

He described the method. The Quakers would not swear, so the old law that every man take the oath of fidelity was revived: refuse it and pay five pounds or leave the colony. "When the Time is come, they are the same as they were; then goes out the Marshal, and fetches their Cows and other Cattle ... On this Account thirty five Head of Cattle, as I have been credibly informed, have been, by the Authority of our Court, taken from them the latter Part of this Summer." Some families had one cow, some two, "and many small Children in their Families, to whom, in Summer-time, a Cow or two was the greatest outward Comfort they had for their Subsistence."

A poor weaver with seven or eight small children, lame himself, had two cows, and both were taken. "The Marshal asked him, What he would do, he must have his Cows? The Man said, That God that gave him them, he doubted not, but would still provide for him." The court then fixed fines for the meetings themselves, ten shillings a meeting, which Cudworth reckoned at one hundred and fifty pounds for Sandwich men, "Newland ... for himself and his Wife" being twenty-four of it and the weaver twenty.

The town was watched. "Sandwich Men may not go to the Bay, lest they be taken up for Quakers," Cudworth wrote, and a man who went on business was put in prison for twenty-four hours while witnesses were sent for. By the colony's newest law, anyone who entertained a Quaker "if but a Quarter of an Hour" forfeited five pounds. Besse follows the letter with a list of other people whose goods were taken at about the same time, for refusing to swear or for absence from public worship. It includes "Peter Gaunt 43 l. 14 s. 6 d.," and the whole list amounts, Besse says, to about six hundred and sixty pounds.

Peter Gaunt's goods and the Butler family's fines are in the colony's own court books, told under "No publicke vizable worship now in the world" and "Daniel Butler's whipping, June 1660." Twenty years later Peter's son Hananiah and Thomas Butler's daughter Dorothy were married at the Sandwich Friends meeting, and within a few years they left for New Jersey.

EXTRA.name: Hananiah Gaunt
EXTRA.place: Oneanickon, Springfield Township, Burlington County, New Jersey
EXTRA.title: Hananiah Gaunt's deeds: 500 acres, a hundred sold, and a share of West Jersey
EXTRA.hook: The East and West Jersey records show Hananiah Gaunt, "of Rhode Island, yeoman," buying 500 acres in May 1685, selling a hundred of them in 1687, and buying into a West Jersey proprietary share in 1690.
body: The New Jersey Secretary of State's calendar of records has three deeds for Hananiah Gaunt. On 11 May 1685 George Hutcheson of Burlington conveyed "to Hananiah Gaunt of Rhode Island, yeoman, for 500 acres in the First Tenth." The Proprietors' survey returns for July 1685 enter "500 a. near Honeonickon, adjoining George Hutcheson," the Indian place-name that became Oneanickon and then Springfield Township. The deed calls him of Rhode Island. An alphabetical list of Dartmouth land owners for 1684-1694 in Lands of Old Dartmouth carries his name; a Ricketson family history notes undivided Dartmouth land deeded by him to William Ricketson on 13 January 1684.

He added to the farm. A later survey is entered for him, "of 220 a. adjoining Samuel Houghton and Tho. Clark; incl. 9 a. of meadow on a brook near Mount Pisgah; 20 a. of the whole being an allowance for highways for other land." A neighbor's survey for Daniel Leeds of 188 acres at Oneanickon is described as lying beside "said Gaunts 9 a. lot," the meadow ground on the brook.

On 18 May 1687 "Hananiah Gaunt of near Oneanickon, yeoman," sold "to William Bustill of Shrewsbury, East Jersey, carpenter, for 100 acres, N. grantor, E. Ralph Trenoweth, part of 500 a., bought of George Hutchinson May 11, 1685." The deed puts Ralph Trenoweth on the east side of the hundred acres and Hananiah's own land on the north.

On 3 November 1690 George Hutcheson, now called a distiller, deeded Hananiah, then "of Burlington Co., yeoman," one twenty-fourth of a share of West Jersey that Hutcheson had bought of Godfrey Newbold of Handsworth, Yorkshire, on 22 August 1684, "excepting 200 acres." A West Jersey share was a proprietary right to a portion of the province's unsurveyed land, and such rights were bought and sold in England and Burlington before the land was laid out.

Hananiah and his brother Israel had exchanged their Sandwich land for New Jersey land on 4 May 1678, the week before his marriage to Dorothy Butler, according to the Sandwich Friends records cited by WikiTree. By 1686 and 1689 the Biddle surveys at Springfield describe other men's land as adjoining his.

EXTRA.name: Richard Browne
EXTRA.place: Podington, Bedfordshire, near Wellingborough, England
EXTRA.title: A "madman" at the table: William Dewsbury and Richard Browne
EXTRA.hook: The Nottingham Friends' family memorandum says our Browne ancestor became a Quaker when William Dewsbury shared his table, and that his landlord then made him pay his rent twice.
body: In 1786 East Nottingham Monthly Meeting entered into its book of births and burials an account of the English father of William Brown the emigrant, written down from the stories of a great-nephew of William's in his eightieth year. It places the father in "Puddington" near Wellingborough, today's Podington, and says he had been "some time in communion with the Baptists, afterwards joining with the sect called Puritans, and is said to have been a teacher among both, and a seeking, religious man." The memorandum calls him William, but the Wellingborough Quaker registers give the father's name as Richard.

The story is that William Dewsbury, "about the first going forth" of that minister, came to the town, and the man noticed "the solidity of his countenance" and asked him in to "break bread." When they sat down the host said grace. Dewsbury sat in a grave manner and answered, "if thou wilt first partake with me I shall be free to partake with thee." After a short silence he was moved to speak, "beginning with these words, 'O Earth! Earth! hear the word of the Lord,'" and the host was convinced. When he came home with Dewsbury his wife asked why he had brought "that madman" to their house. "Why woman," he answered, "he hath brought the Eternal Truth of God to us." She thought it over and was convinced too.

The cost came quickly. The landlord, "a wild airy man and given to sporting," sent his tenant two young hounds to feed and raise. The tenant would not, and the landlord waited. Rent had been paid every half year to a steward without a receipt, so the landlord demanded it again, and said, "except you will take your oath that it is paid, you shall pay it to me." Browne held that Christ had forbidden swearing, so "this Friend had to pay his rent over again," and was then turned off the farm. It took him a considerable time to find another, where he did well. Dewsbury came back, the memorandum adds, and Browne got him leave to speak in the parish church, where "many people were convinced."

Richard died about 1664 by the memorandum's reckoning (a Quaker burial record in the registers gives 1662), and on his deathbed told his wife, "thou shalt live to bring up all our children, and they shall be blessed and be all favoured to keep their habitations in the Truth." William, born about 1656, was the youngest of nine, six other sons and two daughters. The same pages say that when Penn's province was proposed, some Friends doubted whether to go, and Dewsbury, preaching among the Brownes in Northamptonshire, told them: "The Lord is about to plant the wilderness of America with a choice vine or noble seed which shall grow and flourish."

Besse's Sufferings of the People Called Quakers records, in its Northamptonshire section, a meeting at Findon where Daniel Brown and Joane Brown, both "of Puddington in Bedfordshire," were taken with some forty other Friends, held overnight in an alehouse, fined forty shillings each, and sent with the rest to the county gaol for six weeks. Nothing in either source ties them to Richard, and the match rests only on the village name, so it remains a lead.

EXTRA.name: William Brown
EXTRA.place: Marcus Hook and Chichester, Pennsylvania
EXTRA.title: "He is in a wrong spirit": William Brown, his brother James and George Keith
EXTRA.hook: Before the Nottingham Lots, William and James Brown lived at Marcus Hook, where George Keith tried to win James to the separatists and William talked him out of it.
body: William Brown came over about 1682 or 1683 with a first wife, Dorothy, who "could not give up to it cheerfully." The Nottingham memorandum says he felt a clear sense of duty and that "the Lord wonderfully made way for and assisted him," and adds that on the voyage his wife died at sea. Their son Joseph had been born in England on 12 June 1682. William went first to his older brother James, a weaver, who was already at Marcus Hook on the Delaware.

James had been in Pennsylvania before Penn's grant, by Gilbert Cope's reckoning. He married Honour Clayton, whose father William Clayton came in 1677, and on the 20th of the 12th month 1683 (February 1683/4 in modern reckoning) he took a patent for 115 acres on Chichester Creek, which he named "Podington" after the home village. He conveyed it to his son William in 1706.

About 1692 George Keith, once a leader among Friends, split the Quakers of the Delaware. At Chichester meeting Keith "spake or preached largely, using some arrogant and lofty expressions, beyond the simplicity of the gospel." James Brown, "having at first a favourable opinion of Keith," asked his brother afterwards, "what he thought of George Keith now; was not he satisfied?" William, "a deep feeling man," answered, "I am satisfied, but it is in this, that he is in a wrong spirit."

James took it badly and started to leave. William stepped after him and asked whether he remembered "how they used to feel at their meetings when in England, though they were but as lads," the love and melting seasons "under the powerful operation of the pure principle of Love and Light." He went on: "In this country we have come under a different dispensation ... We have been looking out and allowed to provide towards an outward inheritance, and settlements for ourselves and families, free from disturbance or persecution; but let us remember that the truth is still as precious as ever."

The next day Keith held a meeting at the house of Henry Reynolds and called at James's door on the way, asking if he was coming. James hesitated; Keith got down from his horse and went in, saying that if James was growing dissatisfied he would satisfy him, "though he used many words, all did not avail, for James went not to meeting." James later settled in the same neighborhood at Nottingham and died about 1715, "a religious man and of a good character, but not favoured with a capacity or talent equal to his brother William." William's son Richard married Hannah Reynolds of Chichester in 1717; the host of Keith's second meeting was a Henry Reynolds "who lived near."

EXTRA.name: William Brown
EXTRA.place: Nottingham Lots, Chester County, Pennsylvania (now Cecil County line)
EXTRA.title: Lots 23 and 33: William Brown on the Nottingham Lots
EXTRA.hook: William Brown is said to have cut the first tree on the Nottingham Lots in 1701; the plat gives him Lots 23 and 33 and his sons the lots beside them, and the first meeting was held in his house.
body: The Nottingham Lots were thirty-seven rectangular lots of Penn's land laid out in 1701-02 on the border with Maryland. A 1902 bicentennial history of the Brick Meeting House at Calvert, Maryland, says "all agree that William Brown was the first Friend to settle on the Nottingham lots." The family memorandum says he moved his family there in 1702, "accounted far back in the wilderness." The bicentennial history adds a tradition that Penn himself rode out in the early spring of 1701 with a party that included William Brown, James Brown, John Churchman, Edward Beeson and Henry Reynolds, and that in the fall the two Brown brothers went to the site on pack horses from New Castle to clear ground for corn.

The plat as the history gives it assigns "No. 23 to William Brown" and "No. 33 to William Brown," with "No. 14 to James Brown" and Nos. 26 and 27 to James, and "No. 28 to Messer Brown." Messer is William's son Mercer, born in February 1685/6, whose first name was his mother Ann Mercer's maiden name; the history prints it as Messer, as it was commonly written. William's lot was beside a spring about a mile east of the present Rising Sun, near the road to the Brick Meeting House.

Tradition, "which is now upon record," says William "was the first to take his axe in hand and strike it into a tree, one of the monarchs of the forest," and said, "In humble trust we commence our labor." The spring is said to have been an Indian camping ground on the trail from Pennington to the mouth of the Susquehanna, which an old resident, Jesse Pugh, remembered tracing as a boy.

The records are firmer about the meeting. At Concord Monthly Meeting in the 2nd month of 1705, "two Friends of Nottingham desires on behalf of the rest a First Day meeting at the house of William Brown, and a Fourth Day meeting once a month," and Concord Quarterly Meeting on 9 April 1705 "approves of until further order." The first brick meetinghouse followed in 1724. Penn's spoken gift of forty acres for a meetinghouse, burial ground and school in 1701 was the only title Friends had until 1765, when his sons Thomas and Richard Penn issued a patent to William Brown, Timothy Kirk, William Churchman and Benjamin Chandlee in trust.

William Brown the emigrant died, by the family memorandum, on the 23rd of the 6th month 1746 (23 August), "in the 91st year of his age," having lived at Nottingham about 44 years "in good repute for his integrity; being an elder in the Church, and a substantial Friend." Ninety-one would put his birth near 1655; the Wellingborough register gives 1658. His great-nephew and namesake William Brown, a minister, traveled in Europe with John Churchman from 1750 to 1754 and was the man in whose eightieth year the memorandum was written down.

EXTRA.name: Thomas & Agnes (Hawthornthwaite) Croasdale
EXTRA.place: Neshaminy Creek, Bucks County, Pennsylvania
EXTRA.title: Three cows, two mares and 500 acres: the Croasdale inventories
EXTRA.hook: Thomas and Agnes Croasdale lived only two and four years on Neshaminy Creek, and the two estate inventories filed in Philadelphia list what they owned.
body: Thomas Croasdale of New Hay in Yorkshire married Agnes Hathornthwaite of Wyresdale on 1 May 1664, in the Quaker register of Lancaster Monthly Meeting. By deeds of lease and release of 21 and 22 April 1682 he bought a thousand acres of William Penn's province, and on 7 June the Settle Monthly Meeting gave a certificate for a party of its Friends, among them "Thomas Croasdale, Agness his wife & six children." In Pennsylvania 500 acres of the purchase were laid out on Neshaminy Creek near the present Langhorne.

Thomas died on 2 November 1684. His widow was given administration, and James Dillworth and Thomas Constable appraised the goods on 8 December: "his Apparrell 03 00 00; in bedding 07 00 00; in pewter & brass 03 04 00; in bages & Cutions 01 00 00; in Wood vessels 00 15 00; in Chests & boxes 01 00 00; in Linnen 02 00 00; in Iron Ware 04 00 00; in hoggs 05 00 00" (pounds, shillings, pence), "2 Mares 08 10 00" and "3 Cows 1 calf 1 yearling 12 00 00." The total was "47 09 00" and the "500 Ackers of Land" were "not prized."

Agnes outlived him by about two years. The inventory of "Agnes Crossdale of Neshaminah Widdowe," taken by Nicholas Waln and Robert Heaton, starts "Imprimis all the Brass," then "Item all the Pewter," "the wood vessel," "the Potts," "one Bed wth ye bedding belongin" at four pounds, "one Chest ten Shillings," "one Saddle," "Hoggs" at three pounds, "3 Cows 2 Bullocks 1 Heifer" at twenty-four, "2 Mares 1 Colt" at ten, and "500 Acres of Land" at fifty pounds, ending with "one Blankit Some nails all the husbandrie Tooles & hustlement about the House." It totals 106 pounds 5 shillings. She died on 20 October 1686 and her sons William and John were given administration on 1 November 1686. Waln signed with his mark.

The printed inventory is dated the 10th of the 9th month 1685 but registered on the 1st of the 9th month 1686, which does not fit a death in October 1686, so one of the printed years is off. Their six children are in the Settle register: William (born 7 February 1664/5), John, Elizabeth (who died in 1683), Mary, Bridget (30 August 1671) and Alice. Bridget married John Cowgill in 1693. Alice married David Potts, and Mary, William Smith.

Agnes's maiden name may link her to a Friend who was jailed. Besse lists a "William Hathornthwaite" among forty-three Friends arrested at Swarthmoor in January 1660 for refusing the oath and committed to Lancaster Castle, on page 308 of the Lancashire section. Nothing yet ties him to Agnes. Her son William Croasdale, who stayed in Bucks County, made his will on the 30th of the 1st month 1715 (30 March), naming his sisters Mary Smith with eight children and Alice Potts with ten.

EXTRA.name: Ellen Cowgill
EXTRA.place: Middletown, Bucks County, Pennsylvania
EXTRA.title: Two sons in service: Ellen Cowgill's children in 1682
EXTRA.hook: The Settle certificate lists "Ellen Cowgill widow & her children"; two of them arrived as servants, John to the Quaker minister Cuthbert Hayhurst, who was dead within months, and Ralph to a Cheshire settler for four years.
body: Ellen Cowgill is named in the Settle Monthly Meeting certificate of 7 June 1682 as "Ellen Cowgill widow & her children," in a list that goes: Cuthbert Hayhurst "his wife & family," Thomas Wrigglesworth and Alice, Thomas Walmsley and Elizabeth, Thomas Croasdale "Agness his wife & six children," Thomas Stackhouse and his wife, Nicholas Waln "his wife & three children," "Ellen Cowgill widow & her children," and William Hayhurst. No child is named. Genealogists identify Jane, John, Ralph, Edmund and Jennet from Middletown Meeting records and the Board of Property minutes.

John, probably about seventeen, came as a servant to Cuthbert Hayhurst. Hayhurst, born at Easington in Yorkshire about 1633, had been among the Friends imprisoned in the West Riding in the 11th month of 1660 for refusing the oath of allegiance. In 1668 he held a meeting at the house of Richard Betteris in Oxford and was arrested while speaking and held for a month by the vice-chancellor. His neighbor Nicholas Waln wrote that "he went through many great exercises and imprisonments." He died in the first month of 1683, only months after landing in Bucks County.

Ralph Cowgill came by a different ship, landing about 28 September 1682. Under Randolph Blackshaw of Hallingee, Cheshire, a list of Bucks County residents prints: "These servants below came in the ship the 'Friend's Adventure.' The Mr., Thomas Wall. Arrived in this river the 28th 7th M., 1682. Servants to Randulph Blackshaw, William Beasy, Ralph Nuttall, and Ralph Cowgill, each to serve 4 years, and to have 50 acres of land apiece." Passengers and Ships Prior to 1684 (1970) lists both John and Ralph as apparently Ellen's children: John, "servant to Cuthbert Hayhurst" and a probable passenger on the Lamb of Liverpool, and Ralph, "who came on the Friend's" Adventure.

Which ship carried the Settle families has been told two ways. Potts's Our Family Ancestors (1895) and the 1915 Stout family history say they sailed in Penn's own Welcome, and Potts adds that smallpox killed thirty on that ship. The later study says at least four of the seven Settle families sailed on the Lamb of Liverpool, and a Watson family history lists the Lamb, "John Tench, master, from Liverpool," as arriving on 22 October 1682. The party's own certificate does not name a ship.

John Cowgill served his time, married Bridget Croasdale in 1693 at Neshaminy and, after her death in 1701, Rachel Bunting in 1703/4. Jennet Cowgill married Bernard Lane at Burlington on the 2nd of the 12th month 1687/8 (2 February 1688). Ellen is buried in the Middletown Friends cemetery.

EXTRA.name: John Cowgill
EXTRA.place: Blackbird Creek and Duck Creek, New Castle County, Delaware
EXTRA.title: A tan-yard on Black Bird's Creek, and two Cowgill sisters who married two Brown brothers
EXTRA.hook: John Cowgill left Bucks County about 1713, set up a tan-yard on Black Bird's Creek, and his daughters Elizabeth and Ellin married William Brown Jr. and Thomas Brown of Nottingham.
body: John Cowgill, the servant boy of 1682, married Bridget Croasdale at Neshaminy on the 19th of the 8th month 1693 (19 October). Their children were Elizabeth (born the 24th of the 6th month, 1694), Thomas (21st of the 4th month, 1696), John (8th of the 5th month, 1698) and Ellin (14th of the 10th month, 1700). Bridget died on the 26th of the 2nd month, 1701. In 1703/4 he married Rachel Baker, the widow of Job Bunting of Darby, and had four more children: Rachel, Mary, Ebenezer and Eleazer. Quaker months started in March, so the 6th month is August; some family trees convert the first birth to June.

About 1713 or 1714 he moved to the lower part of New Castle County, Delaware. The land records the Stout family history quotes say that on the 26th of the 3rd month 1715 (26 May) a warrant was signed to John Cowgill "for the resurvey of a tract of land in a fork of Appoquinimink Creek," and on the 1st of the 5th month 1715/6 he "desired the grant of about 100 acres of vacant land, near his other tract in New Castle county, where he had planted a tan-yard." On the 10th of the 3rd month 1718 (10 May), "having erected a tan-yard on a branch of 'Black Bird's Creek,'" he asked for another hundred acres on rent.

His sons Thomas and John followed him, and married sisters, daughters of Joshua Clayton of Little Creek Hundred. Thomas had Thomas, Ezekiel and Jane. John married Lydia Clayton in 1720 "of Kent county." The daughters were already settled among the Nottingham Quakers. The Duck Creek Monthly Meeting records the marriage of "Elizabeth Cowgill, daughter of John Cowgill, of Duck Creek in New Castle, and William Brown, son of William Brown, of Nottingham," on 1 December 1715 by the Quaker count (the Nottingham registers say 1715). Her sister Ellin married Thomas Brown, William Jr.'s brother, in 1718/9.

Elizabeth died before 1721 and left a daughter, also Elizabeth, who in 1739 married Edward Norton. William Jr. married Margaret Davis in March 1721/2, died about 1727, and Margaret then married William Kirk. Ellin's husband Thomas Brown died on the 19th of the 12th month 1746/7 (19 February). She married again on the 13th of the 11th month 1768 (January 1769) Lewis Clothier of Kent County, Maryland, and died on the 5th of the 1st month 1772 (5 March), aged 71. John Cowgill himself died on 2 July 1731. His grandson John Cowgill of Little Creek was hauled through Dover in a cart in the Revolution for refusing Continental money; that is told in "Carted through Dover."

Cope's Browns of Nottingham lists the four marriages of William Brown the emigrant and the children of each, and the Maryland Quaker Records for Nottingham Monthly Meeting repeat the Cowgill marriages from the meeting's own books.

EXTRA.name: John Cowgill of Little Creek
EXTRA.place: Little Creek Hundred, Kent County, Delaware
EXTRA.title: Carted through Dover: John Cowgill of Little Creek, 1776
EXTRA.hook: Elizabeth Cowgill's nephew refused Continental paper money on conscience, was declared an enemy to his country by the Kent County Committee in January 1776, and was driven to Dover in a cart with a paper pinned to his back.
body: John Cowgill of Little Creek Hundred was the son of John Cowgill and Lydia Clayton, and the grandson of the tanner John Cowgill of Black Bird's Creek, which makes him a nephew of Elizabeth (Cowgill) Brown, our ancestor. On 4 January 1776 the Committee of Inspection and Observation for Kent County, Caesar Rodney and Thomas Rodney among its members, resolved "that it appears to this Committee, by the confession of John Cowgill, a residenter of Little Creek Hundred, in this County, that he has refused, and, from conscience, shall refuse, to take said Continental money in discharge of debts, or for other purposes, when tendered to him." The committee decided he was "an enemy to his country, and ought to be treated as such by every friend of American liberty; and that they ought to have no further dealings with him."

His daughter Mary Corbit described the arrest in a letter of 1824 to her brother John, who passed it on to Samuel R. Fisher. It began when he asked a tenant to pay rent in specie. He was taken before the Assembly at Dover and threatened with "a heavy fine," and, when he declined to take any part in encouraging war, was let go. Later "going to Meeting on a fifth day, mother and I being in the chaise, and my father on horseback with one of my little brothers behind him," a man in regimentals rode with him half a mile where armed men were waiting. "The child was taken from behind him, and he was ordered to dismount and get into a cart." Friends coming to meeting followed as far as the meetinghouse, where "my father called out and bid us farewell." "A paper was pinned to his back."

Before they entered the town the officer stopped the cart, and, taking his calm for ignorance, said, "Mr. Cowgill you are not aware of the danger you are in!" He answered: "I fear not them that can kill the body, and after that have no more power that they can do; but I fear Him who after he hath killed the body, hath all power." At the liberty pole in Dover it was proclaimed that he had no protection and that anyone dealing with him did so at their peril; "the miller was threatened with the destruction of his mill if he ground for his family, and the school-master forbid receiving his children at school."

The man was let go, and many Friends rode home with him. His daughter wrote, "When we went to bed at night we did not know what would be the issue before morning, and in this way we lived for several years." She told of one of the party who took him that day. The roads were wet and muddy, and Cowgill, seeing the man walking beside the cart, said, "Thee had better get up and sit with me, as the walking is wet and I am fearful thee will take cold." The man said long afterward that he never regretted any act of his life more than being concerned in the affair against "one of the best of men."

Duck Creek Monthly Meeting, on 27 June 1778, received "an account of the sufferings of John Cowgill for refusing Continental Currency" and sent it to the Quarterly Meeting committee. John married Mary Worrell and had a large family; his daughter Mary married William Corbit of Odessa, Delaware.

EXTRA.name: Edward Norton of Armagh and his children
EXTRA.place: West Nottingham, Chester County, Pennsylvania; later Hopewell and Fairfax, Virginia
EXTRA.title: Two Nortons from Armagh and two Browns at Nottingham
EXTRA.hook: Edward Norton's son and daughter, Irish Quakers from Armagh, married a Brown nephew and uncle at West Nottingham in 1739 and 1733, and Mary Norton's widow's settlement was inspected by a Virginia meeting.
body: The Irish Quakers' certificate list for Nottingham Monthly Meeting records two Norton marriages. "Mary Norton, daughter of Edward Norton, 'of ye County of Armagh,' Ireland, was married 9 Mo. 24, 1733, under auspices of Nottingham Mo. Mtg., to Richard Brown, son of William Brown, of West Nottingham." And: "Edward Norton, of West Nottingham, Chester County, son of Edward Norton of 'ye City and Parish of Armagh,' Ireland, deceased, was married 8 Mo. 16, 1739, at Nottingham Mo. Mtg., to Elizabeth Brown, daughter of William Brown."

Richard was the son of William Brown the emigrant and his second wife Ann Mercer, born in 1693; he had married Hannah Reynolds in 1717 and Rachel Beeson in 1730/1 before Mary Norton, who was his third wife by the Nottingham count (Cope lists the same three marriages but gives the third as the 24th of the 5th month). Elizabeth was the daughter of William Brown Jr. and Elizabeth Cowgill, so the bridegroom Edward Norton married his sister Mary's husband's niece. Elizabeth's mother had died before 1721 and her father about 1727, and she married at West Nottingham as an orphan. The meeting's book calls her "dt William & Elizabeth (Cowgill), both dec."

Both couples went to Virginia. Edward and Elizabeth Norton took a certificate to Hopewell Monthly Meeting on 19 January 1739/40, and Richard and Mary Brown with their family took one to Hopewell too. Mary and Richard's three children were Richard (born 18 September 1734, died 4 September 1738), Joseph (1 April 1736, died 19 May 1751) and Mercer (7 May 1740). Richard died before 1747, leaving a will; his widow's second marriage was to Elizabeth's step-family, as below.

The editors' abstract of the Nottingham minutes says that Fairfax Monthly Meeting appointed a committee on the 28th of the 12th month 1746/7 (28 February) to inquire into the settlement of Richard Brown's last will and testament, to protect the children, and that it was found satisfactorily settled. On the 21st of the 1st month 1746/7 (21 March) Nottingham gave William Kirk, the widower of Margaret Davis, a certificate to Fairfax, clear to marry Mary Brown, and in April 1747 he married Mary (Norton) Brown, widow of Richard Brown and daughter of Edward Norton "of Co. Armagh, Ireland, dec." Margaret Davis, who had died in February 1744/5, had been the second wife of Elizabeth's father, so Mary Norton's new husband was Elizabeth's stepmother's widower.

Edward and Elizabeth Norton later lived at Rowan County, North Carolina, according to their daughter Margaret's marriage certificate of 1763, when Margaret Norton married Joseph Chamness at Cane Creek. If the Edward and Elizabeth Norton of that certificate are the couple of 1739, as the names and the Hopewell and Fairfax trail suggest, then Margaret's grandmother was Elizabeth Cowgill of Neshaminy, and the line from the Settle certificate of 1682 runs through Brown and Norton to the Chamness wedding that put the family into Robert Moffitt's household.

quotes.t: Edward Norton, of West Nottingham, Chester County, son of Edward Norton of 'ye City and Parish of Armagh,' Ireland, deceased, was married 8 Mo. 16, 1739, at Nottingham Mo. Mtg., to Elizabeth Brown, daughter of William Brown.
quotes.c: Albert Cook Myers, Immigration of the Irish Quakers into Pennsylvania, 1682-1750 (1902), p. 376

EXTRA.src: Albert Cook Myers, Immigration of the Irish Quakers into Pennsylvania, 1682-1750 (Swarthmore, 1902), Nottingham Monthly Meeting, https://archive.org/details/immigrationofiri00myer_0; Maryland Quaker Records: Nottingham Monthly Meeting (Brown entries for William Jr., Richard and Margaret Davis); Cope, The Browns of Nottingham (1864).
EXTRA.note: The marriages and the Brown relationships are proven by meeting records; that the Rowan County Nortons of 1763 are this couple is probable, not proven.

EXTRA.name: Jacob Perkins Sr. and Jr.
EXTRA.place: Wellingborough (Willingboro), Burlington County, New Jersey
EXTRA.title: A cane and a sword: the Perkins estates of 1731
EXTRA.hook: Within a few months in 1731 two Jacob Perkinses of Willingboro died, the second leaving a will that names Henry Nordyke, who had married his daughter Rebecca that January, as a debtor.
body: In May 1731 administration of the estate of Jacob Perkins of "Wellenborrow," Burlington County, who died without a will, went to his son Jacob Perkins, yeoman. The inventory, made on 20 May by Robert Lucas and Joseph Fenimore, comes to 91 pounds 18 shillings 5 pence and "includes cane and sword, £1.10; debt of 14 shillings from Benja. Perkins; 8 years rent due from Benja. Perkins and Wm. Makintass, £1."

The son, Jacob Perkins Jr., made his own will on 26 October 1731. He left his wife Sarah and his children "Abraham, Rebeckah, David, Mary, Ann, Susannah, Hannah, Sarah, Bethseda and Martha." He disposed of "land in Chester, which I bought of John Ward March 15, 1728," and listed bonds due him "from James Smith, Esq., John Shinn and Henry Nordike." He also left ten pounds to St. Mary's Church, Burlington, the Church of England parish, which points to Church of England ties. His son David was executor and the witnesses were Joseph Fenimore, Eliza Fenimore and Sam. Scattergood. The will was proved on 7 December 1731, and the inventory of 6 December, by Fenimore and Scattergood, was 205 pounds 14 shillings 6 pence.

Henry Nordyke had married Rebecca Perkins at Willingboro on 6 January 1731, the same year. He appears in her father's will as a man who owed him money. Then David died too. His will, made in January 1731/2 "of Wellingborrow, yeoman," leaves his brother Abraham "plantation in Wellingburrow, which came to me by will of my father, Jacob Perkins, dated Oct. 26, 1731," and names his "Sister, Rebecca, wife of Henry Nordike" and "Mother, Sarah Perkins." It was witnessed by Joseph Fenimore, Sam'l Scattergood and Henry Nordike, and was proved on 4 March 1731/2.

So within about a year the Perkins household of Willingboro lost a grandfather, a father and a son, and the new son-in-law Henry Nordyke witnessed the last of the wills. Henry and Rebecca's descendants are the Nordykes of the family tree. Abraham, to whom David left the plantation, was also his executor.

quotes.t: Sister, Rebecca, wife of Henry Nordike. Mother, Sarah Perkins.
quotes.c: Will of David Perkins of Wellingborrow, 1731/2, Calendar of New Jersey Wills, Lib. 8, p. 184

quotes.t: Includes cane and sword, £1.10.
quotes.c: Inventory of Jacob Perkins Sr., 20 May 1731, Calendar of New Jersey Wills, Lib. 3, p. 102

kv: Jacob Perkins Sr. dies intestate; inventory 91 pounds 18s 5d
Jacob Perkins Jr.'s will; proved 7 Dec; inventory 205 pounds 14s 6d
EXTRA.src: Calendar of New Jersey Wills, Administrations, etc. (New Jersey Archives, 1st series), Perkins entries of 1731-32 (Lib. 3 pp. 102 and 169; Lib. 8 p. 184), https://archive.org/details/calendarofnewjer01newj
EXTRA.note: The calendar abstracts the wills; the originals have not been read. That Henry and Rebecca's son Abraham is the Abraham Nordyke who married Mary Rogers in 1761 comes from the family tree, not from these abstracts.

EXTRA.name: Giles County in the Civil War
EXTRA.place: Pulaski and Bee Spring, Giles County, Tennessee
kv: Giles County, Tenn.; Pulaski, Elkton, Prospect, Lynnville
Rev. Abner A. Stevenson and wife Martha; son Gilbert b. 17 Nov 1861 near Pulaski
Bee Spring (listed in the Twentieth Civil District)
EXTRA.src: Goodspeed, History of Tennessee (1886), Giles County chapter, pp. 758-760 and church list in the district descriptions, p. 766 (archive.org: historyoftenness00good).
EXTRA.title: Soldiers on the road to Huntsville: Giles County, 1862-1863
EXTRA.hook: Abner Stevenson's son Gilbert was five months old when the first Federal troops marched into Pulaski.
body: Gilbert Franklin Stevenson was born near Pulaski on 17 November 1861, to Rev. Abner Stevenson and Martha. Goodspeed's county history says what the next four years were like around the family farm. "The county was continually overrun with both Federal and Confederate soldiers throughout the war, being on the line of march from Nashville to Huntsville, Ala. Pulaski, Lynnville, Elkton and Prospect were each visited by Federal troops in large numbers, and Pulaski and Lynnville were fortified." On Fort Hill above Pulaski "a formidable fort or earth-work was erected."

The first Federals to come in any number arrived in April 1862, when Col. Mark Monday brought a detachment of Gen. Negley's brigade from Columbia to drive off John Morgan's cavalry, who were plundering the Federal wagon trains. Gilbert was then about five months old. Monday camped at Pulaski until September 1862. In August 1863 Col. Hayes raided the county with a regiment of cavalry and camped a day and a night in Pulaski. In the same year, in Goodspeed's words, "Lynnville and Elkton were both raided by the Federals, the whole county, in fact, being relieved of horses, cattle and grain."

That October Gen. Wheeler retreated south through the county with Gen. Wilder after him, and in November "Gen. W. T. Sherman and his entire army passed through Giles County, en route to Chattanooga, making a short stop at Elkton." Bee Spring, the Methodist church Elam Stevenson helped found, stood in the Twentieth Civil District with Mount Pisgah and Mount Zion.

The book does not name Abner's household. What it gives is the setting: a Methodist preacher with a farm, a wife, and a new baby on a road that three armies used. Abner's nephews Coleman and Wilbur Stevenson served the other side from their own farms nearby, in the 32nd Tennessee.

quotes.t: The county was continually overrun with both Federal and Confederate soldiers throughout the war, being on the line of march from Nashville to Huntsville, Ala.
quotes.c: Goodspeed, History of Tennessee (1886), Giles County chapter, p. 759

quotes.t: the whole county, in fact, being relieved of horses, cattle and grain.
quotes.c: Goodspeed, History of Tennessee (1886), Giles County chapter, p. 759

EXTRA.note: Place story. It describes the county, not any raid on the Stevenson farm; no source seen says what Abner's family lost or did.

EXTRA.name: John Milton Garrison and the Kentucky General Assembly
EXTRA.place: Warren, later Allen County, Kentucky
kv: 4 Oct 1788, Cowans Ford, Mecklenburg Co., N.C. (WikiTree)
6 Dec 1809, Wilson Co., Tenn., Patsey Cannon
One slave counted in the household (WikiTree transcription)
Act of the General Assembly, session of 1847-48, p. 410, sec. 6
EXTRA.src: Acts passed at the session of the General Assembly for the Commonwealth of Kentucky (1847-48), p. 410, sec. 6 and index (archive.org: actspassedatses72kentgoog); WikiTree Garrison-4365 (biography and census transcriptions) and Cannon-4655.
EXTRA.title: One enslaved person in 1810, and a divorce by act of the legislature in 1848
EXTRA.hook: John M. Garrison's household counted a slave in 1810. Thirty-eight years later the legislature ended his marriage, and he married the neighbor woman WikiTree says he had children with.
body: John Milton Garrison was born on 4 October 1788 at Cowans Ford in Mecklenburg County, North Carolina, and came as a boy with his parents to Warren County, Kentucky. On 6 December 1809 he married Martha "Patsey" Cannon in Wilson County, Tennessee. Their daughter Mary, born 17 October 1811, married Henry Satterfield and is the Garrison link into the Satterfields.

Slavery. WikiTree transcribes the census index entry for "John M Garreson" in Warren County in 1810, and the transcription gives "Numbers of Slaves 1" in a household of five. That is one enslaved person in the household of a man of about 21. The transcribed returns for Allen County in 1820, 1830 and 1840 show no slaves: in each the total of all persons equals the total of free white persons (7, 11 and 7). The 1850 census shows him at 62, a farmer, with real estate valued at $2,250. No 1850 or 1860 slave schedule has been checked, so it is not known whether he held anyone after 1810. The 1810 count rests on a WikiTree transcription of an index, not on the schedule page itself.

The marriage ended in the legislature, by statute. The printed Acts of the 1847-48 session, section 6 on page 410, read: "That the marriage contract now existing between John M. Garrison, and his wife, Patsey Garrison, be and the same is hereby dissolved, and they are hereby restored to all the rights and privileges of unmarried persons." The section gives no reason. The volume's index lists it twice, once under "Garrison, Patsey, an act to divorce" and once, apparently by a slip, under "Harrison, John M."

WikiTree gives a reason from other records, but names no source for it. Its biography says that during the marriage he "fathered children by Sarah Stamps who lived nearby," that he "had the KY legislature declare those children legitimate," and that after the divorce he married Sarah. The 1850 census, as WikiTree transcribes it, lists J. M. Garrison, 62, with an "S" aged 57 and three younger Garrisons aged 21, 19 and 6. The legitimation act has not been located in the volumes searched, so that part is a lead. He died in Allen County on 18 September 1860,

quotes.t: That the marriage contract now existing between John M. Garrison, and his wife, Patsey Garrison, be and the same is hereby dissolved, and they are hereby restored to all the rights and privileges of unmarried persons.
quotes.c: Acts of the General Assembly of Kentucky, session of 1847-48, p. 410, sec. 6

EXTRA.note: The divorce is proven by the printed act. The 1810 slave count is a WikiTree transcription (probable). The Sarah Stamps children and their legitimation are a lead: WikiTree states them without a source and the act was not found.

EXTRA.name: Renting on shares at Hagansport, 1908
EXTRA.place: Hagansport, Franklin County, Texas
kv: U.S. Bureau of Soils, Soil Survey of Franklin County, Texas, 1908
Tenant furnishing everything: half the crop
EXTRA.src: A. E. Kocher and W. S. Lyman, Soil Survey of Franklin County, Texas, in Field Operations of the Bureau of Soils, 1908 (USDA, 1909), pp. 931-947; archive.org: usda-soil-survey-of-franklin-county-texas-1908.
EXTRA.title: What a rented farm at Hagansport meant in 1910
EXTRA.hook: The government's 1908 soil survey says what tenants paid, what the land near Hagansport grew, and why the north end of the county was held back.
body: In April 1910 John C. Satterfield, 46, was renting a farm at Hagansport, and John B. Smith and Emma Liza Langley Smith had farmed there in 1900. The U.S. Bureau of Soils surveyed Franklin County in 1908 and wrote about farming in just that corner, without naming any family.

On renting, the survey says that "the rental paid is on the usual share plan, by which the tenant furnishes everything but the land and buildings and receives one-half the crops. When the tenant furnishes only the labor he is given one-third of the corn and one-fourth of the cotton." In 1900 only 44.1 percent of the county's farms were run by their owners, and the average farm was 77.9 acres. Most land could be bought for $5 to $10 an acre, more in the Sulphur River bottoms. The authors add that "since that date many of the tenants have acquired title."

On Hagansport itself: the town sits on a divide between the Sulphur River and White Oak Creek, with bodies of Wilson clay loam "in the vicinity of Hagansport and Lavada." The survey calls that soil "somewhat better adapted to cotton than to corn," says it was nearly all in cultivation, and gives the cotton yield as "from one-third to three-fourths bale per acre." The bottoms along the river were "more or less subject to overflow." Of the north end of the county, the survey says: "Other small centers in the northern part of the county are Daphne, Lavada, and Hagansport. In this part of the county development is seriously hindered by the absence of adequate shipping facilities."
This is a general portrait. It does not say whether the Smiths owned or rented, or whether the Satterfields farmed on halves or thirds, but it describes the terms on which families like them worked.

quotes.t: The rental paid is on the usual share plan, by which the tenant furnishes everything but the land and buildings and receives one-half the crops.
quotes.c: Soil Survey of Franklin County, Texas (1908), p. 931

EXTRA.note: Place story from a government survey. It names no ancestor; the census facts about the Smiths and Satterfields come from entries already in the app.

EXTRA.name: The fifteen children of Abner and Martha Stevenson
EXTRA.rel: Brothers and sisters of 2nd great-grandfather Frank Stevenson
EXTRA.place: Giles County, Tennessee, with branches in Alabama, Arkansas and Texas
EXTRA.title: Fifteen children at Bee Spring
EXTRA.hook: Frank Stevenson was one of fifteen children of a farming preacher, and a twin; the 1870 census lists eleven of them under one roof.
body: Rev. Abner A. Stevenson and Martha S. Watson were married on 8 December 1838. A family history compiled from the Stevenson family sketches of the 1950s lists their fifteen children, all born in Giles County: Lucinda C. (3 May 1840), William Elam Fletcher (9 April 1842), Lydia Mary Eliza (20 December 1843), Catherine M. Frances (10 January 1846), Augustus Summerfield (30 October 1847), Ellen Tillman and James Willis (twins, 30 January 1850), Larkin Henry (12 October 1852), Amanda Elizabeth (21 October 1854), Julia Ann Desdemona (July 1857), John Edward Thomas (16 September 1859), the twins Gilbert Franklin and George Washington (both 17 November 1861), Wilson McAlister (15 August 1864) and Manerva Jane (22 July 1866).

The 1870 census, as printed on the WikiTree page for Frank, finds the household in District 10 with A. A. Stevenson, 54, Martha, 47, and eleven children: Lucinda 28, James 20, Ellen 20, Larkin 18, Amanda 16, Julia A. 14, John E. 12, George W. 8, Gilbert 8, Mack 5 and Manerva J. 3. The two eight-year-olds are the twins. By 1880 the house was nearly empty: Abner, 63, "Farming Preacher," Martha, 56, Gilbert F., 18, Wilson M., 16 and Jane M., 12, with three hired or fostered Whittaker children and a one-year-old grandchild named Berry Andrew, born in Alabama. The Andrew grandchild was probably the youngest son of Abner's daughter Eliza, who had died in November 1878 (lead).

Several of the dates check against the Bee Spring graveyard. W. Mack Stevenson is on the cemetery list as born 15 August 1864 and dead 30 June 1940, which matches Wilson McAlister. Nathan A. Stevenson, 12 November 1870 to 21 July 1936, is Abner's grandson Nathaniel, William's son. Werner W. Stevenson, 4 March 1880 to 23 June 1974, is James Willis's son. Abner himself lies there, as does Martha S., 19 February 1823 to 12 July 1887.

The children scattered. Lucinda married Perry Pittman Williams and died in 1920; Eliza Mary married John Newton Andrew on 20 December 1870 and died in 1878; Frances married J. M. Whitaker and died on 18 April 1889; Summerfield went to Arkansas and was buried near Crowley's Ridge; Ellen married James Marion Britton; Julia went to Texas as John Newton Andrew's third Stevenson wife; Edward died in El Paso; George became a judge at Lubbock; James Willis became a Methodist minister; Manerva married Andrew R. Merrill and moved to Ardmore, Tennessee. Frank went to Indiana. Each has a short story of her or his own in this section.
EXTRA.src: Robert Casey, Interactive Family Histories, "Stevenson, Arrington and Tucker Families," Master Publication pp. 3-98 to 3-120 (http://www.rcasey.net/master/steelam.htm and steabner.htm); WikiTree profiles (api.wikitree.com) for Gilbert Franklin Stevenson (Stevenson-12558), Parsis Jane O'Neal (O'Neal-3514) and Daniel Waters O'Neal (O'Neal-2667), with the 1870, 1880 and 1910 census transcriptions printed there; Bee Spring Cemetery listing, Giles County, Tennessee (Giles Co. TNGenWeb cemetery page); Goodspeed list of Elam Stevenson's children, p. 872.
EXTRA.note: The Casey family history names the fifteen children and their births; the 1870 and 1880 census households and the cemetery dates fit it, but the family history has no sources for the exact days.

quotes.t: Farming Preacher
quotes.c: Abner A. Stevenson's occupation, 1880 U.S. census, 10th District, Giles County, Tennessee

EXTRA.name: George W. and Edward Stevenson
EXTRA.place: Giles County, Tennessee; Texas
EXTRA.title: Two Stevenson brothers go to Texas
EXTRA.hook: One brother became a judge at Lubbock and the father of thirteen; another died of smallpox at El Paso in June 1886, working for the railway.
body: Frank Stevenson had a twin. George Washington Stevenson was born on the same day, 17 November 1861, and the 1870 census lists both as 8 years old in the same Giles County household. In May 1881 the Pulaski Citizen noted that "Judge Geo. Stevenson, son of Rev. A. Stevenson, returned from Texas last week." The family history says that George later lived at Lubbock, Texas, where he was a judge, and that he was the father of thirteen children. It names none of them.

John Edward Thomas Stevenson, born on 16 September 1859, appears in the 1870 census as "John E," 12. The family history says Edward "moved to Texas where he worked for the Texas and Pacific Railway" and "died of smallpox in El Paso, Texas on June 26, 1886." He would have been 26. The Texas and Pacific reached El Paso in 1881, so the job fits the date.

The pull of Texas runs through this family. In January 1881 their father "abandoned the idea of going to Texas." Their sister Julia Ann followed her husband John Newton Andrew there, and by the 1870s their sister Ellen Britton's growing family was moving between Giles County and Texas. When Frank and Parsis lived there in the 1890s and 1900s, three of their children were born in Texas.

quotes.t: Edward Stevenson moved to Texas where he worked for the Texas and Pacific Railway. Edward Stevenson died of smallpox in El Paso, Texas on June 26, 1886.
quotes.c: Casey family history, Master Publication 3-109

quotes.t: Judge Geo. Stevenson, son of Rev. A. Stevenson, returned from Texas last week.
quotes.c: The Pulaski Citizen, 5 May 1881, p. 2

EXTRA.src: The Pulaski Citizen, 5 May 1881, p. 2 (Library of Congress); Robert Casey, Interactive Family Histories, "Stevenson, Arrington and Tucker Families," Master Publication pp. 3-98 to 3-120 (http://www.rcasey.net/master/steelam.htm and steabner.htm); 1870 U.S. census, District 10, Giles County, as transcribed on the Frank Stevenson WikiTree page.
EXTRA.note: The El Paso death and the Lubbock judgeship come from the family history alone, which has no source for them. A Texas death record or a Lubbock County court record would settle both.

EXTRA.name: Julia Ann Desdemona (Stevenson) Andrew
EXTRA.place: Giles County, Tennessee; Rockwall and Wilbarger Counties, Texas
EXTRA.title: One widower, three Stevenson wives
EXTRA.hook: John Newton Andrew of Giles County married a Stevenson cousin, then a Stevenson sister, then Frank's other sister; the last wife took him to Texas.
body: John Newton Andrew was born in Giles County on 20 February 1841. His first wife was Mary Hamilton, a granddaughter of Rev. Elam Stevenson through Elam's daughter Catherine. His second, on 20 December 1870, was Eliza Mary Stevenson, Frank's sister, who bore him four sons (Baxter, Abner, Truman and Perry) and died on 16 November 1878. His third was Eliza's younger sister Julia Ann Desdemona Stevenson, born in July 1856 or 1857. The family history notes that Julia was thus "John's third marriage to a Stevenson woman."

Julia and John had four children, Ray, George, Tina Tisha and Alice. WikiTree places a son, Roy Jackson Andrew, at Rockwall, Texas, on 30 July 1893 and at his death at Wilbarger County, Texas, in 1964. John died on 28 March 1909 and Julia on 3 July 1928 at Vernon, Wilbarger County, according to WikiTree; its biography page gives 1925 as her death year, so the date is not settled.

Rockwall comes up again in this family. A WikiTree profile for the first husband of Parsis O'Neal, Frank's wife, puts his death in Rockwall County in 1901. If Frank and Parsis were among the Giles County Stevensons around Rockwall in the 1890s, the Texas births of their children Willie, Frank and Elisha would be explained (lead; see the Louderback story).
EXTRA.src: Robert Casey, Interactive Family Histories, "Stevenson, Arrington and Tucker Families," Master Publication pp. 3-98 to 3-120 (http://www.rcasey.net/master/steelam.htm and steabner.htm); WikiTree profiles Stevenson-5863 (Julia Ann Desdemona), Andrew-1921 (John Newton Andrew) and Andrew-1917 (Roy Jackson Andrew).
EXTRA.note: Julia's death year is given as 1925 and 1928 in different WikiTree fields, and her birth as 1856 and 1857. A Texas death certificate or Vernon cemetery record would settle it.

EXTRA.name: Ellen Tillman (Stevenson) Britton
EXTRA.place: Giles and Crockett Counties, Tennessee; Texas
EXTRA.title: Ellen Stevenson and the Brittons
EXTRA.hook: A twin born in 1850 who married a Giles County farmer, went to Texas and back, and raised seven children.
body: Ellen Tillman Stevenson was born on 30 January 1850, the twin of James Willis. On 24 December 1871 she married James Marion Britton, born on 3 March 1840 in Giles County, the son of Wilson Britton and Elizabeth Ragains. His brother John Frank Britton died in Collin County, Texas, in 1890.

Her seven children were born in several places: Logan Harwell Britton on 17 September 1872 (at Wichita Falls, Texas, according to WikiTree, and he died at Wichita Falls on 25 March 1950); Sarah Beulah on 24 January 1873 in Tennessee; Amanda Elizabeth on 6 February 1877 (Dallas, Texas, by the family history; Giles County by WikiTree); an infant daughter on 6 March 1880; Wilson Arrington on 12 May 1882 at Friendship, Crockett County, Tennessee; James Wilson Lafayette "Fate" on 8 December 1884; and Carlos Erskine on 15 May 1890. The 1880 census finds the family in Crockett County, Tennessee, and by 1900 they were back in Giles County.

James died on 18 September 1913 in Giles County and Ellen on 4 March 1927 (Find a Grave gives 4 February); both lie at Mount Zion (New Zion) Cemetery near Pulaski. Their daughter Amanda married Eli Bascom Pitts on 2 March 1892 and had eleven children. Sarah Beulah married Samuel McNeese and had eight, including twins who died the day they were born, 10 June 1902.
EXTRA.src: Robert Casey, Interactive Family Histories, "Stevenson, Arrington and Tucker Families," Master Publication pp. 3-98 to 3-120 (http://www.rcasey.net/master/steelam.htm and steabner.htm); WikiTree profiles Stevenson-3637 (Ellen Tillman), Britton-1643 (James Marion Britton) and Britton-2364 (Logan Harwell Britton).
EXTRA.note: Birthplaces and the month of Ellen's death differ between the sources; the family history and WikiTree each have errors that the other does not.

EXTRA.name: Rev. James Willis Stevenson
EXTRA.place: Giles County, Tennessee
EXTRA.title: A third-generation preacher with three wives
EXTRA.hook: Frank's brother James Willis, a twin of Ellen, became a Methodist minister, married three times, and lived until 1943.
body: James Willis Stevenson, born on 30 January 1850, was the twin of Ellen. The family history calls him a Methodist minister. His first wife was a cousin, Nancy J. Stevenson, and their only son was Werner Wesley, born on 4 March 1880. After Nancy died he married Elizabeth A., and then Beatrice, born in October 1870 in Alabama. The 1900 census finds James and Beatrice in Giles County, and he later lived at Ardmore, Tennessee.

His second and third marriages gave him another ten children: Bessie (1885), Bertha (1887), Coleman (1893), Cletis Z. (1897), Lydia M. (1898), and Nore, Clower, Elizabeth, Charlie and Talmadge Dewitt. He died on 9 November 1943 and was buried at Bee Spring, the church his grandfather founded.

Werner Wesley (1880-1974) stayed in Giles County and married Lila Mitchell. Their daughter Nannie married Robert Hulsey, born in January 1904; a family letter of 1997 from "Nannie (Stevenson) Hulsey" is one of the sources for the family history. No connection between this Giles County Hulsey and Katie Stevenson's husband Oscar Hulsey has been shown (lead).
EXTRA.src: Robert Casey, Interactive Family Histories, "Stevenson, Arrington and Tucker Families," Master Publication pp. 3-98 to 3-120 (http://www.rcasey.net/master/steelam.htm and steabner.htm) (James Willis Stevenson, Werner Wesley Stevenson); Bee Spring Cemetery listing, Giles County, Tennessee (Giles Co. TNGenWeb cemetery page); 1900 and 1920 censuses, Giles County, as cited in the family history.
EXTRA.note: The 1943 death date comes from the family history; the cemetery list used here has no matching entry for him.

EXTRA.name: Rev. William Payne Stevenson and Malinda (Rowe)
EXTRA.place: Giles County, Tennessee
EXTRA.title: A preacher with soldier sons and a short-lived brood
EXTRA.hook: Elam's oldest surviving son raised eight children on a Giles County farm, buried four before 1857, and sent two sons into the Confederate 32nd Tennessee.
body: William Payne Stevenson was born on 27 September 1810 in North Carolina, the oldest son of Rev. Elam Stevenson. On 14 October 1830 he married Malinda Rowe in Giles County. Goodspeed (1886) says he "has four brothers who are ministers of the gospel," and that he settled on his farm in 1838. He lived to 14 January 1892; Malinda died on 21 January 1888. He is buried at Bee Spring.

The family history lists nine children: an infant son who lived and died in 1831; Coleman Lafayette (26 December 1832); Elam R. (1835); Joseph J. (1837); Sarah Ann P. (10 March 1840); Wilbur Marion (20 January 1841); Presley W. (8 September 1847); William F. (19 January 1853); and John Henry (1856). Six of the nine did not reach adulthood. The family history gives Presley W.'s death as 30 June 1849 (the cemetery list reads 30 July), Elam R. on 2 August 1854, William B. F. on 19 August 1854 and Joseph J. on 15 February 1856. Sarah died on 10 February 1846.

The two grown sons went to war. Goodspeed says Coleman "enlisted in the Thirty-second Tennessee Regiment of Volunteers" in 1862 and "served until the close of the war," taking part "in most of the principal battles." The same book says the 32nd was organized at Camp Trousdale in the summer of 1861, with four Giles County companies, and went first to East Tennessee and Kentucky. Goodspeed's orders of battle for the Army of Tennessee place the 32nd in Brown's Brigade of the division of Gen. C. L. Stevenson (no kin), and the county chapter says it was reorganized at Jackson, Mississippi. Wilbur Marion served in the same regiment until the fall of 1864, "when left the service due to ill health."

Coleman raised not only his own sons but three orphaned Jackson nieces of his wife (Martha V., Nancy M. and Mary J.). He died on 24 October 1908. Wilbur married Martha Jane Hampton on 9 November 1865. She died on 28 December 1918 and he died the next day, 29 December 1918, in Giles County. The sources do not give a cause, but their dates fall in the winter of the great influenza epidemic (lead).

quotes.t: He has four brothers who are ministers of the gospel, and his father was also a very prominent Methodist Episcopal minister.
quotes.c: Goodspeed, History of Tennessee (1886), Giles Co., sketch of Coleman L. Stevenson, p. 872

quotes.t: In 1862 Mr. Stevenson enlisted in the Thirty-second Tennessee Regiment of Volunteers, and served until the close of the war.
quotes.c: Goodspeed, p. 872

EXTRA.src: Goodspeed, History of Tennessee (1886), Giles County, Biographical Appendix, pp. 871-872; Goodspeed, Giles County military chapter, p. 758-759; Robert Casey, Interactive Family Histories, "Stevenson, Arrington and Tucker Families," Master Publication pp. 3-98 to 3-120 (http://www.rcasey.net/master/steelam.htm and steabner.htm) (William Payne Stevenson, Coleman Lafayette, Wilbur Marion); Bee Spring Cemetery listing, Giles County, Tennessee (Giles Co. TNGenWeb cemetery page).
EXTRA.note: The influenza suggestion is only a guess from the dates. Neither source states a cause for the 1918 deaths.

EXTRA.name: Bee Spring Cemetery, the Stevenson burials
EXTRA.rel: Place the family lived and was buried
EXTRA.place: Bee Spring Methodist Church, near Bunker Hill and Bryson, Giles County, Tennessee
EXTRA.title: The Stevenson row at Bee Spring
EXTRA.hook: Four Stevenson burials between 1 February and 3 March 1856, two more in August 1854: the graveyard Elam founded shows how hard those years were.
body: Elam Stevenson bought fifteen acres for $20 in 1815 to found Bee Spring church. The cemetery behind it lists about seventy-five Stevenson entries. The tall stone over Elam and Lydia reads, on Elam's side, "Erected to the memory of Reverend Elam Stevenson, born September 24, 1787, died March 13, 1875. Nearly 62 years a minister of the gospel. He was pure in heart and life." On the back: "Erected to the memory of Lydia Stevenson, born August 16, 1787, died March 6, 1872. Nearly 70 years a Methodist. She consecrated her household to God and the church."

The listing shows how the family's children died. In the summer of 1854: Citty on 20 June, Elam R. on 2 August and William B. F. on 19 August. In the winter of 1856: Louisa (Coleman's young wife) on 1 February, Joseph J. on 15 February, Ann Eliza on 2 March and James Elisha on 3 March. An "infant" is dated 6 October 1831 (the first child of William and Malinda). Several more are listed only as "child" or "infant." The list does not record causes.

The family also kept its dead close. Rev. Abner A. is listed there with his wife Martha S. (1823-1887); his brother Rev. James C. (23 June 1813 to 23 February 1899) lies beside Margaret Caroline (8 December 1816 to 11 February 1886); Willis McKendree is there (18 January 1818 to 6 February 1900), as are Coleman L. (1832-1908), with Dorcas (1832-1892), and Thomas C. (1825-1906). The congregation also buried a Stevenson as late as 1994. The Pulaski Citizen noted in 1878 that "Here repose the sacred dust of old Father Stevenson and his beloved consort."

quotes.t: Nearly 62 years a minister of the gospel. He was pure in heart and life.
quotes.c: Elam Stevenson's gravestone, Bee Spring Cemetery, as quoted in the Casey family history, p. 3-98

quotes.t: Nearly 70 years a Methodist. She consecrated her household to God and the church.
quotes.c: Lydia Stevenson's gravestone, same stone, reverse side

TNGenWeb cemetery page) (burial dates for Stevenson entries); Robert Casey, Interactive Family Histories, "Stevenson, Arrington and Tucker Families," Master Publication pp. 3-98 to 3-120 (http://www.rcasey.net/master/steelam.htm and steabner.htm) (gravestone inscriptions, p. 3-98); The Pulaski Citizen, 30 May 1878, p. 1.
