EXTRA.name: Catherine A. (Stevenson) Hamilton
EXTRA.place: Giles County, Tennessee; Limestone County, Alabama
EXTRA.title: "They who bear the cross shall bear the crown"
EXTRA.hook: Elam's eldest child moved to Alabama with her husband, raised nine children, and is quoted on her gravestone; her sons went on to Texas and Arkansas.
body: Catherine A. Stevenson was born on 2 October 1808 in North Carolina, the oldest of Elam and Lydia's eleven children. She married William B. Hamilton, born in 1808 or 1809 in South Carolina. Their nine children were Lydia J. (1832), Mary A. (1834), James (1839), Elam Carr (1 February 1842), Clatinda I. (20 January 1844), George Worth (1846), Thomas C. (1848), Gilbert William (1850, in Alabama) and John Baxter (30 April 1853, in Limestone County, Alabama). The family was in Limestone County in 1860, 1870 and 1880.

William died on 8 September 1872 and was buried in the Wallace Cemetery in Limestone County. Catherine died on 2 December 1888, and the same cemetery has her stone: "Mrs. C.A. Hamilton born October 2, 1808 died in great peace December 2, 1888. They who bear the cross shall bear the crown." A grandson, Robert J. Hamilton of Ripley, Alabama, described her as "a short, chubby, and very cheerful little lady."

Her children moved west. Her son George became a Methodist minister. Clatinda never married and died on 4 March 1892. Gilbert William married Martha J. Thorpe and lived in Greene County, Arkansas, where their daughter Bessie was born on 31 March 1880; Martha died on 19 May 1881, Gilbert on 6 June 1896, and both were buried at Pruetts Chapel. John Baxter married Mary Arantha Lynch in Kaufman County, Texas, on 31 January 1884 and had nine children there. Her daughter Mary A. became the first wife of John Newton Andrew, who later married two of Frank's sisters.

quotes.t: Mrs. C.A. Hamilton born October 2, 1808 died in great peace December 2, 1888. They who bear the cross shall bear the crown.
quotes.c: Gravestone, Wallace Cemetery, Limestone County, Alabama, as quoted in the Casey family history, p. 3-99

EXTRA.src: Robert Casey, Interactive Family Histories, "Stevenson, Arrington and Tucker Families," Master Publication pp. 3-98 to 3-120 (http://www.rcasey.net/master/steelam.htm and steabner.htm) (Catherine A. Stevenson, pp. 3-99 to 3-103); WikiTree Stevenson-8354 (Catherine A. Stevenson) and Hamilton-23815.
EXTRA.note: A 1950 Skinner family genealogy on archive.org (ancestryofcaroly00skin) prints a chart of Elam Stevenson (1787-1875) and what appears to be the opening of his will in Giles County Court, 1875, via the Hamilton line; the book is not available in full text and was seen only in search snippets.

EXTRA.name: Elam Augustus Stevenson
EXTRA.place: Giles County, Tennessee; Arkansas; Winston County, Alabama
EXTRA.title: A doctor and preacher who moved to Arkansas in 1858
EXTRA.hook: Abner's younger brother carried the family trade to Arkansas, taught his sons the pulpit, and is buried at Booneville, not far from Danville where Frank later lived.
body: Elam Augustus Stevenson was born on 3 February 1829 in Giles County, the son of Rev. Elam and Lydia. He joined the Tennessee Conference of the Methodist Episcopal Church, South. The Minutes of the 1858 Conference record "Elam A. Stevenson, transferred to Wachita Conference" (Ouachita, in Arkansas). A 1930 Arkansas biography of his son says he "came to Arkansas and became pastor at El Dorado and Princeton" in 1858. His son James Baxter was born at Richmond, Arkansas, on 24 October 1860, and WikiTree puts Thomas Elam's birth at Booneville in April 1857, a year before the Minutes record the transfer, so he was in Arkansas earlier than 1858 (lead).

Ten years later he was back in Tennessee, where the 1870 census shows "E A Stephenson," 40, with Alabama-born wife H. S., 27, and sons Thomas, James and John. In 1875 the Minutes list him as "readmitted" and then "transferred to White River Conference," and appoint "Wittsburg, E. A. Stevenson," in the White River Conference of northeast Arkansas. The 1880 census finds him at Addison, Winston County, Alabama, aged 51 and married to Hannah, listed as a "Doctor & Preacher" with seven children at home. Hannah Celia Carolan, born in 1844 at Somerville, Alabama, died on 26 October 1884 at Carolan, Logan County, Arkansas. Elam A. died on 17 April 1886 and is buried at Oak Hill Memorial Cemetery, Booneville.

The 1930 biography says he "was a graduate of the Vanderbilt University" at Nashville. Vanderbilt did not open until 1875, when he was already 46, so the claim must be a family exaggeration. It also names his wife as "Earl (Cook)," which none of the census records supports, so the sons by his first marriage and by Hannah are not yet separated (lead).

quotes.t: Elam A. Stevenson, transferred to Wachita Conference.
quotes.c: Minutes of the Annual Conferences of the Methodist Episcopal Church, South, 1858 (archive.org item 27838123.1858.emory.edu)

quotes.t: Wittsburg, E. A. Stevenson.
quotes.c: Minutes of the Annual Conferences, MECS, 1875, appointments (archive.org item 27838123.1875.emory.edu)

EXTRA.src: Minutes of the Annual Conferences of the Methodist Episcopal Church, South, 1858 and 1875 (Emory/Internet Archive 27838123.1858 and .1875); Arkansas and Its People (1930), vol. 4, sketch of James Baxter Stevenson (archive.org arkansasitspeopl0004vari); WikiTree Stevenson-15611 and Stevenson-15610 with the 1870 and 1880 census transcriptions; Goodspeed list of Elam's children, p. 872.
EXTRA.note: This Elam A. Stevenson is called "Elam A., Jr." in the Casey family history, which gives his wife as Mrs. Hannah Celia Wright.

EXTRA.name: Rev. James Baxter Stevenson
EXTRA.rel: First cousin of 2nd great-grandfather Frank Stevenson
EXTRA.place: Richmond, Booneville and Atkins, Arkansas; Oklahoma City
EXTRA.title: Frank's cousin the Arkansas Methodist
EXTRA.hook: A cousin of the Hulsey ancestor Frank preached in Yell County in 1883, was the first pastor of Oklahoma City's Methodist church, and is the Rev. J. B. Stevenson whose 1932 letter is quoted for the family's years of preaching.
body: James Baxter Stevenson was born on 24 October 1860 at Richmond, Arkansas, the son of Rev. Elam A. Stevenson. His 1930 biography says he "grew up in Tennessee, to which State his father had returned when he was six," and that at nineteen he "returned to Arkansas and settled in Booneville, Logan County" (the 1930 text is hyphenated across a line). He was licensed to preach on 21 September 1881. In 1883 "the Arkansas Conference sent him to Yell County, where he remained for two years" and then to the Mulberry Circuit and to Paris, Logan County.

He became "the first pastor of the Methodist church in Oklahoma City" and later served at Guthrie, Fort Smith, Conway, Batesville, Morrillton, Dardanelle, Fayetteville, Paragould, Russellville and Ozark. The Conference Minutes confirm some of this: "Conway Station, J. B. Stevenson" in 1892, "Van Buren Station, J. B. Stevenson" in 1896, "Morrillton Station, J. B. Stevenson" in 1900. From 1927 he was pastor at Atkins. He married Lulu Briggs on 14 May 1885. They had four children, among them Eugene Hendrix, a Rhodes Scholar who studied at Oxford and took a doctorate at the University of Pennsylvania.

This is the J. B. Stevenson who wrote in 1932 that "Uncle Jimmie preached 63 years, Uncle Abner 54 years, Uncle John 48 years, my father E. A. Stevenson 38 years, Uncle Gilbert 25 years." The Giles County site that printed the letter calls it a letter to "Eugene Hendricks Stevenson," which fits his son Eugene Hendrix (lead). His Yell County parish of 1883-85 is the county where Frank Stevenson was living at Danville in 1910, and his father's burial place at Booneville is in the next county.

quotes.t: Uncle Jimmie preached 63 years, Uncle Abner 54 years, Uncle John 48 years, my father E. A. Stevenson 38 years, Uncle Gilbert 25 years.
quotes.c: Rev. J. B. Stevenson, 1932 family letter, Giles County TNGenWeb

quotes.t: In 1883 the Arkansas Conference sent him to Yell County, where he remained for two years.
quotes.c: Arkansas and Its People (1930), vol. 4

EXTRA.src: Arkansas and Its People: A History 1541-1930, vol. 4, sketch of James Baxter Stevenson (archive.org arkansasitspeopl0004vari); Minutes of the Annual Conferences, MECS, 1892, 1896 and 1900 (archive.org 27838123.1892, .1896, .1900 emory); letter of 1932 listed in the Giles County TNGenWeb Stories index.
EXTRA.note: The 1932 letter is attributed on the Giles County site to "Rev. J. B. Stevenson, Elam's grandson"; James Baxter, then 72, is the grandson of that name found in the Minutes and the Arkansas biography.

EXTRA.name: Rev. James Calvin Stevenson and Margaret Caroline (Brown)
EXTRA.place: Near Bryson, Giles County, Tennessee
EXTRA.title: Golden-wedding preacher, and a general in the family
EXTRA.hook: "Uncle Jimmie," who preached 63 years, planned a golden wedding for October 1885; a great-grandson was probably the lieutenant general who died in Iceland in 1943.
body: James Calvin Stevenson was born on 23 June 1813 in North Carolina and brought to Giles County as a babe. On 19 November 1835 he married Margaret Caroline Brown, born on 8 December 1816. County marriage returns of the 1850s and 1860s name "James C. Stevenson" as the officiating minister at several weddings, among them Swinney-Dyer on 19 January 1852, Young-Huff on 3 November 1852, Stovall-Stephenson on 3 September 1860 and Woodard-Barnfield on 25 August 1862.

On 20 August 1885 the Pulaski Citizen's county correspondent visited "our old friends, Rev. and Mrs. Jas. C. Stevenson of near Bryson," who "speak of celebrating their golden wedding in October." Margaret died on 11 February 1886. James lived until 23 February 1899 and is buried beside her at Bee Spring. His ten children included Catherine Eliza (1838) and another daughter, Sarah, who married James Hollon.

Catherine Eliza married William Thomas Andrews in 1856. He was a minister, born in Alabama in 1838, the son of David Andrews and Eliza Brown. Their sons became a minister (John), a physician (Charles) and a writer and real estate man (James David Andrews, a "newspaper reporter and author"). The Casey family history adds that James David married Lula A. Maxwell and that their son Frank Andrews "was a general and died off the coast of Iceland." That fits Lt. Gen. Frank Maxwell Andrews, killed in an airplane crash in Iceland on 3 May 1943. Wikipedia records him as born in Nashville in 1884 and as a great-great-nephew of the Tennessee governors John C. and Neill S. Brown, which fits the Brown mother in this line. No record that names his parents has been seen, so the identification is probable, not proven.

quotes.t: speak of celebrating their golden wedding in October
quotes.c: The Pulaski Citizen, 20 Aug 1885, p. 3

quotes.t: Frank Andrews was a general and died off the coast of Iceland.
quotes.c: Casey family history, p. 3-107

EXTRA.src: Robert Casey, Interactive Family Histories, "Stevenson, Arrington and Tucker Families," Master Publication pp. 3-98 to 3-120 (http://www.rcasey.net/master/steelam.htm and steabner.htm) (James Calvin Stevenson, Catherine Eliza Stevenson); The Pulaski Citizen, 20 Aug 1885, p. 3; Bee Spring Cemetery listing, Giles County, Tennessee (Giles Co. TNGenWeb cemetery page); Giles County marriage returns (Giles Co. TNGenWeb marriage index, grooms S-Y); Wikipedia, "Frank Maxwell Andrews," early life.
EXTRA.note: The family history gives 14 January 1892 as James C.'s death, which belongs to his brother William Payne on the cemetery list. The cemetery date of 23 February 1899 is used here. The Andrews connection comes from the family history only.

EXTRA.name: The O'Neal brothers of Gibson County
EXTRA.place: Gibson and Pike Counties, Indiana; Missouri
EXTRA.title: Parsis's brothers stayed home
EXTRA.hook: Five of Daniel and Vashti O'Neal's sons and their youngest daughter lived out their lives in or near Gibson County, Indiana, while Parsis and Mary went west.
body: Daniel Waters O'Neal and Vashti Pearson had ten children, and six of them are traced to adulthood on WikiTree. William Allen was born on 15 April 1863 in Tennessee (WikiTree; the 1880 census says Indiana), and died on 11 September 1933 in Pike County, Indiana, with burial at Blackfoot Cemetery. His wife was Nancy Jane Mason, born in 1865 at Oakland City, who died there on 20 June 1923.

John Sherman was born on 15 January 1866, a few months after the regiment mustered out, and died at Somerville on 19 July 1940. He married Jane Minerva Mitchell. George Johnson was born on 16 August 1875; the 1880 census says in Missouri, so the family spent some time there in the 1870s (WikiTree says Tennessee). He lost his first wife, Adella Douglas (born 1875), on 27 February 1906, married Sarah Eleen Reed, and died at Somerville on 12 June 1965 at 89. Daniel Clinton, born 9 June 1878, married Flora Nellie McGregor and died on 3 March 1954. David Commodore, born at Somerville on 22 March 1881, married Birdie Viola Rembe and died at Evansville on 7 May 1955.

The youngest, Charity Louisa, born on 19 December 1887, was the only daughter besides Parsis and Mary to live to adulthood. She married Fred Skomp, born on 7 May 1884 in Greene County, Indiana. He died at Hobart, Indiana, on 5 August 1949, and she died at Valparaiso on 15 November 1979. Vashti's 1919 obituary named her five living sons as William, John, George, Clinton and Commodore, and the daughters as Mrs. Frank Stevenson of Valiant, Oklahoma, and Mrs. Fred Skomp of Somerville.
EXTRA.src: Obituary of Vashti O'Neal, Jan 1919 (Find a Grave 24711779); WikiTree profiles O'Neal-3565, 3566, 3567, 3568, 3569, 3570 and spouse pages; 1880 U.S. census, Columbia Twp, Gibson Co., Indiana, as printed on the Parsis O'Neal WikiTree page.
EXTRA.note: Death dates after 1900 are taken from WikiTree and are not checked against Indiana death certificates.

EXTRA.name: Mary Elizabeth (O'Neal) Farris Rinker Wilson
EXTRA.place: Gibson County, Indiana; Missouri; Arkansas; Tuttle, Oklahoma
EXTRA.title: A hundred years from Indiana to Oklahoma
EXTRA.hook: Parsis's oldest sister married three times, raised her children in Arkansas, and was feted at 100 by the Tuttle Times.
body: Mary Elizabeth O'Neal was born on 16 November 1860 in Gibson County, Indiana, the first child of Daniel and Vashti, ten months after their marriage. By 1878 she had married David Raliegh Farris, born in 1856 in Indiana. Their son Elmer Cooper Farris was born on 25 September 1878 at Princeton and died in Sequoyah County, Oklahoma, in 1948. A second son, Daniel Riley, born in Arkansas on 23 March 1881 and recorded as Fairce, died at Mead, Oklahoma, in 1968.

On 10 February 1884, in Arkansas, Mary married Joseph McConnell Rinker, 29, born in Iowa. WikiTree lists their children: Lydia Bell (1885, Sunset, Arkansas), Armenda Mae (1888), Cynthia Jane (1890), Joseph Jonathan (1892, Fayetteville), Vasha (1895, died 1897), Oscar Ashel (1897), Letha Agnes (1900) and Alta (1902, died 1906). Joseph was in Roger Mills County, Oklahoma, in 1910 and died on 27 May 1919 at Wapanucka.

Her obituary in the Tuttle Times of 22 December 1960 says Mrs. Mary Elizabeth Wilson, 100, "was born in Gibson County, Indiana, near Evansville, and spent most of her early life in Missouri, and raised her children in Arkansas. She first came to Oklahoma in 1907 and moved to Tuttle, from Faxton, in 1926." She "celebrated her 100th birthday in Nov 16, 1960, and passed away at her home on Wednesday, Dec 14, 1960." Survivors included "3 sons, 3 daughters, 51 grandchildren, 150 great-grandchildren, & 73 great great grandchildren." She was buried in Fairlawn Cemetery. Her third husband, James Calvin Wilson, born in 1867 at Princeton, Indiana, is listed with her on WikiTree.
Katie's brother Eddie was born in McCurtain County, Oklahoma, in July 1907, the same year Mary's obituary says she first came to Oklahoma.

quotes.t: She first came to Oklahoma in 1907 and moved to Tuttle, from Faxton, in 1926.
quotes.c: Tuttle Times, 22 Dec 1960, obituary of Mrs. Mary Elizabeth Wilson, as transcribed on WikiTree O'Neal-2666

EXTRA.src: Tuttle Times, 22 Dec 1960 (transcribed in Find a Grave 41943603 and WikiTree O'Neal-2666); WikiTree Rinker-451, Farris-3080, Wilson-112326 and the children's profiles.
EXTRA.note: Names and dates for her children and husbands are from WikiTree; the Rinker and Wilson marriages are not checked against a county marriage register.

EXTRA.name: Katie Stevenson's brothers and sisters
EXTRA.rel: Brothers and sisters of great-grandmother Katie (Stevenson) Hulsey
EXTRA.place: Indiana, Texas, Oklahoma and Arkansas
EXTRA.title: Seven children in the 1910 census
EXTRA.hook: The 1910 census at Danville, Arkansas, lists Katie, the baby, with six older brothers and sisters born in Indiana, Texas and Oklahoma.
body: The 1910 census, enumerated at Danville, Yell County, on 18 April, lists Frank Stevenson, 51, "Clergyman," his wife Jane, 41, and these children: Delphia, 18, born in Indiana; Willie, 16, Texas; George, 12, Indiana; Frank, 8, Texas; Elisha, 6, Texas; Eddie, 2, Oklahoma; and Katie, under one year, Arkansas. Frank and Jane told the enumerator they had been married 25 years and that seven children had been born. These are the seven.

Delphia was the oldest daughter. In her own obituary in 2009 Katie was said to have been preceded in death by "daughters Delphia and Mary," so she named a daughter for her sister. Willie was born in Texas about 1894. George Sherman Stevenson died on 3 June 1978 at Kilgore, Gregg County, Texas, and his mother Parsis Jane (O'Neal) Stevenson is named on the Texas death certificate cited in WikiTree. Frank, born about 1902 in Texas, is "Frank Lester" in other trees. WikiTree's list of the children calls the sixth one "Allen" where the census has Elisha.

The youngest brother, Horace Edward "Eddie," was born on 13 July 1907 in Garvin, McCurtain County, Oklahoma. He married Edith Marie Shunkey (born 29 July 1911 at Muskogee, died 2 April 2003 at King City, Oregon), and he died on 1 February 1998 at Portland, Oregon.

Other trees give a different list for the same parents: Iva Myrtle (1884), Adison Galiton (1886), Nellie Vashti (1889), Frank Lester (1902), Horace Edward (1907) and Katie. Iva Myrtle, Adison and Nellie would have been 26, 24 and 21 in 1910, so they could have been grown and away; WikiTree's list does not include them, and their link to this family is not documented (lead).
EXTRA.src: 1910 U.S. census, Danville, Yell Co., Arkansas, as transcribed on the WikiTree pages for Parsis Jane O'Neal (O'Neal-3514) and Gilbert Franklin Stevenson (Stevenson-12558); WikiTree Stevenson-5100 (Horace Edward Stevenson); Texas death certificate 1978, George Sherman Stevenson, cited on WikiTree O'Neal-3514.
EXTRA.note: Delphia, Willie, George, Frank, Elisha and Eddie are the names on the 1910 census page; the later given names in other trees are not proven. The census is also the only record yet seen for Willie and Delphia.

EXTRA.name: Otho Louderback
EXTRA.rel: Possible first husband of 2nd great-grandmother Parsis O'Neal
EXTRA.place: Pulaski County, Arkansas; Illinois; Rockwall County, Texas
EXTRA.title: A sixteen-year-old bride in Pulaski County
EXTRA.hook: An Arkansas marriage index records Parsis J. O'Neal, 16, marrying a 40-year-old Otho Louderbank on Christmas Day 1884, and her grave memorial still carries the Louderback name.
body: The WikiTree page for Parsis Jane O'Neal quotes a FamilySearch index of "Arkansas Marriages, 1837-1944": "Parsis J O Neal and Otho Louderback were married 25 December 1884 in Pulaski County, Arkansas. Otho was 40, Parsis, 16 years old." The index spells the groom "Louderbank." Pulaski County is Little Rock. In Gibson County, Indiana, at the 1880 census, Parsis, 11, had been in her father's household. Parsis's sister Mary was also in Arkansas by February 1884.

William Ortho Louderback was born about 1836 to 1844 at Princeton, Gibson County, the same county as the O'Neals. WikiTree gives his death in 1901 in Rockwall County, Texas, and lists a daughter, Henrietta Louderback, born in Illinois and dead in Texas in 1955, as a child of Parsis and him.

The Find a Grave memorial that WikiTree cites for her grave at Hugo is titled "Parsis Jane O'Neal Louderback (26 Mar 1868-26 Jan 1956)," so she was remembered under the Louderback name to the end, while the same WikiTree page lists the Stevenson children after the note "Marriage to Stevenson ..... Citation Needed." The 1910 census says Frank and Jane had been married 25 years, which would put that wedding in 1885, months after the Louderback record. Either the 1910 answer is loose, or the Stevenson household began without a recorded marriage, or the Louderback marriage ended early. No record seen settles it. Willie, Frank and Elisha Stevenson were born in Texas after 1894, where Otho Louderback died in 1901 (lead).
EXTRA.src: WikiTree O'Neal-3514 (Parsis Jane O'Neal), Louderback-86 (William Ortho Louderback) and Louderback-85 (Henrietta Louderback), quoting "Arkansas Marriages, 1837-1944," FamilySearch F73Z-LQF; 1910 census, Danville, Yell Co., Ark.
EXTRA.note: The marriage record itself has not been seen. Both the Louderback surname index and the bride's age should be checked against the Pulaski County, Arkansas, marriage register for 25 December 1884.

TIMELINE.t: Thomas Gaunt marries Susan Bate at Rotherham on 28 August; their only child, Peter, is born at Lincoln the next June.
Henry Croasdale, yeoman of Newhey in the Forest of Bowland, makes his will on 21 September and is buried at Waddington on 10 October.
Peter Gaunt tells the Plymouth Colony court at its March session that he knows of no public worship in the world he can join.
Peter Gaunt and three other Sandwich men are fined twenty shillings each on 2 March for appearing before the Plymouth court with their hats on; Thomas Butler is cleared.
Daniel Butler, brother of Dorothy Butler, is publicly whipped at Plymouth for rescuing a 'Strang Quaker' from the Sandwich marshal.
William Croasdale of Newhey dies on the 29th day of the 11th month and is buried at Settle Meeting, Newton.
Hananiah Gaunt marries Dorothy Butler at Sandwich, Massachusetts, on 10 May, a week after posting their intention at the Friends meeting.
The Lamb carries the Settle Meeting Quaker families, including the Cowgills and Croasdales, to Pennsylvania; they arrive in October.
Ralph Cowgill arrives in the Delaware on 28 September on the Friend's Adventure, indentured to Randolph Blackshaw for four years and fifty acres.
Thomas Croasdale dies on 2 November on Neshaminy Creek; his goods, apart from 500 acres 'not prized,' are appraised at 47 pounds 9 shillings.
Hananiah Gaunt takes up 500 acres at Hananicon, Springfield Township, New Jersey.
George Hutcheson sells Hananiah Gaunt 'of Rhode Island, yeoman' 500 acres in the First Tenth of West Jersey on 11 May.
Anthony Champneys and Anne Pitts marry at St James, Duke's Place, London, on 23 September.
Hananiah Gaunt sells 100 acres of the 500 to William Bustill, a carpenter of Shrewsbury, on 18 May.
Land surveyed for William Biddle in Springfield, Burlington County, is described as adjoining the land of Hananiah Gaunt.
Dennis Garrett of Baltimore County dies on 2 September of a sword blow; his son-in-law John Cole and his widow Barbara Garrett are named as witnesses at the trial of John Oldton.
John Cowgill marries Bridget Croasdale at Neshaminy, Bucks County, on 19 October.
A 67-acre tract, Cole's Addition, is surveyed for John Cole on 29 May on the north side of the Patapsco, on the site of Baltimore.
John Chamness marries Ann Weary at St John's Church, Wapping, London, on 4 January.
Nottingham Friends begin meeting at the house of William Brown on the Nottingham Lots; Concord Monthly Meeting approves in the 2nd month of 1705.
Barbara Garrett Broad deeds land to her grandson Dennis Garrett Cole in Baltimore County, Maryland.
Anthony Chamness is born in East Smithfield, London, to John and Ann Chamness.
Elizabeth Cowgill of Duck Creek, daughter of the tanner John Cowgill, marries William Brown Jr. of Nottingham.
Hananiah Gaunt's will names his daughter Mahitable Staples.
Henry Stevenson marries Ann Curlett at Saul parish, Downpatrick, on 2 June.
Joseph Cole's will names his wife Susanna and daughter Sarah.
Anthony Chamness is indentured in London for service in Maryland.
Henry Nordyke marries Rebecca Perkins in Willingboro, New Jersey.
Jacob Perkins Sr. of Willingboro dies intestate in May with a cane and sword in his inventory; Jacob Jr. makes his will on 26 October naming Henry Nordike as a debtor.
Charles Davies marries Hannah Matson, "daughter of John Matson of Merion," in Pennsylvania.
Mary Norton, daughter of Edward Norton of Armagh, marries Richard Brown at Nottingham Meeting.
Anthony Chamness marries Sarah Cole.
Thomas Rogers marries Ann Staples at Upper Springfield Meeting, New Jersey.
John Cole, Senior, aged about 67, testifies in March at a Baltimore County land commission on the bounds of Cole's Adventure.
Edward Norton, son of Edward Norton of Armagh, Ireland, marries Elizabeth Brown at West Nottingham Meeting.
William Kirk, widower of Margaret Davis, marries Mary Norton Brown, widow of Richard Brown, under the care of Fairfax Monthly Meeting in Virginia.
Anthony Chamness moves his family from Monocacy, Maryland, to Carver's Creek Meeting, North Carolina.
Cane Creek Monthly Meeting is organized, with Anthony Chamness as overseer.
Cane Creek Monthly Meeting is set up in the tenth month; the Davis family book names Charles and Hannah Davies as charter members, having come south from Radnor and Hopewell.
Thomas Staples's will names his granddaughter Mary Rogers.
Robert Johnson marries Virginia Elmore of Louisa County, Virginia, on 19 November; in 1766 Cedar Creek Meeting sends them to North Carolina by certificate.
Mary Rogers marries Abraham Nordyke in Burlington County, New Jersey.
William Moffitt marries Mary Davies, and Joseph Chamness marries Margaret Norton, at Cane Creek Meeting.
Joseph Chamness marries Margaret Norton at Cane Creek on 17 March, sixteen days before William Moffitt marries Mary Davies there.
At Cane Creek on 17 March, Joseph Chamness and Margaret Norton are married before twelve witnesses, among them Anthony and Sarah Chamness and Edward and Elizabeth Norton, who sign the certificate.
William Marshall conveys 26 acres on Cane Creek to trustees for the use of Cane Creek Meeting, the ground where the meeting-house and burial ground stand.
William Moffitt proves a deed from Thomas Cox to Jacob Grigg at the Orange County court in May.
Deep River chooses William Moffitt to attend the Regulators' first general meeting.
William Moffitt witnesses the will of William Cox; the Orange County court at Hillsborough records it proved on his oath in February.
Governor Tryon refuses to pardon William Moffitt and twelve other Regulators.
William Moffitt signs the Regulators' Advertisement No. 8 on 30 April as "William Maffet."
The Regulators name "Wm Maffit" first on the committee to petition the Governor, 21 May.
The Regulators' committee, William Moffitt among its eight signers, sends the Governor its narrative; it records William finding no such Act in the laws as the deputy sheriff claimed.
William Moffitt signs the Regulators' letter to Tryon as his troops march on Hillsborough, and heads the signers of their Address.
On 29 September the Hillsborough Superior Court quashes an indictment for riot that names William Moffitt.
A general pardon on 9 September covers all persons concerned in the Regulator insurrection.
William Sample and his wife Esther each sign a will in Mecklenburg County, North Carolina, on 26 January; he dies that month.
Abraham and Mary Nordyke move from New Jersey to Virginia and join Hopewell Meeting; their son Micajah is born in Stafford County that year.
Anthony Chamness, after two marriages, marries Margaret Evans Williams, a widow; he dies the next September.
On 4 January the Kent County Committee in Delaware declares John Cowgill of Little Creek, a nephew of Elizabeth (Cowgill) Brown, an enemy to his country for refusing Continental money.
Joseph Chamness marries Hannah Beeson at Deep River Meeting after Margaret Norton's death.
William Brown's recollections of his father's fines are written into the East Nottingham Meeting minutes on the 28th of the 1st month.
Abraham Nordyke's family transfers its membership to Deep River Meeting, North Carolina, after eight years in Georgia.
Ashley Johnson of Louisa County, Virginia, deeds all his estate to his son Elijah for the keep of himself and his wife Martha.
Mary Moffitt, daughter of William, is said to marry William Wilkinson on 26 March (the 26th day of the 3rd month).
William Moffitt makes his will, leaving his wife Mary the wagon and the still.
Robert Moffitt, son of William & Mary, marries Martha Chamness at Centre Quaker Meeting.
Westfield Monthly Meeting asks advice on members removing to the Scioto River; the Moffitt family record puts Hugh Moffitt in Ohio this year or the next.
The Nordyke family moves to Lost Creek Meeting, a few miles north of Knoxville, Tennessee.
The Nordykes move from Tennessee to a new farm near New Vienna, Ohio, and help found East Fork Meeting.
Ephraim Satterfield marries Ruth Knowles in Warren County, Kentucky, on 12 November.
J. M. Garrison marries Patsey Cannon in Wilson County, Tennessee, on 6 December.
Giles County, Tennessee, is formed from Maury County; Elam Stevenson's family arrives four years later.
John M. Garrison and Martha "Patsey" Cannon marry in Wilson County, Tennessee, on 6 December. The 1810 Warren County census, as transcribed on WikiTree, counts one slave in his household.
Rev. Elam Stevenson moves his family to Giles County, Tennessee, by pack horse.
Elam Stevenson and his family settle, in a neighbor's later recollection, near Bee Spring church, Giles County, Tennessee, in 1815 or 1816.
Allen County, Kentucky, is cut from Warren and Barren counties, where the Garrisons and Satterfields had settled.
The Centre branch of the North Carolina Manumission Society reports sixty-five members in April, the largest of its branches.
Mary Moffitt, William's widow, dates her will "the 23rd day of the 9th month."
Mary (Davies) Moffitt, the Regulator's widow, dies and her 1820 will is filed in Randolph County.
Silas and Hannah (Wilkinson) Moffitt reach their Hamilton County, Indiana, farm on 8 October after a trip from Randolph County in a single four-horse wagon.
U.S. Army founds Cantonment Towson near the Kiamichi and Red rivers.
Joshua Knowles writes his Warren County will on 11 November, naming his daughter Ruth Saterfield; it is proved in October 1832.
Rev. Philip Bruce dies in Giles County in May; Elam Stevenson, by his own account, closes his eyes and helps shroud him.
The Hall County, Georgia, census lists seventeen Hulsey households, including Salathiel.
The Choctaw removal from Mississippi begins.
About 2,500 Choctaw exiles are landed at Arkansas Post between 26 November and 8 December in a blizzard; the Pisachubbes later said they came with the first group.
By family tradition, the Pisachubbes arrive from Mississippi with the first group of exiles and settle at Fort Coffee.
Gilliam Graves marries Mary Tyler on 18 August in Randolph County, North Carolina.
Rev. Alfred Wright organizes Wheelock Church in the Choctaw Nation in December; he is buried in its graveyard in 1853.

On 6 February the treaty captains of Nittuckachee's district write from Horn Prairie that Doaksville is where annuities are received and that white traders have built 'a small town' below the Kiamichi.
Fort Coffee is founded in June on the Arkansas River, replacing Fort Smith's garrison; it is abandoned on 27 July 1838.
Nathan Moffitt marries Rebecca Williams in Randolph County, North Carolina, on 13 October.
Vincent B. Tims witnesses the Treaty of Doaksville.
Doak & Tims sign a contract on 1 January with Captain R. D. C. Collins to feed about 200 Chickasaw emigrants at Doaksville for twelve months, at thirteen cents a ration.
Rev. Abner A. Stevenson marries Martha S. Watson on 8 December in Giles County, Tennessee; they have fifteen children by 1866.
Archibald O'Neal brings his family from Tennessee to Gibson County, Indiana; he dies there on 25 April 1841.
Yell County, Arkansas, is organized on 5 December, with seats at Danville and Dardanelle.
A clerk at the Doaksville trading house writes home on 17 April that "Mr. Tims one of the men I am living with" is in New York buying a stock of goods.
Montgomery County, Arkansas, is organized on 9 December.
Vincent B. Tims runs the Doaksville office for letters to the Agent for Claims.
Spencer Academy opens north of Doaksville.
The Doak and Tims partnership at Doaksville is dissolved by mutual agreement.
A New Orleans commission house advertising in the Washington (Arkansas) Telegraph names "Doak & Tims, Doaksville, C. Nation" among its references.
Vincent B. Tims attends the Red River Raft Convention for the Choctaw Nation.
John Satterfield's Warren County will is proved on 10 November; the same year the Kentucky legislature dissolves the Garrison marriage.
The Kentucky General Assembly divorces John M. Garrison and his wife Patsey in Section 6 of Chapter 600, approved in February.
The Kentucky General Assembly dissolves the marriage of John M. Garrison and Patsey Garrison by an act printed on page 410 of the 1847-48 Acts.
The Texas Supreme Court decides Love v. Doak & Tims, a suit over a Doaksville store account that ran from 1840 to 1844.
Nathan Moffitt's family, lately from North Carolina, is farming in Lawrence County, Arkansas.
Nathan Moffitt is farming in Strawberry Township, Lawrence County, Arkansas, with eight children.
The census taker in Union County, Georgia, finds Salatheil Hulsey, 43, with a wife and eight children in the house; Benjamin is 6 in the transcription.
The Union County, Georgia, census lists Salathiel Hulsey, 43, with a household that includes Robert, Jesse, Jennings and Benjamin.
Nathan Moffitt's son Patrick is born in Lawrence County, Arkansas, in May.
V. B. Tims of the Choctaw Nation is listed among the stockholders of the Cairo & Fulton Railroad Company of Arkansas, with 10 shares.
Gilliam Graves is appointed guardian of the children of Samuel and Sarah Graves in Montgomery County, Arkansas.
In the summer, two Stevenson boys, Elam R. (2 August) and William B. F. (19 August), are buried at Bee Spring.
Between 1 February and 3 March, four Stevenson burials are recorded at Bee Spring: Louisa, Joseph J., Ann Eliza and James Elisha.
Sicily Shaw and J. H. Leak advertise the 268-acre farm of the late Noble Shaw near Oak Ridge, Guilford County, for sale on 16 April.
Elam A. Stevenson transfers from the Tennessee Conference to the Ouachita Conference in Arkansas; his son James Baxter is born at Richmond in 1860.
James H. Satterfield marries Melissa Gibson in Allen County, Kentucky.
Doaksville Constitution ratified, creating Cedar County among others.
Daniel O'Neal marries Vashti Pearson on 5 January in Gibson County, Indiana.
A Robert R. Hulsey, 27, is counted in Hempstead County, Arkansas, with a baby son named Salathel G.
Daniel W. O'Neal enlists in the 42nd Indiana Infantry.
Daniel O'Neal's regiment marches into Nashville and finds an unlocked pork-house.
Coleman L. Stevenson of Giles County enlists in the 32nd Tennessee.
At Perryville on 8 October the 42nd Indiana loses 166 men, one-third of the regiment.
The first Federal troops in number reach Pulaski in April; Gilbert Stevenson, born 17 November 1861 nearby, is five months old.
Coleman L. Stevenson enlists in the Confederate 32nd Tennessee Infantry and serves to the end of the war; his brother Wilbur Marion serves until the fall of 1864.
Capt. William M. Cockrum of Company F, 42nd Indiana, is wounded and captured at Chickamauga on 20 September and spends eight months in Libby Prison.
A Benjamin F. Hulsey is on the roster of the Union 4th Arkansas Cavalry, recruited in Montgomery County.
Gilliam Graves, 45, volunteers at Cedar Glades, Arkansas, for the Union 4th Arkansas on 14 January.
V. B. Tims, postmaster at Doaksville, writes to the Confederate Post Office Department on 16 August, 9 September and 1 November.
On 1 July the postmasters along the Washington-Doaksville mail route petition Gen. S. B. Maxey for mail service; V. B. Tims signs for Doaksville.
On 1 March, Dr. Brown of Cedar Glades, Arkansas, is shot down; on 10 March Union men of Montgomery County petition for cavalry.
David W. Wallam of Company F, 42nd Indiana, is killed at Altoona on 31 May; David W. Johnson is killed at Atlanta on 14 August.
Gilliam Graves, 45, volunteers for the 4th Arkansas Cavalry (Union) at Cedar Glades on 14 January.
Chief Peter Pitchlynn, then General Stand Watie, surrender at Doaksville, near the Tims family home.
Daniel W. O'Neal applies for a Civil War disability pension in December 1865.
Stand Watie surrenders at Doaksville on June 23.
The 1884 county history lists Daniel W. O'Neal of Company F as a veteran who mustered out with the 42nd Indiana on 21 July 1865.
Lt. John Q. A. Steele of Company F, 42nd Indiana, is killed instantly at Bentonville.
James H. Satterfield moves his family from Allen County, Kentucky, to Dakota County, Minnesota; they return to Kentucky in 1875.
The Rev. Elam Stevenson, 81, dictates his recollections of early Methodism in Giles County; the Bee Spring society, he writes, was organized in 1814.
Nathan Moffitt has moved the family to Dent County, Missouri.
A. M. Satterfield is born on 23 July in Minnesota, where her father James H. Satterfield had taken the family from Kentucky; she dies at 21 in 1892 and is buried in Butler County.
On 20 December Eliza Mary Stevenson marries John Newton Andrew, who later also marries her sister Julia.
Spencer Academy's superintendent teaches 'Swing Low, Sweet Chariot' to the Fisk Jubilee Singers.
Rebecca (Williams) Moffitt dies in Oregon County, Missouri, and Nathan remarries.
Jesse Graves marries Sarah Emma Fisher at Mountain Township, Montgomery County, Arkansas, on 2 April.
Hugh Watt, second husband of Parses (Shaw) O'Neal, dies in Gibson County on 20 September; he was born in County Down, Ireland.
Jesse Graves, 18, marries Emma Fisher, 15, at Jack Phillips's house in Mountain Township, Montgomery County, on 2 April.
William Thomas Camp is hanged at Princeton on 22 November for a murder near Haubstadt, the first legal execution in Gibson County.
Nathan Moffitt dies in Oregon County, Missouri, on 23 December.
Stone County, Arkansas, is organized on 21 April with Mountain View as its seat; Garland County, with Hot Springs, had been set up on 5 April.
Rev. Elam Stevenson dies on 13 March at the home of W. M. Stevenson near Bethany, Giles County, "in his 88th year," according to the Pulaski Citizen.
On Sunday evening, 27 February, a cyclone wrecks the south side of Princeton, Indiana.
The Official Register lists Doaksville, Choctaw Nation, with V. B. Tims as postmaster, paid $37.77 for the year.
James H. Satterfield marries Lucinda Belle Phelps in Butler County, Kentucky.
Henry and Hannah Moffitt are farming in Randolph County, Arkansas, with Josephine and baby Jesse.
Henry and Hannah Moffitt are starting out as farmers in Randolph County, Arkansas.
The Pulaski Citizen reports that Rev. Abner Stevenson has "abandoned the idea of going to Texas"; in May his son Judge George Stevenson "returned from Texas."
Sarah Rebecca Graves is born on 5 May, the day her mother Margaret dies.
Margaret Crumpton, who married Jesse Graves in January, dies on 5 May, the day Sarah Rebecca is born.
On 25 December Parsis J. O'Neal, 16, is indexed as marrying Otho Louderback, 40, in Pulaski County, Arkansas (lead).
A Kentucky history book prints the Satterfield family's account of three generations.
Edward Tims is one of four named candidates for Principal Chief in the Choctaw election of 4 August; Thompson McKinney wins.
Edward Stevenson, a Texas and Pacific Railway man from Giles County, dies of smallpox at El Paso on 26 June.
Edward Ward Tims is appointed postmaster at Doaksville.
Edward W. Tims and Willie Maxwell marry on 29 April in Towson County, by R. S. Frazier, according to the certificate copied into the Dawes file.
Joseph P. Thompson marries Betsy Tims near Doaksville.
John Morgan Shackleford marries Lizzie Newton in Etowah County, Alabama.
Tom Moffitt is born at St. James, Stone County, Arkansas, on 17 February.
Joseph P. Thompson is elected to the Choctaw House, one of its youngest members.
Grady Moffitt is born near Mountain View on 6 November.
John C. Satterfield marries Samantha Johnson.
Joel J. Thompson is born on 29 January near High Hill, the family's second son.
A. M. (Satterfield) Coots dies on 25 May, aged 21, a year after her wedding.
Company F, 42nd Indiana, dedicates its 28-foot limestone monument at Oakland City, with eleven Andersonville dead named.
Mary Tinsley Shackleford is born in Alabama on 4 June.
Atoka Agreement signed April 23, setting up allotment of Choctaw land.
Simon is born; his grandmother Emeline is the midwife and swears the enrollment affidavit.
The family applies for enrollment on 1 May; Simon is born on 4 May; Ella dies on 22 May.
On 22 August a student list from Armstrong Academy puts "Harrison Pisachubbe" on the Choctaw rolls a second time; he is William H. Pisachubbe, already enrolled.
Oscar Smith, 10, is in John and Emma Smith's household in Franklin County, Texas.
Henry Moffitt owns his Stone County farm free of mortgage, with six children at home.
Mitchell and Mildred Tims's daughter Else dies on 25 November, a year old.
On 19 October a Doaksville notary tells the Dawes Commission that Rosey Wilson was registered as Rosey Ann Tims, daughter of Emaline Tims.
Henry H. Moffitt dies at Mountain View, leaving Hannah a widow for 22 years.
Joseph Thompson builds the big white house near High Hill and paints it.
Sarah Rebecca Graves marries George Washington Hulsey on 22 December.
Joseph P. Thompson and Robert Tims swear on 13 April before the notary at Doaksville that Ella N. Thompson died on 22 May 1899.
The Thompson family's Choctaw enrollment is approved.
On 8 December Willie J. Tims testifies at Tuskahoma that she married Edward Tims in 1888 near Doaksville.
Joseph Thompson selects the family's allotments at Atoka, including 160 acres for four-year-old Simon.
Joseph W. Thompson is born on 5 March; Emeline Tims later swears to the birth as midwife.
Corinne post office opens; Joel later says it replaced Doaksville as the family's post office.
William Roy Hulsey, eldest of George Washington and Rebecca's ten children, is born.
Willie Tims's son Wilson, born in 1904, is found to have died before the 4 March cutoff; the Principal Chief writes to the Commission on Willie's behalf.
The Satterfield family moves from Butler County, Kentucky, to Franklin County, Texas.
Mount Olivet Cemetery is established at Hugo, first called Burgoyne Cemetery.

The government's soil survey of Franklin County, Texas, reports that tenants on the usual share plan give half the crop, and that development around Hagansport is held back by poor shipping facilities.
A tornado destroys Bee Spring church in Giles County on the night of 29 April; the congregation rebuilds at Bryson.
Oscar Smith, 19, and Pearl Satterfield, 11, are neighbors at Hagansport, Texas.
Joseph Thompson is recorded farming his own allotment at Wilson, with both parents born in Mississippi.
Frank Stevenson, a preacher like his father, is living in Danville, Arkansas, with baby Katie.
Hannah Moffitt is a widow in Stone County with her sons Thomas and Grady; Grady is making barrel staves.
The Satterfields and the Smiths are neighbors at Hagansport, Texas, where Oscar Smith, 19, and Artie Pearl Satterfield, 11, live on facing census pages.
The Hot Springs Sentinel-Record lists a deed from "B. F. Hulsey and wife" to C. Floyd Huff among Garland County transfers (possibly Benjamin F. Hulsey).
The Marmon Wasp, built by the Nordyke cousins' firm, wins the first Indianapolis 500.
On 16 August the Interior Department marks Harrison Pisachubbe's roll number a duplicate of William H. Pisachubbe's.
Oscar Smith marries Artie Pearl Satterfield.
Grady Moffitt and Mary Tinsley Shackleford marry about this year.
The Secretary of the Interior approves removal of restrictions on Joseph Thompson's land on 28 March.
Grady Moffitt, timberman at Ervin, and Robert Pisachubbe, farmer at Speer, register for the WWI draft.
Samantha Satterfield marries Alex Stephens at Mount Vernon, Texas, on 28 July.
On 28 July Samantha Satterfield marries widower Bird Alexander Stephens at Mount Vernon, Texas; they move to Oaks Township, Choctaw County, Oklahoma.
Pvt. Edmond Tims is killed near St. Étienne, France.
Camp Pike's base hospital admits 214 influenza cases on 23 September; George W. Hulsey, working on the camp, had filled out his draft card on the 12th.
Edmond Tims, a company runner in Co. D, 142d Infantry, is killed at St. Etienne, 8 or 9 October.
Grady Moffitt is a tenant farmer at Wilson, Choctaw County, with Mary and their sons.
Betsy Thompson's petition to remove restrictions is approved on 30 April.
Edmond Tims of Hugo is listed among Oklahoma's killed in action in Soldiers of the Great War, and as a private of Co. D, 142d Infantry in the Honor Roll of Chastaine's Story of the 36th.
Hannah (Grimes) Moffitt dies at Herpel, Arkansas, on 4 April.
Benjamin Franklin Hulsey dies at Story, Arkansas, on 16 December.
George Paul Hulsey, the tenth and last child of George Washington and Rebecca Hulsey, is born.
Stella (Satterfield) Riddle dies on 25 January, aged 17, and is buried at Chillicothe, Hardeman County, Texas.
Jimmie Gaynell Moffitt, three, dies; Henry Wayne follows in 1937.
Oscar Hulsey marries Katie Stevenson on his 17th birthday.
Samantha (Johnson) Stephens dies on 1 October and is buried at Soper, Oklahoma.
Grady and Mary Moffitt and their six boys are living with Mary's parents in Martin County, Texas.
Simon and Frances Thompson share a home at Jeter with Robert and Lizzie Pisachubbe.
Nancy (Wilborn) Graves, Sarah Rebecca's stepmother, dies on 20 November.
Joel J. Thompson tells the family's story to a WPA interviewer in Hugo.
The Methodist Indian Mission lists Peter Thompson and Mitchell Tims, both of Fort Towson, among the Choctaw District's church school superintendents.
The census finds Grady Moffitt and Oscar Hulsey nearly a year without work; Simon Thompson's farm feeds twelve.
The Methodist Indian Mission of Oklahoma meets at Hampton's Chapel north of Fort Towson; the roll lists J. B. Tims of Fort Towson and Robert J. Tims of Idabel as local deacons.

James Brown Tims, born at Doaksville on 25 June 1864, dies at 77; the conference prints a memoir saying "he loved everybody and everybody loved him" and that he had been a member of the Choctaw Council.
On 27 April the "Old Man's Draft" registers Charles Oscar Smith (52) and Robert Pisachubbe (53).
John Winfred Moffitt enlists in the U.S. Navy on 17 December.
John Winfred Moffitt, Navy corpsman, is aboard ARD-19 at Leyte when it is attacked from the air.
ARD-19 is commissioned at Alameda on 22 March; John's service on her begins.
ARD-19 reaches Manus in the Admiralty Islands at the end of August.
The Rev. Robert James Tims dies on 12 September and is buried at Idabel; his nephew's memoir says he was born six miles north of Fort Towson, "the son of Vincent and Emiline Tims."
USS Chief sails for San Francisco in March; John is discharged on 9 May.
John Moffitt marries Faye Smith in Paris, Texas.
Dois Moffitt, a Navy cook through the war, dies after a diving accident in the Red River.
Katie Hulsey moves to Hugo, Oklahoma.
The conference minutes give High Hill's church school superintendent as Pete Thompson of Fort Towson, probably Peter P. Thompson.
Frank Stevenson dies in Hugo; his stone at Mount Olivet reads 1860-1950.
Parsis Jane Stevenson dies; her Mount Olivet stone is listed as 1956.
Mary Elizabeth (O'Neal) Wilson, Parsis's oldest sister, dies at Tuttle, Oklahoma, on 14 December, a month after her 100th birthday.
The Chico Enterprise-Record prints the obituary of Robert Y. Shackleford, naming his sister 'Mamie Moffett' of Oklahoma.
Mary Tinsley (Shackleford) Moffitt dies in Paris, Texas, on 26 August.
Mary Tinsley Moffitt dies on 26 August and is laid at Shoat Springs.
Charles Oscar Smith dies on 17 August; Artie follows in 1983. Both are at Grant Cemetery.
Grady Moffitt dies on 21 June and is buried at Shoat Springs Cemetery.
Descendants place a large Chamness memorial stone in the Cane Creek Friends cemetery for Anthony and Sarah.
The Lamar County Echo prints Hazel King's obituary on 1 January, listing her Shackleford brothers and sisters.
Oscar Hulsey dies at his home at Holly Creek on 17 June.
Oscar Hulsey is buried at Wheelock Cemetery after a funeral at 2 p.m. on the Sunday following his death on 17 June.
Katie (Stevenson) Hulsey dies at 98 on 30 January.
